title: Skip the run: here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by experts | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re nursing a joint, have an existing condition or just don’t feel like running, these exercises help get your cardio in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Whether you’re nursing a joint, have an existing condition or just don’t feel like running, these exercises help get your cardio in
Content: For those with existing joint issues, other cardio activities may be better alternatives.Photograph: Gary Yeowell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFor those with existing joint issues, other cardio activities may be better alternatives.Photograph: Gary Yeowell/Getty ImagesWell actuallySkip the run: here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by expertsWhether you’re nursing a joint, have an existing condition or just don’t feel like running, these exercises help get your cardio inRae WitteTue 4 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe runner’s high might be contagious. In 2024, the fitness tracking app Stravarecorded a 59% increasein users attending social running events and run clubs globally. Applications for London’s marathonhave increased 40%since 2024, whileNew York City’s received about 20% moreapplicantsthis year. Overall, an estimated 56 million Americans regularly run on a treadmill and 51 million jog, according to areportfrom the Sports and Fitness Industry Association.But running has a reputation for being rough on our joints. There is some good news for those chasing the high: one2023 studyfound little relationship between recreational running and arthritis of the hip or knee, and another suggests that the impact of runningcauses cartilage to adapt, fortify and thickenover time.However, for those with existing joint issues, other cardio activities may be better alternatives. Here’s what experts say about running, joint health and good alternatives.How does running affect lower-body joints?Running is a full body activity, but some areas are more affected by it than others.‘Smaller doses of exercise are a miracle cure’: 14 expert tips to protect your jointsRead more“Most people come in with knee issues,” said Lauren Borowski, a primary care sports medicine specialist at NYU Langone’s Sports Medicine Center. Pain in the hips, ankles, feet and low back are also common.“When running, you’re essentially landing in a single leg squat, and it’s a lot of repetitive pressure. It’s three to four times your body weight in every step,” Borowski said. “When the muscles are not ready to receive the extra weight, [the impact goes] more directly to the bones and the cartilage.”What can make a joint unhealthy or painful?“Unhealthy” joints can show up as a variety of things. Injuries such as a torn meniscus in the knee, hamstring strains, ankle sprains, achilles tendinitis, shin splints, plantar fasciitis and stress fractures can make running painful. So can “osteoporosis or osteoarthritis, where the bone tissue is starting to break down”, said Dr M Claire Coopes-Meske at Good Reps Physical Therapy.With conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or arthritis related to inflammatory bowel disease, there is “a lot of known inflammation that’s attacking [the] cartilage”, Borowski said. Broken down cartilage further exposes the bone to stress.Some pains are legitimate cause for concern and need attention from a healthcare provider. Alexis Colvin, orthopedic surgeon at Mount Sinai hospital and the chief medical officer of the US Open, recommends seeing a doctor sooner rather than later “if the knee is swollen or the pain is really persistent even after a day or two and it’s affecting their regular activity” – or if you are constantly taking painkillers to try to mitigate the pain.Which cardio options are easier on the joints?Motion is healing and essential for healthy joints, saidCoopes-Meske. “Any time we’re moving a joint, [synovial] fluids are released into the joint space that provide nutrition and lubricate the joint.”Additionally, diversifying your exercise is essential for general health. Borowski recommends focusing on four categories: strength training, for the muscles; cardio respiratory exercise, which strengthens the heart and lungs; balance work; and mobility and flexibility training.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionImproved performance, freedom of movement and less pain: how to start a mobility practiceRead moreIf the impact of running is inhibitive for you, experts recommend the alternatives below to help you dodge physical stress on your bones and cartilage:Cycling:If the knee cannot withstand the impact of running, biking is an option. “It’s a really great tool for range of motion,” Borowski said. Cycling stimulates the production of synovial fluids and allows for a range of leg extension. Coopes-Meske pointed out that people can adjust the resistance, speed and distance to vary workload. Increasing these measures requires more from muscles without the additional stress of impact on the joints.Rowing: Rowing is also great for those who are looking to avoid joint impact but may not be ready for weight-bearing exercises. It offers a greater range of motion than cycling, depending on how much your knee can bend. If your range is limited, modifications are available. For instance, on a rowing machine, you can adjust how much your knees are bent in the starting position and how much you straighten them when driving your seat back, making for a shorter stroke.“The intensity, resistance and speed can also be adjusted based on their capabilities as well,” Coopes-Meske said. Rowing requires a lot of work from the hips, core and upper body, so its benefits go beyond the legs.Swimming:For those with bone or cartilage issues that experience a lot of swelling, swimming is a great cardio option, said Coopes-Meske. It’s a full body workout and puts minimal stress on the joints. It’s excellent for building lung capacity and heart strength, and there’s an added bonus for swollen joints: “The hydrostatic pressure from the water can help push the swelling out of that area,” she said.It doesn’t do much for bones or muscles, or from a strength standpoint, because water doesn’t provide much resistance, said Borowski: “But it’s great for mobility and range of motion of those joints.”Incline walking:Incline walking reduces load on the joints while increasing heart rate. Unlike swimming, cycling and using the rowing machine, walking is a load-bearing exercise because you’re supporting your bodyweight against gravity while on your feet. “We still want to load those bone tissues, because the body starts to rebuild those areas and help build up the bone as well,” Coopes-Meske said.Load-bearing exercises are important because the physical stress stimulates bone-forming cells to produce new bone tissue. This increases their density, which can slow age-related bone density loss and help with osteoporosis. “We still want to load those bone tissues, because the body starts to rebuild those areas and help build up the bone as well,” Coopes-Meske said.Walking, however, avoids the harsh impact of running, and doing it at an incline gets your heart rate up quicker. Depending on whether you are using a treadmill or walking outdoors, you can also adjust the speed and incline depending on your symptoms, capabilities and the terrain.Rollerblading, ice skating or cross-country skiing:Booted activities such as rollerblading, ice skating and cross-country skiing can be good alternatives for those with injured or weak ankles. “The boots come up much higher on your ankle, providing extra support,” said Coopes-Meske. Running and walking both involve heel strikes – the initial contact your heel makes with the ground. These activities eliminate the impact from heel strikes and focus on continuous gliding motion. They are great for strengthening the glute muscles, hamstrings and quadriceps, and deliver a full body workout with minimal stress on the knees and ankles.Other options:As long as you are diversifying your movement and covering the four buckets Borowski referenced, many cardio alternatives are suitable. For instance, Latin, hip-hop, house or ballroom dance classes and Zumba. (Skip ballet, which can involve high-impact leaping.) Be mindful of how much jumping is involved in any of these options, but there are typically lower-impact modifications for these movements. They are a great way to get your cardio in, mix it up and have fun.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyRunningHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat: why our cities can't cope | Opinion |  Presented by Kirsty Major ; produced by Bryony Moore and Lauren Hurrell ; executive producer Barbara Speed | The Guardian
description: The UK and Europe have been facing extreme heatwaves - Greenpeace recorded temperatures of up to 53C at one London playground in recent weeks. The Guardian’s deputy opinion editor Kirsty Major goes in search of playgrounds that are adapting to our new reality.

title: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways
Content: Euston, we have a problem: commuters heading to and from the capital often face extremely busy services.Photograph: Robert Stainforth/AlamyView image in fullscreenEuston, we have a problem: commuters heading to and from the capital often face extremely busy services.Photograph: Robert Stainforth/AlamyRail transportA rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only trainThis evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangwaysSammy Gecsoylerand Amee JoshiTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.“There’s been a couple of times where everyone’s boarded and then the train’s been cancelled and we all had to get off,” he says. On another occasion, his journey home took five hours because this service was delayed, meaning he missed a connecting train.This rush-hour service, operated by London Northwestern Railway (LNR), is the busiest commuter-only journey in England and Wales, according to figures by the Department forTransport.Overall, it’s the second busiest commute, the No 1 being a morning Thameslink service from Bedford to Three Bridges – which passes through three international hubs: St Pancras International, and Luton and Gatwick airports.We decided to join commuters getting the packed, two-hour-plus service on Thursday evening. According to the DfT, the service had a load factor – how many people are on a train compared with its maximum capacity – of 170% when the analysis was carried out last autumn. LNR says the number of seats on the service has increased from 460 to 812 since the data was gathered.There is the familiar scrum moving towards the train after the platform is announced, an infamous tradition at Euston station. At first it seems as if this crop of commuters has lucked out, as it isn’t overly busy. But as the clock approaches 5.46pm, the carriages begin to heave with people.Some fan themselves to keep the summer heat at bay. When the train is finally on the move, most gangways are cluttered with unlucky commuters unable to snag a seat. Some stand but others sit, bearing the rough and tumble of the shifting metal surface underneath.View image in fullscreenDaniel Garill regularly travels on the service.Photograph: Sammy Gecsoyler/The GuardianAmong them is Daniel Garrill, 23, who regularly gets this service. “I know I’m going to be sitting in some dodgy spot,” the data analyst says, having never got a seat during the week.He travels between London and Manchester at least twice a week, meaning he has to bring a suitcase – which is tricky because there’s “nowhere to put your bag either”. He has to keep fiddling with his luggage to ensure it doesn’t escape down the carriage.On the other side of the gangway is Akshay Vaghela, 31, who is commuting to Rugby. He says he is forced to stand half the time, and more often than not is “resigned to finding a seat on the floor”. This train is particularly busy because it is cheaper than the shorter Avanti service also heading to Crewe.“I’ve gotten used to it because I know what booking this service means. It’s a free-for-all for the seats, otherwise you’re standing,” he says. Despite the train being kitted out with air conditioning, Vaghela says it’s still “stuffy, hot and sweaty” because there are so many people on it. “Unless you’ve got water, you’re struggling until you get home,” he says.View image in fullscreenAkshay Vaghela often has no choice but to sit on the floor for long stretches of his journey.Photograph: Sammy Gecsoyler/The GuardianThere is a chance things might not stay this way. Andy Burnham, newly installed as prime minister, has had rail operators in his sights for a while, making headlines for calling out poor performers while mayor of Greater Manchester.He has previously said nationalising railways is a “no brainer” and launched the Bee Network as mayor, which brought privatised bus and tram networks into the local government’s control and capped fares at £2. Rail services across Greater Manchester willstart to jointhe network by the end of the year.He faced a rude reminder of the state of our railways last month. After his election as MP for Makerfield, he took a 10.54am Avanti West Coast train from Manchester to Euston. The service was delayed by 21 minutes, making him eligible to claim compensation.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also faced a bumpy train journey, saying she sat on the floor of a packed service from London Paddington to her constituency in Swindon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAndy Simms is thankful he has a short journey.Photograph: Sammy Gecsoyler/The GuardianBurnham hinted in May that there could be a swifter move towards rail renationalisation – a number of operators were brought under state control while Keir Starmer was prime minister – saying it would “reduce train fares and make them affordable to people again”.Vaghela is optimistic that Burnham will enforce some change. He says “priority routes like this one which connect main parts of the country should be looked at”, especially because “everyone’s paying the same price and some people get seats and others don’t, there’s a disparity there”.As we advance further down the carriages, we squeeze past commuters packed together by the platform doors, sidestep buggies and grab on to windows, poles or even fellow passengers to avoid tumbling to the floor.Standing among a group of commuters in a packed gangway is retiree Andy Simms, 65. He has a lucky escape, only having to bear the service for half an hour. He’s getting off at the first stop: Milton Keynes Central.Simms isn’t too bothered about the packed train. “It’s fine but busy,” he says, though he admits: “If you’re doing this every day it must be very annoying, especially if you’re paying for a season ticket.”Overall, he thinks trains are better than he remembers. “Things used to be a lot worse on trains back in my youth. It was scruffy, dirty and violent,” he says.On the prospect of Burnham making changes to the rail system, he’d rather he keep his focus elsewhere. “I think social care is more important than train journeys. I’d rather he fix that than this,” he says, while holding on to a pole behind for balance.An LNR spokesperson said: “Our services to and from Euston are extremely popular, which is why we have made a major £1bn investment in new trains to provide extra space for our customers.“Since this data was gathered we have added hundreds of extra seats to this particular service, increasing its capacity by 77% and significantly reducing its load factor to provide more comfortable journeys for passengers.”Explore more on these topicsRail transportPublic transportTransportRail industryTransport policynewsShareReuse this content

title: The truth about blushing: why we do it, how we can resist it – and why it’s actually good for us | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Humans are the only animals whose faces redden with embarrassment. Should we see that as an affliction, or as a blessing?
Author: Joel Snape
Headline: Humans are the only animals whose faces redden with embarrassment. Should we see that as an affliction, or as a blessing?
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Jamie Garbutt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Jamie Garbutt/Getty ImagesSecrets of the bodyLife and styleThe truth about blushing: why we do it, how we can resist it – and why it’s actually good for usHumans are the only animals whose faces redden with embarrassment. Should we see that as an affliction, or as a blessing?Joel SnapeTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Blushing is the most peculiar and most human of all expressions,” Charles Darwin once wrote, and he wasn’t wrong. Though certain species of bird pinken up as a means of communication, and uakari monkeys have red faces when in good health, we seem to be the only animal that flushes as a sign of embarrassment.“It’s a very truthful signal,” says Prof Sophie Scott, the director of the Institute for Cognitive Neuroscience at University College London. “It’s not fakeable, and there aren’t many things that humans do that fall into that category. You can’t blush on command.”You might, of course, hate it when it happens, but it’s a useful signal, one way or another. So what is it actually signalling? And is there any way to stop it?To get the “Why does it happen?” question out of the way, blushing is caused by your sympathetic nervous system – the same one that kicks in when you’re stressed or frightened – triggering your fight-or-flight response. Your brain releases adrenaline, which widens the blood vessels in your face (known as vasodilation), increasing blood flow to the skin and producing a visible shift in colour.“It’s more noticeable as a redness if your skin is pale, but everybody blushes,” says Scott. “In people who don’t have pale skin, it’s more a darkening of the skin, but your skin also does get hotter. So there’s this hall of mirrors effect: you know you’re blushing, other people know you’re blushing, and they knowyouknow you’re blushing.” Which, of course, can make you blush even more. Other animals might exhibit involuntary physical reactions such as laughing, or screaming in terror, but blushing seems to be unique to us because it’s linked to our theory of mind: our ability to guess what other people are thinking.This is important because we’re social animals: cooperation is what allowed us to survive and thrive when we were still hunting our food with pointed sticks. In early human societies, committing a faux pas, making a mistake or challenging a leader might have led to physical confrontation or expulsion from the group. It’s likely that blushing emerged as a way to signal recognition of rule-breaking, or genuine remorse: a way to de-escalate possibly deadly situations without any physically risky behaviour.“It seems to be associated with increased trustworthiness,” says Scott. “When somebody blushes easily, you’re more likely to know if they’re lying to you, for instance – or even if you don’t, you think that you can. That bonding and closeness is also what helps us work in groups. We’re apex predators because we can work cooperatively and, usually, read each other’s intentions really clearly.”Obviously, blushing can still be useful today for all of the reasons above. If we’ve dropped a clanger at work, it can be helpful to have an unfakeable signal that we genuinely regret it. But if we’re prone to blushing and hate it, is there anything we can do?The short answer is very little. But it also might not be the disaster you think. Frequent blushersseem to view blushing more negativelythan people who don’t blush all that much: if you’re aware that you blush a lot, it can create feelings of shame or self-awareness. If you’re an infrequent blusher, on the other hand – or you don’t tend to notice when you do it – then you might associate it with getting an unexpected compliment, being publicly recognised for an achievement or doing a bit of light-hearted flirting.The good news is that, whatever it feels like, you might not actually be blushing much more than anyone else. “Our research indicated that when embarrassed, people who weren’t frightened of blushing blushed as much as people who were frightened of blushing – they just didn’t notice it so much,” says Prof Peter Drummond, the lead authoron a studyexamining the gap between actual and perceived blushing. “When we brought this to their attention, they started to becomemoreconcerned about blushing. In this way, being worried that you might blush could actually trigger it in certain situations. However, it’s comforting to know that most people don’t even notice that others are blushing during social interactions because their attention is focused on speaking or thinking about what to say.”If this alone isn’t a comfort, then cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which aims to reframe your feelings about blushing, is one option. Another is task concentration training (TCT), a form of therapy developed specifically for people whose anxiety is anchored to visible body sensations such as blushing, trembling or sweating. TCT argues that your attention is a finite resource, and so if you deliberately direct it to external data – the tone of someone’s voice, say, or what else is going on in the room – you’ll be less likely to focus on how red your face feels.What does stress really do to our bodies – and when does it become a big problem?Read more“The aim of TCT and CBT is to manage anxiety about blushing rather than the blushing response itself,” says Drummond. “Even so, given that being worried about blushing can become a self-fulfilling prophecy, reducing that anxiety can reduce how often we blush.”Finally, it’s worth considering that, even if you hate it when you blush, there’s a decent chance that it’s doing you good overall. “I think of blushing as a ‘letting off steam’ response, as it shares the same physiological mechanism as flushing during exercise,” says Drummond. “Although we might feel hot and bothered when we blush, we generally feel better once we cool down. In fact, blushing might help dissipate unpleasant emotions such as anger, embarrassment and shame, just like flushing helps to dissipate heat generated during exercise.”In other words, it’s showing other people you’re sincere while also helping to calm you down. Nothing at all to be ashamed of.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis | Oil | The Guardian
description: Iran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damage
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Iran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damage
Content: The impacts this summer include Europe’s worst ever heatwave, the latest to be categorised by scientists as ‘impossible’ without human-caused global heating.Composite: Guardian Design/Reuters/EPA/AP/Getty Images/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe impacts this summer include Europe’s worst ever heatwave, the latest to be categorised by scientists as ‘impossible’ without human-caused global heating.Composite: Guardian Design/Reuters/EPA/AP/Getty Images/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOilRevealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisisIran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damageJillian AmbroseandDamian CarringtonTue 4 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareEight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.The windfall war profits have reignited calls for oil and gas supermajors such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for the environmental damage caused by “cashing in on human misery” and fund a rapid transition to renewable energy.Guardian analysis found that the eight listed oil producers made almost $93bn (£69bn) in the three months to the end of June – the first full financial quarter after the US-Israeli war on Iran triggered a surge in global oil prices tohighs above $126 a barrel.Graph showing changing oil pricesThe companies have used thebiggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s historyto almost double their combined profits from just under $50bn in the same period last year, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left paying the price in higher bills and climate chaos.The data suggests the eight oil companies – Aramco, BP, Shell, Equinor, TotalEnergies, Eni, Chevron and ExxonMobil – made more than $700,000 of profit every minute over the spring quarter.While their market valuations were swelling by about $600bn to above $3tn, temperatures built towards arun of deadly heatwaves, all made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels.Carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel firms weredirectly linked to fatal spells of hot weatherfor the first time by scientific analysis published last September. It found the emissions from any one of the 14 biggest companies were each enough to cause more than 50 heatwaves that would otherwise have been virtually impossible.View image in fullscreenBlackheath in south London, a wide open common usually known for its sweeping green spaces and views, has been left looking scorched and barren by the severe drought that was officially declared across more than half of England in late July 2026.Photograph: Fraser Gray/ShutterstockThe biggest oil profits in the spring quarter were raked in by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, Aramco, which reported a 34% increase in its quarterly net income to more than $33bn, even as its infrastructure wasdamaged by drone and missile strikesfrom Iranian and Houthi forces.Quarterly profits for the eight oil companiesSaudi Aramco’s fossil fuel production has made it responsible formore carbon emissions than any company in history, according to the database Carbon Majors, followed by Chevron and ExxonMobil and with Shell and BP in the top 10. Saudi Arabia has for decades led successfulefforts to block and delay international climate action.On Tuesday, BP became one of the last big oil companies to publish its results for the April to June period, reporting quarterly profits of $5.73bn – the highest since the first year of Russia’s full-scale war on Ukraine and more than double the $2.5bn of the previous three months.Graph showing rising oil company profitsPatrick Galey, the lead on fossil fuels at Global Witness, said: “BP’s sky-high profits are a scandalous reminder of who’s been cashing in on human misery this year. While wildfires threaten communities across the world, drought bites and energy costs spiral, ordinary families are paying the price for big oil’s prioritisation of shareholder wealth over a livable planet.”He added: “It’s time to make oil giants pay up to repair the climate breakdown they’re driving. Think how many fire and flood defences we could build, or how many solar panels we could install, if big oil paid their fair share in taxes.”Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control.”BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, defended the company’s profits by saying it was “focused on the things we can do to try to help address the situation” such as reliably producing more of the oil products that were in short supply.The company has been cutting the amount it spends on green energy since it dropped its environmental ambitions in a“fundamental reset” early last year, reducing its annual energy transition budget from $5bn to $1.5bn-$2bn.In recent years BP has spun off its UK offshore windfarms into a joint venture and sold its US onshore wind business, and on Tuesday it announced it would sell its $4bn US biogas business, which captures methane from landfill sites and is the largest renewable gas producer in the US.It is in advanced talks to sell its solar power business, Lightsource, to a consortium backed by Kuwait’s sovereign wealth fund, according to the Financial Times.On Friday, BPput its North Sea oil and gas business up for saleafter more than 60 years operating it, reigniting calls for the UK government to rule out the development of two controversial North Sea fields in the ageing basin.Shell last week reported itssecond highest quarterly profits everas its net income jumped to $9.84bn, despite producing less gas from its Qatar gas plant due to billions of dollars’ worth of damage caused by the war. Equinor’s profits climbed to $3.2bn in the same period, up from $1.8bn in the spring quarter last year.In the US, the profits reported by Chevron and ExxonMobilprovoked criticism from Donald Trump. The US president accused the pair of “making too much money” from his war on Iran and warned that they would be made to return profits to the public, as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings.Chevron reported net income of $12.2bn for the second quarter, a more than fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.Graph showing rising global temperaturesGaley said: “You know big oil is taking us for a ride when one of their biggest allies, Donald Trump, is telling them to rein their profiteering in.”The impacts this summer include Europe’sworst ever heatwave, another categorised by scientists as “impossible” without human-caused global heating. About 20,000 people are estimated to have died due to the extreme temperatures, including close to3,000 in the UKin May and June alone.South Korea andJapanhave also experienced record-breaking heat of up to 42.5C, with the Korean weather agency instructing people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, while the climate crisis pushed uptemperatures across much of Africain July. Global heating makes every heatwave more intense and more likely, and rising global temperatureskill one person a minutearound the world, a report in the Lancet estimated in October.The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “Around the world, climate-driven disasters are reaching nightmare proportions. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”View image in fullscreenA firefighter works to extinguish an advancing wildfire near Formariz in Zamora province, Spain, on 29 JulyPhotograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersEurope’s succession of heatwaves hassucked soils dryand led to extreme drought, damaging food supplies frommaize to sunflowers to salad. At least9m tonnes of grainare expected to be lost, with the UK, for example, facing its worst harvest on record.The arid conditions have also enabledhuge wildfires in France, Spain,Portugal and Greece, causingbillions of euros of damage. The blazes send toxic air pollution soaring and in the US and Canada the fires from 15-23 July are estimated to havecaused about 4,000 deathswithin a week of exposure. The climate crisis is making fire weather worse and about1.5 million people a yearhave their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.In south Asia, the climate crisis is supercharging extreme rainfall – air that is 1C warmer holds 7% more water. More than40cm of rain fell in 24 hoursin Chattogram in Bangladesh in early July, for example, leading to flash flooding. Floods and landslides have taken lives and livelihoods inPakistanandIndia. There have also beendozens of fatalities in north-west China, where many thousands of people have been evacuated due to heavy storms.The eight oil companies were contacted for comment.The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: on Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts – including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh, Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.live.

title: Electronic tagging system failing to alert authorities of probation breaches, watchdog warns | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Probation inspector for England and Wales says ‘clunky’ system needs huge increase in staff
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Probation inspector for England and Wales says ‘clunky’ system needs huge increase in staff
Content: The number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled in five years.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled in five years.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyPrisons and probationElectronic tagging system failing to alert authorities of probation breaches, watchdog warnsProbation inspector for England and Wales says ‘clunky’ system needs huge increase in staffRajeev SyalHome affairs editorTue 4 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe electronic tagging system that will be relied upon to monitor thousands of offenders released early from prison is failing to alert the authorities of potential breaches of conditions, a watchdog has warned.Martin Jones, HM inspector of probation inEnglandand Wales, said the system relied on hard-pressed police and probation officers looking up individual cases and then deciding whether potential breaches needed to be investigated further.He said it needed to be updated to send alerts to the authorities if a former inmate breached an exclusion zone from which they were banned.His demand comes after the government announced that up to 5,000 prisoners would be released from 1 October to ease the prison overcrowding crisis. At present, there are 86,500 people behind bars with 2,400 spare places.Andy Burnhampaused the schemelast month and on Tuesday heannounced plans to exclude prisonersguilty of rape, serious child sexual abuse offences and grooming, reducing the number of releases by 1,000. Killers and domestic abusers will still be eligible for early release, the Ministry of Justice has confirmed.Line graph showing projected prison population in 2030The prime minister has assured the public that offenders will face tighter community supervision, including new GPS monitoring.Jones, in an interview with the Guardian, said he had recently launched an inspection of offender tagging, and had seen that the system was coming under strain and needed to be upgraded to “minimise the risk to the public”.“Some of the systems are pretty clunky and it’s far too reliant on people looking for the information rather than the information being fed or pushed to practitioners as a matter of course,” he said.“Tagging has potential to improve public perception of victims’ safety. But only if it used properly and if there is a wider system and enough staff to support that. If not, there is a risk that you give false assurances to the public.”The number of people in England and Wales beingelectronically monitored has doubledto 28,700 in five years, and the number of newly tagged each year is expected to rise to 22,000 from 2027. Jones said this expansion needed a huge increase in staff to monitor offenders.The prison population has fallen under LabourAn early review of Jones’s inspection, across six regions in England, found:Probation officers wrongly assuming they would be notified about breaches of exclusion zones, when they were required to conduct a specific search.Data was not being actively monitored or analysed to reduce risk to the public.“Significant complexity” was involved in managing the monitoring process, leaving probation officers “overwhelmed and disengaged” by the volume of correspondence.Jones said: “My concern is this: have the processes and the system kept apace with the number of people being tagged? Because ultimately all tagging gives you is information about where somebody is at a particular point in time. You are relying on having sufficient police officers and probation officers to look at that information and make a decision about how it informs your picture on the activities of that individual.”Last monththe National Audit Office foundthat the rapid expansion of electronic tagging to reduce pressure on prisons would put public safety at risk unless there were robust improvements.‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release schemeRead moreJones also called for the government to ensure that there were enough staff inapproved premises, which are hostels set up to monitor 2,000 of the most serious offenders when they are first released from prison.“Our research shows that approved premises work. [They] are extremely effective at managing people after their initial release from custody. What a missed opportunity if those premises cannot remain open because of our insufficient staff,” he said.After a review of the plans, rapists and serious child sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators, will no longer be eligible for the early release scheme. But those given custodial sentences for domestic abuse, and criminals guilty of manslaughter, will still be eligible to be freed halfway through their sentence.Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has apologised to families affected, saying they were “carrying the can from previous failures”. He acknowledged the proposals had “created harm” for those grieving, such as the wife of PC Andrew Harper, Lissie.“I would express how angry I am, too, at being in a situation where we’re having to make significant changes that do have real impacts on people’s lives, so that we are able to have a functioning prison system,” he said.Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, said her family was “paying the price” after learning her son’s killers remained eligible for early release under the plans.Sarah Champion, the Labour MP for Rotherham, has written to Burnham, telling him that victims would “remain in a state of fear and limbo” unless domestic abusers were no longer included in the early release scheme.She told the prime minister: “I fully support the government’s ambitious goal to reduce violence against women and girls and tackle serious sexual offences. However, without reinstating the exemption to the early release scheme, I fail to see how that is possible.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charity Commission to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlements | Charities | The Guardian
description: Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint made by Labour MP about the funds
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint made by Labour MP about the funds
Content: Israeli settlers look at nearby Palestinian towns from an outpost in Yitzhar, Occupied West Bank.Photograph: Marcus Yam/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers look at nearby Palestinian towns from an outpost in Yitzhar, Occupied West Bank.Photograph: Marcus Yam/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesCharitiesCharity Commission to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlementsOfficial action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint   made by Labour MP about the fundsHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn official investigation has been launched into charities in England and Wales donating funds to illegal Israeli settlements inPalestine.The Charity Commission will aim to establish the amount of charitable funds going to illegal settlements, whether the spending was in furtherance of their purposes and any regulatory action that may be necessary.The investigation follows the Guardian’s reporting about the issue. Last year, it revealed thattwo UK charities had transferred approximately £5.7mto the Bnei Akiva Yeshiva high school in Susya, in the Israeli-occupied territory.In June, the Guardian published details of a formal complaint made by the Labour MP, Melanie Ward, to the regulator in which she said that32 charities in England and Wales had donated at least £28mto Israeli settlements that are illegal under international law. The Guardian understands that the inquiry is a direct response to Ward’s complaint.Announcing the investigation, which will initially focus on eight unnamed charities, Stephen Roake, assistant director, high risk compliance at the commission, said: “Serious allegations have been made about UK charities operating in illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine, so our first step is to establish the facts. Only then can we determine if regulatory action is required, based on our findings and the evidence we see.“Our fact-finding will also help us develop regulatory guidance for charities, which will to help ensure public trust and confidence in charities.”In June, the then foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper,said in parliamentthat she had asked the regulator to investigate the issue, telling MPs that “charity systems are abused to funnel support to illegal settlements” and “some evidence suggests that rules are being broken”. She expressed concern about “UK gift aid [tax relief] being funnelled to illegal settlements”.Responding to Cooper, Ward said her and 140 Labour colleagues wanted to see a ban rather than an inquiry. She told MPs that the commission appeared to have been made aware of the issue of donations to settlements in July last year – when the Guardian published its first story on the matter – but “has done nothing so far”.The regulator said the eight charities are among those that have been identified in concerns recently raised with it and that it would look at the location of their respective partners and how recently alleged activity occurred. It said it would consider naming them when it publishes its findings.The commission added that it planned to extend the number of charities under investigation over time.It said it has shared information about the scope of its inquiry with the police and HMRC. The Metropolitan police’s war crimes unit has said that it is not currently investigating any charities in relation to donations to illegal settlements.Last month, the Guardian revealed that a British charitywas funding a religious school at the heart of expansion plansfor the illegal Israeli settlement in the Palestinian city of Hebron.Friends of Yeshivat Shavei Hevron, which was approached for comment at the time, sent nearly £200,000 to the school between 2019 and 2024.Construction of a new dormitory for the school was approved in June, after the far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, unilaterally broke a decades-old international agreement on control of Hebron to give Israel planning authority.Abtisam Mohamed, a Labour MP and member of the foreign affairs committee, said that while she and other parliamentarians welcomed news of the investigation, “we know there is evidence of at least 32 charities engaging in this abhorrent practice. The Charity Commission must investigate them as well and move quickly to stamp out this behaviour altogether.“Funding illegal Israeli settlements is extremist activity linked to the violence and dispossession of Palestinians and bears no relation to charitable activity.”Explore more on these topicsCharitiesCharitable givingEnglandWalesIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bid | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Jordan FA president has accused Fifa of “blackmail”, claiming it threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The Jordan FA president has accused Fifa of “blackmail”, claiming it threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election
Content: Prince Ali bin al-Hussein (left), the president of the Jordan Football Association, says players have not been paid for their appearance at last year’s Arab Cup.Photograph: Mike Nelson/EPAView image in fullscreenPrince Ali bin al-Hussein (left), the president of the Jordan Football Association, says players have not been paid for their appearance at last year’s Arab Cup.Photograph: Mike Nelson/EPAFifaFifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bidJordan FA president says Fifa threatened to block fundsSecretary general calls selloff plan ‘sad and reproachable’Nick AmesTue 4 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, has accused Gianni Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”, claiming that Fifa threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election.In a major intervention Prince Ali, who ran for theFifapresidency against Infantino in 2016 and finished third, listed a number of problems dogging the global governing body and said Jordan’s players have not yet been paid for appearing in the Arab Cup last year. Prince Ali is head of the West Asian Football Federation, which includes influential states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates that have thus far backed Infantino to stay on.Concacaf countries considering withdrawing support for under-fire Gianni InfantinoRead moreIt came on a day when Infantino’s authoritywas dealt a further blowas two more key allies distanced themselves from his failed World Cup private investment plan. His No 2, the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, was revealed to have called the botched Fifa Forward Enterprise a “sad and reproachable series of events” in an email to the organisation’s staff. Meanwhile the former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who is now Fifa’s chief of global development, said the project’s withdrawal was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”.Infantino is steadily losing backing from countries who previously had sent letters to endorse his continuation for a fourth term in charge. It is understood that Greece is the latest federation to have pulled its support, following the lead taken by countries such as England, Wales, Finland and Serbia. More European federations are expected to follow in the coming days, while a number of nations in Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – are also giving serious consideration to withdrawing their backing.Prince Ali’s statement, published on X, painted the picture of a small country facing a litany of roadblocks when it came to receiving help from the global governing body. Jordan competed in their first World Cup this year but he explained some of their fans had not received visas, despite purchasing tickets, and expressed anger at being taxed by the US for being based in the country.“We have been waiting for reward money for our players since December for the Arab Cup in Qatar, which is a Fifa event,” his statement read. “The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet, while at the same time Fifa brags about how many billions they have in reserve.View image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (centre), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström (right), with Arsène Wenger during the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock“It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, Fifa has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters – until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out.“We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that.”Other countries are understood to have been put under concerted pressure to formally back Infantino before the Fifa election in March, although details of how it was applied remain unclear in those cases.Grafstrom’s email had urged Fifa staff to keep morale high after what was perceived to be a successful World Cup. His message stopped short of criticising Infantino by name and promised to shield colleagues from the strife enveloping their organisation.“A sad and reproachable series of events – which were thankfully concluded with the FFE project permanently abandoned – for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality,” read a section of the email.11:54Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president? - The LatestHe referred to “a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept” and said: “Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure.”Wenger, who assumed his current position in November 2019, confirmed he had been among the many senior Fifa staffsidelined by Infantino’s plan. “I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports,” he said.“The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity.”Fifa was contacted for comment regarding Prince Ali’s accusations.According to reports, Infantino has called Fifa staff to a crisis meeting in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, today as he tries to cling to his position.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoArsène WengerFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Government contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rules | Unemployment | The Guardian
description: Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Content: The first secretary of state, Louise Haigh (left), says new rules will ensure £90bn spent annually on government contracts can help ease unemployment.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe first secretary of state, Louise Haigh (left), says new rules will ensure £90bn spent annually on government contracts can help ease unemployment.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAUnemploymentGovernment contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rulesLouise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groupsAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.As part of a government push to reduce the number of peoplenot in education, employment or training (Neets)in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, said the move would help small businesses who often find themselves locked out of contracts because of the requirements, which big businesses know how to get around.“Every pound of taxpayer money should be spent in a way that benefits local communities – creating good jobs and giving young people the skills they need for the future,” said Haigh. “For too long, securing government contracts has been a tick-box exercise that fails to deliver the positive change that people feel in their pocket and see in the places they live.“We are doing things differently. These new rules will ensure the £90bn that is spent each year through government contracts supports British jobs, skills and people in every postcode.”Central government departments are required to weigh up the social value of government contracts, which counts for 10% of the decision. Under new measures this will be increased to 20%, but instead of considering social good, government buyers will be pushed to secure contracts with companies creating local jobs that pay above the minimum wage, offer training, work experience or plug local skills gaps.Contracts worth less than £1m will be exempt from the requirement, which ministers hope will make it easier for smaller companies to compete.The plans were criticised by environmental and green campaign groups, which said that job creation should not be a trade-off with protecting the environment.“Protecting the environment and helping young people into good work are mutually beneficial and one shouldn’t come at a cost to the other,” said Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy. “Companies should be held to account with environmental targets to help achieve a better future without leaving young workers behind.”‘They’re anxious about everything’: life for young people seeking work in Dudley and LewishamRead moreFriends of the Earth’s head of campaigns, Rosie Downes, said: “Encouraging companies to create good local jobs is crucial, but it shouldn’t be an either/or with efforts to safeguard our environment.“Communities are already paying the price of environmental inaction, with the UK on course for record levels of heat-related deaths this summer and our natural world in sharp decline.”Sarah Williams, the director of strategic partnerships at Green Alliance, said: “The UK is facing a growing youth unemployment crisis, so businesses should be encouraged to create good jobs and opportunities for young people. But scrapping requirements on climate and sustainability is simply not the answer. It’s not an either/or choice.”The move is also likely to spark concern among anti-trafficking and equality campaigners. ALaboursource said the government knew it would face criticism for scrapping some of the current social value indicators.“What companies have to do at the moment feels too much like a box-ticking exercise and it’s just red tape instead of being useful,” they said. “We are trying to make sure that the government pound is being used to invest in companies that want to invest directly in young people in their areas, and it brings real results and doesn’t just look good on paper.”Suppliers will be assessed on their commitment to backing British jobs and developing skills, and specifically targeting support for young Neets, care leavers and people with long-term health conditions.Explore more on these topicsUnemploymentLabourLouise HaighnewsShareReuse this content

title: MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review finds | MI6 | The Guardian
description: UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
Content: MI6 headquarters at Vauxhall Cross, London. The service was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenMI6 headquarters at Vauxhall Cross, London. The service was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants.Photograph: ReutersMI6MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review findsUK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’Nadeem BadshahTue 4 Aug 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMI6 has been ranked as the most powerful foreign intelligence service inEuropeahead of France and the Netherlands, according to a peer review.The British intelligence agency scored 251 points in the research and was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants and penetrating the ruling elites in Russia, China, Iran and Turkey, according to the review by 60 professionals from 25 countries.France’s General Directorate for External Security (DGSE) finished in second place with 169 points for its global reach and operational capability, the Times reported.The Netherlands, Ukraine and Germany complete the top five, while Slovakia’s service was rated the worst.The review was conducted by French magazine L’Express, which contacted people in stateservices de renseignements(intelligence services) to rate their counterparts in the western-allied countries.Britain caught in ‘space between peace and war’, says new head of MI6Read moreBritain was the first to warn Ukraine about the likelihood of the Russian invasion that began in February 2022, and has been a staunch ally of Kyiv.Ralph Goff, a former chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia at the CIA, told the magazine: “The British are in the lead on the Ukrainian file. We are right behind them.”Robert Gorelick, a former CIA station chief, added: “The United Kingdom has by far the strongest secret services in Europe.MI6is extraordinary.”Last year,Blaise Metreweli became the first woman to lead MI6, taking over from Sir Richard Moore.A former head of the DGSE said: “The British have the ability to play the long game, investing in sources over a 10-year horizon, somewhat like the Russians. And they have a taste for dirty tricks.”The DGSE, which was depicted in the French series The Bureau, was rated as one of the world’s best in counter-terrorism.The service is renowned for its clandestine operations to “eliminate” people deemed a threat to French security. François Hollande, the former French president, spoke publicly about ordering at least 40 operations to assassinate “high value” targets in the Middle East and Africa, according to a 2017 book.A Polish intelligence executive told L’Express: “It is the only service in continental Europe with near-global reach.“They combine technical collection, human intelligence and operational action capabilities.”Explore more on these topicsMI6EspionageUK security and counter-terrorismFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: AI-generated stories rated better quality than human-written ones, study finds | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Researcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsolete
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Researcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsolete
Content: Many participants were not able to detect when they had been misled about the origins of the text in the short stories.Photograph: Sergey Mironov/AlamyView image in fullscreenMany participants were not able to detect when they had been misled about the origins of the text in the short stories.Photograph: Sergey Mironov/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)AI-generated stories rated better quality than human-written ones, study findsResearcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsoleteNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom Homer’s Odyssey to Agatha Christie’s crime fiction, humans have produced plenty of tales to grace the bookshelf. But research suggests artificial intelligence may now be providing some competition.In a studypublished in the journal Judgment and Decision Making, 1,682 adults were asked to read one of six short stories, three of which were written by humans andthree by ChatGPT. Each AI story had a similar theme to one of the human-authored works.The team told participants whether their story was written by a human or AI, but this information was not always correct. The researchers then asked participants to rate how absorbing and engaging they found the story, and its quality.Participants who read an AI-generated story rated it as more absorbing and of higher quality than those who read a story written by a human. However, participants gave higher ratings to stories they had been told were written by people.Dr Deena Skolnick Weisberg, a senior author of the research from Villanova University in Pennsylvania, said: “AI systems can already generate short stories that are seen as being at least as good as – if not better than – human-written stories. We should update our views of AI’s abilities accordingly.”However, Weisberg, who is herself a creative writer, said that did not mean writing should be left to AI, noting that novels produced by tech were probably going to be different from those written by humans.“We may need to make room for AI-generated novels, and for AI/human co-written novels, but that doesn’t mean that there’s no longer space for us to appreciate the process of human creativity,” she said.“Humans write as a form of creative self-expression or to challenge ourselves, or to make sense of our experiences. The fact that AI can generate human-like stories doesn’t change any of that.”Google Earth’s potential disinformation nightmareRead moreThe results also suggest attitudes to AI matter: participants with more positive attitudes toward AI gave higher ratings to stories they were told were produced by ChatGPT than those with a less positive outlook.The researchers carried out two further experiments in which 905 adults were given two of the six short stories – both on the same theme and only one of which was penned by a person. They were then asked to guess which was written by a human and which by AI.In one experiment, about 40% guessed correctly, a result that is worse than chance, while in the other experiment 52% guessed correctly.“There is no general evidence that participants were able to distinguish human-written from AI-generated stories,” the authors write.The researchers found that while participants’ self-reported expertise with fiction was not linked to how accurately they guessed, greater expertise with AI systems was.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“AI writing has a particular style that we can learn to recognise with practice – just as we can learn to recognise different human authors’ unique styles,” Weisberg said.Weisberg suggested that the preference for stories labelled as beingwritten by humans was linked to a desire for authenticity, but that people actuallypreferred AI-generated stories because they were easier to read and digest.However, Luke Kennard, a professor of film and creative writing at the University of Birmingham, who was not involved in the work, emphasised that AI was highly contentious.“Because we’re human, we tend to personify AI and imagine it as some kind of glowing robot with a benign and neutral face, when it’s really just predictive code based on a massive stolen database of actual writing, physically based in vast, expensive anddestructive datacentreswith catastrophic repercussions for the surrounding communities,” he said.Kennard also stressed that AI was nota “tool” similar to spellcheck or a thesaurus, but an existential threat.“Of course it’s capable of spitting out a coherent and even enjoyable poem with the right prompting and finessing. Given that it’s been trained on thousands of years of human work, it would be embarrassing if it wasn’t,” he said. “I suppose the question we should be asking is: is it worth it? And the answer is absolutely, categorically, it is not.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)FictionCreative writingComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release scheme | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Partner of woman killed by dangerous driver among those who say they are devastated at killers leaving jail early
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Partner of woman killed by dangerous driver among those who say they are devastated at killers leaving jail early
Content: Frankie Jules-Hough was killed when Adil Iqbal crashed into her car on the M66 in 2023.Photograph: GoFundMe/PAView image in fullscreenFrankie Jules-Hough was killed when Adil Iqbal crashed into her car on the M66 in 2023.Photograph: GoFundMe/PAPrisons and probation‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release schemePartner of woman killed by dangerous driver among those who say they are devastated at killers leaving jail earlyJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Calvin Buckley, whose pregnant partner was killed by a dangerous driver in 2023, secured a tougher sentence for the man who took her life, he felt some justice had been served. Now, under plans to release prisoners early to ease overcrowding, Adil Iqbal, who filmed himself speeding at 123mph before he crashed into 38-year-old Frankie Jules-Hough, may serve less time in prison than he would have under his original sentence.“He could actually serve less time than he originally was going to before we appealed,” Buckley said. “We’ve fought for a tougher sentence. What is the point of having an actual sentence if the government can just reduce that?”Victims and bereaved family members who fear perpetrators could be released early under government plans to free up prison space say they are deeply concerned at the prospect of dangerous offenders walking the streets.Gemma Chappell, the great-aunt of Maya Chappell, who was shaken to death aged two by her mother’s boyfriend in 2022, said the early release scheme was further traumatising bereaved families.Maya’s mother, Dana Carr, was sentenced to nine years in prison after being found guilty of child cruelty by neglect and allowing her child’s death, but Chappell has been told she is set to be released early under the scheme.“I think it’s terrible. I think victims are not being heard. We should be allowed to grieve, we should be allowed to have our trauma,” she said.Chappell said it was “ridiculous” that Carr had made no admission of guilt and applied to have her sentence reduced, which was denied, but was now set to be released early anyway due to overcrowding.She said she welcomed Andy Burnham’s intervention to exempt rapists, serious child sexual abuse offenders and those convicted of grooming from the early release plans but said it didn’t go far enough.“There’s still victims and families out there who remain deeply concerned about these dangerous offenders getting out early, and we’re one of them. Justice should always be about public safety and the victim’s voice first,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.A former prison officer, Chappell said she wanted the government to invest more money in prison buildings instead. “Letting serious offenders out on to the street is not the answer,” she said. “We need some clarity on what’s going to happen if these offenders do get out because this affects our lifetime, not just the next couple of months.”Adil Iqbal in 2023.Photograph: Greater Manchester police/PABuckley said he was devastated to find driving offenders would not be exempted from the plans. “To kill somebody and to have your [prison] sentence reduced is just not right. Our justice has been taken away,” he told BBC Breakfast.“I understand there is a crisis, I agree that it needs to be addressed, but not at the expense of victims. For me it is another example of road victims not being treated the same as other offences.”Iqbal was originally sentenced to 12 years for killing Jules-Hough and her unborn child, Neeve. This was increased to 15 years by the court of appeal under the unduly lenient sentence scheme.Buckley said he was told Iqbal would serve a minimum of two-thirds of his original 12-year sentence – eight years – in prison. But under the new plans he could be eligible for release after half of his 15-year sentence, or seven and a half years.The government has also been criticised for its decision not to exempt domestic abuse perpetrators from the early release scheme.Alice Russell-Harris, the public affairs lead at Refuge, said the organisation was “deeply alarmed” and that the move would “put many domestic abuse survivors at risk”.She said releasing domestic abusers early would “heighten survivors’ fears for their safety” and the charity was aware that perpetrators “frequently breach conditions to continue their campaign of abuse”.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PAThe family of PC Andrew Harper, who was killed while responding to a report of a burglary in 2019, said they were devastated to learn two of the men jailed for his death would stillbe eligible for release.Harper was killed after being dragged behind a car for a mile. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter, could apply for early release after serving half of their sentences.“Andrew deserves better than this and so do we,” his mother, Debbie Adlam said. “It feels like we’re letting Andrew down again. We’ve been through the justice system, we thought we’d done as best as we could. Apparently, the situation is, if nothing was done, then the prison system would fall completely. But we’re paying the price for it.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door review – Theresa May is full of bluster in this fascinating deep dive | Television | The Guardian
description: This lively look at the 2018 novichok attack is full of strange and intriguing detail – even if May and Amber Rudd’s contributions don’t get the scrutiny they deserve
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This lively look at the 2018 novichok attack is full of strange and intriguing detail – even if May and Amber Rudd’s contributions don’t get the scrutiny they deserve
Content: State of shock … Theresa May in The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door.Photograph: Propagate/Passion PicturesView image in fullscreenState of shock … Theresa May in The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door.Photograph: Propagate/Passion PicturesTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door review – Theresa May is full of bluster in this fascinating deep diveThis lively look at the 2018 novichok attack is full of strange and intriguing detail – even if May and Amber Rudd’s contributions don’t get the scrutiny they deserveJack SealeTue 4 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It doesn’t sound like something that happens in your town.” The 2018 poisoning of former Russian military officer turned British double agent Sergei Skripal, along with his daughter Yulia, was extraordinary because of where it took place. Not that there are many locations where Russian agents using a chemical weapon against a former asset would be normal – but it would be relatively easy to comprehend in Paris, London or Berlin. In the quiet Wiltshire cathedral city of Salisbury, the contrast between everyday life and lethal international espionage was acute.That’s the most prominent of many angles taken by The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door, a not quite comprehensive but still nicely busy feature length documentary that offers a compendium of ways in which the Salisbury attack was fascinating and deeply strange.We meet a cross-section of Salisburians, starting with artist Meg Edgar, quoted above, who acts as a barometer for citizens’ fear and bewilderment. Rev Kelvin Inglis is closer to the event, having tended to a distressed flock after the attack: “The ugliness of the world was suddenly on our doorstep,” he says, with the deft flourish of the sermon writer. More involved than him is shopkeeper Ebru Ozturk, who used to enjoy a chat with a cheerful regular who bought the same items every few days: Russian sausage and scratchcards.Skripal, who had been spiked with a monstrously powerful nerve agent from a group of chemicals known as novichok, is profiled with help from the journalist Mark Urban, who recalls researching a book on Russian intelligence and learning not just that Skripal lived in Salisbury, but that one could simply go and visit him. His house featured a twee china ornament of a thatched cottage on the mantel, and a half-made Airfix model of HMS Victory. Skripal had been sold a dream of old England by MI6: having served four years in a labour camp after Vladimir Putin’s regime identified him as a traitor, he moved to Salisbury and enjoyed a happy, trivial existence. In lieu of an interview with the now unavailable Skripal, we spend time with ex-KGB agent Viktor Makarov, who is now in hiding somewhere in England. He likes scampi and chips.The novichok was identified byscientists at Porton Down, ending a period of manic uncertainty for the government, represented here by the then home secretary Amber Rudd and then prime minister Theresa May. It must have been an unforgettable episode in their careers, but none of their recollections quite bring it to life.Rudd and May are preoccupied with blustering about how jolly awful the Russians’ behaviour was, particularly the brazen denials that the then national security adviser Mark Sedwill slightly grandly refers to as “disinformation”. May is keen to communicate how determined she was to “hold them to account”, which ultimately took the form of diplomatic expulsions. Whether the UK could have taken more robust action, for instance by flushing dodgy Russian money out of London, is barely discussed. Nor is there analysis of the effect on Vladimir Putin of Skripal, embarrassingly for the Russian premier, surviving the attack, or of how the incident affected Putin’s feeling that he could act with impunity, and whether this influenced his invasion of Ukraine. Instead, we get the usual performatively withering stuff about him being a corrupt autocrat who was bullied at school and whose vengefulness masks weakness.Back in Salisbury weeks after novichok was unleashed, the fallout continued to be a mixture of eccentric and tragic. In archive footage – generally presented here in that now familiar post-Adam Curtis style, with moments where the camera wobbles or refocuses left in for added spookiness – we see Rev Inglis conducting a “cleansing” ceremony to symbolically rid Salisbury of poison, this being an event where he throws two glass jugs of water on to the brick paving outside a crystals shop. But we also hear, in a present-day interview,the desperately awful story of Charlie Rowley, a man who was trying to make a new life for himself and his partner Dawn Sturgess, and was foraging in bins for any items that could be gifts for her. He was delighted to come across what seemed to be a tester bottle of perfume. Some time later he presented it to Dawn, she sprayed it on her wrist, and shortly afterwards she was dead. Skripal’s assailants had casually binned their disguised vial of novichok when they were done; Charlie lost the love of his life in the most phenomenally unlikely fashion.The last blast of dark absurdity came when the Russian agents who had conducted the attack responded to being unmasked by denying their involvement on the propaganda channel Russia Today, in an interview during which they and the host both seemed to be stifling a laugh. There was nothing funny about the Salisbury poisonings, but their elusive quirkiness makes them unique.The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door aired on Sky Documentaries and is available on NowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewNovichok poisoningsEspionageDocumentaryTheresa MayAmber RuddRussiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Google Earth’s potential disinformation nightmare  | Technology | The Guardian
description: A new feature briefly allowed Google Earth users to overlay AI-generated images on locations of their choosing
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: A new feature briefly allowed Google Earth users to overlay AI-generated images on locations of their choosing
Content: A Google Earth satellite screengrab of the seventh district in Tehran.Illustration: Google EarthView image in fullscreenA Google Earth satellite screengrab of the seventh district in Tehran.Illustration: Google EarthTechScape newsletterTechnologyGoogle Earth’s potential disinformation nightmareA new feature briefly allowed Google Earth users to overlay AI-generated images on locations of their choosingThis was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives.Sign up to receive it here.Johana Bhuiyan,Dara KerrandNick Robins-EarlyTue 4 Aug 2026 09.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 17.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. This week we’ll be discussing a regrettable decision by Google Earth, the dramatic fall of the “Nostradamus of AI”, and what happens whenAIagents go rogue.Google Earth pauses new AI feature for satellite imagesLast Thursday, Google announced that users of its satellite-imagery software, Google Earth, could create AI-generated images to overlay on any location they looked up.
