The tool could be used to “help students visualize the past”, “create professional real estate plans” to envision the final result, or “give your favorite place a makeover”, Google suggested in its announcement. Nearly immediately, users began testing the limits of the feature. Turns out there weren’t many.Henk van Ess, an AI researcher and investigator, posted images he created showing refugees near the Mexican border. He also said he “planted a nuclear plant in Iran”. “What on earth is Google doing?” Van Essposted on X. Another image he generated showed a crater from a bomb near a fake hospital he created in Gaza. We tested the feature too. The process just required choosing a location, clicking “create image” and entering a prompt. We chose to show “refugees swarming New York”. The image it created was not ultra-realistic, but it was still troubling.View image in fullscreenGoogle Maps screengrab with AI overlay.Illustration: Google MapsSatellite imagery has become widely used by journalists, researchers and investigators to shed light on the breadth and realities of global crises, especially in places that are otherwise inaccessible. The utility of satellite images first became apparent in 2020, after BuzzFeed News won a Pulitzer for a series that exposed the location and expansion of China’s Uyghur detention camps. The imagery captured, for the first time, factories within the walls of the camp. The journalists worked with satellite firm Planet Labs, which is backed by Google and acquired satellite startup Terra Bella from the tech giant in 2017.The use of satellite imagery to better understand and uncover global crises really took off in the last two years as reporters and the world sought to better understand the mass destruction Israel has wrought on Gaza. Satellite imagery of Gaza before and after Israel’s years-long rampage on the 365 sq km stripshows cities completely leveled.Satellite imagery was also used to expose the human toll of the crisis in Sudan. Images captured from space inNovember 2025showed stains that resembled blood and what researchers believed were human bodies scattered near the besieged city of El Fasher, which was under siege by paramilitary fighters from the Rapid Support Forces.So a feature that allows you to “transform” satellite imagery, as Google described it, is a potential disinformation nightmare. Satellite imagery lends a degree of authority, authenticity and veracity to claims and has been used as a mechanism to better understand inaccessible global events. It feels more indisputable than images captured by humans on the ground, which face more public skepticism – even when they’re real – as AI-generated images proliferate. Enabling anyone to create any image overlaid on satellite photos of real places may make it impossible to suss out the truth.Unsurprisingly, Google rolled back the feature so it can create more guardrails, meaning they may bring the feature back. “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world,” the company wrote. “We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies.”‘Nostradamus of AI’ sees $45bn hedge fund unravel practically overnightView image in fullscreenLeopold Aschenbrenner, once hailed as ‘the Nostradamus of AI’, saw his multibillion-dollar hedge fund decimated last week as many of its investments withered.Illustration: Guardian DesignThe popular podcaster Tim Ferriss once called Leopold Aschenbrenner “the Nostradamus of AI”, saying that the 24-year-old investor and his theories on the future of artificial intelligence were “as close to clairvoyant as you could possibly be”. But that lore hasn’t been borne out.Last week, Aschenbrenner saw his multibillion-dollar hedge fund decimated as his many investments withered. By Thursday, the fund had no choice but to sell the majority of its public holdings to a rival.Aschenbrenner isn’t a household name, but he is well-known in Silicon Valley circles. When he graduated college, in 2021, he started working for the now defamed crypto exchange FTX. When the exchange collapsed, he joined OpenAI. Aschenbrenner was later fired from OpenAI for reportedly leaking sensitive information to the husband of an Anthropic executive,according to the Wall Street Journal. At that point, in 2024, Aschenbrenner wrote a 165-page essay called Situational Awareness: the Decade Ahead, which catapulted him toward fame in the tech world.The essay laid out his theories on AI, saying that the technology had set in motion “extraordinary techno-capital acceleration” and that “before long, the world will wake up”. As his essay gained momentum, Aschenbrenner collected prominent Silicon Valley investors for his hedge fund, also called Situational Awareness. The fund grew exorbitantly.Situational Awareness didn’t adhere to the usual cautions of Wall Street, however. Instead, it took the gamble of borrowing money to buy stocks, a strategy that doesn’t have a safety net when stocks go south. And, as AI stocks took a downturn this past month – with doubts of the technology’s potential swirling – the hedge fund was forced to pay back skittish lenders. Situational Awarenesssold off its investments in a fire salewith its billions now dissipated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAI models go on hacking spreesView image in fullscreenThe Claude AI app on a smartphone.Photograph: AnthropicOver the past several weeks,Anthropicand OpenAI have revealed that their artificial intelligence models carried out unauthorized hacking operations against outside organizations. The hacks took place during their tests of yet-to-be released AI models, which were supposed to happen within isolated, controlled environments.In OpenAI’s case, an autonomous AI agent carried out a days-long hack in early July against Hugging Face, a developer platform that hosts AI models. It also hacked a customer of the AI startup Modal Labs. Anthropic similarly revealed last week that its AI models hadhacked into three undisclosed organizationsduring a cybersecurity test, in part because human error gave it access to the public internet during the test.The reports of rogue AI agents breaking out of their testing sandboxes to carry out attacks have, unsurprisingly, drawn huge amounts of tech and media attention amid heightened cybersecurity concerns and distrust of the industry. They have also divided tech experts over whether these hacks are as consequential as they seem and how to stop them in the future.One of the longstanding problems of AI development is that models can act in unpredictable ways when directed to complete a task. An AI instructed to win a racing game may not solely try to drive fast to succeed, for instance. It may also look for loopholes in the game or shortcuts in the course. This is a well-known phenomenon that is usually described as models “cheating” or “lying” during testing.OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face was an extreme example of this type of behavior and one that highlights how advancements in AI have exacerbated these unsolved problems. Models that go rogue to achieve their goals are now powerful enough that the unintended consequences can be much more damaging and far-reaching than finding a glitch in a video game.While cybersecurity experts agree that AI has become incredibly capable at finding security vulnerabilities, somealso cautioned that OpenAI’s hacking incidentfit into one of the company’s well-worn marketing narratives – that its technology was scarily powerful and therefore exceedingly valuable. Others, meanwhile,described it as a wake-up callabout the threat of AI as a cybersecurity nightmare, with the technology rapidly gaining new capabilities.Regardless of whether the hacking incidents mark a new frontier or merely play into industry talking points, they highlight the lack of coherent policy and industry standards surrounding the technology. As AI experts Bruce Schneier and Barath Raghavanargued for the Guardian, the industry has been focused on whether AI can reach a goal without enough scrutiny of how it gets there:Dozens of benchmarks and leaderboards tell us how well these AI models write code, perform logical reasoning, and pass standardized legal and medical exams. But there is nothing that scores whether a system does what you actually meant. We need to develop a measure for this, test it regularly, and push for improvement. We’re not going to have trustworthy AI agents without it.Read more:Apple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access dataCould AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answerChina’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White HouseHow to keep your Claude chats and Google files private | US newsUS bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’Explore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘When you kill it, it doesn’t die’: the jellyfish that has cracked the secret of immortality | Marine life | The Guardian
description: Turritopsis dohrnii has the ability to turn back into a baby jellyfish and grow up all over again
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Turritopsis dohrnii has the ability to turn back into a baby jellyfish and grow up all over again
Content: The Turritopsis dohrnii can survive adverse conditions such as high temperature, physical cutting, starvation and chemicals in water.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Turritopsis dohrnii can survive adverse conditions such as high temperature, physical cutting, starvation and chemicals in water.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Marine life‘When you kill it, it doesn’t die’: the jellyfish that has cracked the secret of immortalityTurritopsis dohrnii has the ability to turn back into a baby jellyfish and grow up all over againRevealed: the top ten invertebrates of the yearPetra StockTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImmortality is generally considered the realm of the gods or science fiction, a fantasy that’s actively pursued by tech entrepreneurs in macabreexperimentsthat include injecting “young blood”, cryopreservation, or resurrection in an AI afterlife.But one ethereal, thimble-shaped jellyfish has already cracked the code.As associate professor Maria Pia Miglietta, a marine biologist at A&M University, explains,Turritopsis dohrniihas an incredible ability to cheat death.“Turritopsis is unique, because when faced with unfavourable conditions – and I mean high temperature, physical cutting, starvation, chemicals in the water, you name it – when you try to kill the jellyfish, it doesn’t die.”Most normal jellyfish start off life as larvae. They metamorphose into polyps (tiny, stationary soft bodies) that bud off swimming medusas, which grow up to become adult jellies. Eventually, after reproducing, most will stop swimming, crumble a little and then die.But the immortal jellyfish escapes that fate. It reverts to a juvenile form, and starts its life cycle again.The process is called “cellular transdifferentiation”, Miglietta says. The jellyfish looks like it’s dying and sinks to the bottom. Then – like a butterfly returning to a caterpillar – it shrinks into a ball, and within 24 to 48 hours, buds off a new polyp with the same identical genome, she says.View image in fullscreenThe Turritopsis dohrnii starts its life cycle again in a process known as ‘cellular transdifferentiation’.Photograph: Adisha Pramod/AlamyIt’s one of “nature’s coolest tricks”, says Guardian reader Raquel López-Aragón. “When this jellyfish gets old or gets hurt, instead of just dying like most animals, it transforms itself back into a baby jellyfish and grows up all over again. It can do this as many times as it wants, which means theoretically it never has to die from getting old, it just keeps hitting the reset button on its life.”In the lab, where Miglietta studies them, these jellies can theoretically live for ever. However, for some in the wild, getting eaten may eventually end that dream run.Globally, there are eight accepted species of Turritopsis – but (so far) only one holds the key to eternal life.Immortal jellyfish are only a few millimetres in size. But, if you know what to look for, they can be found in many places, from the Mediterranean sea, to the Atlantic, from the coast of Japan to Panama and Brazil.As another reader remarks, the immortal jellyfish does “exactly what it says on the tin”. “They have the very enviable ability to simply turn back into a juvenile at any sign of stress, which is something that I’m sure we all wish extended to humans.”With their delicate bodies and veil of tentacles, Dr Lisa-ann Gershwin, a biologist specialising in jellyfish, describes Turritopsis as “exquisite” and “the most beautiful little creature”. But what makes them remarkable is their capacity for reincarnation.Since ancient times, humans have speculated about eternal life, she says, it’s one of the things that unites us all.“It’s so hardwired in humans to not want to die. And I think the drive that we have to survive, and the absurdity of that being in a jellyfish – the juxtaposition of those two just entertains me to no end.”It’sInvertebrate of the Year again! From 3-12 August, every day wewill be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when youhave got to hear about all of them, wewill open the voting so that you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us at environment.desk@theguardian.com with Invertebrate in the subject line.Explore more on these topicsMarine lifeInvertebrate of the year 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: No smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy Cricket | Comedy | The Guardian
description:
Having cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015
• Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Having cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015• Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80
Content: Letters from ‘Mammy’ … Jimmy Cricket performing in A Night Of 100 Stars in 1990.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLetters from ‘Mammy’ … Jimmy Cricket performing in A Night Of 100 Stars in 1990.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockComedyNo smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy CricketHaving cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80Mark LawsonTue 4 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the comedian Jimmy Cricket chose the catchphrase, “And there’s more!” he may have reflected that the words would one day have a poignant irony. As has now happened after his death, aged 80.The stage name was adopted by James Joseph Mulgrew, from Cookstown in Northern Ireland, when he worked as an entertainer at the Butlin’s and Pontins holiday camps from the 1960s at a time when these summer resort venues were an academy for UK entertainers.Both Jimmy and Jiminy Cricket were rooted in polite euphemisms for the expletive “Jesus Christ!”, but Mulgrew, a committed churchgoer and carefully clean comic, is unlikely to have been motivated by the oath. Whether deliberately or by luck, his chosen pseudonym was likely to pique the interest of fans of Disney’s Pinocchio(in which Jiminy Cricket is a key character), those interested in orthopteran insects in general and lovers of the greatest summer game. The Irish climate and distraction of more historically Irish sports might have restricted the resonance of that reference back home but it proved useful to schedulers in Britain. Jimmy’s Cricket Team was the title of his successful BBC Radio 2 series from 1990, making the return to wireless writing of Morecambe & Wise’s greatest writer, Eddie Braben.View image in fullscreenSuited and Wellington booted … Cricket in And There’s More in 1985.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockAt that time, BBC Radio was tapping into the peak of Mulgrew’s public popularity, encouraged by his biggest television visibility, from 1985-88, on an ITV show titled after his catchphrase, And There’s More. The words perfectly suited a show featuring short sketches, songs and standup. Fronted by Mulgrew as Cricket, the 24 episodes included regular appearances by comedy actors Nicholas Smith (Are You Being Served?) and Joan Sims (Carry On) and guest slots for Hazel O’Connor, singing, and Rory Bremner, impersonating.As Cricket, he wore a stage costume of too-short formal trousers (possibly a homage to the similarly attired Max Wall), funny hats and Wellingtons on the wrong foot. That – alongside the somewhat silly professional moniker – led some wrongly to assume that he was a children’s entertainer.It was not, though, entirely misleading. He aimed at adults the sort of material that classified him as what used to be called a “family entertainer” – no smut, no swearing and little songs in which his retained native accent allowed him to rhyme “faffing” with “laughing”.The purity and implied puritanism of his comedy was perhaps rooted in a Roman Catholic upbringing in Northern Ireland in the 1950s, a creed and era noted for their censoriousness. The lasting impact of his upbringing was also evident in many references in his routines to letters from his “Mammy”. Though uncontroversial at the time, one aspect of the act – many gags relating to “Irish logic” – might now be regarded as offensive, although, in common with Jewish comedians, Mulgrew would have claimed a birthright to explore stereotypes within his own tribe.Though the hold of the faith diminished for many of his Ulster generation, Mulgrew remained practising, receiving in 2015 a papal knighthood, Catholicism’s highest honour, from Pope Francis. The citation mentioned the recipient’s charitable work; although the Argentinian pontiff was something of a joker himself, the honour is unlikely to have been for comedy. (Mulvey’s Northern Irish peer, Frank Carson, though rather less scrupulously clean mouthed, had received the same honour from Pope John Paul II, creating an intriguing trend among Northern Irish jokers of that generation.)The highest profile period of Mulgrew/Cricket’s career overlapped with the so-called Troubles in Northern Ireland, its associated atrocities often featuring in the headlines of news bulletins abutting his TV and radio appearances. The performer, though, was wary of sectarianism – holiday camp performers largely targeted those unlikely to be paying customers – and, in turn, didn’t suffer much bigotry, although, as with Carson, few impressionists could resist a go at the Ulster brogue.“Always let your conscience be your guide,” sings Jiminy Cricket in Pinocchio and that was the credo of his near namesake during a career in which he aimed to provide unthreatening fun – and succeeded.Explore more on these topicsComedyTV comedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rod Liddle obituary | Newspapers & magazines | The Guardian
description: Provocative journalist whose invective-laden columns targeting the liberal-left were laced with an ebullient humour
Author: Stephen Bates
Headline: Provocative journalist whose invective-laden columns targeting the liberal-left were laced with an ebullient humour
Content: A tousled and dishevelled figure, Rod Liddle believed that the alleged sacking of the old order had ‘left us fraught and clamorous, unhappy, isolated and averse’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA tousled and dishevelled figure, Rod Liddle believed that the alleged sacking of the old order had ‘left us fraught and clamorous, unhappy, isolated and averse’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNewspapers & magazinesObituaryRod Liddle obituaryProvocative journalist whose invective-laden columns targeting the liberal-left were laced with an ebullient humourStephen BatesTue 4 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf the first rule of column writing is to be read and the second and third to be interesting and provocative, the journalistRod Liddle, who has died aged 66after a short illness, certainly met the bill.His columns in theSunday Times, the Spectator and the Sun, and his Saturday morning shows for Times Radio, gave his fans, mainly on the political right, all they needed to fulfil their prejudices, laced with a satirical edge and verve. He could fill the 2,500-seater London Palladium, as he once did for his conversational show.A tousled and dishevelled figure, shirt flapping open, Liddle’s iconoclastic targets in recent years have included bureaucrats, politicians, “thought police”, campaigners for gay and trans rights and, above all and constantly, the supposed politically correct, liberal-left elite alleged to be undermining the stolid, respectable working classes, leaving them feeling left behind and ignored.The columns regularly became boisterously laden with invective moderated by an ebullient, wrecking-ball humour and were the subject of regular complaints by those who did not see the joke.Welsh nationalists were “miserable, seaweed munching, sheep bothering, pinch-faced hill tribes” and grievance groups indulged in “furious yapping”; others were waxen-skinned spaffgoblins. The alleged sacking of the old order had “left us fraught and clamorous, unhappy, isolated and averse”, never mind that some of his readers espousing such views were inflamed and confirmed in their opinions precisely by his prose.The one person to whomhe felt he owed an apologywas the Labour politician Harriet Harman for a crude snub, saying that he had not thought how the remarks would affect her. Liddle was thefirst journalist to be censured for a blogby the Press Complaints Commission in 2010 after alleging that the majority of violent crime in London was carried out by“young men from the African-Caribbean community”.It was an irony that some of his most ardent fans were among those he had mocked inregular columns for the Guardianfor more than three years between 1999 and 2003. When in 2002 he had derided conservative members of the Countryside Alliance who had demonstrated against the Blair government as “angry ruddy-faced people”, going on to say “you may have forgotten why you voted Labour in 1997 but then you catch a glimpse”, he was condemned by the Telegraph and the Sun, which he would subsequently go on to write for.Liddle was born in Sidcup, Kent, into a respectable, church-going family, the son of Margaret (nee Clee), who worked for the then Department of Health and Social Security, and Edwin, who came from a north-east family of railway workers but was himself an Inland Revenue clerk. They moved back up north when Liddle was eight to the Middlesbrough “select” suburb of Nunthorpe, a description that he later characteristically described as like saying “a select suburb of Mogadishu”.He was educated at the Laurence Jackson comprehensive school and Prior Pursglove sixth form college, undergoing as he did so a rite of passage as a punk, a sartorial style that never completely left him, and briefly joining the Socialist Workers party. Canvassing for Labour at the 1983 general election, he claimed his appearance must have cost Labour 5,000 votes.Liddle joined the South Wales Echo as a journalist, and then moved to London to study social psychology at the London School of Economics and worked as a researcher for the Labour party before joining theBBCas a trainee producer.View image in fullscreenRod Liddle in his time as producer of the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianIn 1998 he was made editor of the Today programme onRadio 4and became perhaps the first to be widely known beyond the corporation. He undoubtedly made the previously rather cosy programme sound more aggressive and competitive, with more use of investigative journalism, and increased its audience figures accordingly.It was under his watch in 2003 that the BBC was engulfed in a furious row with the Blair government over allegations that a dossier alleging that the Iraqi government was preparing weapons of mass destruction had been “sexed up” as a pretext in advance of the Iraq war – a story that led to the suicide of theweapons expert David Kelly, who had been the unwitting source of the reporter Andrew Gilligan.Liddle defended the programme and the BBC vigorously in columns for the Guardian against the government and other newspaper attacks, reserving deepest scorn for Peter Mandelson, whose briefings he claimed had heightened the row.It was Liddle’s increasingly outspoken columns for the paper that goaded the corporation into requiring that he either gave them up or left the BBC. Choosing the latter course, he soon found himself in demand by the Sunday Times and others for his pugnacious commentaries, delivered professionally on time and to length. A novel and books of his writing followed, including Selfish Whining Monkeys in 2014 and The Great Betrayal (2019), stating why in his view the Brexit referendum vote had been undermined by, naturally, the liberal elite and politicians.While at the BBC in 1993, Liddle began a relationship with Rachel Royce, a reporter, whom he married in a ceremony in Malaysia in 2004. The relationship had already produced two children, Tyler and Wilder, but Liddle left the honeymoon early to his wife’s fury whenshe discovered he had done so to continue his affairwith Alicia Monckton, a receptionist at the Spectator magazine who was half his age. Following the divorce from Royce, Liddle married Monckton in 2008 and the couple had a daughter, Emmeline.Alicia and the three children survive him.Roderick Edwin Liddle, columnist and broadcaster, born 1 April 1960; died 2 August 2026Explore more on these topicsNewspapers & magazinesBBCRadio 4Sunday TimesThe SunThe SpectatorobituariesShareReuse this content

title: The best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – tested | Life and style | The Guardian
description: They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterLife and styleReviewThe best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – testedThey’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommendsThe best air fryersCaramel QuinTue 4 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.If you’re at a restaurant and hear a ping a couple of minutes before your meal arrives at your table, it’s unlikely to be a good sign. But microwave ovens are a brilliant tool in the home kitchen. They’re fearsomely fast at heating up – or even cooking – food when you’re time-poor and lacking the energy to make something wholesome after a hard day at work. And in hot weather, cooking by microwave isn’t just quick: it also won’t warm your home.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Microwaves work best for heating food with a high water content (they make the water molecules in food vibrate to create heat). However, before testing, I asked around to find out what people use theirs for most, with a view to using this information to shape my tests. I learned a few things – like lots of people eatmug cakes. Who knew? And that wheat bags are a popular alternative to hot-water bottles. But the majority of folk use their microwave for reheating cold cuppas, defrosting frozen batch-cooked meals, warming food, popping microwave popcorn – and, of course, cooking jacket potatoes more quickly. I used these insights to shape my testing.Ease of use is important, too. Most of us only ever use a few buttons on repeat, often having to reach for the instructions if we want to use some of the smarter functionality these appliances now come with – some can even air-fry.Microwaving can be healthy and fast, and it uses less energy than an oven. So, if you want to discover the best microwaves for your needs, read on.At a glanceBest microwave overallPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fry£379 at AmazonBest budget microwaveSalterDuoWave 2-in-1£184 at CurrysBest microwave for controlsLGMH6565CPS NeoChef£148.98 at LGWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist who’s been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with my children and several pets, meaning there were plenty of mouths for the extra food I was making while testing these microwaves. The humans got a lot of jacket potatoes and beans; the animals helped with the rest … which is how I discovered that hens love poppadoms!How I testedView image in fullscreenMicrowave magic … every model was put through the same tests, from jacket potatoes and baked beans to defrosting and popcorn.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI selected 10 microwave ovens from leading brands at various price points. The models differed in capacity and features but were similar in other ways. They all had a dial and buttons for control on a panel on the right-hand side. They all opened to the left, other than the Samsung Combi microwave, where the door opens downwards. And they all had a one-metre power cable at the rear that came from the top right (looking front on).I used each model to prepare the same set of foods. I made microwave popcorn, cooked jacket potatoes (200 to 250g each), and heated up 150g of baked beans.Next, I used each microwave to heat 250ml of chilled (starting at 9C) tap water for two minutes, using a digital thermometer to check its temperature after heating. I also used the defrost settings on a 500g block of ice in each microwave for 10 minutes, weighing how much ice was left. Finally, I cooked poppadoms to evaluate a microwave oven’s ability to cook evenly, and frozen oven chips in those models that come with an air-frying feature.None of the food I made went to waste, with the chickens happily eating any leftover popcorn and – surprisingly – the poppadoms, and the dog eating everything else.With testing done and dusted, any models that weren’t collected by the manufacturers were donated toFurnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes social housing for survivors of domestic abuse.The best microwaves in 2026View image in fullscreenHot competition … the microwaves battling it out for a place on your worktop.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest microwave overall:Panasonic NN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryfrom£379£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonWhat we loveHuge capacity; proper jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveBulky; greasy fingerprints show up on itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonThis microwave is huge, arriving with the biggest capacity on test. The turntable sits on a roller with six wheels, rather than the usual three, and the controls are a dial with a button at its centre, plus six clearly labelled buttons. Helpfully, the display features scrolling text, so you always know what you’re doing, and you’ll find a list of all the programmes inside the door, so you never need to consult the instructions to make full use of it.Why we love itPerformance was excellent: the microwave cooked popcorn fast, the poppadoms evenly, heated my mug of water to 75C and defrosted the ice well. I used a special programme to cook the jacket potato, which took 15 minutes but was well worth the wait. In fact, the Panasonic was the only microwave on test to produce a jacket potato that could have passed for oven-baked.This model also offers grill, convection oven and air-fryer cooking – personally, I think those last two are the same thing. Again, though, performance impressed. It comes with a circular rack, a crisper tray and a wire basket, which I used to air-fry frozen chips to perfection.If you want a microwave that does it all and gives you extra cooking capacity – essentially, an extra shelf’s worth of oven – this is the one to buy.It’s a shame that …fingerprints show on the brushed stainless steel finish.Dimensions:56 x 45 x 34cm (WDH)Power:1,000W (1,300W grill)Capacity:34lTurntable diameter:36cmOther cooking options:oven, grill, air fryerPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryfrom£379£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonWhat we loveHuge capacity; proper jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveBulky; greasy fingerprints show up on itBest budget microwave:Salter DuoWave 2-in-1SalterDuoWave 2-in-1from£184£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterWhat we loveGood value; a whole shelf for air fryingWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need the instructions for some functionsView image in fullscreen£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterThe “duo” in the name refers to the fact that this microwave doubles as an air fryer. And it performed brilliantly on all fronts. If you don’t have the worktop space or the budget for the Panasonic, the Salter is a great buy.Microwaving is on a standard glass turntable, but you air-fry on a full-width, rectangular roasting tray that slides into the unit like a shelf, with a rectangular mesh basket that sits on top of this tray.Why we love itIt’s clever. Most microwaves have a jacket potato programme that takes five minutes, but that’s never quite enough: I experimented and found 5mins 20secs was the optimum time. The Salter automatically went for 5mins 20secs and cooked it perfectly.It’s quick, too, heating my mug of water to an impressive 73C and cooking two poppadoms quickly and evenly. I used the basket to air-fry frozen oven chips, and they were ready within 15 minutes.Controls are intuitive, with a button in the middle of the dial. It was easy to figure out how to defrost, and I could do so by time or weight.It’s a shame that …there isn’t a list of all the programmes inside the door.Dimensions:45 x 52 x 30cm (WDH)Power:900WCapacity:26lTurntable diameter:31cmOther cooking options:air fryerSalterDuoWave 2-in-1from£184£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterWhat we loveGood value; a whole shelf for air fryingWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need the instructions for some functionsBest microwave for controls:LG MH6565CPS NeoChefLGMH6565CPS NeoCheffrom£148.98£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks classy and packs a good grillWhat we don’t loveThe musical alerts are an acquired tasteView image in fullscreen£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonThis feels like a high-end microwave for a mid-market price. The design is sleek, with a full-width door and a control dial that you can push in to sit flush when not in use. Inside the door is a list of all the programmes.The cooking area is impressive, too: the turntable sits on a roller ring with six wheels, rather than the usual three, so it doesn’t wobble. It comes with a circular rack and a crisper tray, too.Why we love itThe look is high-end and performance impressed, too. My mug of water was heated to 72C, and the 14-minute programme for the jacket potato gave decent results. The “healthy fry” setting did a great job of frozen oven chips as well – cooking them to perfection in 15mins 30secs, without the need to turn them midway.It’s a shame that …I couldn’t find a setting to defrost by time, so I had to do it by weight. Nevertheless, it worked well, defrosting more than half my ice in 10 minutes. Also, its alerts are a bit musical, which you’ll either love or loathe.Dimensions:48 x 39 x 27cm (WDH)Power:1,000W (900W grill)Capacity:25lTurntable diameter:29cmOther cooking options:grillLGMH6565CPS NeoCheffrom£148.98£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks classy and packs a good grillWhat we don’t loveThe musical alerts are an acquired tasteFor more, read our guide tothe best air fryersskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox.
