It has a generous capacity and plenty of cooking options, including oven, grill, air fryer and steam. It comes with two circular racks (so you can cook on two levels at once), a crisper tray and a plastic steamer. Unusually, the door opens downwards like an oven.It’s also smart: the SmartThings app lets you view cooking progress, get notifications, and even control the microwave from your phone. You can connect it to voice assistants, too, but I didn’t find this especially useful.It didn’t make the final cut because …cooking performance was so-so. My water heated to only 66C; it was slow to cook a jacket potato, and air-frying chips was a 19-minute programme – slower than most dedicated air fryers and closer to an oven.Dimensions:52 x 52 x 33cm (WDH);power:900W (1,500W grill);capacity:32l;turntable diameter:34cm;other cooking options:grill, oven, air fryer, steamSamsungCombi All-In-One 32L MC32DB7746KCE3from£298.99£349 at AO£298.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLarge capacity and app controlWhat we don’t loveNot the best, nor the fastest, on testCaso MCG 25 Ceramic ChefCasoMCG 25 Ceramic Cheffrom£159£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoWhat we loveIts flatbed design means more cooking capacityWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsView image in fullscreen£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoBest for:a larger flatbedThe flatbed design means this model has more usable space than a microwave with a turntable. For example, I could fit in three poppadoms without any overlapping, which is good for a mid-size microwave. However, they cooked unevenly: I had to flip them over and give them another minute.It did a good job of heating baked beans, but it was slow to cook the jacket potato and the popcorn.It didn’t make the final cut because …I hated the controls. It is a truth universally acknowledged that all microwaves should have a button you can bash for 30-second increments. But this one does 30 seconds, a minute, then goes up in minutes (to a maximum of 10 minutes).Dimensions:49 x 48 x 29cm (WDH);power:900W (1,200W grill, 2,050W oven);capacity:25l;turntable:31 x 32cm (flatbed);other cooking options:grill, ovenCasoMCG 25 Ceramic Cheffrom£159£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoWhat we loveIts flatbed design means more cooking capacityWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsBeko MCF25310BekoMCF25310from£179£179 at Very£179 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat controls and good jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveIt didn’t defrost well enoughView image in fullscreen£179 at Very£179 at AmazonBest for:amid-price combi microwaveThis is a combi: a microwave, grill and oven that can combine cooking styles. However, performance was a mixed bag. It turned out a jacket potato in 6mins 30secs – which, although no replacement for an oven-cooked spud, was better than a microwaved one. It heated my mug of water to 76C, but defrosted less than 20% of my ice.I was a fan of its controls, though: a dial with a button in the middle, plus six clearly labelled buttons.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found it confusing; sometimes it would keep cooking, but the timer didn’t go down. Plus, defrosting yielded disappointing results.Dimensions:48 x 44 x 28cm (WDH);power:900W (1,950W grill, 1,950W oven);capacity:25l;turntable diameter:27cm;other cooking options:grill, ovenBekoMCF25310from£179£179 at Very£179 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat controls and good jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveIt didn’t defrost well enoughRussell Hobbs RHFM2365BRussell HobbsRHFM2365Bfrom£119£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesWhat we lovePowerful microwavingWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesBest for:a flatbed microwave on a budgetDoing away with a turntable means flatbed microwaves can fit in more food. For example, this one is compact but can accommodate a large 30cm dinner plate. On the downside, flatbed microwaves often struggle to cook evenly, and this model was no exception in my tests. I could fit two (and even three at a squeeze) poppadoms at a time, but while they were fully cooked at the centre, the sides were underdone.The microwave was powerful, though, heating my mug of water to an impressive 72C.It didn’t make the final cut because …it looks classy but the controls proved annoying. There’s no button in the middle of the dial and I had to read the manual to look up programmes.Dimensions:47 x 38 x 30cm (WDH);power:800W;capacity:23l;turntable:33 x 31cm (flatbed) ;other cooking options:noneRussell HobbsRHFM2365Bfrom£119£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesWhat we lovePowerful microwavingWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsTower T24041BLKTowerT24041BLKfrom£79.99£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmWhat we loveIt’s cheap and fairly powerfulWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for a big dinner plateView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmBest for:priceAt RRP, this was the cheapest microwave tested – but you get what you pay for. The styling is simple but old-fashioned. Overall, it looks pretty basic.When it comes to performance, while my mug of water was heated to only 64C, more than 60% of the ice was defrosted in just 10 minutes.Capacity is small, though: it could cope with only one poppadom and couldn’t accommodate my 30cm dinner plates. Also, it has eight preset programmes, but they’re not listed conveniently on the appliance itself, so you’ll be reaching for the instructions.It didn’t make the final cut because …I liked it, but I think it’s worth spending a bit more on the Salter.Dimensions:45 x 35 x 26cm (WDH);power:800W;capacity:20l;turntable diameter:26cm;other cooking options:noneTowerT24041BLKfrom£79.99£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmWhat we loveIt’s cheap and fairly powerfulWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for a big dinner plateWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenChoosing the purrfect microwave … think about capacity, cooking modes and available space before you buy.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianWhat microwave capacity is right for me?The room inside a microwave is usually measured in litres, but that’s the total volume, right up to the corners. I’ve included turntable diameter, so you can measure your dinner plates to see if they’ll fit. Some microwaves have a flatbed design, with no turntable. While you can fit more into these models, cooking can be uneven.Do I need a microwave?A microwave is a valuable tool in the kitchen, if you have the worktop space for it. If space is tight, look for one that’s shallow enough that you can make good use of the space in front of it to prepare food.Microwaves are best at heating, reheating and defrosting food with a high water content. They’re great for reheating everything from batch-cooked meals to a forgotten cuppa.Models that feature oven capabilities or air frying are great because they offer valuable extra cooking space, but only if you have the worktop space. It’s like having an extra shelf’s worth of oven – perfect when you’re cooking for lots of people.What microwave wattage do I need?Microwave power is measured in watts – this is a measure of cooking power, rather than electrical draw. The models on test range from 800W to 1,000W. They will all cook your dinner, but the higher-power appliances will do it faster. This shouldn’t use more electricity overall (and, therefore, money and carbon) as they use more per minute but take less time.Other features to look out forLarger microwaves sometimes offer grill, oven and air fryer modes – or all three. I considerair fryersand small convection (fan) ovens to be the same thing: they cook food by circulating hot air, and they’re faster than ovens thanks to their small size.Combi cooking is when one of these styles and microwave cooking are combined for the best of both worlds. For example, you can cook a crispy-skinned jacket potato in less than 20 minutes.Some microwaves also come with a set of plastic dishes for steam cooking. This works well, but do remember that you’ll need to find space in your kitchen to stow any accessories. Some people also prefer to avoid microwaving in plastic where possible.For more:The best toasters for toast, bagels and crumpetsThe best slow cookers for effortless homemade mealsThe best rice cookers for gloriously fluffy grains at homeThe best soup makers for healthy, thrifty mealsCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotmentExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterFoodGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siege | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: The long read: Soon after my first visit to Ukraine four years ago, I began language lessons. It taught me more than I ever expected
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: The long read: Soon after my first visit to Ukraine four years ago, I began language lessons. It taught me more than I ever expected
Content: Illustration: Nataliia Shulga/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nataliia Shulga/The GuardianThe long readUkraine‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siegeSoon after my first visit to Ukraine four years ago, I began language lessons. It taught me more than I ever expectedCharlotte HigginsTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareAlmost as soon as I returned from my first reporting trip toUkraine, in October 2022, I decided to start Ukrainian lessons. Not as an act of solidarity, exactly, but as a marker that I was committed to returning. I wanted to know some Ukrainian in order to feel less helpless, to edge towards a better understanding of what I was reporting, and to be more courteous to those whom I encountered. And I hoped, in time, to be able to pull myself through a piece of poetry in the original.I began meeting Olha, my teacher, by weekly video call later that autumn. She was in Ivano-Frankivsk, her home town in the far west of Ukraine, I was in London. With endless patience and humour, she led me by the hand through the unfamiliar letters of her language, those elegant, sensuous shapes of the Cyrillic alphabet.I have not yet fully internalised them, as I have the Roman alphabet, whose shapes are so much part of me that I don’t see them any more. The unfamiliarity of Cyrillic characters, by contrast, allows me to enjoy the exhilarating ski-slope swoop of the Л (l), the generous expanses of the Ю (yu), and the majestic architecture of the Ж (zh), which spreads out its arms and legs like candelabra. (Enjoy, please, the extravagant double Ж in Запоріжжя – Zaporizhzhia – which has a particularly graceful etymology: it means “beyond the rapids”.) And, though I shrink from trying either to write or decode the curlicued Ukrainian cursive, just forming these letters is a joy for the hand: the twin sweep of a З (z) and the harsh angles of a Д (d), which I like to write as a triangle with a pair of sharp, inward-facing tails dangling from it.Then there is the special category of Cyrillic letters reserved only for the Ukrainian language. You may see, for example, on a Ukrainian necklace or bracelet, or on a T-shirt, the letter Ї – like our letter I, surmounted by a diaeresis. The character, which expresses the sound “yi” – as in Kyiv (Київ) – is absent from the Russian variant of the alphabet, and thus operates as a subtle signifier of allegiance. In occupied Mariupol, in 2022, the letter Ї was seen scrawled in chalk on the ­streets – a single letter as an act of defiance. I enjoy the fact that in the transliteration of my surname, Гіґґінс, there is another Ukrainian-only letter, Ґ, which, from its jaunty upturned serif, one can tell is the rare hard g, most commonly employed for loan words; it was removed from the alphabet in Stalin-era reforms, and formally given back a place in the Ukrainian alphabet after the fall of the Soviet Union and Ukrainian independence in 1991.There is a text artwork that I love, by the sculptor Nathan Coley, installed in a library in Edinburgh, which consists of the sentence: The Basic Material is Not the Word but the Letter. I often think of it when navigating a forest of Cyrillic signs. Thick accumulations of Ukrainian consonants conspire against my tongue and my memory: airless crushes of them, like the compressed folds of a concertina. I cannot tell you how many repetitions it took to memorise незважаючи на (nezvazhayuchy na) – “despite” in Ukrainian. It seemed important to master this phrase. How else could I say, “despite the war”? Emblematic of the many sound collisions in Ukrainian is the magnificent single letter Щ, expressed in English as “shch” – as in “fresh cheese” , as one of my grammar books puts it. After much deliberation, I have only come up with one word in English (with the exception of those we have borrowed, such as borshch) that contains this fricative-affricative alliance: “pushchair”. Four whole letters in English for a single pair of glorious, fat loops in Ukrainian.I had studied classics at university, and recklessly, perhaps arrogantly, felt that I needn’t be defeated by a tricky language. I knew, at least, what I was getting into with Ukrainian nouns, which, like those in Latin and Greek, come in three genders – masculine, feminine and neuter – and are inflected, meaning their endings change depending on what role they perform in a sentence. Even so, I feel that seven case endings, which is one more than Latin, and two more than Greek, is a lot. Their usage is almost baroque in its excess: I have a kind of stunned respect for a language in which some numbers – but by no means all, and for no perceptible reason – demand to be followed by the genitive case. One says п’ятдесят доларів (pyatdesyat dolariv), meaning $50, the genitive case; but п’ятдесят два долари (pyatdesyat dva dolary), $52, using the ordinary nominative. On the other hand, $51 has yet another ending, because the crucial extra dollar bill you have added to your 50 means that it is, according to the Ukrainian language, a singular, however hard you may protest that you are, in fact, clutching a fistful of dollars.View image in fullscreenA billboard shows a stamp issued in Ukraine on the invasion’s first anniversary. It reads ‘FCK PTN!’, set against a Banksy mural on a ruined house in Borodyanka.Photograph: Dominika Zarzycka/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockI had heard rumours of the perils of Ukrainian “verbs of motion”, which turned out to be more than well founded. Speakers of Slavonic languages describe movement at a level of subtlety that, to an anglophone, seems absolutely bewildering. Ukrainian has two basic verbs where we have one to express the idea of “to go” – the first used for travelling on foot and the second for travelling by some form of transport. Both of those, in turn, come in different forms depending on whether you are moving in one direction only, or going there and back again. That is true for other verbs of motion, right down to, say, the verb to crawl. Is your baby moving across the floor in one direction? Or is she planning on taking an indirect route, or perhaps undertaking this journey regularly? Answer these questions before selecting your verb form!Learning Ukrainian, it turned out, was more than a side-interest, an extracurricular activity. It forced me to look at myself in entirely new ways. In my 50s – treading the pleasant plateau of knowing broadly how to do my job after all these years – it was confronting to be back at the bottom rung of knowledge, out of my depth. There would be moments – when Olha was speaking to me, or when I was trying to keep up with what Ukrainian friends were saying, or even during a seemingly predictable encounter in a cafe – when I would feel an unfamiliar, blind panic rising to engulf me. It would start out well, I would be clinging on to comprehension, and then there would be a block, a word or phrase I would snag on, or an unexpected conversational current – and I would lose my grip. I recognised the feeling from only one other area of my life: playing chamber music. When you lose your place in a Beethoven quartet, say, and everyone else is moving onwards at speed, you can feel stranded, as if you are watching the vessel of the music slip into the distance without you. The redeeming fact is that attempting to speak even terrible Ukrainian in Ukraine is met, in my experience, with a response on a scale set between courteous acceptance and ecstatic (and undeserved) gratitude.But my new language was also the language of war. From the very first, the experience was quite unlike that of studying Italian, the only other modern language in which I can claim any kind of proficiency – a language, for the learner, full of the pleasures of ordering cappuccino and gelato, for asking directions to the duomo, and exclaiming over the splendour ofil paese più bello del mondo– the most beautiful country in the world. The very first sentences in Ukrainian that I read – when Olha introduced herself – were coloured by her wistfulness for a life that war had forced her to leave behind: До війни я жила в Києві. Я дуже люблю це місто і хочу знову там жити. “Before the war I lived in Kyiv. I love this city very much and want to live there again.”It would be wrong to suggest that every lesson was filled with darkness. We laughed a lot. Olha often steered us towards a world of red wine and ice-cream, of opera and music and reading. The Ukrainian delight in the consumption of delicious food (a constant pleasure, thanks to the excellence of produce grown in the чорнозем, orchornozem, the fertile black earth) was present in our lessons. Soon I learned the words смачний (smachnyi), tasty, and смачного! (smachnoho!), bon appetit! – lip-smackingly onomatopoeic vocabulary, full of the joy of the Ukrainian table. But the war leaked into every lesson. Indefinite pronouns were explained to me via the example Ніхто не любить Путіна – “No one likes Putin”. The impersonal expressions communicating necessity, треба and потрібно (trebaandpotribno), were illustrated via a speech made on the eve of war by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, then commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces, about the urgent need to be equipped for battle. Треба готуватися до війни – “We must prepare for war.” Нам треба мати ресурси, потрібно 300 танків – “We need to have resources, we need 300 tanks.”View image in fullscreenPeople shelter inside a subway station during an air-raid alert in Kyiv, May 2023.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersMy vocabulary grew to include the words for drone and rocket, explosion, bomb shelter and air-raid alarm. There is a Telegram channel that is commonly consulted when an air-raid alert goes off in Ukraine, as it provides details on whether there are drones on the way, or ballistic missiles, and their direction of travel. For ease I switched this channel to English, using an automatic translate function. With every new siren, it leapt into life, asking, “Why the anxiety?” It took me a while to figure out that the word used for air-raid alarm, тривога (tryvoha) also means “anxiety” in Ukrainian. (The English word “alarm” behaves similarly, being both the mechanism that produces the sound, and the feeling it engenders.) But still, every time I checked it I imagined it was asking me, yet again, a sarcastic question about my state of mind.As Christmas 2022 arrived, Olha and I read a speech of Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s that contained a nice example of the compound future tense formed by an auxiliary verb and the infinitive: Ми будемо співати колядки – голосніше ніж генератор. “We are going to sing carols – louder than a generator.” The noisy chugging of generators side by side on a pavement, servicing a row of shops during a blackout, would become a familiar music to me. In the same speech, the president also provided an introduction to impersonal adverbial constructions suggesting a state or condition. Нам може бути темно, холодно і складно. Але нам більше не страшно. “It may be dark, cold and difficult for us, but we are no longer afraid.” That winter truly was dark. Even in far-western Ivano-­Frankivsk, Olya was affected by Russian attacks on power infrastructure designed to freeze Ukraine into submission. Blackouts meant the cancellation of several lessons.In time a kind of intimacy sprang up between us: there is something vulnerable-making about learning a language, when your normal ease of expression crumbles and you have to start again like a child acquiring speech for the first time, but oh, so much more slowly. You open yourself up to being and sounding foolish as you reach for ways to say what you mean. You build fragile little linguistic structures, and they collapse time and time again. You want to cry like a child with frustration. Olha – younger than me by a good 15 years – reassured me like an encouraging parent.Soon I was speaking excitedly of plans for another reporting trip. Olha’s notes recorded our dialogue. У які міста ти будеш їхати? Я буду їхати у Київ, у Ізюм, у Харків і теж яхочу їхати у Херсон. “What cities are you going to go to?” “I am going to go to Kyiv, Izium and Kharkiv, and I want to go to Kherson, too.” Olha must have asked what my partner thought of all this – an extremely good question. I offered the truthful although carelessly incomplete reply, Мій чоловік розуміє, як це важливо для мене. “My partner understands how important this is to me.”When I returned from that trip – it had been my first time to eastern Ukraine and to territories recently clawed back from Russian occupation – Olha asked for my impressions. I described seeing зруйновані вулиці, мости, будинки – “destroyed streets, bridges, buildings”. Це було дуже стресово для тебе? “Was it very stressful for you?” she asked. Another good question. Було стресово бачити міста зруйновані. “It was stressful to see destroyed towns,” I replied, evasively, perhaps enjoying wrapping my tongue around the word зруйновані –zruynovani, ruined. At that moment I lacked either sufficient insight into my own emotions, or the linguistic skill to explain precisely how stressful this trip had in fact been. It was a world away from any kind of journalism I had done before: the mass grave site; the hours with the grieving parents of a killed son; the sorrow of it all.In Lviv, a couple of months ago, I attended an intensive language programme. I put great hope into this course, as if it were not a series of lessons but rather a magical linguistic wand that would offer me the gift of tongues. When we arrived – the 20-odd students, an eclectic group of mainly Americans, some with Ukrainian roots, some at university, some volunteering for the Ukrainian cause in one way or another – we were given a written test and an interview. On the basis of this, I was placed in what became understood as the “top class”. I spent two weeks in this class, with three excellent female classmates, taught by a gentle and learned teacher, having my sense of myself as a competent person systematically undone. No English was uttered in these classes, as we discussed such subjects as the wartime rifts in Ukrainian society and were tasked with preparing presentations to the assembled staff and student body – something I would shudder to do even in English.View image in fullscreenA customer browsing the shelves in Sens bookshop in Pechersk, Kyiv.Photograph: Emre Çaylak/The GuardianEvery evening, I went home to my flat fighting the urge to weep, convinced that there had been an error and I was simultaneously “holding everyone up” and “letting the side down”. One of the Americans – a level-headed economist who, when she finished her course, was told she held the record for speed of learning – gently pointed out that we had been placed in our classes based on our scores in a test. Perhaps, she offered, my response was gendered? Would many men be flailing around in quite this level of self-doubt? I despairingly messaged a colleague and friend who’d learned Russian as a teenager, who briskly informed me that he had cheated an aptitude test in his youth precisely to be in a confounding top class; that he had observed at work that I was a very competitive person; and that I should sit back and enjoy the sensation of not being the best at something.I had not expected to be recalibrating my relationship with myself, or to be confronting the gap between my own and others’ perceptions of myself, in this way. There were other moments of inner tumult, too – the day we discussedVictoria Amelinain class: a Ukrainian novelist who had become a friend, and who died of her injuries after a Russian cruise missile targeted a pizza restaurant she had just sat down in. Or the morning we were asked to read out our favourite Ukrainian poem. I chose a very recent work: My Day, by poet and film-maker Iryna Tsilyk. It anatomises the peculiar state of being that engulfs people living behind the lines, where incompatible experiences (sheltering in the corridor from an air raid, making pancakes for your son’s breakfast, attending a funeral, dithering over whether to buy zinfandel or pinot noir in a supermarket aisle) are crammed together in bizarre and uncomfortable proximity. I read it aloud, as directed, fairly competently until the line “I cried in the park” (Плакала в парку –plakala v parku), at which point I felt a surging desire to cry myself. Natalya, our teacher, gently took over the reading. It wasn’t just me feeling overwhelmed at times. You don’t turn up in wartime Ukraine for an intensive language course just for the hell of it.I try not to envy the young. There are many reasons not to. But I did come to envy brains that could more readily absorb, memorise and parrot languages than mine. Ukrainian vocabulary is, to me, truly difficult to remember. It is an Indo-European language, which helps up to a point – it shares deep roots with English, such that some basic words are familiar (such as мати, сестра,maty,sestra– mother, sister). But it is a much more distant relation than, say, German, or the Romance languages. In Italian, for example, the verb “to use” isusare. Fine, done. In Ukrainian, the verb “to use” is використовувати,vykorystovuvaty. No apparent connection to English, an absolute pain to memorise,sevensyllables.And yet, while ordinary, everyday words such as the verb “to use” seemed almost unconquerable, somehow I found it easy to memorise words and phrases in two distinct categories: pointlessly poetic, or plain rude. For my own satisfaction, for example, I made an English translation of Tsilyk’s My Day. It contains a line about the sound of distant rockets; the noise is described as шелест (shelest), a word that describes the whisper of leaves in the wind. I spent ages puzzling over how to translate the word in the context of her poem, since, though I could see that a very distant rocket might make a kind of shivering sound like a wind-shaken tree, the English word “rustling” felt wrong, and I couldn’t imagine rockets doing it (I settled on “eerie thrum” in the end, although I’m not entirely satisfied with it). Of course, that left me with a perfect recall of the Ukrainian word for “rustling” – but what good was this piece of knowledge, when I couldn’t even remember the verb “to use”? My friend Mariana cheerfully informed me that the word, in verb form, appeared in an older famous poem, by Pavlo Tychyna, dating from 1911: Ви знаєте, як липа шелестить / У місячні весняні ночі? (“You know how the linden rustles / On moonlit nights in spring?”). I memorised it with ease. I suppose it might come in handy sometime, if I’m ever passing a lime tree with a Ukrainian on a breezy May evening.In 2025, Ivisited the Kharkiv studioof the artist Pavlo Makov. He was finishing a work – a large, bright drawing in pastels – of a very battered-looking, ordinary plant. A weed, many people would say, but it is not a weed: it is a humble and in its way rather handsome plant, which also grows in Britain and the US, with oval leaves and modest flowers on little spikes, often seen on verges and in the cracks in the pavement. I confess I did not know the English word for it, until I sent a photo to my brother, a botanist: it is the common plantain. (Not to be confused with the fruit, a different species altogether.) In Ukrainian, Makov told me, it is called подорожник,podorozhnyk– because it lives along (по,po) the road (дорога,doroha). The drawing was, he told me, a kind of portrait of himself and other Ukrainians, who – battered but alive, ragged but tough – are metaphorically living by the road, just a rocket or drone strike away from losing a home and being displaced. Подорожник is also known as a healing plant in Ukraine – you pick a leaf and press it against a scratch or a sting. Now, every time I see this inconspicuous little plant in England – something I couldn’t name in my own language before I could in Ukrainian – I am tugged back to Kharkiv, my mind filled with thoughts of lives full of instability, but pursued with a kind of rooting toughness.View image in fullscreenArtist Pavlo Makov at his studio in Kharkiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAs for the bad words – yes, I can swear like a Mykolaiv dockworker, and have a repertoire of disreputable phrases, many of them learned on long car journeys on reporting trips. On one occasion, I was in the car with two much younger female colleagues. We were looking at some photos. I regret to inform you of the occasional low level of chat among us, but one of these photos was of a good-looking young man, with a hipster moustache. Finding a boyfriend, for many of my female Ukrainian friends, presents certain difficulties: men are absent, at the front, on the whole. But I’m always keeping half an eye open for them. Just in case. As we appraised this particular image, one of us giggled and uttered the phrase усики – пропуск в трусики (usyky –propusk v trusyky) which I suppose, loosely translated, means, “a ’tache is a pass to your panties”. Utterly memorable, nicely rhyming in Ukrainian, it stuck at once. Not entirely useless, either, if you decouple the vocabulary from the particular phrase: пропуск,propusk, could be your pass for a festival or workplace, or the gap left on a form for you to fill in your information. Tрусики,trusyky, is a perfectly respectable word for underwear. As a phrase used in its entirety (judiciously, of course, in the right company), it causes Ukrainian men to finger their upper lips nervously and Ukrainian women to erupt in laughter.Even when I was not working on Ukrainian stories, and was immersed in writing about culture in the UK or the US, that act of plugging away, however slowly, at Ukrainian kept a thread of connection with the country, and with my friends there. Though, at times, it would have been easier to forget about Ukraine, because the memories could be so painful: the rescue workers gently easing a corpse from the ruins of the smashed Kyiv apartment building; the crumpling face of the mother who had lost her son; the young artist with the radiant eyes who was haunted by guilt after a brother soldier had been killed beside him. Through all of this, it was impossible to forget that, though I wasn’t learning Ukrainian to make any kind of political point, the Ukrainian language itself was deeply concerned with the war.The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, repeatedly claimed that the invasion, or special military operation as he initially called it, had been mounted in order to rescue Russian speakers in Ukraine from a repressive state. This seemed especially ironic given that the Russian military bombed and killed thousands of civilians in, for example, Mariupol, a largely russophone city. In the wake of the invasion, and Putin’s propaganda, many Ukrainians have switched away from the Russian language (including the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy). New Ukrainian-language bookshops have blossomed, despite the war, on the streets of Kyiv and other cities. “People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Bohdana Laiuk, an editor and cultural manager, now Ukraine’s deputy minister for culture, told me. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.” Since the Maidan protests of 2013-14, and especially since 2022, embracing the Ukrainian language has, for many, been an active, personal act of decolonisation.But the politics of language are also a matter for passionate debate. “If you are ever short of conversation at a Ukrainian party,” joked Olha once, “just ask about language.” I remember witnessing an argument between two friends. One, much more positive about Russian-speaking Ukrainians, was an academic based in western Ukraine. The other was a Ukrainian-speaker from the Kharkiv region, who remembered being bullied as a child for speaking his own language in the big Russified city, and who argued that the Ukrainian language should be protected by strong legal frameworks.View image in fullscreenBreaktime at a Ukrainian language evening class in Kharkiv, April 2023.Photograph: Ed Ram/The GuardianArtist Pavlo Makov, who was born in 1958, took a different view again. Although he was born into a Russian family, his father insisted he should be able to speak Ukrainian. So he grew up bilingual, loving Ukrainian-language children’s books and comics. “Being a citizen of Ukraine means much more to me than the fact that I am ethnically Russian,” he said. But “we should maintain our knowledge of Russian”, he argued: Ukrainians needed to understand the country across its eastern border. For him, it was a complex and personal matter. “Russian is the language of the enemy, yes – but it was also the language of my mum.”I talked to friends who had stopped using the Russian language. It takes years to set aside the language of your mum. Even if you speak your chosen language perfectly, you might think in the old language, or dream in the old language, and when that is all past, there are still things that may persist in the old language – memories of the books you read when you were little, for example. One of my friends, writer and cultural manager Sasha Dovzhyk, wrote a remarkable essay about her rejection of Russian. “My mother tongue tastes like ashes,” she wrote. “I felt the taste of my mother tongue most acutely while driving through Borodianka, Bucha and Irpin two months after these Ukrainian towns in the Kyiv region were liberated by the Ukrainian army from the Russians’ ‘brotherly’ embrace.” Her rage and horror turned inwards, into her own body, into the very words she had first formed as a baby on her mother’s lap. “Russian,” she wrote, “is my mother tongue and liberation means ripping it out of my throat.”You think about time a lot when you are learning a language. How much time do I have to devote to this pursuit? How much time will it take me to get where I want to be, linguistically? The curious thing was that the horizon of desire kept receding into the distance, and likewise, the time it might take me to get there also moved into the barely perceptible future. When I first started Ukrainian, I wanted only to be able to read road signs, exchange pleasantries and order coffee, but soon my desires stretched – from booking a pedicure on the phone, say, to understanding my friends so that they didn’t always feel the need to switch to English. At the same time, I had to keep revising my short-term expectations downwards, making peace with the fact that, after four years, I was still only OK at Ukrainian, and often stumbled over basics.Ukraine’s death-defying art rescuersRead moreOne day, early in 2026, I went to a gallery in London showing a work called Repeat After Me, by the Ukrainian artists’ collective Open Group. I had first seen this work in 2024 in Lviv, then later that year at the Venice Biennale. The work is a video installation, with screens on which Ukrainian refugees imitate the sounds of war, and then invite visitors to “repeat after me”, karaoke-style. On one screen, Svitlana, from the Luhansk region, re-created the sound of a Ka-52 Alligator – a Russian attack helicopter designed to take out tanks and infrastructure. Antonina came next, singing the mournful, gut-clenching wail of the air-raid siren. Iryna imitated a T-80 tank, while Boris, from Mariupol, mimicked the keeeeen-thunksound of aerial bombing. “Repeat after me,” he said, “so you’ll remember.”This was also the language of war, a new unwritten dialect of violence that Ukrainians had learned and absorbed not out of choice, but because they needed to – so you could hear the direction the Shahed drone was moving in, or differentiate between the outgoing crump of air defence and the sharp blast of incoming explosions. At the gallery opening I chatted with one of the artists, Anton Varga, who complimented me on my Ukrainian – so much improved, he said, since the last time he’d heard it. I thanked him. But it was not because of my diligence, I realised. It was just that time had passed. Even a lazy student – or to be kinder to myself, a time-poor student – will get somewhere after four years. My progress, I understood, was just a clock – a clock that marked the painful pace of war.This is an adapted extract fromUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, published on20 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOnWednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. WithOlia Hercules,Sasha Dovzhyk,Olesya KhromeychukandShaun Walker. Book ticketshere

title: We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zone | Rebecca Solnit | The Guardian
description: Summer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joys
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Summer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joys
Content: ‘Summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianOpinionClimate crisisWe launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zoneRebecca SolnitSummer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joysTue 4 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTShareFar beyond the fires raging acrossEuropeand North America, the smoke, dangerous to breathe, hangs in the air, dimming the view, changing the very color of sunlight into something grimly unsettling.An estimated 20,000 are said to have died in the extreme heat in Europe earlier this year, and heat is climate change’s quiet killer, compared with the dramatic violence of death by fire or flood. In eastern Washington, 600 homes have just burned down, and in both Europe and North America, firefighters have died in the effort to contain the climate-fueled firestorms.Once, across much of the the world’s temperate zones, we looked forward to summer as a time of delights, from summer’s bounty of fruits, long days, warmth, school holidays, activities like camping and swimming, travel and adventure. Now many of us dread it.Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder | Bill McGuireRead moreSummer was the sweet season celebrated in poetry and song, often pictured as a gentle goddess; now it is too often a threat and a misery. All this makes me think of Bill McKibben’s 2011 book Eaarth, a proposal that we can understand climate change as equivalent to moving to a more perilous, unwelcoming planet than the gentle, stable one we evolved over the 12,000 years since the last ice age.I know that there are parts of the world where summer was already harsh, intense – 20 years ago, my friend Mark Klett, a photographer living near Phoenix, Arizona, joked: “Phoenix has two seasons: summer and hell,” summer being January and February; hell being the rest of the year.But even in Phoenix, summer is now more intense; there, people get severe burns from falling down on superheated asphalt. It’s changed everywhere.I’ve driven toNew Mexicoalmost every summer since 1989. A few years ago, I found that I feared heat for the first time: the temperature in Needles, a California desert town on the Colorado River near the Arizona border, was going to be 116F (46.6C). I didn’t know if my car could survive temperatures like that, and I feared what survival would look like for me if the air-conditioned car broke down on the highway. (I managed it by staying on the edge of the Mojave Desert the night before and darting across the low desert to Flagstaff, which at 7,000ft elevation stays cooler, and pressing on to New Mexico the next day.)I’m in New Mexico now, as I write, enjoying the beauties of its incomparable skies and summer thunderstorms, but 37 summers since I started coming, summer is not what it used to be. It’s hotter.The monsoon rains are less reliable and often more violent when they come; one New Mexico town,Ruidoso,has over the past few years been beaten up repeatedly by flood and fire. Like so many westerners, I have too often breathed in the toxic smoke of burning forests, have followed the news of forests and towns being consumed by flames, have friends whose homes have been reduced to ash and rubble, have seen brick chimneys standing above the blackened ruins of a neighborhood.As I hear about summer tourists sweltering miserably from Japan to Spain, I wonder if, going forward, travelers will shift peak vacation times to spring and fall, if schools will change when students have their holidays.Keeping them indoors in air-conditioned spaces may be even a safety measure for those who lack such protection at home. Summer has too often, in too many places, become something to brace against, prepare for, and dread: the season of danger, heat, fire, misery. The New Yorkerreports: “ A conflagration west of Bordeaux, described as four times the size of Paris, prompted the largest peacetime evacuation in the country’s history: 220,000 people.”I study the boreal forest. This summer wildfires came for my home | Julee BoanRead moreIt’s as if we launched a war against nature, and that has turned place after place into something that resembles a war zone. The climate movement is a peace movement, a movement to end this war and its casualties.We often talk about what climate change has wrecked in terms of what’s material, tangible, structures lost to fire, flood, or sea level rise, trees dying, species threatened, glaciers melting in warmer weather. But summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.There have been youth-led lawsuits against the producers of climate chaos and the governments who’ve refused to act adequately – essentially for robbing them of their future. Robbing us all of the immeasurable joys of summer as it was is part of that theft. It’s not the main reason that climate action matters so much, but it’s a reminder that what we’re losing is not only the terms of our survival and our safety, but our freedom and pleasure.Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. Her newest book is The Beginning Comes After the End: Notes on a World of ChangeExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionNew MexicoEuropeExtreme weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to Burnham | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Meg O’Neill is overseeing rapid clearing of the decks at BP after strategic muddle of recent years, with ‘message’ for new PM
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Meg O’Neill is overseeing rapid clearing of the decks at BP after strategic muddle of recent years, with ‘message’ for new PM
Content: BP’s Eastern Trough Area Project oil platform about 100 miles east of Aberdeen. BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenBP’s Eastern Trough Area Project oil platform about 100 miles east of Aberdeen. BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale.Photograph: ReutersNils Pratley on financeBPBP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to BurnhamNils PratleyMeg O’Neill is overseeing rapid clearing of the decks at BP after strategic muddle of recent years, with ‘message’ for new PMBP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gasRevealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisisTue 4 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.44 EDTShareBP will ignore “sentiment” and “history” in pruning its portfolio of assets,says its new-ish boss, Meg O’Neill. She demonstrated as much last week when putting the company’s 60-year-old North Sea oil and gas businessup for sale, explaining on Tuesday that “it just doesn’t compete” in the internal battle for capital.Now comes a disposal that sends an equally unsentimental message about priorities. The US biogas business, Archaea, which was a prized acquisition in the brief green-tinged era of Bernard Looney, is on the block less than four years afterBPbought it for $4bn (£2.98bn).Back in 2022, Looney, O’Neill’s predecessor-but-one,cooed over Archaea, which taps methane from landfill sites. It was “a fantastic fast-growing business” that would add “distinctive value” and “support our net zero ambition”. One hefty write-down later, the operation is judged surplus to requirements because it’s too capital-hungry for a group in debt-reduction mode.The clearing of the decks at BP is happening quickly after the strategic muddle of recent years. A sale of the solar power unit Lightsource is close but, as with the North Sea assets, it’s not just the green assets that are a target. A major refinery in Gelsenkirchen in Germany has gone. So, too, the Austrian fuel stations. And the sale of the lubricants business Castrol was under way before O’Neill arrived. By the end of the year, reckons BP, it will have reached its target to get net debt below $18bn, 12 months ahead of schedule.The process will have been massively assisted, of course, by theboom in profits and cashflowthat followed the surge in oil and gas profits with the Iran war. BP’s profitsmore than doubledto $5.73bn in the three months to the end of June.Cue understandable outrage among campaign groups but zero surprise on the part of City analysts. BP sold its oil at an average of $94 a barrel in the second quarter, up from $67 in the first, enjoying only a slightly smaller increase in the price of natural gas. Profits were obviously going to be enormous,just as they have been at other oil majors. That is doubly so when constraints in the global flow of oil meant refining the stuff – where BP is also big – became a licence to print money in the period.View image in fullscreenMeg O’Neill said BP would ignore ‘sentiment’ and ‘history’ in pruning its portfolio of assets.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/PAFor O’Neill, the next question from investors will be when she is going to rejoin other majors and restart share buy-backs, which werecancelled in Februarywhen the strain on the balance sheet was more acute than it is now. She dodged the question on Tuesday – but shareholders will expect an answer from a straight-talking chief executive soon-ish.Still, she was clear in the advice she had given to Andy Burnham if the new prime minister wished,as he says he does, to take a “pragmatic” approach to the North Sea.“The message I left him with was: the UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas,” O’Neill said. “The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat is the case for more (or just more stable) domestic volumes, even as the UK keeps decarbonising: you do it to minimise imports, particularly of liquefied natural gaswith its higher associated emissions. The UK’s net import dependencywas 43.5% in 2025.There’s no chance of O’Neill reversing BP’s exit from the North Sea, it seems, but the other implied message in her comments about the competitiveness of the basin wasn’t hard to grasp. If Burnham wants to boost domestic supplies, it won’t be enough just to approveAdura’s Jackdaw and Rosebank fieldsfor production. There will also have to be a rethink onthe energy profits levy, AKA the windfall tax that dates from 2022, to incentivise investment.Politically speaking, it is tricky to lower the level at which windfall rates apply at a moment when the Iran war has created a fresh corporate profits bonanza globally. Burnham has said he was“looking at” the levy. It is one of the unavoidable big choices forOctober’s budget.Explore more on these topicsBPNils Pratley on financeOil and gas companiesEnergy industryOilFossil fuelscommentShareReuse this content

title: What if older people refuse help outside the family? This is the taboo that could wreck care reform | Emily Kenway | The Guardian
description: Many fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on board, says Emily Kenway, a social policy doctoral researcher
Author: Emily Kenway
Headline: Many fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on board, says Emily Kenway, a social policy doctoral researcher
Content: ‘People’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change.’Photograph: Phanie/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘People’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change.’Photograph: Phanie/AlamyOpinionCarersWhat if older people refuse help outside the family? This is the taboo that could wreck care reformEmily KenwayMany fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on boardEmily Kenway is the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve ItTue 4 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTShareLisa*has used her local glazier so many times that he gives her a discount. For months, when care workers arrived at her mum’s home, they would find the front door locked and the elderly woman – who has dementia – resolute in her determination to bar their entry. Often, the only solution was to break the glass in the front door. When I met Lisa, who was a participant in aresearch projectI ran, her mother had finally accepted help, but it had taken years of frustration and smashed glass. Unlike Lisa, Lily* never got to acceptance. After two years spent trying to persuade her elderly father to accept social care, she lied. He thinks the people who visit twice a day are nurses, legally required to dispense his dementia medication.Experiences like these are common among people caring for ageing parents. They present an uncomfortable challenge for those who, like our new prime minister, Andy Burnham, wish tofix our care system. Many people are like Lisa and Lily: they are providing eldercare notbecause of the lack of social care, but because their ageing relatives will not accept external help, or at least not without a years-long fight.Numerousstudies have shownthat people with dementia are prone to refuse medical and wider forms of care. More broadly, we know that people’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change: what your loved one thinks they’ll want in the future isn’t necessarily what they’ll accept when that future comes. There is a lag between ageing parents developing care needs and accepting external forms of help, and it’s in that lag that family members step in. There isn’t enough formal evidence of this problem – too few studies askwhypeople receive the type of care they do, rather than assume it’s due to absent alternatives. But in one of the few studies to pose this question, published in theJournal of Nursing Managementin 2007, “frail older people” attributed their reluctance to their fear of losing independence, and the humiliation and embarrassment they felt at the idea of being deemed needy.It is an understandable fear. In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence. You only need to look around at the paltry nods to accessibility in our public spaces or thedegrading assessmentsof people seeking to claim disability benefits. For people who have lived their lives independently and able-bodied, the slip into dependency can be hard to accept. This is why Lily’s father finds nurses more tolerable than care workers: he doesn’t want to needcare,butmedicine– with its connotations of formalisation and expertise – is more acceptable. My mother was the same; after a lifetime being able-bodied, cancer took her mobility. But the notion of a rota of workers trooping into her home was unconscionable; they would be a physical affirmation of her frailty. Nobody wants to need care, so why are we assuming everyone will take it up?There are more granular reasons for refusal too. In the same research in which I worked with Lisa and Lily, Malik*, a British Muslim, explained why his family would not use external care: “It’s a cultural thing, it’s also a religious thing … responsibility for the parents just lives within the family.” Numerous reports have shown that Black and minority ethnic people areless likely to useformal services – this appears to be partly because of community norms that locate responsibility for care within the family, and also because services may lack culturally appropriate options. And lest we forget, the state is not considered a friend by all: past experiences of discrimination may reduce the uptake of services.Last year, I raised this issue at an event packed with thinktankers and policy advisers working to fix our care system. In response, an attender asked, “What’s the risk of saying this?” She meant that talking about refusal of social care risks undermining the political case for its improvement. We may inadvertently strengthen rightwing arguments that care is a familial concern (by which they mean female family members should do it all for free), rather than something to be funded by government. In contrast, the political left locates care as a state responsibility, transferring it into the paid labour market (albeit still usually performed by women, for almost-free).My heart sank as the people around her concurred – the prevailing feeling in the room was that good progressives should not talk about this problem in case we undermine long-fought campaigns to make social care a political priority. And, of course, many thousands of peopleareabsolutely desperate for adult social care – according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services,at least 400,000 peopleare on waiting lists in England alone. But I saw in my mind the innumerable family carers I have met like Lisa, Lily and Malik. I saw the carers’ groups in which people have talked of their loved ones’ refusals. What does it mean if we allow political discomfort to get in the way of truth? And the truth of eldercare is that ageing parents will often refuse support even when they need it, at least for a while.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOur culture fears getting older. But there is a different way to think about the passing of time | Kelley SwainRead moreThere is some evidence that improving social care is actually part of the solution to its refusal: a studyexamining preferencesin countries in the OECD found that “older adults in countries with greater national expenditure on old age support … showed a stronger preference for formal care”. Nobody wants to deal with bad service, and social care is no different. This bodes well, but alone it will not be enough. We need to undo people’s view of dependency as a source of shame. This requires a culture shift. I don’t know how we achieve it, but centring the principles of the disability justice movement is a good place to start. This movement has worked indefatigably to show that people are worthy beyond their productivity, and that interdependence is a fundamental of existence rather than a personal failing. Too few of us have imbibed this wisdom, and the consequences are being played out in households everywhere; we must change that for future generations.Culture change takes time, time in which thousands of people like Lisa will continue to struggle with their ageing relatives’ refusals of support. Any realistic package of reforms must acknowledge this situation, providing improved rights and resources for family carers alongside reforms to social care. Time will tell if the government will face this reality, or whether some things remain too inconvenient to acknowledge.Emily Kenway is a social policy doctoral researcher at the University of Edinburgh and the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve It*All names have been changedExplore more on these topicsCarersOpinionCare workersSocial careAgeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia Tait | The Guardian
description: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Author: Amelia Tait
Headline: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onWeddingsThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your weddingAmelia TaitSure, it’s about jealousy, infidelity and paranoia, but the Killers’ biggest hit is a dancefloor banger: any marriage that starts without it is guaranteed to end in divorceTue 4 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareI’ve been to two weddings where the bride and groom refused to play theKillers’ pop-rock hit Mr Brightside, and both ended in divorce. Well, not yet or anything – but I’m sure it’s coming. How happy can a couple really be if they’re not willing to play the biggest banger to ever bang moments after their hearts have been bound together as one? There are some things that should never be missing from a wedding unless you outright detest your guests. Canapes, yes. Cake, sure. And the opportunity to scream, “Comin’ out of my cage and I’ve been doin’ just fine” next to someone’s Auntie Debs? Undoubtedly.Why should a song about jealousy, paranoia and infidelity pump through the speakers on your special day? Because everyone knows it. Mr Brightside is thethird most sold and streamedsong in the UK, and it’s the longest-charting single in this country’s history, even though the Killers are (somehow) American. Unlike much else these days, the track transcends borders. In 2025, YouGov asked more than 1,000 Americans which songs they knew all the words to, and Mr Brightside came in15th place. The songs above it included The Star-Spangled Banner, Happy Birthday and Jingle Bells.Four years ago, my husband and I fought over our wedding playlist because he (I possibly unfairly believed) wanted to look cool and cultured, and I wanted to serve up a cheeseboard of belter after belter. In the end, our elderly Sicilian DJ forged his own path, playing The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air theme tune twice in quick succession, to my husband’s consternation and my utter delight. Was that DJ simply confused by our shared language barrier?No. He knew something, I think, that so many couples refuse to accept: your wedding playlist is not about you. Your wedding day is, sure. The dress, the venue, the food, the poems – they can all be a careful curation of your tastes. But the playlist belongs to the people. And the people demand to dance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Killers’ Mr Brightside becomes biggest song to never reach UK No 1Read moreDancing Queen. Come On Eileen. Jolene. Many failsafe wedding staples unite the generations by ending in an emotive “een”. But another way to be sure a song will set fire to the dancefloor is to ask yourself a very simple question: can my guests do a series of impassioned hand gestures as they scream-sing? Mr Brightside encourages listeners to not only touch their chests, but also take a drag of a phantom cigarette. The song allows us to bring a little finger-and-thumb-shaped phone to our earstwice– once to call an imaginary cab and once to answer the phone to destiny.This, in the end, is all that most of us come to a wedding to do. And as the track comes to a close, we can heed its final call to open up our eager eyes. Because in that moment, we’re all Mr Brightside.Amelia Tait is a freelance features writer and the author of Lily Tripp: Diary of an Accidental Time TravellerExplore more on these topicsWeddingsThe hill I will die onThe KillersPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left  | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Migrants being escorted in Ceuta, Spain, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenMigrants being escorted in Ceuta, Spain, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersOpinionMigrationCeuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the leftJonathan LiewIt was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment tooTue 4 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.07 EDTShareThe live streams are still running, training their cameras on the beach at Ceuta, where nothing is happening. The self-styled citizen journalists are still pounding the streets, capturing their shaky smartphone footage.Zia Yusufof Reform UK was out there at the weekend, wearing a crisp white shirt and smart tailored trousers, lest anyone confuse him with the other brown people there. The bad brown people.Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world? How did it manage to pique the interest ofDonald Trump and Elon Musk, to feature on NBC’s Nightly News, not – shall we say – a programme massively predisposed to spotlighting news stories from continental Africa? What about it so exercised Europe’s heads of government? What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph?Certainly not any kind of urgent or imminent threat to our own borders, much less the borders of the United States. The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla operate under special exemptions from the Schengen area, rendering it almost impossible for an undocumented migrant to reach mainlandSpain, about 12 miles away across the Mediterranean. Once many of the migrants realised this, they duly left.Nor any kind of humanitarian concern for those who drowned or were killed in the crowd crush. “About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day. Still, the sudden influx created a crisis for Spain’s pro-immigration government. Nearly three dozen died.” So read aNew York Times subheadingon Friday. And once you fight your way past the tortured syntax, did you notice anything unusual there? First the integrity of the border, then the political ramifications, then the people who died: the hierarchy of rightwing immigration discourse expressed in three perfect sentences. The death toll has since risen toeither 72 or 88– authorities disagree on the number – and nobody seems over-fussed either way.Rather, Ceuta functions as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies. If the historian Mike Davis once described the US-Mexico border wall as“a political stage set”, then in the age of the deepfake and the troll-farm, Ceuta has proved a similarly fertile source of content: the border interface reimagined as digital theatre, mass migration as primetime television.View image in fullscreenMigrants who entered the Spanish enclave by swimming or on foot from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Reduan/EPAThe rich irony here is that from a securitisation standpoint, Ceuta functions almost exactly as it was intended. A six metre-high barbed-wire fence, reinforced by watchtowers and a network of video cameras, separates it fromMorocco. From Ceuta, an internal checkpoint guards the only ferry route to mainland Spain. The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management.None of which seemed to matter in the slightest as European leaders queued up to give the Pedro Sánchez government a ritual horse-whipping. Italyreintroduced air and sea border controlswith Spain. Emmanuel Macrondeployed mobile unitsto the Spanish border to strengthen controls. Giorgia Meloni – backed by Finland, Denmark and Czechia – has argued that Spain’s membership of the Schengen areashould be suspended.And of course these are primarily domestic politicians catering to a domestic market, ahead of an electoral cycle in which incumbents in France, Italy and Poland are being outflanked by nativist insurgents to their right. Sánchez himself faces the ballot box in 2027, an election in which his government can boast strong economic growth and which his rightwing opponents will therefore be desperate to turn into a referendum on immigration.So that’s the political angle. But really the spectacle of Ceuta represents a more primal and guttural need, particularly in the English-speaking world, for the inflammatory anti-immigration crusade to beseenas well as spoken. The photos and footage coming out of the enclave in recent days, all shot from distance and almost never in closeup, are all geared towards a single end: to encourage the viewer to see these brown bodies as a single mass, each indistinguishable from the other, the accountants and surgeons from the bomb-makers and rapists, the living from the dead.And so, by small degrees, the line between nationalism and pure-blood white supremacy blurs a little more. Indeed, the very idea that a single border crossing 1,000 miles and two seas away from us is somehow our urgent problem, only really makes sense in a worldview whose real distinction is not between “Britain” and “abroad” but between an imagined white ChristianEuropeand a savage brown other.For all this, the right does not act alone. The palpable relief on many parts of the left as most of the original 60,000 migrants returned to Morocco spoke of a worrying acquiescence: a tacit acceptance of the dangerous trope of migration as a prima facie problem. Here’s a radical thought: what if migration is only a problem to those who want it to be? What if we started seeing the mass movement of people less as an existential threat and more as a simple inevitability of human existence? Nine years ago the great Gary Younge set out in the Guardiana utopian vision of open bordersand no immigration controls. What happened to that sense of vision and idealism? When did border discourse, the conversation on why and how we move, become something to be feared and not embraced?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen saysRead moreWhether Ceuta was an accidental security lapse or a deliberately engineered event is actually beside the point. The point is that as the global right grows in confidence, as the migration industrial complex thirsts for new content, new border porn, there will be more Ceutas in the future. People will keep migrating and die trying, and because this is good telly it will keep happening. “Today more than ever,” writes the sociologist Mimi Sheller in her bookMobility Justice, “these borderlands are soaked in the blood of white nationalism, ethnic profiling, and enforced death in the no man’s land.”The endgame here is massacres, vigilante violence, not “stop the boats” but shoot the boats, the border reimagined as a computer-game war zone. The endgame is what the likes of Musk and his far-right meat puppets are already depicting: a world where zombie armies of “military-age males” invade our virgin turf, and the problem is not the forces that drove them from their homes, but your“suicidal empathy”, because these are not equal humans deserving equal treatment. These are the stakes. And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
