title: After five brutal years of Taliban rule, Afghan women and girls need our help – and I have a plan | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: Even in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help them, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: Even in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help them, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Schoolgirls read the Qur’an inside a traditional classroom in Salihan, Kandahar, 8 July 2026.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSchoolgirls read the Qur’an inside a traditional classroom in Salihan, Kandahar, 8 July 2026.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAfghanistanAfter five brutal years of Taliban rule, Afghan women and girls need our help – and I have a planGordon BrownEven in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help themTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTShareNext weekmarks the fifth anniversary of the takeover of Afghanistan by the Taliban asUS coalition troops were evacuatedfrom the country. That’s five years for the terrorists to have consolidated their grip, so now is a good time to reflect on what the “coalition of the willing” left behind.Through vindictive edict after edict, these five years have broughtan ever-escalating repression of Afghan girls and women– with far too little done by any outside authority to speak up or stand up against the most egregious denial of girls’ rights in the world today.Barely reported was the shocking massacre in June by troops whofired on a group of women’s rights protestersas they demonstrated against girls’ exclusion from education and the enforcement of strict dress codes. They were marching under the banner “Azadi”, meaning “freedom”. Two people, including a young boy,were shot deadand several were injured.In the most medieval of ways, the Taliban are also imposing even harsher lawsto legitimise child marriageand provide legal exemption for domestic violence perpetrated by husbands, including against school-age girls.‘When she turns eight they will take her’: rising number of Afghan girls being sold into child marriageRead moreAccording to UN observers, these girls, often sold into marriage or forced to become child brides, are victims of a new form of crime:gender apartheid. Historians will look back and ask why it is that, after landing more than 1 million coalition troops, suffering more than3,500 deaths and 23,000 injuriesand spendingin excess of $1tn, we have been unable to prevent the Taliban destroying the most basic of rights. But perhaps more important, and with the Taliban entrenched in Kabul and religious leaders regularly sending out instructions from Kandahar, the question for now is: what can we do immediately to improve the lives of girls and women?Can we help them fulfil their potential? Globally, the proportion of women aged 20-24 who were married before 18 hasdeclined over the past decade, and Unicef suggestsat least 25m child marriagesthat could have involved school-age brides have been prevented. Yet an estimated12 million girlsunder 18 are still married off each year when they could be at school.The issue is acute in the Afghanistan the coalition left behind, where girls are banned from secondary schooling and Afghan women are bannedfrom university, public sector employment and even workwith NGOsand charities. They are forbidden to travel or to enter many public places, from parks to restaurants, unless accompanied. And with the Taliban confident that they can act with impunity, a dozen recent anti-girl, anti-women injunctions are tightening their grip. In one recent case, a 15-year-old Afghan girl isreported to have been killed, along with her mother, by a Taliban official after he tried to abduct her for a forced marriage.It is appalling, and it does speak to the particular brutality of the Taliban. Pakistan’s Sindh province, by contrast,has enactedone of the strongest legal frameworks in the developing world against child marriage, criminalising marriage under 18 and introducing penalties for those who facilitate it.Bangladesh, too,has enacted new laws. A stronger birth registration system has made it harder to conceal a girl’s age, closing off a common pathway into early marriage. At the same time, programmes providing small-scale financial support to poor families have enabled girls to remain in education. Save the Children reports that inone programme in Bangladesh, the offer of financial support helped more than 1,000 girls stay in school and avoid early marriage. Child marriage is not simply a cultural practice, as often portrayed. It is also driven by poverty, as much as weak enforcement of the law.View image in fullscreenGirls studying in a secret school at an undisclosed location in Afghanistan.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesThere are “child marriage-free zones” in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, where young people come together to support any school friend who is being married off against her will. Young people become known as“wedding busters”because of their willingness to intervene. With assistance and will, so much is possible.It is no accident that the Taliban have focused so much attention not just on denying women rights but specifically on denying them an education, because they know, as we do, that schooling is the most potent enabler. Across the world, it is the single most powerful protection against early marriage. Organisations such asGirls Not Brideshave established that every additional year a girl spends in secondary education significantly reduces the likelihood that she will be married as a child.If we could open the doors to quality schooling, ensure girls had access to safe spaces and provide financial support for their families, tens of thousands more could get that education. Even in Afghanistan, that is no pipe dream. Through Unicef andEducation Cannot Wait, and with secret, on-the-ground support, girls are learning in unconventional ways: often online, sometimes in underground schools or in family homes, unseen by the authorities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Nobody is coming to help us’: Afghan teenage girls on life without schoolRead moreBut there is so much more to be done, not least because thousands of girls have had to leave the country to obtain schooling, and with tension rising betweenAfghanistanand Pakistan, one favoured route out of the country is fast closing.Britain’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced that under the newimmigration and asylum bill, there will be two routes under a refugee resettlement scheme for students that could help girls get the education they have been denied. The first is through recognised charities sponsoring girls coming to the UK. The second is through colleges and universities offering scholarships.That’s good, but we must go further. I believe a fund must now be set up in support of Afghan girls who are threatened with being married off against their will. It should offer them bursaries to continue their education, if necessary outside their home country. And as UN special envoy for education, I am happy to work with any charity or educational institution that wants to assist girls in defence of their human rights.It may be a small gesture, but five years after they were condemned toTalibanrule, isn’t it time to truly support all the girls who risk their freedom and their lives for an education, and the hope of a meaningful existence? They yearn for things we take for granted. It is our moral duty to help them.Gordon Brown is the UN’s special envoy for global education and was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010The future starts with us:Gordon Brown in conversationOn Thursday 10 September, join Hugh Muir and Gordon Brown to discuss the intricate connections between global instability and civic decline, aas explored in Brown’s new book, The Future Starts With UsBook ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsAfghanistanOpinionTalibanChild marriageViolence against women and girlsWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite  | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Feigning friendship? Katie Miller at the White House on 30 May 2025.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFeigning friendship? Katie Miller at the White House on 30 May 2025.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesOpinionAnthony FauciAsking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocriteArwa MahdawiThe vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning planTue 4 Aug 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.12 EDTShareYou should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy andMuslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics tostart a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich?While I may not need to inform you that the Millers arebad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, wasforced to appearat a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Bidenpreemptively pardonedFauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration.While the Millers were not directly involved in the Fauci hearing, they did make an interesting cameo.Paul releasedmore than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary from 2019 to 2022, which revealed that Fauci regularly talked to Katie, then a communications aide to vice-president Mike Pence, about her health concerns.“I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day,” Fauci wrote in notes dated 9 May 2020. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone.”View image in fullscreenTarget of vitriol … Dr Anthony Fauci at a Senate hearing in Washington on 29 July.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFauci seemed to like Katie, who he described as “tough, smart, but great”, and she seemed on good terms with him. Fauci also sent the Millers a baby gift and, per his diary, the couple called him to say thank you. “We had a nice discussion about life after Trump,” he wrote in December 2020.I don’t think any more gifts are going to be exchanged, however, because Katie has thrown Fauci under the bus. It’s very embarrassing for a Maga bigwig like her – someone who hasamplified vaccine-sceptic viewsand publicly called forFauci to be jailed– to be revealed as having privately asked him for medical advice. Katie has tried to explain away the relationship by insisting that she had simply been feigning friendship as part of a cunning plan.Katie toldthe political news website Notus that she’d been cordial with Fauci so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”. She added that she understood “how to manage somebody like him”. Some of the information about her seems to have been redacted. Notus reports that the original Fauci journal entries released “mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times”.After the diary entries became public, Katie attacked Fauci on social media and accused him of being fame-hungry. “Every man who has a journal is a narcissist,” she wrote onX on Thursday. “Dr Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponised my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandise himself. As they say, keep your friends close and your enemies closer … this man should be in prison.”Katie isn’t entirely wrong about Fauci enjoying fame. His journal entries contain cringeworthy details about flattering press coverage and celebs fawning over him. Julia Roberts, he wrote, “said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous”. Barbra Streisand apparently also chatted to Fauci about vaccines. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” he wrote in February 2021. “I told her that I work listening to her songs on Alexa. She really did not know what Alexa was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening …”Still, this was a private journal, and we’ve all been embarrassing in private haven’t we? Plus, if Roberts was gasping over me, you best believe I’d be telling dear diary. Fauci getting carried away by his sudden fame is understandable; there is no vaccine for being cringe. One day, however, I hope there will be a cure for the harm people like the Millers have inflicted on the body politic.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on 80 years of public funding for the arts: more vital than ever | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Arts Council England has been much criticised in recent years. A new chair offers hope for a weary cultural sector
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Arts Council England has been much criticised in recent years. A new chair offers hope for a weary cultural sector
Content: The Glastonbury festival is supported by Arts Council England.Photograph: Joe Maher/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Glastonbury festival is supported by Arts Council England.Photograph: Joe Maher/Getty ImagesOpinionArts Council EnglandThe Guardian view on 80 years of public funding for the arts: more vital than everEditorialArts Council England has been much criticised in recent years. A new chair offers hope for a weary cultural sectorTue 4 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 20.24 EDTShare“Ido not believe it is yet realised what an important thing has happened,” the economist John Maynard Keynes wrote inThe Listener in July 1945. “Patronage of the arts has crept in. It has happened in a very English, informal, unostentatious way – half baked if you like.” He was referring to the wartime Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts (Cema), which would become the Arts Council of Great Britain. Keynes died a few months before it was granted a royal charter on 9 August 1946. A body to secure and distribute government cultural investment was created – an important thing, indeed.The Arts Council initially funded46 institutions, including the Royal Opera House andBristol Old Vic, the first publicly funded regional theatre in the UK. Over eight decades it has contributed to the making of world-renowned treasures such as the Southbank Centre and Royal Shakespeare Company. Today it supports nearly 1,000 organisations from the Proms to Glastonbury, local libraries, comedy venues and community arts centres, as well as individual artists. In 1994 it was devolved into national councils. This weekDawn Airey, the former head of Channel 5, took over as chair of Arts Council England (ACE) from Sir Nicholas Serota.View image in fullscreenDawn Airey, the new chair of Arts Council England.Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianGiven the Arts Council’s fundamental dependence on the economy and political will, it is no surprise that his nearly decade-long tenure was turbulent. Under the Conservatives, ACE’s budget wasreducedby about 30%. As Sir Nicholas put it in an introduction toMade in England, a collection of essays marking its 80th anniversary, the health of the culture sector relies on “one sobering, practical reality … money”.In recent years, ACE has beenaccusedof crippling bureaucracy, favouring grassroots organisations over prestigious establishments, and straying from Keynes’s foundational “arm’s length” principle. “The Arts Council is not altogether on our side,” John Gilhooly, the director of the Wigmore Hall,toldthe BBC. It pulled out of the Arts Council last year. English National Opera and other classical music organisations suffered major budget cuts in 2022. Contrary to ACE’s promise to take high-quality culture to “every corner of the country”, cuts to Glyndebourne resulted in thecancellationof its 2023 tour.Let’s Create, the controversial strategy set up in 2020 to diversify and redistribute funds outside London, was blamed for many of these problems. It wasscrappedinresponseto last year’s criticalArts Council reviewby the former Labour arts minister Lady Margaret Hodge, who accused it of stifling“innovation and creativity”. But inclusive ambitions should not be abandoned with the red tape. Access and excellence are not mutually exclusive.For all its shortcomings, Lady Hodge concluded that the Arts Council“remains a vital national body”. It is even more important in times of austerity: without public funding, many institutions would not survive. With a new chair – and a new prime minister – this is a moment of hope for a weary creative sector. Apetitionby Campaign for the Arts urges Andy Burnham to follow the example of Clement Attlee’s Labour government, which established the Arts Council “from the rubble of the second world war”, to make “arts and culture an integral part of their plan to rebuild the nation”. There is much to be done before the Arts Council celebrates its 100th birthday. Without Keynes’s “half baked” scheme, England would be much poorer, in every sense.Explore more on these topicsArts Council EnglandOpinionPromsFestivalsGlastonbury festivalSouthbank CentreMusic festivalsDawn AireyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Burnham and the devolved nations: a test for the new politics in Westminster | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister has unveiled his plans for English devolution. The picture in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is much less clear
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister has unveiled his plans for English devolution. The picture in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is much less clear
Content: Andy Burnham, right, with Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, in Glasgow on 23 July.Photograph: Alastair Grant/Pool AP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, right, with Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, in Glasgow on 23 July.Photograph: Alastair Grant/Pool AP/APOpinionDevolutionThe Guardian view on Burnham and the devolved nations: a test for the new politics in WestminsterEditorialThe prime minister has unveiled his plans for English devolution. The picture in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is much less clearTue 4 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTShareAfter early statements of intent on homelessness and social care, Andy Burnham capped his opening two weeks in office byaddressingwhat one might call the English question. Plans for greater fiscal devolution to England’s mayoral authorities, unveiled last week, are part of what is perhaps the primary raison d’etre of Mr Burnham’s government: the need to rebalance power and resources, in a country where they have been skewed disproportionately towards London and the south-east. As the designated administrative hub of that political project, thecreationof No 10 North in Manchester symbolises the ambition.Beyond England’s borders, however, the picture is much less clear. May’selectionsin Scotland and particularly Wales were a disaster for Labour and Mr Burnham’s predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. Progressive nationalist parties now rule in each of the devolved nations. How the prime minister chooses to engage with them will be a test of the kind of politics of compromise and consensus-building he has said he is committed to.Early meetings with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Scottish and Welsh first ministers, have beenreportedas positive by both sides. But the challenge for Mr Burnham will be how to combine a conviction that power should be devolved as locally as possible, with the need to respect the status and prerogatives of different national administrations. The prime minister hasarguedthat “the people of Dundee and Bangor feel just as distant from Holyrood and the Senedd as they do from Westminster”. That seems like a stretch, but Westminster should not in any case claim the right to bypass the devolved administrations in attempting to solve the problem.View image in fullscreenNicola Sturgeon launches the SNP s final poster of the general election 2015 campaign.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSir Keir at times adopted precisely that approach, at one pointwarningministers against being “overly deferential” to the Scottish and Welsh governments. That didn’t do Labour’s popularity much good in either country. Wales has a population of roughly the same size as Greater Manchester, yet the Welsh government does not, for example, have the powers the mayoral authority does over policing. If Mr Burnham is to be consistent in his devolutionary logic, that kind of anomaly should be addressed.Inevitably there will be frustrations, rows and disagreements, not least overcallsfor theBarnett formulafunding arrangements to be updated. The Scottish National party, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin will all have a powerful motive for taking credit for what goes right, and blaming Mr Burnham’s government when things go wrong. Matters in Wales are further complicated by the minority status of the Plaid government, which Welsh Labour has refused to support and which has yet tosucceedin passing a budget.But Mr Burnham’s direction of travel can be the right one for the devolved nations as well as the English regions. A confidence-building early move would be to repeal contentious powers granted by the post-Brexit United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020, which allow London to distribute funds across the UK in a variety of policy areas. As the Institute for Government hassuggested, Mr Burnham could instead fund the devolved governments to establish their own priorities.Devolution, and the possibilities it could unleash, were at the heart of Mr Burnham’s rise to Britain’s highest political office. Entirely understandably, his first moves have reflected the regional backdrop to that ascent. He should also follow his instincts in the rest of the United Kingdom.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Social care is for us all, and we all must fund it | Social care | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the new prime minister’s commitment to a fair system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the new prime minister’s commitment to a fair system
Content: Andy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers, volunteers and social care stakeholders in London, 29 July.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers, volunteers and social care stakeholders in London, 29 July.Photograph: ReutersSocial careLettersSocial care is for us all, and we all must fund itReaders respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the new prime minister’s commitment to a fair systemTue 4 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePolly Toynbee (Battles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes that, 29 July) is right that reforming England’s broken social care system will require winning the “attention, hearts and minds” of a public that knows little about it. Yet one of the biggest barriers to reform is that social care itself remains widely misunderstood, and public debate often reinforces narrow assumptions about who uses it.Social care is too often equated with care homes and dementia services for older people. While these are vital, they are one part of a wider system. Demand has grown fastest among working-age disabled adults who are largely missing from the public and political narrative. As such, the assertion by Polly Toynbee that “the old must pay for the old” is incorrect.Social careis relied on by people of all ages.Public debate not only misunderstands who uses social care, it often overlooks what social care makes possible. Social care should enable people to live independently, sustain relationships, take part in education and employment, and contribute to their communities. At its best, it is not simply about meeting needs but about creating the conditions for people to live full and meaningful lives.Most people will need care, provide care, or both, during their lives. Only when society understands the scope, value and reach of social care will meaningful reform become politically possible.Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of GlasgowPolly Toynbee asks: “Why do we endure this barely regulated, barely inspected patchwork of confusion” that constitutes Britain’s social care “system”? There are two main reasons. First, care provision has been regarded by governments as a domestic responsibility, overwhelmingly women’s work.This patriarchal assumption was built into the welfare state from birth. The strain that this has placed on generations of, again mainly women, has been documented. Yet, the state has held firm in believing that providing support risks the family giving up caring. Research, including my own, has shown this assumption to be entirely false.Second, we live in a deeply ageist society. Ageism “others” older people and diminishes their worth. Ageism allows the endless annual toll of cold-related deaths, and now heat-related ones.This scandal has persisted long enough, but now there is a prime minister who appears to understand why social care is so important and why it is in such a parlous state.Alan WalkerProfessor of social policy and social gerontology, University of SheffieldI’m in my 70s and my one concern is being able to pay for care that I may need as I get older. I live in a modest house and have a small amount of savings, so I know that this money could soon run out if I ever needed care later in life. I would love to have the peace of mind knowing that I would get care even if it meant paying a percentage of my estate on death or increased taxes.It would salve so many worries for people who don’t want to be a burden on their children and to know that they can at least pass on some inheritance. If for some reason you don’t need care then you’ll have been lucky, but at the moment it’s so unfair that your care depends on wealth, where you live and the type of illness you have. I really hope Andy Burnham gets this sorted.Janet TouheyNewark, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: North Sea oil is a litmus test for Burnham | Oil | The Guardian
description: Letters: John Barstow says oil expansion is a necessity, while David Parker wonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: John Barstow says oil expansion is a necessity, while David Parker wonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industry
Content: The Brent oil field in the North Sea.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Brent oil field in the North Sea.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyOilLettersNorth Sea oil is a litmus test for BurnhamJohn Barstowsays oil expansion is a necessity, whileDavid Parkerwonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industryTue 4 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareNorth Sea oil expansion is a necessity (Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling, 31 July). I state this as an environmentalist – not despite. Oil is a feedstock, not mere fuel. Oil is necessary for the day-to-day maintenance of wind turbines, nuclear plants and rail. Hence oil is part and parcel of supply chains for green tech. A domestic oil base brings such supply chains closer. This also underscores the case for approval of coking coal extraction in Cumbria. Green tech needs high-grade steel and high-grade steel needs coking coal.There are much better ways of helping the environment, such as more tree planting and stopping plastic waste being dumped into our seas. The carbon sink factor would be helped. A major expansion of the UK’s North Sea oil sector will make a more cohesive UK, complete with more jobs in Scotland and the north of England, including in supply manufacturing chains.On these grounds, the full approval of North Sea oil expansion is an absolute litmus test of Andy Burnham’s credibility given his talk of reindustrialising.John BarstowFittleworth, West SussexBurnham’s avowed pragmatism appears to be disappointingly deficient as far as North Sea oil is concerned. His pragmatic antennae should be telling him that new drilling will bring insignificant gain in exchange for a considerable dent in the renewed optimism and the support which he has so far generated.Rightly or wrongly, he will be perceived to have bowed to the oil and gas lobby, which is intent on burning the planet. He is reported as saying: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.” Wrong. The question is which side is our prime minister on and seen to be on: the planet’s or that of the fossil fuel industry?David ParkerHolmfirth, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Scrapping foreign doctors scheme will hurt the NHS | Doctors | The Guardian
description: Letter: The move is regressive and removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, writes Dr Peter Trewby
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The move is regressive and removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, writes Dr Peter Trewby
Content: ‘International exchanges built over decades have ended abruptly.’Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAView image in fullscreen‘International exchanges built over decades have ended abruptly.’Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PADoctorsLettersScrapping foreign doctors scheme will hurt the NHSThe move is regressive and removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, writesDr Peter TrewbyTue 4 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareThe decision to abolish the medical training initiative (MTI) scheme (Medical colleges condemn scrapping of NHS placements for overseas doctors, 31 July) risks reversing years of progress in medical diplomacy and repeating earlier mistakes in the UK’s treatment of international medical graduates (IMGs).In the early 2000s, in response to perceived workforce shortages, the government actively recruited IMGs and established a new GMC exam centre to process applicants at scale. Thousands came to the UK, but the number of available posts was insufficient. The government responded by ending the permit-free visa, which had allowed IMGs to work in the UK, so doctors could now only apply for posts when no UK graduate had applied, regardless of relative merits. International exchanges built over decades ended abruptly.Following strong lobbying by the medical royal colleges, the MTI scheme was introduced to allow suitably qualified doctors to come to the UK for a maximum of two years before returning home. The scheme benefited the UK, theNHS, international graduates and UK trainees, while also serving as an effective example of UK soft power.Abolishing the scheme removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, and risks signalling again that nationality takes precedence over merit. For an NHS that prides itself on its inclusivity, this is a serious regression.Dr Peter TrewbyRetired consultant physician and former director, international medical graduates, Royal College of PhysiciansHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Forget the goals and PBs – just enjoy it | Sport | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Recreational sport | Happy WhatsApps | Woodlice woes | Guessing game | Lost in film
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Recreational sport | Happy WhatsApps | Woodlice woes | Guessing game | Lost in film
Content: Run for fun – not for bragging rights.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenRun for fun – not for bragging rights.Photograph: AlamyBrief lettersSportLettersForget the goals and PBs – just enjoy itRecreational sport | Happy WhatsApps | Woodlice woes | Guessing game | Lost in filmTue 4 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareWhat happened to the joy of recreational sport (‘I spent a week crying. I’ve never had an injury in my life!’ Why do so many fitness fans end up needing surgery?, 3 August)? It’s like modern life – goal and target-oriented. PBs, how many laps, lengths, miles? Have to get the laps in, even if the back is killing me. Why? Is it about bragging rights? As a lifelong sports and exercise enthusiast aged 77 and still loving it, I really don’t understand the motivation for wilfully destroying your body in the name of sport.Barbara SmythCheltenham, GloucestershireMy experience of WhatsApp blue ticks differs (Letters, 29 July). During the Covid pandemic, every day I rejoiced in seeing the blue tick on a message from a family member who lived alone and had Covid: they were still alive.Ann NewellThame, OxfordshirePatrick Barkham wouldn’t be so fond of woodlice (‘Bumbling, mumbling’ tidiers of our world: the unexpected superpowers of the common woodlouse, 3 August) if, like me, he found them every day munching into his ripening strawberries on his allotment.Malcolm RiversIsleworth, LondonYour dailyCountry Diarycolumn is always informative, but I encourage readers to join the game it offers. I cover up the name of its author before reading the column and then guess whether it was written by a man or a woman. I’m correct 99% of the time. No disrespect to the contributors is intended.Ros CordinerLudham, NorfolkRe the articleFrom The Wizard of Oz to Trainspotting: 25 films to watch before you turn 25 (2 August), someone at the Guardian has an optimistic idea of the paper’s readership profile.Mike Hine (age 79¾)Kingston upon Thames, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him? | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The president is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the governing body
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The president is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the governing body
Content: Gianni Infantino speaks at the podium during the 76th Fifa Congress in April.Photograph: Bob Frid/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino speaks at the podium during the 76th Fifa Congress in April.Photograph: Bob Frid/EPAFifaExplainerThe Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him?Gianni Infantino is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the presidentNick Ames,John Duerden,Alexander Abnos,Osasu ObayiuwanaandMarcela Mora y AraujoTue 4 Aug 2026 16.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pressure is growing on the Fifa president,Gianni Infantino, with many countries withdrawing their support following the bungled World Cup sell-off. However, how key is Infantino’s relationship with each confederation and is it likely that an election contest will actually happen? We look at the key considerations, confederation by confederation.1) How does each confederation view Infantino’s re-election?Uefa(Europe) has firmly led the moves under way to achieve Infantino’s removal. The threat last week to boycott all Fifa competitions if the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme was not scrapped contributed hugely to its failure. In a scathing statement on Saturday, Uefa said the current Fifa leadership had “not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family”, and pledged to push for change. Some Uefa member associations, including the English and Welsh FAs, havewithdrawn their letters of supportfor Infantino’s re‑election and efforts are continuing to ensure others follow suit in a bid to weaken his position irretrievably.Nick AmesReports ofAFC(Asia) support for Uefa are premature; the confederation is divided. The AFC has spoken out, strongly in relative terms compared to its usual pronouncements, against the proposed World Cup deal and has called for reform of Fifa. The AFC has been a staunch supporter in the past but if it looks as if Infantino is in trouble the AFC leadership, which was genuinely angry at how the proposal was made (probably more so than the actual details of the deal), could switch sides, which would probably confirm Infantino’s downfall if Uefa and Concacaf oppose but it is not a foregone conclusion – some in Asia are not convinced that Uefa has the numbers. The big problem is that, while the AFC leadership may want Infantino out, most individual Asian federations do not want him to be replaced. The AFC president, Sheikh Salman, has ambitions of his own and has been historically successful at preserving AFC unity but this will be tricky especially as west Asian nations such as Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia support Infantino and are influential in Asia. It could be that the only way to ensure Asian unity is to have an Asian candidate. Jordan’s Prince Ali bin Hussein’sclaim of “blackmail”could prove a significant moment, however.John DuerdenWenger and Infantino’s No 2 Grafström criticise ‘sad and reproachable’ World Cup planRead moreConcacaf(North and Central America, and the Caribbean) is among the confederations that have come out strongly against Infantino and his FFE proposal, first directly rejecting it and then releasing a statement after it was withdrawn that took direct aim at Infantino. A release speaking on behalf of Concacaf’s 41 member associations called the plan “a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first”, and a “unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership” and said that “a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative”.That is about as direct a call for no confidence in Infantino as you are likely to get outside of an election itself. It should be noted, of course, that the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is also aFifavice-president and would be a leading candidate to run for president should there be a united desire among confederations to oust Infantino. Montagliani has kept silent on the subject when asked in the past but this statement, which speaks for him, shows at the very least he is not immune to the idea of going against Infantino.Alexander AbnosView image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani, pictured consoling Lionel Messi after the World Cup final, is a potential successor to Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAPatrice Motsepe, president of theConfederation of African Football, has said the 54 member associations are in unanimous support of Infantino’s re-election in Morocco next year.Osasu ObayiuwanaSince the rumpus over Infantino’s proposed FFE brokeand died, the South American confederation,Conmebol,has been notably silent. Its president, Alejandro Domínguez, has been posting birthday wishes to individuals, clubs and institutions from Uruguay where he is visiting ahead of the 2030 centenary of the first World Cup. Unlike Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC, which publicly opposed Fifa’s aborted FFE proposal, Conmebol took several days before issuing a fence-sitting statement stressing football first, and requesting further information and clarification. That was the only official response at all, and there has been absolute silence since.“Conmebol’s current position is best described as cautious support rather than open confrontation,” says Marina Mendez, a director of AD Sporting Industry Professionals and a friend of Conmebol who consults on football in the region. “The distinction is politically significant. It suggests Conmebol wants to preserve its institutional relationship with Fifa and maintain room for negotiation, rather than join a public campaign against Infantino. This should not necessarily be interpreted as unconditional personal loyalty. Conmebol’s approach is pragmatic: it is protecting South American football’s access, influence and negotiating position within Fifa while assessing how the international balance of power develops.”Brazil and Argentina are the main countries, and Domínguez looks after the relationship with both, with most of the other countries expected to follow suit. “They are not federations likely to confront Infantino directly because they will always prefer to be on the right side of the non-Europeans,” says an industry insider who does not wish to be named.Marcela Mora y AraujoIt remains to be seen what the 11Oceania Football Confederationmember associations will do. New Zealand, the leading member of the confederation, was quick to come out against the World Cup proposal – though the reaction of the OFC itself was noncommittal – and there is still support for Infantino among the other federations.John Duerden2) What are the historical links to Infantino?UefaThe parties go back a long way. Infantino was Uefa’s secretary general from 2009 until 2016 and it backed him strongly when he first ran for the Fifa presidency. But there has long been push and pull between the global governing body and that of football’s most powerful continent. Relations have deteriorated in recent years, Uefa fending off Infantino-led initiatives such as abiennial staging of the World Cupand a proposed investment in 2018 by SoftBank. Things appeared to reach a head in May 2025 when delegates from several European federationswalked out of Fifa’s annual congress in protestat Infantino’s late arrival. They accused him of pursuing “private political interests”. That turned out to be the tip of the iceberg. The past year’s near-interminable list of Fifa-related controversies have further ensured that the differences between the two are irreconcilable.NAAFCIt has been a close relationship, Salman and AFC have backed Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election. It is not just about money either, though this is of course important. He is seen as approachable, available and open. Fifa has historically been seen as a European (and to a lesser extent South American) institution in Asia, and while Infantino is from Uefa, he is seen as a leader who gives equal weight to all. One president said to me that in the past, conversations with Fifa were like receiving decrees from above but now there is a genuine dialogue. World Cup expansion has gone down well,64 teamswould be welcomed too, and there are more tournaments held in Asia these days. Infantino has already been reminding Asia about this.JDView image in fullscreenSheikh Salman and the AFC have backed Gianni Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election.Photograph: Vincent Thian/APConcacafInfantino’s most direct relationship has been as the president under whom the World Cup was awarded to the US, Mexico and Canada, after a bid from the US lost out to Qatar for the 2022 hosting rights. Aside from that, there was not much of a direct, historic relationship between Infantino and Concacaf – at least, not until the letter released by the confederation over the weekend.AACAFInfantino’s association with African football began in 2016, when he backed Ahmad Ahmad of Madagascar totopple the late Issa Hayatou as CAF presidentin March 2017. Being an eyewitness to that election, at the African Union HQ in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, I recall the anger with which Hayatou confronted Infantino and Fatma Samoura, then Fifa secretary general, over their involvement in an election.Infantino, under Ahmad’s ill-fated four-year tenure between 2017 and 2021 – which ended in his untimely removal from office over ethics violations – got Fifa to take over the daily administration of the CAF from August to December 2019, with Samoura going to Egypt to take charge of the organisation. Many in African football saw this as a neo-colonial act and a direct violation of the CAF’s autonomy and independence. Infantino was involved in the ascension of Motsepe to the presidency in March 2021.OOConmebolAlong comes Infantino, the Uefa salvation who promises an anti-corruption ticket. After Julio Grondona’s death, an AFA (Argentina Football Association) election found more votes than members and Fifa intervened, naming a committee of industry insiders to oversee a cleansing of the house. Infantino was present in the AFA headquarters at its inaugural press conference. Imagine Infantino launching an English FA governance intervention.In 2018, in Buenos Aires for a Libertadores final to be played by two clubs from the same city for the first time in Argentina’s history (policing was a mess and fan violence before the second leg led to its suspension andeventual move to Madrid) Infantino was invited by the then president of Argentina, Mauricio Macri, to be guest of honour at the G20 held in the city later that week.Infantino, as we know him today is created then, photographed gifting football shirts to the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Donald Trump, POTUS at the time. “Yes, that G20 was key for Infantino, because he’d inherited a corruption scandal. He needed to instil the belief that football would cease to be a mafia, that he would achieve this. And he managed,” Macri, now president of the Fifa Foundation, told the Guardian: “From an ethical point of view he is impeccable. There is nothing odd in Fifa today, Fifa manages fortunes, more than ever, because Infantino is successful; he organises competitions that are more and more profitable, and it’s all above board. I should say the same applies to Conmebol.”The Conmebol president, Nicolás Leoz, fell in the same Fifagate swoop, although he had left office in 2013. A series of interim and short-lived presidencies ensued until January 2016 when current president Domínguez took his post. Unanimously voted in by the 10 member associations, he pushed for every professional club to have a female team and introduced “hydration” breaks before this World Cup, albeit less structured ones. Infantino has also maintained a functional and stable relationship with the AFA president, Claudio “Chiqu” Tapia. “This relationship is politically relevant because Macri has been an opponent of “Chiqui” Tapia,” Mendez says. “This demonstrates Infantino’s ability to maintain links with both sides of Argentine football’s internal power structure.” Tapia was approached for comment.MMAView image in fullscreenClaudio Tapia of Argentina’s FA has a stable relationship with the Fifa president.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersOFCLike Asia, Infantino has worked hard to build relationships both of the personal and financial kind. It is common to hear officials describe him as a friend. The expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams finally gave Oceania an automatic World Cup spot – something that Fifa had promised in the past but never delivered. And the idea of having more spots in a 64-team competition was also attractive. Under Infantino,New Zealand co-hosted the Women’s World Cupwith Australia. Fifa also supported the establishment of the Oceania Professional League that kicked off in January to provide much-needed pro club football for the region.JD3) How financially dependent is the confederation on Infantino and Fifa?UefaNot at all. While the World Cup is Fifa’s most essential driver of revenue, Uefa can lay claim, among other things, to the highly lucrative Champions League and the vast sums that it attracts on an annual basis. Expanding its tournaments and staging them more often is one of the only ways available for Fifa to keep pace. Private investment would not harm its cause, either. Uefa’s annual revenues have recently totalled around double those of Fifa; as things stand football’s powerhouse can cope perfectly well on its own.NAAFCLike always in Asia, it varies. There are rich federations on either side of the continent but in between there are some that are almost completely dependent on Fifa money. Bhutan, for example, gets $1.5m a year, which makes up the majority of its budget. Even Australia, which has reached the knockout stages of the past two World Cups, has lost around $17m over the past two years, which may explain its rather vague statement calling for more time when the plan was first heard.JDView image in fullscreenPaul Okon Engstler, Jackson Irvine and Harry Souttar after Australia’s World Cup exit; even their federation, one of AFC’s richest, loses money.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersConcacafThis is a very top‑heavy confederation, perhaps more so than any other in the world. The US and Mexico have been regional powers for most of the past 30‑40 years, and recently Canada has shown signs it can compete on the field and is addressing business issues off of it. Just below them is a middle class consisting of Panama, Jamaica, Costa Rica and Honduras. The remaining 33 Concacaf nations are fairly small by comparison, and thus naturally more reliant on funding from Fifa via the forward programme and other initiatives. The fact that smaller Caribbean nations feel empowered to join with the big dogs says a lot about how at risk they feel they may be without Infantino at Fifa’s helm.AACAFThe confederation funds activities from its own commercial revenue, so it is not dependent on Fifa and Infantino in that sense. But the majority of CAF’s 54 member associations are financially challenged and are dependent on the annual grants that the world governing body gives them to meet their operating costs.OOConmebolIt represents only 10 nation members. Variations among them notwithstanding, the federations are self-sufficient economically and their local leagues are attractive and profitable. Their national teams are the No 1 sporting attraction, pulling in vast numbers of fans who are emotionally attached to their heroes, who in turn love to play for their country. The main sources of revenue for clubs are TV rights, marketing and the sale of players. For this, the top market is the Premier League (which operates entirely outside the FA and therefore Fifa) and the other European leagues, which are also largely independent of their FAs. Montevideo has produced more World Cup players than any other city in history, so even a financially struggling association such as Uruguay’s continues to rely more on the income from the development of youth talent than Fifa aid. There were six Argentinian managers with extensive international trajectories at this World Cup. Exporting home‑grown talent, of which there is plenty, is a bigger source of revenue than Fifa project distribution funds. Two of the most colourful stories of the World Cup, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha and the New Zealand defender Tim Payne, transferred to Chilean and Paraguayan clubs respectively following their popularity during the tournament. Popularity due in no small part to the efforts of streamers and influencers from Argentina and Brazil.MMAOFCOceania is made up of small federations that tend to be reliant on what Fifa gives them. So the recent World Cup proposal would, had it gone through, have made a huge difference financially.JD4) Would a breakaway cause an existential threat?UefaEurope has the strongest club and international teams in the world. Parting ways from Infantino and Fifa would be unlikely to cause serious damage, although it could cause issues with clubs who have been looking to expand their global reach through the revamped Club World Cup. It is plausible that bigger teams from other continents would seek to join forces with Uefa and compete in new tournaments given the kudos and financial opportunities available when competing with the majority of the sport’s giants.NAView image in fullscreenEuropean clubs such as Chelsea have been looking to expand their global reach through Fifa’s revamped Club World Cup.Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAAFCIt is a generalisation but, in Asia, Fifa as an institution does not make the headlines that it does in western Europe. Usually, interest in a country comes when they are affected specifically by a decision, as when bidding for a tournament. In my experience, there just isn’t the same interest in the day‑to‑day running of the organisation. Breaking with Infantino would not be a massive threat to Asia but there is some concern about a return to a more Europe‑dominated Fifa, if that were to materialise. While pretty much everyone has supported Infantino from 2016 until the past few days, Asian federations that have done so are seen in some quarters as being corrupt and/or greedy but the Europeans, who did exactly the same, are now trying to paint themselves as the moral guardians of the sport.JDConcacafIf a breakaway would cause an existential threat, then Concacaf is living it right now. One could certainly read it as a principled stand, but it’s hard to separate the confederation’s statement with Montagliani’s current position as Infantino’s most likely successor, should the latter need to stand down.AACAFThe relationship between Infantino and Africa’s 54 national associations is largely seen as a “master-servant” one, in which he basically tells the FA/federation heads, through Fifa officials, to do his bidding. Those who do not toe the political line of Zurich, as decided by Infantino, may well end up having their books audited over how they have spent their Fifa grants. Many FA/federation presidents faced Fifa ethics proceedings and subsequent bans as a result.OOConmebol“There’s no morality involved, just politics,” the industry insider says. Mendez concurs: “It’s not a simple case of morality, it’s a power struggle and a rupture in perspectives about football in general and the business of football in particular. Today, Eurocentrism is dominating, and things like sponsored hydration breaks and Super Bowl-style half-time shows impose a North American regard hitherto unseen.”MMAOFCOceania welcomed the fact that Infantino had a “global” mentality and went out of his way to engage with smaller nations far from the centre of global football power. If the confederation does break away, it would want something similar in the opposition candidate and not a return to the old days when the confederation was an afterthought in the corridors of power.JD5) How important is the current and historical relationship?A strong relationship between Uefa and Fifa would make for a far more harmonious global football scene but, as described above, there is huge work to do before that can be repaired.NAIt’s very important – barring some new organisation stepping in to run world football in a better way, Fifa is Concacaf’s best link to the traditional power centres of world football. The US, Mexico and Canada derive a lot of their value as federations from how they’ve been able to perform at men’s and women’s World Cups – that’s not something they’ll want to give up lightly, which is perhaps why they did not threaten a boycott the way Uefa did.AACAFAfrica’s political power within Fifa began to rise in 1974, when João Havelange successfully courted the continent as a block and made it an important pillar of his electoral victory over Sir Stanley Rous in Germany, becoming the first and only non-European, to date, to be Fifa president. Sepp Blatter, Havelange’s successor in 1998, also leveraged Africa’s support in a similar fashion to defeat the Uefa president Lennart Johansson. Delivering on his promise to the continent that it would host a World Cup during his presidency, which South Africa did in 2010, bolstered his popularity and support base on the continent. But the last 10 years of the Infantino presidency have made many resent the undue influence of the world governing body in Africa’s affairs.OOView image in fullscreenSepp Blatter, pictured with the then South Africa president Jacob Zuma at the 2010 World Cup, cultivated support in African football.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianConmebolFifa as we know it was essentially invented, developed and moulded by the Brazil and Argentina federation presidents Havelange and Grondona respectively. They specifically wanted to break Europe’s stronghold. Initially, they started funding grassroots via “partnerships” with big brands, which benefited from reaching wider markets. A vivid example is the giant sign with a Coca-Cola bottle on every corner of the pitch, seen in places such as Russia and China where advertising was otherwise prohibited, every single time a corner kick was awarded. After Havelange’s time at the helm was up, Blatter took the lead. Blatter kept Grondona close by, his right-hand man, while the business venture grew and grew, and places for other confederations increased. When Fifagate blew up, most leaders close to the top faced trials and disgrace; Grondona was saved by death.Infantino’s reign was a continuation of keeping Conmebol as a key ally. The historic power derived from on-the-pitch success in the region, and the crown jewel that is Lionel Messi, have contributed to keeping the small confederation big. “The relationship is neither purely personal nor purely institutional. It is built on mutual strategic value,” says Mendez. “The coming election will be Uefa versus footballistic populism,” the industry source said. “Conmebol owns Fifa.”MMAExplore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest padding | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Riders at the Tour de France Femmes were subject to extra clothing checks before Tuesday’s stage following claims some could be using extra padding to seek an aerodynamic advantage
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Riders at the Tour de France Femmes were subject to extra clothing checks before Tuesday’s stage following claims some could be using extra padding to seek an aerodynamic advantage
Content: The peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenThe peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest paddingChest fairings could smooth airflow around the bodyWarning came before time-trial stage to DijonJeremy Whittlein DijonTue 4 Aug 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRiders in theTour de France Femmeswere examined for hidden aerodynamic enhancements, or chest fairings, before the race’s time trial stage to Dijon on Tuesday, in a clampdown on the latest attempts to circumnavigate cycling’s rules.Changes to body morphology to improve aerodynamics are banned under InternationalCyclingUnion rules. The UCI’s commissaires were looking for padded chest fairings that would artificially improve airflow and reduce wind resistance.Tour de France Femmes: Reusser aces stage four time trial to snatch yellow jerseyRead moreIn June the male rider Jan-Willem van Schip was disqualified in a French race for inserting a water bottle into the front of his racing jersey on the basis that it enhanced his aerodynamics and speed.The UCI directive that selected riders have extra checks before the stage to Dijon came at the instigation of some teams who had noticed changes to rider physiques before time trials.Stijn Steels, director of the AG Insurance-Soudal team, said he first noticed suspicious padding at the Paris Olympics in 2024. “There was a rider who suddenly had huge breasts,” Steels told the Belgian newspaper Het Laatste News.“Last year, many riders filled their bust area completely with ice or other items to create a larger volume, which gives a much better aerodynamic effect. It’s only a few watts difference [in power], but a few watts matter a lot in a time trial. It’s possible and it does make a difference, but I wouldn’t risk it.”Stephen Delcourt, manager of the race favourite Demi Vollering’s FDJ United-Suez team, said: “We never play with the rules like this. If they want to have controls for this, it’s because someone is doing it. Every season everybody does more work in wind tunnels and looks at equipment from the handlebars, the bike, the helmet. But we don’t play with the rules, we are always transparent.”The former world champion Marianne Vos, teammate to the defending Tour de France champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, supported the clothing checks. “It’s good that they try to enforce the rules,” Vos said. “Everybody is looking for the best aerodynamics, so there are some games. But there are rules to live by.”In a statement to the teams taking part in the Tour Femmes, the UCI said “particular attention” would be paid to ensure cyclists complied with regulations over “non-essential items or other accessories worn by a rider that could alter their physique”.Vos said of the checks: “I don’t think it’s really body searching, so I don’t have a problem with it, as long as it’s not too invasive.”Rolf Aldag, team manager to Kasia Niewiadoma, winner of the Tour Femmes in 2024, saw little difference between the clothing inspections and standard doping controls. “You have to enforce the rules,” Aldag said. “Otherwise, don’t make them. If there’s something to check, then it should be checked. They do that every time they do a doping control. So do we question doping controls?“If we question it due to the privacy of an athlete, then you have to skip doping controls too, which we all agree that we should not do. It’s the same rule for the men and they would also be checked. I think there’s nothing wrong with that.”Bert Blocken, professor of aerodynamics, aerospace and mechanical engineering at Scotland’s Heriot‑Watt University, said a chest fairing can alter airflow around the body and reduce aerodynamic drag, allowing riders to conserve energy.“You don’t gain tens of seconds on a time trial, but over 20-30km, it can make a decisive difference,” Blocken said, adding that it could mean a gain of 0.78 seconds per kilometre.The UCI’s directive has led to accusations of sexism as no clothing checks were carried out either before, or after, the men’s Tour de France time trial, between Évian‑les‑Bains and Thonon-les-Bains on 21 July.Philip Roodhooft, manager of the Fenix-Premier Tech team that won three stages in the men’s Tour in July, said that he was “not surprised that people are exploring it”.Roodhooft said: “When you see that the men try things with water bottles placed in strategic spots, then I can imagine that women are thinking about it as well. Still, it’s not good that it happens because it’s still cheating.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stokes decoded: his concerns for Joe Root and hopes for ‘great man’ Stephen Fleming | Ben Stokes | The Guardian
description: What England’s former captain did – and didn’t – say in two-hour podcast interview with his old teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: What England’s former captain did – and didn’t – say in two-hour podcast interview with his old teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler
Content: Ben Stokes says he is feeling ‘chilled right now’ after retiring from international cricket.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenBen Stokes says he is feeling ‘chilled right now’ after retiring from international cricket.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PABen StokesAnalysisStokes decoded: his concerns for Joe Root and hopes for ‘great man’ Stephen FlemingAli MartinWhat England’s former captain did – and didn’t – say in two-hour podcast interview with his old teammates Stuart Broad and Jos ButtlerTue 4 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTShareOver the course of two hours chatting to his old friends Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler on their podcast, Ben Stokes sounded at peace with his decision toretire from England dutyfive weeks ago. Dare we say it, refreshed and ready to go again.Beyond playing for Durham and in franchise cricket, Stokes is “definitely” retired, however, and there was not even a hint of a possible U-turn when the home Ashes rolls around next summer. Nor, given his character, was this first interview since calling it a day ever going to be one stuffed with regret.There was an admission from Stokes he put “way too much” on his own shoulders as England captain, rather than delegate to others. And there was a comment that the team could have communicated better in Australia last winter, not least when they tossed away a commanding position duringthe series openerin Perth.Ben Stokes rules out 2027 Ashes return but ambition is ‘to coach England one day’Read moreStokes spoke openly about cricket’s relationship with alcohol, insisting the sport – not just the England team – has a drinking culture out of step with increased professionalism. “[It] has been the same since the 1980s,” he said. “As the game has got better and better and better, that thing has just stayed around.”But, equally, he was never going to own up to too many of the team’s shortcomings during the 4-1 Ashes defeat that English cricket is still struggling to shake off. Nor was he going to look back with much sheepishness regarding the farewell against New Zealand at Trent Bridge that many felt was a bit too self-indulgent.Indeed, beyond the team’s lack of game awareness at times, few decisions in the past year would have been made differently. Everyone was on the same page in Australia and there was no tactical divergence from Brendon McCullum. Noosa – the mid-tour break that invited headlines and questions about the team’s penchant for a good time off the field – would be repeated.But for all that this was to be expected from an all-action all-rounder who, like Ian Botham before him, prefers to forge ahead rather than look back, there were interesting elements – not least when discussing his successor as Test captain.Stokes and Joe Root are as tight as you get in English cricket and needless to say there were best wishes as regards the future of the side. In Stephen Fleming, Stokes believes England have selected a “great man”, having worked with the New Zealander previously at Chennai Super Kings in the Indian Premier League.But, despite this hopefulness, Stokes also went on to share his concerns that Root is about to re-enter what became an “unhealthy relationship” with the job at the end of his first spell in charge – concerns that he is not alone in harbouring.“He just always puts the team first and he always comes second,” said Stokes. “That’s my only concern with it, knowing what he went through last time. Because I don’t want to see that ever happen again. I care for Joe a lot.”View image in fullscreenBen Stokes (right) says he worries about Joe Root returning as England Test captain because Root ‘puts the team first and he always comes second’.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPAs he said at the end of his last Test, Stokes felt HarryBrook should have been promotedfrom vice-captain. And here he went on to question the message it sent, likewise Brook not stepping up while Stokes was suspended for the second Test against New Zealand and Root first dipped his toe back into the water.Though these comments added up to some rare direct criticism of the current regime, just as telling were the moments when Stokes chose not to answer. The most glaring of which came when discussing the infamous night out with Gus Atkinson after the Lord’s Test this summer and the disciplinary action it triggered.A question about the team’s curfew and who knew what was sidestepped, making way for some in-jokes about being better off heading to McDonald’s for a Filet-O-Fish that night. But there was more than a hint of disquiet about handling of events by his now former employers at the England and WalesCricketBoard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’m not going to lie and say that there might have been some other things that contributed to the decision [to retire],” said Stokes. “But I’m not here today to go into all that detail. I think there’s a time and a place for that.The Spin | Joe Root stands alone after old mate Ben Stokes runs out of roadRead more“And now isn’t that time because, you know, I don’t want to come across as, you know, bitter towards anyone yet. Cause I’m chilled right now.”The word “yet” was a telling one, with Stokes citing a desire not to damage the England team but probably aware that divulging too much right now might devalue a future book or some such. By his own admission, the chief driver for retirement was having strung himself out during the five-month gap after Australia.Aside from a fractured cheekbone sustained in the nets at Durham, albeit not relevant to him calling it a day, he insisted – Stokes owned up to over-thinking and over-training during this protracted down time, to the point of returning anything but Test-ready.Interestingly, Stokes went on at one stage to say that McCullum might still be the Test head coach – not simply reduced to the white-ball role – had he not retired from England duty. Unfortunately, his reasoning was not explored further.But listening to him speak, and noting another shouldering of arms when asked about his relationship with the team director, Rob Key, it was hard to escape the notion that had regime change come sooner and more fully, Stokes might not have been speaking as a former England cricketer.Explore more on these topicsBen StokesEngland cricket teamCricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Tearful Jack Draper loses on comeback from injury at Canadian Open | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Jack Draper was in tears during his 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jack Draper was in tears during his 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open
Content: Jack Draper of Great Britain plays a backhand against Térence Atmane.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper of Great Britain plays a backhand against Térence Atmane.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesJack DraperTearful Jack Draper loses on comeback from injury at Canadian OpenBriton withdrew from Wimbledon with bruised boneDraper in tears during 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 loss to Térence AtmanePA MediaTue 4 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Draper was in tears during a first-round comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open.The Briton was competing for the first time sincepulling out of Wimbledonwith a recurrence of a bruised bone in his left arm, and was beaten 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 in Montreal.Draper pulls out of Wimbledon with arm injury in fresh blow to British hopesRead moreThe 24-year-old was visibly upset during a changeover in the third set. His serve speed had significantly dropped, and he appeared concerned about his left arm.He has a wildcard entry for the Cincinnati Open, beginning next week, but there will be doubts about his involvement after this defeat, as well as regarding his fitness for the US Open.Draper pulled out of the DC Open in Washington last week, as well as missing Wimbledon.He reached a career-high ranking of No 4 in the world last summer, but has been plagued by injuries since and has spent the better part of a year on the sidelines.Draper’s fellow Briton Jacob Fearnley reached the second round in Montreal with a 7-6, 6-4 victory over Adrian Mannarino.Meanwhile, world No 2 Carlos Alcaraz has withdrawn from the Cincinnati Masters as he continues his recovery from a wrist injury that has sidelined him since April. The Spaniard had been slated to make his return in the tournament to prepare for the US Open, the final Grand Slam of the year, which starts on 30 August in New York.Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talks | Mohamed Salah | The Guardian
description: The Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor have begun transfer ⁠negotiations with Mohamed Salah and hope to sign the former Liverpool player this week
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor have begun transfer ⁠negotiations with Mohamed Salah and hope to sign the former Liverpool player this week
Content: Mohamed Salah in action for Egypt against Iran at the World Cup in the US this summer.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenMohamed Salah in action for Egypt against Iran at the World Cup in the US this summer.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersMohamed SalahTrabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talksClub chair says forward will have medical on WednesdayEgypt international left Liverpool after nine yearsReutersTue 4 Aug 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor say they have begun transfer ⁠negotiations withMohamed Salah, with the club chair adding they hoped to sign the Egypt forward later this week.“Negotiations have been launched ⁠to transfer professional footballer ⁠Mohamed Salah, ​who is in a free status, to our club,” the club said in a statement.Frank Lampard hails ‘huge’ signing as Coventry seal record £22.5m Rushworth dealRead moreSpeaking to the broadcaster ⁠A Spor, the Trabzonspor chair Ertugrul Dogan said that while the transfer was not completed, Salah is expected to arrive ⁠in Istanbul for a medical on Wednesday and then go to Trabzon to sign with the ​Black Sea side.He did not confirm ‌when the contract would be ‌signed, but said it would likely be on Thursday.Salah left Liverpool this summerafter nine ‌years, having scored 257 goals in 442 appearances, where he won the Premier League twice and the Champions League once.In the 2024-25 season Salah scored 29 Premier League goals and provided 18 assists, equalling the league record for most goal involvements in a season andsetting the record for a 38-game campaign.He was named Premier League Player ‌of the Season and won the Golden Boot and the Playmaker Award, becoming the first player to take all three in one campaign.His output ​waned last season, with seven goals and seven assists in 27 league matches and he was left on the bench in Champions League games, leading to a public spat with Liverpool’s then-manager Arne Slot.The 34-year-old began his career in Europe at Swiss side Basel in 2012 and ⁠later joined Chelsea. He also had brief stints at Fiorentina and Roma between 2015 and 2017 ​before joining Liverpool.Trabzonspor – generally ​considered to be the fourth-biggest team in Turkey after Istanbul ​sides Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, and ‌Besiktas – finished third ​in the Super Lig ​last season and will enter the Europa League playoffs.Salah had been close to joining Istanbul club Besiktas, whose football director Onder Ozen said negotiations had stalled over financial and image-rights demands, according to local media.Explore more on these topicsMohamed SalahTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland risk ECB ire by agreeing to play five matches against Afghanistan | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Ireland’s decision to stage a full one-day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer could cost them lucrative future fixtures against England
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Ireland’s decision to stage a full one-day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer could cost them lucrative future fixtures against England
Content: Ireland, who beat India in a T20 series in June, are playing five one-day internationals against Afghanistan this month.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenIreland, who beat India in a T20 series in June, are playing five one-day internationals against Afghanistan this month.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PACricketIreland risk ECB ire by agreeing to play five matches against AfghanistanFirst ODI of series will take place in Bready on WednesdayEngland refuse to face Afghanistan due to Taliban regimeExclusive byMatt HughesTue 4 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland’s decision to stage a full one‑day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer couldcost them lucrative future fixtures against England.The England and WalesCricketBoard is understood to be unhappy about the series, which starts on Wednesday, ­taking place as England refuse to play Afghanistan outside ­International Cricket ­Council global events because of what the ECB chair, ­Richard Thompson, has described as the “gender apartheid” of the Taliban regime.Durham sitting pretty in One-Day Cup despite Ben Stokes’ golden duckRead moreThe ECB’s policy is backed by the UK government, but Cricket ­Ireland has taken a different view and has developed close relations with the Afghanistan Cricket Board, ­offering it five ODIs this month, all of which will take place in Northern Ireland.
