In a reciprocal arrangement Ireland will play Afghanistan in the UAE next March for one Test, three ODIs and three T20 fixtures.England played a one-off Test against Ireland at Lord’s as prepara­tion for both the 2019 and 2023 home series, but the ECB has opted for a warmup Test against Bangladesh instead next year.England’s men played ­Afghanistan in a Champions Trophy group game in Lahore last year after a specially convened ECB board meeting approved the fixture, which was criticised strongly by a cross‑party group of 160 MPs, who had urged them to withdraw in a joint letter.The ECB will not schedule any bilateral cricket against ­Afghanistan, however, and this summer organised a tour of England for the Afghan Refugee Women’s team, as well as ­inviting them to the T20 World Cup final at Lord’s. The Afghanistan women ­players fled the country with the majority relocating to Australia after the Taliban retook control in 2021 and enforced a ban on female sport.While Afghanistan are the only ICC full member not to operate a ­women’s cricket programme the world ­governing body has not banned them. Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand also refuse to play Afghanistan in ­bilateral series, however, with ­Ireland ­joining West Indies, ­Zimbabwe and the four Asian ICC full members in granting them fixtures.The ECB’s relationship with Cricket Ireland has been delicate for some time, as England have declined an invitation to join a proposed new Euro Nations Cup tournament also involving Scotland, the Netherlands and Italy next year because of their congested calendar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile England’s men played three T20 internationals in Ireland last September the ECB sent a second-string team and there are no more matches in the calendar. England’s women, however, will host Ireland in a three‑match ODI series next month.Explore more on these topicsCricketECBIreland Cricket TeamAfghanistan cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coach | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: Manchester United are closing in on their new head coach after the departure of Marc Skinner
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester United are closing in on their new head coach after the departure of Marc Skinner
Content: Manchester United are expected to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach.Photograph: Callum Landells/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United are expected to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach.Photograph: Callum Landells/Getty ImagesManchester United WomenManchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coachOlid expected to meet players on WednesdayUnited squad pays tribute to former head coach SkinnerTom GarryTue 4 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United are set to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach to replace Marc Skinner,following his exiton Monday, multiple sources have told the Guardian.Talks with the 40-year-old are understood to be very advanced and she is expected to be introduced to the United squad on Wednesday.United are confident that the Spanish coach is the right person to lead them into a new chapter, as first reported by the Telegraph, as the Women’s Super League club focuses on developing young, homegrown players.Marc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thin | Tom GarryRead moreOlid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last term on a dramatic final day of the season, but it had already been confirmed in April that she was to leave the Edinburgh club this summer by mutual agreement. She was in charge of Hearts for five years and also guided them to the 2024 Scottish Cup final, where they were beaten by Rangers.She has previously coached in the United States with Houston Dynamo, working with their women’s team and their under-19s men’s squad, before she had a spell with the Catalan Football Association.United are understood to be impressed by her playing style and her ability to develop and improve players, and they carried out extensive background checks on Olid prior to publicly announcing Skinner’s departure on Monday, with succession planning having already been well under way.Skinner left partly because of frustration at United’s transfer strategy. The club are understood to feel the current level of spending across the WSL is unsustainable and they want a different approach, focusing on their own younger talents and improving their academy to deliver longer-term success.View image in fullscreenMarc Skinner left Manchester United party because of frustration over the club’s transfer strategy.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersUnited finished fourth in the WSL last term. They start the new season away to big-spending London City Lionesses on 4 September.The news comes on the day that the United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will “stick together” and be ready for the new WSL season, despite Skinner departing.Le Tissier and the rest of the playing squad were informed bySkinner that he would be leaving, in a meeting on Monday morningshortly before the news was announced, and on Tuesday Le Tissier and her England teammate Ella Toone paid tribute to Skinner for his contribution to the club over five years in charge, which included winning the2024 Women’s FA Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLe Tissier said the “energy he brought to the club was amazing”, while Toone told reporters: “He wanted to tell the team before it came out. It was nice that he was able to tell us [and] he was able to say goodbye, because he’s done a lot for the club. We can’t thank him enough for everything he’s done, the hard work and the passion that he’s put into leading this team.”Le Tissier said that neither she nor Toone have been consulted on who the next head coach should be but added: “I think the club have been pretty clear with what they’ve said, bringing through the youth, that’s what something Manchester United has been kind of made for, and they’ve always done that historically. I think they’ve been pretty clear with that. When we speak to the new manager, the ambitions will be clear.“Me and Tooney are at Man United because we want to win and we’ll be doing everything we can to make that happen. We’ve got a great team, a great squad, great girls. I’m ready to do that.“No matter who comes and goes, we’ve always had that togetherness and that fight for each other and we stick together in tough moments. There’s been a few over the years and we’ve always come through as a team, and, yeah, this one might be difficult right now, we’re in the start of pre-season and we want to make sure that we’re 100% ready for the start of the season.“We spoke to the girls today, we’ll stick together, we always do. We’ve got to go out on the pitch, enjoy playing football and being with each other and we’ll get through it.”Explore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meeting | European Union | The Guardian
description: Migration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for Europe
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Migration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for Europe
Content: People wait on the beach in Ceuta for food provided by the Red Cross on Monday after arriving from Morocco.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople wait on the beach in Ceuta for food provided by the Red Cross on Monday after arriving from Morocco.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersEuropean UnionEU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meetingMigration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for EuropeExplainer: Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?Jennifer Rankinin BrusselsTue 4 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU’s top official on migration has criticisedSpain’s plan to regularise undocumented migrantsas “not a good signal” for Europe, after an emergency meeting intended to draw a line under divisions on theCeuta crisis.Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for migration, said that while the EU could not currently see a direct link between events in Ceuta and Spain’s regularisation plan, the policy was “definitely not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.It was a rare note of discord as the EU sought to move on from an acrimonious row, caused after tens of thousands of migrants arrived – and mostly left – the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged video conference on Tuesday, intended to learn lessons from the politically divisive Ceuta crisis and chart next steps.Spain’s government saidat least 75 people had diedtrying to reach the territory last week, although Ceuta authorities on Monday put the death toll at 88, with at least 11 more on the Moroccan side of the border.About 70,000 of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta had left, Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, told reporters on Tuesday. He described the EU meeting as constructive, saying ⁠member states had ​recognised Madrid’s “immediate and efficient” response.View image in fullscreen‘A test of our resilience’: Magnus Brunner speaking on Wednesday.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPABrunner said the past few days had been “a test of our resilience” and the EU’s external border. The situation, he said, was under control; no one had moved to mainland Spain and the EU’s border-free Schengen zone had not been affected.The message of unity came after several EU member states heavily criticised Spain. Twenty two signed a letter, organised by Italy and Denmark, that implicitly criticisedMadrid’s plan to regularise 500,000 undocumented migrants and asylum seekersas a “pull factor” for “illegal migration”. Nearly 1.2 million people have applied for the scheme.Asked about Spain’s regularisation policy, Brunner said it was not discussed on Tuesday, but added: “I always say to this regularisation discussion … it’s not a good signal, definitely not a good signal for the rest of Europe.”He went on: “I do understand that it is a member state’s competence. And I do understand that Spain did it because it’s mainly about Latin Americans speaking the same language, having the same culture, but the signal for the rest of Europe is not a good one, definitely not.”Brunner declined to criticise Italy’s decision to reintroduce air and sea border checks with Spain for one month, afterthe Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said such moves were informed by “prejudice, fake news, ignorance and political interest”.Brunner said any suspension of Schengen rules had to be proportionate and temporary, adding: “I have some understanding of this reaction of the Italians, because the citizens are concerned.”France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said EU ministers had agreed the Schengen zone was “not the problem”. France was one of the few member states not to sign the letter of 22 EU leaders indicating readiness to reintroduce border checks, although it did step up its own controls.Denmark’s interior minister, Morten Bødsko, said he was “very satisfied” with Spain’s handling of the crisis, but doubled down on the message that the EU needed tougher border controls, adding: “Uncontrolled immigration is a threat to Europe and Denmark.”10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestMinisters broadly endorsed a five-point plan set out by European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, who proposedfurther action to strengthen Europe’s external borders, including an early-warning system and better cooperation with non-EU countries on migration.A statement published by the EU council after the meeting said there was “a common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight”.Ministers emphasised the need to improve “situational awareness, which could be achieved by further developing early-warning systems such as pre-frontier intelligence and social media monitoring” and efforts to “counter malicious external actors engaged in foreign information manipulation and interference”, the statement said.The EU’s foreign policy service was investigating the possible role played by Russian disinformation, but it was too early to reach conclusions, Brunner said.Migration has been a deeply divisive issue for the EU since the 2015-16 crisis, when more than a million people sought asylum in the union. As far-right and nationalist parties seek to outflank mainstream rivals on the issue, tensions remain high, despite fewer people making irregular crossings.The EU’s border agency, Frontex, reported 178,000 irregular border crossings in 2025, down 26% on the previous year and the lowest since 2021, when much of Europe was in Covid lockdown.Irregular arrivals in Spain (36,683) were significantly lower than inItaly(66,328) and Greece (51, 399), as well as attempted and successful crossings to the UK (65,891), according to Frontex.The 2015-16 crisis paved the wayfor a sweeping overhaul of the EU’s asylum and migration rules, which came into force in June.Brunner emphasised the need to implement the EU’s migration pact, playing down a suggestion from Greece that further emergency measures were required.The Greek prime minister, Kyriákos Mitsotákis, inan article for Politico, said countries should be able to suspend asylum applications for newly arrived people when facing “exceptional situations of extreme and disproportionate pressure”. Europe was facing the “deliberate instrumentalisation of migration by state and non-state actors”, he wrote, saying the pact did not provide the tools for these scenarios.Brunner disagreed – “the pact does offer solutions for this” – while not ruling out changes, saying EU leaders would discuss a “strategic way forward”.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionSpainItalyMigrationImmigration and asylumEuropePedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdom | X | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook
Content: Yahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist, is one of those affected by the account blocking.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist, is one of those affected by the account blocking.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianXElon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdomExclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and FacebookGeneva AbdulTue 4 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk’s X has become the latest major US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi Arabian dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.Earlier this year, the Guardian reported that platforms includingSnapchat and Meta’s Facebook and Instagramhad blocked dissidents’ accounts over allegations by Saudi authorities that they were violating local law.At the time,X, formerly Twitter, said it had notified users that it had not taken any action following requests by Saudi authorities, and it “strongly believes in defending and respecting the voice of our users”.However, since mid-July more than 60 accounts on the platform have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia through geoblocking, which prevents users inside the kingdom from viewing the content, according to the London-based human rights organisation ALQST.Those affected includeYahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist who runs ALQST, and Abdullah Alaoudh, a US-based activist and vocal critic of Saudi human rights violations. Others affected include exiled activists, Saudi academics and independent media.Alaoudh, a senior policy adviser for Gulf issues at the American Committee for Middle East Rights, said: “I think it’s horrible because we were fighting tyrants back home and now we’re fighting tyrants and their cronies here where we are in exile.“It’s censorship – and what’s even worse is that they did not say we violated X’s rules or Meta’s rules.”Account holders received emails from X informing them that their content had been withheld in the kingdom “in order to comply with X’s obligations under Saudi Arabia’s local laws”.A Saudi decree attached to the letters and seen by the Guardian said the accounts had transmitted material that “infringes on public order, religious values, public morals or the sanctity of private life”.Abdullah Aljuraywi, a monitoring and campaigns officer at ALQST, whose X account was also blocked inside the kingdom, said: “The news was sadly not very surprising, given that the authorities have a long history of silencing criticism at home and treating Saudis who speak out from abroad, especially those still connected to people inside the country, as a threat.“What is even more concerning is that technology companies have helped enable this suppression, instead of protecting the freedom of speech they often say they support.”ALQST has called on X, Meta,Snapchatand YouTube to restore access to the accounts and provide transparency over how the decisions were reached.Meta previously told the Guardian that when it received reports of content violating local law but not the company’s own community standards, the company may restrict the content’s availability in the country where it was alleged to be unlawful.X and the Saudi embassy in London have been approached for comment.Other accounts targeted include those of Ghanem al-Masarir, a prominent Saudi satirist. Earlier this year a British court ordered Saudi Arabia topay him £3m in damagesafter his iPhones were hacked and he was physically attacked outside Harrods in central London.In May, al-Masarir was notified by YouTube that two of his accounts, with more than 800,000 subscribers combined, would be blocked in the kingdom after legal complaints made from a “government entity”. YouTube did not respond to a request for comment.The same month, X emailed al-Masarir informing him of the request from Saudi authorities alleging that his account violated Saudi law, with an attached decree. By July, the company had notified al-Masarir that his content had been withheld in the kingdom to comply with local laws.“I’m not surprised that Saudi has asked to block, but I’m surprised Elon Musk has listened,” al-Masarir said. He predicted “other authoritarian countries around the world” would follow suit.Explore more on these topicsXSaudi ArabiaSnapchatFacebookInstagramMetaInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of people | Guatemala | The Guardian
description: Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert
Content: The Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes.Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes.Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty ImagesGuatemalaGuatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of peopleEruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alertAgence France-Presse in San Juan AlotenangoTue 4 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people living on the slopes ofGuatemala’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning.By Tuesday, rivers of lava were streaming down the 3,763-metre (12,346-foot) volcano, which is located less than 100 kilometres (62 miles) fromGuatemalaCity. Ash rose six kilometres (3.73 miles) into the red sky.“Since early morning it was active. That night, the alarm was raised that we needed to evacuate,” a local resident, Alejandro Garcia, 68, told AFP.Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, Garcia said, describing terrifying scenes of lava tumbling down the mountainside.Firefighters said they transported at least 350 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality.Evacuees are staying in a community hall, where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown.“If there were any chance of moving to a different house, it would be better, because you’re always afraid since the volcano doesn’t give any warning,” Lidia Ortiz, 40, said at the shelter.Escuintla, to the south, was sheltering dozens more families, including children, local authorities reported.“If an evacuation is ordered or conditions pose a risk to your life, follow the principle of self-evacuation,” Conred spokesperson Valeria Urizar said in a video posted on social media.The country’s Institute of Volcanology warned of hot volcanic debris flows down Fuego’s slopes, with communities on the western and southern flanks at the greatest risk.Fuego had been erupting for 23 hours straight by Tuesday morning, it said, although the intensity was easing.“We’ve already gotten used to having the volcano constantly active, but this time it was really too much,” 50-year-old resident Sonia Vasquez said.Guatemalan authorities urged “precautions with air traffic”, but there has so far been no impact on the capital’s international airport.The education ministry ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes in communities within two municipalities near the volcano.Guatemala volcano: rescuers battle boiling ash to recover Fuego’s deadRead moreTraffic police also closed a road encircling the mountain range that connects the south coast with the colonial city of Antigua, the country’s main tourist destination and a Unesco World Heritage site.Guatemala lies on the Pacific ‘ring of fire’ and experiences frequent seismic and volcanic activity.There have been several such mass evacuations in recent years because Fuego erupted.Authorities evacuated more than 500 people last year after Fuego spurted gas and ash, with residents moved to shelters from communities near the crater.Another eruption in 2023 pushed around 1,200 people to evacuate.In 2018,215 people were killed and a similar number left missing when rivers of lava poured down Fuego’s slopesand destroyed a village.Explore more on these topicsGuatemalaVolcanoesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area | Washington state | The Guardian
description: Suspect had a prior conviction for shooting his father in Arizona, reportedly after he told his son to do the dishes
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Suspect had a prior conviction for shooting his father in Arizona, reportedly after he told his son to do the dishes
Content: A view of a neighborhood burned by the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington on Monday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenA view of a neighborhood burned by the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington on Monday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersWashington stateMan charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the areaSuspect had a prior conviction for shooting his father in Arizona, reportedly after he told his son to do the dishesRichard LuscombeTue 4 Aug 2026 16.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities on Monday charged a man inWashington statewith starting a wildfire that has consumed almost 4,000 acres and forced tens of thousands from their homes.Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for setting the Old Trails fire, the largest ofthree devastating wildfiresburning through the region.He was found in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter – and was identified by witnesses who spotted him kneeling in grass close to where the blaze began over the weekend.At apress conferenceon Monday night, John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, said Farinacci had been apprehended quickly.“As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr Farinacci,” Nowels said. “This was fantastic, very quick work by everybody involved.”Nowels also offered details of the suspect, including that he had a prior conviction in Arizona for manslaughter. According to the Phoenix New Times, the victim was Farinacci’s father, who wasshot and killedat their Mesa home in 2010, reportedly after telling his son to do the dishes. Farinacci was later found injured by a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Farinacci, then aged 21, pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. A judge found he was mentally fit to assist in his own defense, though defense lawyer Jose Colon continued to raise questions about his mental health and said that he had been hospitalized multiple times for psychiatric treatment, court records show.Beth Farinacci, who had married Aaron Farinacci’s father, said second-degree murder, not manslaughter, would have been a more appropriate way to resolve that case.“Manslaughter is for when someone accidentally kills another person. It is not for someone who intentionally points a loaded gun at their father and shoots him in his face and back,” she wrote in a letter to the judge.It was also reported that Aaron Farinacci had been contacted by police twice before during fire investigations.Spokane police responded to reports of several fires on 8 July 2025, near Farinacci’s apartment. The area near the Spokane River involved several “bus-sized” fires and prompted a significant emergency response, according to a police record.TheWashington statepatrol made contact with Farinacci the following month while pursuing a suspect in a wildfire at Riverside state park. They found him on a park bench, “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. They took photos of him. He was wearing a green T-shirt just like the one he was seen wearing on Saturday, the document says.Farinacci was expected to make his first court appearance Tuesday, Nowels said, as crews continued to battle the fires that have expanded across the county.The Old Trails fire started on Saturday north-west of downtown Spokane. The blaze jumped the Spokane River and ripped through neighborhoods that some residents were able to return to on Monday.“There’s nothing to save,” said Miriam Sim, 76, as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruined home where they had lived since 2005.In one Spokane neighborhood, blackened vehicles, a boat twisted by the heat and melted plastic recycling bins remained. Across the street, lawns were still green and houses were spared, as residents continued to run hoses or sprinklers to water their properties.More than 67,000 people were told to evacuate the three fires – Old Trail, Autumn Lane and Fairview – that by early Tuesday had burned about 16 sq miles (41 sq km) of Spokane, although orders in some areas were downgraded late on Monday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElsewhere across the state, where extreme high temperatures and a fourth year of drought conditions have taken hold, at least 15 wildfires were burning, covering at least 390 sq miles.Washington state’s entire congressional delegation wrote to Donald Trump on Monday urging the president to approve an expedited emergency declaration. Bob Ferguson, the state’s Democratic governor, said he spoke to the White House over the weekend after making his own emergency declaration.“Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers,” the politicians’ letter said.No deaths or major injuries have been reported, although Cpl Mark Gregory, a spokesperson for the Spokane sheriff’s office, said on Monday that 14 remained unaccounted for. They were, he said, probably people who had not been in contact since evacuating and were not truly missing or in danger.More than 1,000 firefighters, many from out of state, arrived by Monday to help tackle the blazes, a number expected to double in the coming days, authorities said. Crews continued to fight the fires by land and air, with Nowels warning the public during the Monday press conference not to interfere with aerial operations by using drones.Abulletinissued by the National Weather Service (NWS)’s Spokane office on Tuesday morning warned that challenging conditions would persist through the remainder of the week.“Extensive amounts of smoke will continue over the region, maintaining unhealthy air quality,” it said.“Dry conditions and breezy winds increase Friday and Saturday across portions of central Washington, bringing elevated fire weather conditions.”Hundreds of homes, businesses, and other structures have been destroyed in what Dave Upthegrove, Washington’s commissioner of public lands, called “anextraordinary wildfire seasonacross the Pacific north-west”.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsWashington stateWest CoastWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Devastating LA wildfire sparked by utility company tower, long-awaited report finds | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower
Content: Trees sway in high winds as the Eaton Fire burns in Altadena in January last year.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APView image in fullscreenTrees sway in high winds as the Eaton Fire burns in Altadena in January last year.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APLos AngelesDevastating LA wildfire sparked by utility company tower, long-awaited report findsInvestigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service towerAssociated PressTue 4 Aug 2026 15.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe deadly 2025 Eaton fire in theLos Angelesarea was caused by equipment belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday.Los Angeles county fire officials found that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service, according to the report.“After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service SouthernCaliforniaEdison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement.It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 sq miles (57 sq km).View image in fullscreenThe Eaton fire in Altadena in January 2025.Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty ImagesKathleen Dunleavy, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, said the utility had received the report and was reviewing it.“We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning,” Dunleavy said. She said SCE previously acknowledged “it was likely our equipment was associated with the ignition of the Eaton fire”.She said the utility continued to support the communityas it recovers.SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles county agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena.The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles county declined to comment about the latest court filings.The Los Angeles county arson fire investigation unit jointly conducted the investigation with California department of forestry and fire protection. It found electrical arcing on the utility’s out-of-service tower sparked the dry brush below and that the utility was responsible for maintaining and operating its electrical lines and equipment “in a manner that would minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfire posed by them.”Their homes burned in the LA wildfires. A year later, thousands still can’t returnRead moreThe blaze was sparked during extreme weather conditions that included high temperatures, low humidity and powerful winds. Two “electrical arcing events” occurred in quick succession, causing an unknown burning material to fall from the tower to the ground below, according to the report.Within 12 seconds, dry grass and brush was ignited and the fire swiftly developed “into a conflagration engulfing the areas of the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre and La Cañada Flintridge”, the report said. It took more than two weeks to fully contain the wildfire.The report cites an interview with a Pasadena resident who called 911 on 7 January after spotting flames across the canyon from his home’s rear window. The caller described it “as a 10in x 10in fire at the base of a high-voltage electrical tower”, the report said.The Eaton fire burned at the same time as the Palisades fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views.The man accused of sparking the Palisades fire will be tried again this fall after his first federal arson caseended in a mistrialin June. Prosecutors said Jonathan Rinderknecht used a barbecue lighter on 1 January 2025 to spark a blaze that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up 7 January.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesWildfiresCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nobody cares’: the Turkish farmers bearing the burden of UK’s plastic waste problem  | Plastics | The Guardian
description: Britain exported 139,000 tonnes of rubbish to Turkey last year, leaving smallholders and poor districts of Adana to cope with the debris, microplastics and toxic smoke
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: Britain exported 139,000 tonnes of rubbish to Turkey last year, leaving smallholders and poor districts of Adana to cope with the debris, microplastics and toxic smoke
Content: Plastic waste dumped and burned in Adana, Turkey, 2021.Photograph: Caner Ozkan/Greenpeace/PAView image in fullscreenPlastic waste dumped and burned in Adana, Turkey, 2021.Photograph: Caner Ozkan/Greenpeace/PASeascape: the state of our oceansPlastics‘Nobody cares’: the Turkish farmers bearing the burden of UK’s plastic waste problemBritain exported 139,000 tonnes of rubbish to Turkey last year, leaving smallholders and poor districts of Adana to cope with the debris, microplastics and toxic smokeUK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartlandSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighand Ayça Aldatmaz in AdanaTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlastic debris clings to the reeds in a waterway metres from where Ayhan*, a farmer in Adana, southernTurkey, is harvesting aubergines. “We get pollution from all sides here,” he says, referring to the plastic recycling zone upstream, as well as a nearby textile plant that he suspects is making the water acidic. “The plastics are all there, by the bank, and the fumes come this way.”Between May 2021 and July 2024, 13 British companies sent 545 shipments of household and supermarket plastic waste, totalling 52,000 tonnes, to the Kemal Deniz recycling zone, under a mile from Ayhan’s aubergine fields, according to data analysed for the Guardian by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), an international NGO.New research has also been sharedwith the Guardian that shows high levels of microplastics, as well as plastic debris, in Adana’s waterways, including one next to Kemal Deniz.Fires from abandoned piles of unrecyclable plastic in the region create toxic smoke over neighbourhoods and fields, locals said.“Every year we install the greenhouse tarps, and when we bring them down we have to clean the surface because we find a black coating, coming from the fumes of these places,” says Ayhan.In January, canal water flooded on to his land after heavy rain, destroying seven hectares (17 acres) of crops, he claims. “We had to plant new ones. But what can we do? Nothing. Nowhere to file a complaint – nobody cares.”View image in fullscreenA recycling facility by a canal in Adana.Photograph: Ayça AldatmazAdana sits in Turkey’s Çukurova plain, one of the country’s most fertile regions, rich in cotton, soya beans and citrus fruits.But sinceChina’s 2018 banon plastic waste imports, Turkey has become the primary destination for plastic waste from the EU and UK. Adana receives 60% of Turkey’s plastic waste imports – an influx that has overwhelmed local treatment infrastructure and sparked widespread illegal activities, including dumping and burning, according toinvestigations by environmental groupsand journalists.Sedat Gündoğdu, a Turkish marine biologist at Sabancı University’s Istanbul Policy Center, who has been monitoring pollution in the region, says many of the recycling facilities discharge wastewater directly into canals and channels used for irrigation.Samples of water he took from a canal downstream from Kemal Deniz, adjacent to Ayhan’s fields, show a 10-fold increase in concentrations of microplastics compared with sites upstream, according toresearch he publishedin Environmental Monitoring and Assessment.Ayhan does not use the canal for irrigation, but the waterway next to his fields feeds into other canals that are used by farmers to water their crops, according to Gündoğdu.“[The recycling facilities] are discharging this polluted water into the canals,” Gündoğdu says. “Farmers then use that water as an irrigation source.” He also found pellets, films and fragments “highly characteristic of recycling processing” waste.He found that other canals downstream of recycling facilities in Adana separate from those in Kemal Deniz had even greater concentrations: at 132-fold that of upstream. The canal network traverses agricultural fields, leading to the Seyhan River and ultimately the Mediterranean Sea.View image in fullscreen‘The plastics are all there, by the bank.’ Unrecyclable waste is often just dumped in Kemal Deniz.Photograph: Ayça AldatmazThe Kemal Deniz zone is a sprawling, heavily guarded site that houses a series of storage warehouses and recycling facilities, some with the names of Turkish recycling companies, some with no visible identification. Piles of plastic lie scattered around the site, outside and inside the facilities. Security guards on motorcycles patrol the dirt roads around it.An analysis of import/export data carried out for the Guardian by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) found that 13% of the UK’s exported plastic waste to Turkey was sent to the Kemal Deniz zone between May 2021 and July 2024. Thirteen British companies shipped waste, the top three exporters being ProtoGreen, Vanden and Eurokey.There is no suggestion that, by shipping plastic waste to Turkey, the British companies are doing anything illegal. The companies do, however, have a duty under various regulations to ensure the plastic they export is recycled in an environmentally sound manner.Turkey is the third-highest contributor to plastic leakage into the Mediterranean from mismanaged waste after Egypt and Italy, according to a2020 International Union for Conservation of Nature report.From entanglement and ingestion by marine species to the disruption of food chains, plastic wreaks havoc on marine life. Microplastics have also been found tohinder photosynthesisin plants and marine algae, the foundation of the ocean food web.People living near the Kemal Deniz zone who have spoken to the Guardian say fires from waste plants in Adana create toxic smoke over residential areas four to five times a year.View image in fullscreenSome canals in Kemal Deniz have 132 times the level of microplastics seen upstream of recycling plants.Photograph: MikeDotta/ShutterstockThe city is divided along socioeconomic lines: the north, where the wealthy live, and the south, made up of poorer residents and migrants, where the recycling facilities are located, according to Yaşar Gökoğlu, a spokesman for the environmental group Adana Ecology Platform.“Even under normal working conditions, chemical pollution, water, air and soil pollution negatively affect their lives,” he says.Last year, residents protested with Adana Ecology Platform outside the city law courts, after a blaze at a recycling facility near the Küçükdikili neighbourhood burned for 36 hours, creating a plume of thick toxic smoke that settled over the neighbourhood and nearby fields. The fenced-off facility is just over a mile north-west of the Kemal Deniz recycling zone. Fires have also happened at Kemal Deniz, according toreports.A graph showing the levels of plastic waste sent to Turkey by the EU and UK between 2016-25.Unlike the facilities at Kemal Deniz – which, the Guardian has established, is supplied by British companies – we could not determine whether the plastic waste entering this facility, half a mile west of Küçükdikili, was imported or domestic. However, a pile of waste that included British packaging was dumped on the roadside nearby.A businessman, who spoke on condition of anonymity, says: “Every month, between the first and fifth of the month, deliveries come. Trucks line up during those days on the street leading to the facilities.“There are fires every summer in this area; there is a school right next to it. The neighbourhood is really concerned about it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe man said he had written a letter of complaint about the facility, but had not sent it. “Who is going to care?” he says.View image in fullscreenA protest by local residents and the Adana Ecology Platform environmental group. The banner reads: ‘Plastic waste imports should be banned.’Photograph: Umut ÖzşimşekMuch of the plastic arriving in Adana includes mixed, dirty and contaminated plastic that ends up abandoned and burned, according to local people. TheUnion of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects estimatesthat unrecyclable material makes up almost 50% of the country’s plastic waste imports from the EU.The UK, one of the world’s largest exporters of plastic waste, shipped out 675,000 tonnes in 2025 – its largest amount in eight years – of which almost140,000 tonneswas shipped to Turkey. The EU’s plastic waste exports to Turkey that yearreached more than 500,000 tonnes.But while theEU has recently imposed stricter controlson its plastic waste exports to prevent environmental exploitation abroad, the UK government continues to export plastic waste – to countries not part of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, a club of wealthy countries.Amy Youngman, a legal specialist at the EIA, said: “The highest pollution levels in [Gündoğdu’s] study are directly linked to identifiable industrial sources. UK waste drives the very operations contributing to this pollution, and without it this harm would not occur at this scale, if at all.”View image in fullscreenA recycling plant in Kemal Deniz. The EU exported more than 500,000 tonnes of plastic waste to Turkey in 2025.Photograph: Ayça Aldatmaz“The UK should take immediate action to end this colonial practice by phasing out plastic waste exports, strengthening traceability and enforcement, regulating microplastics and reducing plastic production to address the root causes of pollution,” she said.James McLeary, the managing director of Biffa Polymers, said the UK needed to take “greater responsibility” for its own plastic waste and has called for targeted reforms. “Plastic waste should be processed within controlled environments in the UK wherever possible, rather than exported,” he said.The UK government should ban the export of unprocessed plastic waste, reform the current system that incentivises exporting plastic waste rather than recycling it domestically and support domestic recycling, he added.Over recent years, 21 plastic recycling and processing facilities have closed in the UK.A spokesperson for Eurokey, one of the top three UK exporters of waste to Turkey, said it only worked with “accredited partners” approved by the UK environment agency, and was surprised to learn of the findings. It no longer sent plastic waste to Turkey, they said.View image in fullscreenWaste bearing the logos of UK brands by the side of a road.Photograph: Ayça Aldatmaz“The reason plastic waste is sent abroad is that there is not enough domestic infrastructure to deal with it, but Eurokey is building its own recycling plant in Corby to address this,” they added.A spokesperson for Vanden, another top exporter of waste to Turkey, said: “Any evidence of environmental harm should be investigated by the appropriate competent authority in Turkey.”Vanden undertook assessments, they said, including visits and inspections of Turkish recycling facilities via representatives in the country.While “no regulatory system can eliminate the risk of non-compliance by individual operators”, they said it would be “inaccurate” to characterise Turkey’s plastic waste import regime as unregulated. The spokesperson added that controls at national and facility level had “strengthened considerably” over recent years.“We recognise the importance of ensuring that materials exported from the UK are recovered in an environmentally sound manner, and we support robust oversight throughout the recycling supply chain.”ProtoGreen declined to comment.ADepartment for Environment, Food and Rural Affairsspokesperson said: “There are already strict controls in place on the export of waste set out in UK legislation.“Businesses involved in the export of waste from the UK are required to ensure that the waste they ship is managed in an environmentally sound manner, and we have already taken action to further reduce our need to export plastic waste.”The Turkish government was approached for comment but did not respond.*Name has been changed to protectidentityExplore more on these topicsPlasticsSeascape: the state of our oceansRecyclingEthical and green livingWastePlastic bagsPollutionTurkeyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK plastic manufacturer could face legal action over toxic emissions | Chemical industry | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzene
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Exclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzene
Content: Huntsman Polyurethanes’ chemical plant is in Teesside, north-east England.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenHuntsman Polyurethanes’ chemical plant is in Teesside, north-east England.Photograph: HandoutChemical industryUK plastic manufacturer could face legal action over toxic emissionsExclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzenePippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA plastic manufacturer in the north ofEnglandis facing potential legal action over emissions of benzene, a carcinogenic chemical with no safe level, the Guardian can reveal.TheEnvironment Agency(EA) is considering taking legal action against Huntsman Polyurethanes in Teesside for a potential breach of licence, which is a criminal offence.Campaigners say it has shone a light on the toxic nature of the global plastics industry and that workers and the local community have been put at risk.Huntsman Polyurethanes, a petrochemical company that manufactures chemicals to produce plastic, sits within the sprawling Teesside chemical cluster in the seaside town of Redcar, North Yorkshire. The factory is part of Huntsman Corporation, a publicly traded global producer and marketer of chemical products whichboastedrevenues of $6bn in 2025.In 2023, Huntsman decommissioned a process that was reducing its benzene air emissions and replaced it with an alternative method controlled by a third party.However, EA documents show this new process “periodically paused”, with benzene consequently emitted directly to the air. The documents also show the EA was aware of this problem in 2023, but did not investigate until this year.During this time, the benzene emissions from the site rose from 13 tonnes in 2022 to 17 tonnes in 2024, according to EA records.Benzene, which is used to make some plastics, is carcinogenic to humans andcausesleukaemia. According to theWorld Health Organizationthere is no safe level of exposure.In an inspection report from March, the EA recorded several permit breaches in relation to the benzene emissions. The document states benzene is a carcinogen and it is “reasonably foreseeable that the deficiencies in the management system will cause multiple emissions, that when agglomerated, may result in a significant impact on the environment or human health until resolved through compliance”.Failure to comply with an environmental permit is a criminal offence.A Huntsman spokesperson said the benzene emissions were not illegal and were “fully compliant with our permit conditions”.However, the EA told the Guardian: “We are considering further enforcement action with our legal team in relation to these permit breaches and have informed the UK Health Security Agency and the Health and Safety Executive so that they can assess any public or occupational health risks”.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreHuntsman was instructed by the EA to carry out modelling to assess the impact of the benzene emissions in March 2026. The modelling found “significant” breaches of air quality standards in all scenarios considered. These standards are legally binding and are set to protect human health from toxic pollutants. In one scenario, the benzene emissions were predicted to exceed the 24-hour limit by 933%.However, the EA told the Guardian an internal review of the modelling found the impacts to be “not insignificant but predicted environmental concentrations remain below the relevant environmental standards”.“Our air quality experts have assessed environmental and human health impacts – their feedback indicates that these emissions do not pose a significant risk to local sites such as nearby schools,” the spokesperson added.However, David Santillo, a senior scientist with the Greenpeace Research Laboratories at the University of Exeter, said these emissions are “very significant” and described the Environment Agency’s slow action as a “travesty”.“The Environment Agency should be there to prevent this kind of thing, not just to document it and request more and more reports,” he said.The EA said Huntsman “failed to act proactively” but it also “recognised that further follow-up sooner could have supported more timely implementation”. It added that its recent interventions have led to “significantly improved performance of the abatement system on site”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlly Lewis, professor of atmospheric chemistry at the University of York, said benzene is one of the most harmful air pollutants to human health and that the EA “seems to be allowing an obvious degradation in air quality and an increase in a pollutant that causes cancer on the basis that it’s fine as long as you stay below a somewhat arbitrary value”.“If this is our national approach to managing risk and chemicals it seems remarkably laissez-faire and hands off,” he said.Roel Vermeulen, professor of environmental epidemiology and exposome science at Utrecht University, said the modelling report flags a plausible problem that should be taken “very seriously”.He said measurements of the benzene levels outside people’s homes and in other places in the community should “begin immediately” and this should be in parallel with reducing emissions.A spokesperson from Huntsman said its own air monitoring data “indicates that concentrations beyond the site boundary are below applicable air quality standards”. It also said its “long-term personal monitoring programme highlights that there are no real-world instances of exceedance of exposure limits for personnel on site.” The company refused to share this data with the Guardian and has not shared it with the EA.Campaigners say the benzene emissions from this factory point to a broader problem with the global plastic industry. A recentGreenpeace reportsaid pollution from plastic waste is only one aspect of the “devastating impacts of plastics”, with the hazardous chemicals used in plastic production also “poisoning people and the natural world”.International researchhas linked living close to plastic production facilities with negative health outcomes. TheBoston College Global Observatoryfound that plastic production workers are at increased risk of a range of cancers, including leukaemia.“You can’t manufacture plastics without creating pollution and the plastics then create pollution of their own. It’s a messy business right the way through,” Santillo said.Carole Zagrovic, who worked as a community development specialist in Redcar for Friends of the Earth for around a decade in the early 2000s, said back then people in the area “talked about cancer like it’s the flu. They had become blase and hardened towards it,” she said.Zagrovic said she was “appalled” that pollution like this was ongoing and said it seemed like nothing had changed despite her years of campaigning.A spokesperson for Huntsman said: “Huntsman’s benzene emissions are fully compliant with our permit conditions, including our 2024 emissions, as governed by the Environment Agency.”An EA spokesperson said: “We have been carrying out extensive regulatory work in response to concerns about emissions from this site, including inspections and compliance reporting which uncovered several breaches. We are considering further enforcement action in relation to these breaches and are working with the operator to ensure site improvements are rapidly delivered, due to our action, controls have been improved and emissions associated with process vent gases have reduced significantly since early February.”Explore more on these topicsChemical industryEnglandEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Campaign warns of perils UK waters can pose for dogs and owners | Dogs | The Guardian
description: Dogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or people
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Dogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or people
Content: Emma-Jane Thomas with Bruno: ‘We’ve had all this hot weather … and it’s easy to not realise the dangers.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma-Jane Thomas with Bruno: ‘We’ve had all this hot weather … and it’s easy to not realise the dangers.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDogsCampaign warns of perils UK waters can pose for dogs and ownersDogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or peopleNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith its gentle rippling water, tall purple flowers and rustling trees, Earlswood Lakes near Solihull in the West Midlands seems the perfect spot for dogs to paddle. But their owners have been warned that the otherwise idyllic open water could prove perilous to pets.“We’ve had all this hot weather and millions of families are now spending time around open bodies of water, and it’s easy to not realise the dangers,” said Emma-Jane Thomas, rehoming manager atDogsTrust Kenilworth during a walk around Earlswood.“Dogs love water and it’s great exercise and enrichment for them. However, not all dogs are natural swimmers,” she added. “Even strong swimmers can get into difficulties in the water.”Accompanying Thomas is Bruno the dalmatian who is clearly eager to go for a dip. But he’s been kept on a short lead. Dogs Trust has launched a new campaign with the catchline “If in doubt, keep your dog out”, in an attempt to reduce the injuries and fatalities that can occur among dogs and their owners around lakes, canals, rivers and the sea.Data from the Royal National Lifeboat Institute obtained by Dogs Trust shows that 308 dog-related incidents in open water in the UK were recorded between 2021 and 2025, almost all taking place on the coast. About a third occurred between June and September of those years.Separate figures from the National Water Safety Forum show there were 10 accidental deaths due to drowning in England between 2019 and 2025 linked to animal rescue, and 12 linked to dog walking.Data from the Canal & River Trust shows that dog-related incidents in the UK reached a five-year high in 2025, increasing by 39% compared with the previous year.Dogs Trust notes that many cases were related to dogs – or people attempting to rescue them – needing help after entering the water. Strong currents and fatigue can pose a risk, too.“When you’re thinking about open bodies of water, it’s always stop, check and think about what could be the dangers,” said Thomas, noting many are not clearly visible on first sight. “Steep banks could be an issue if a dog gets in and then swims around, [and] can’t find a way out again,” she said. “Hidden debris under the water – trolleys, broken glass, lots of weeds or branches. Blue-green algae is a danger to dogs.”View image in fullscreenSign alerting walkers at Earlswood to dangers of blue-green algae.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThomas also cautioned against attempting a rescue should a dog get into trouble.“If your dog’s in difficulty, it could then be two emergencies, not just one,” she said. “If you can see a safe place where your dog can exit the water, call your dog there with their recall. If you can’t do that, call emergency services and they will come and assist with dog emergencies.”Even on a picturesque summer’s day Earlswood is far from hazard-free, with a small yellow sign alerting walkers to dangers of blue-green algae.Such cyanobacteria thrive in warmer weather, forming blooms and scums – and some release toxins.“Not all blue-green algae blooms and scums are toxic, but you can’t tell just by looking at them, so it’s best to assume they are,” theEnvironment Agency notes.Emily Mills, veterinary projects manager at Dogs Trust, said: “Dogs can become unwell from drinking contaminated water or simply cleaning it from their fur after swimming. Symptoms can be seen as little as 15 minutes after exposure and may progress rapidly to become fatal.”Walking her rescue border collie Billy, local resident Sally said the blue-green algae was a concern – adding that Billy was always kept on a lead.View image in fullscreenBlue-green algae can contain toxins.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“But there’s more dogs off the lead than on the lead when you walk around here. And it is a worry that there isn’t enough signage around,” she said.An online Dogs Trust survey of 2,000 owners in the UK, conducted in June, revealed that many may be unaware of such risks, with 33% reporting they did not believe blue-green algae posed a serious risk to dogs.The survey also found 19% of dog owners were unaware calm-looking water can still pose serious risks, and 80% said they’d enter water to rescue their dog, despite the risk to themselves.“Dogs love the water, we know that, and we absolutely don’t want to stop that,” said Thomas. “The reason that we’ve put the campaign out is so that owners and dogs can continue to enjoy these types of areas safely, so that when they do come here, they are aware of the risks.”Explore more on these topicsDogsAnimalsPetsHealth & wellbeingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey gives UK poetry sales an epic boost | Books | The Guardian
description: Poetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poem
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Poetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poem
Content: Bringing Homer to a new audience. … Matt Damon (Odysseus) and Zendaya (Athena) in The Odyssey, directed by Christopher Nolan.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenBringing Homer to a new audience. … Matt Damon (Odysseus) and Zendaya (Athena) in The Odyssey, directed by Christopher Nolan.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesBooksChristopher Nolan’s The Odyssey gives UK poetry sales an epic boostPoetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poemEmma LoffhagenTue 4 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK poetry sales are on course to reach a record high this year, buoyed by the success ofChristopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptationof Homer’s The Odyssey.Poetry sales surpassed £8m during the first 30 weeks of 2026, an increase of 13.3% on the same period last year, according to data from market researchers NielsenIQ.The category is expected to exceed £15m in annual sales for the first time since accurate records began and could reach £17m if its current momentum continues through the autumn.Homer’s 2,700-year-old epic poem has accounted for a significant share of this year’s growth after Nolan’s adaptation – starring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Anne Hathaway – brought the ancient Greek epic to a new audience. UK print sales ofThe Odysseyincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.Editions of The Odyssey and The Iliad have generated £980,000 in poetry sales so far this year – equivalent to £1.20 of every £10 spent on poetry books in Britain.Nolan’s adaptationstormed the global box office,taking $264m (£198m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening.The Odyssey by Homer, translated by Emily WilsonHomer could now challenge the record for the highest annual sales by a poet in the UK. The current benchmark was set by Canadian poet and Instagram sensationRupi Kaur,whose books, such as 2015 hit Milk and Honey, generated £1.2m through NielsenIQ BookScan’s Total Consumer Market in 2017.The Nolan effect is also being felt in the US. Print sales across all editions of The Odyssey areup 76% so far this year,according to Circana BookScan figures.But the poetry boom extends well beyond ancient epic. Even when sales of The Odyssey and The Iliad are removed from this year’s and last year’s figures, the category is still up 7.2% and remains on course for its best year. The three years from 2023 to 2025 were the category’s most lucrative on record.Much of this has been driven by more commercial, social media-friendly poets. Scottish writer Donna Ashworth remains Britain’s bestselling living poet of the decade, with her 2025 collection To the Women selling almost 34,000 copies this year. However some traditionalists have questioned whether her uplifting, aphoristic work is poetry or self-help.“The poetry sector was already enjoying an upwards trajectory before Chris Nolan tackled The Odyssey, helped in recent years by the popularity of Instapoets, including Rupi Kaur, repositioning the poetry sector from a more academic category into a lifestyle, gift and self-development genre,” said Philip Stone at NielsenIQ.The year’s breakout poetry bestseller is from the London-based actor and poet Lucas Jones, whose debut collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, is 2026’s bestselling poetry title by value, generating £400,000, according to the Bookseller.Classicist Emily Wilson’s acclaimed 2017 translation has been the main beneficiary of The Odyssey’s surge in sales.Wilson herself made headlines last week whenshe criticised the film,saying “it has nothing convincing to say” and that it “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”.In a scathing article for the London Review of Books, she wrote: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”She added: “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”Audiobook versions of The Odyssey have also experienced renewed interest: Stephen Fry’s reading has entered Spotify’s UK audiobook top 10, while Ian McKellen’s narration has appeared in the equivalent US chart.Explore more on these topicsBooksPoetryHomerThe OdysseyChristopher NolanFilm adaptationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Star Wars dubbed into Welsh for first time for S4C broadcast | Wales | The Guardian
description: Rhys Ifans, Matthew Rhys, Aimee-Ffion Edwards and Mark Lewis Jones among actors voicing characters from 1977 blockbuster
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Rhys Ifans, Matthew Rhys, Aimee-Ffion Edwards and Mark Lewis Jones among actors voicing characters from 1977 blockbuster
Content: The classic 1977 movie Star Wars has been dubbed into Welsh – Cymraeg – for the first time.Photograph: Lucasfilm/DisneyView image in fullscreenThe classic 1977 movie Star Wars has been dubbed into Welsh – Cymraeg – for the first time.Photograph: Lucasfilm/DisneyWalesStar Wars dubbed into Welsh for first time for S4C broadcastRhys Ifans, Matthew Rhys, Aimee-Ffion Edwards and Mark Lewis Jones among actors voicing characters from 1977 blockbusterSteven MorrisTue 4 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are a few links between theStar Warsfranchise and Wales, including the secretive building of the Millennium Falcon in an old hangar in the far south-west of the Celtic nation.But until now, speakers of Welsh – Cymraeg – have not been able to hear the words of Luke Skywalker, Han Solo and Princess Leia spoken in their own language.On Tuesday, however, it was revealed that a Welsh-language version of the 1977 blockbuster Star Wars will be shown on the Welsh television channelS4Cand its platforms from Christmas Day.Rhys Ifans, who has appeared in Harry Potter and Spider-Man films as well as Notting Hill, voices the Jedi master Obi-Wan Kenobi.Matthew Rhys, a winner of a Primetime Emmy, voices Han Solo, and Aimee-Ffion Edwards, best known for her roles in Peaky Blinders and Slow Horses, is Princess Leia.Mark Lewis Jones, who had a role in the 2017 Star Wars film The Last Jedi, is the Welsh Darth Vader.The rising talent Osian Morgan voices Luke Skywalker, and Rhys Ifans’s brother, Llŷr, C-3PO. The Ifans siblings won plaudits for their 1997 cult film Twin Town.The announcement was made at the National Eisteddfod, the vast music and poetry festival taking place in Pembrokeshire.View image in fullscreenThe National Eisteddfod was held this year in the Garreg Las area near Cardigan, North Pembrokeshire.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianThe Welsh version of the film has been produced by Lucasfilm and Disney in collaboration with S4C and the Welsh government via its CreativeWalesagency. Its Welsh title is Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (New Hope), reflecting the 1977 film’s later title on reissue, Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope.The producer Michael Kohn, the director of distribution operations at Lucasfilm, said the company was excited about the project, which coincides with the movie’s 50th anniversary in 2027.“I’ve been involved in a few Indigenous dubs of Star Wars over the years that aim to preserve and revitalise interest in learning the language,” Kohn said. “They have been tremendously successful not only in their communities but internationally as well. The chance to celebrate the Welsh language through Star Wars is one we couldn’t pass up.”A version of the Millennium Falconwas created at a hangar at Pembroke Dock,not far from the current Eisteddfod site. Built out of wood and steel in 1979 for Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back, released in 1980, it was constructed under the code name “Magic Roundabout”, though local people knew what was going on.View image in fullscreenA 2022 exhibition at Pembroke Dock, west Wales, told the story of how, in the 1970s, a version of the Millennium Falcon was secretly built there.Photograph: Martin Cavaney/Pembroke DockScenes for Lucasfilm’s 1988 fantasy film Willow and the 2024 television series Star Wars: The Acolyte were also shot in Wales.Another Welsh connection is the Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan, who was born in Pembrokeshire.“Wales has such a rich history of storytelling and a beautiful lyrical language,” Brennan said. “We have never before had a translation of Star Wars into Welsh and I am so thankful, that in celebration of our 50th anniversary, we have been able to work with some incredible Welsh talent to make that a reality.“Welsh speakers will finally be able to enjoy the film in our native language and my hope is that it will have the same emotional impact as if you were watching the film again for the first time.”View image in fullscreenStar Wars characters in Cardiff  last year.Photograph: Ian Cook/CameraSport/Getty ImagesGeraint Evans, the S4C chief executive, said: “It’s such an iconic film to so many generations of fans across the world. It’s a fantastic opportunity to promote the Welsh language.”The Welsh government is aiming to have a million people speaking Cymraeg by 2050.The first minister,Rhun ap Iorwerth, who is fluent in Welsh, said Star Wars was one of the most influential films of his childhood.“Its appeal shows no sign of waning,” he said. “To see a Welsh-language version, using the talents of some of our best actors, is fantastic. We already produce world-class TV and film here in Wales and I’m really looking forward to seeing Star Wars in Welsh.”And yes, there is a very nice translation for “May the force be with you”: “A boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi.”As for the beloved opening line, “A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away …” : “Amser maith yn ôl, mewn galaeth bell bell i ffwrdd...”Explore more on these topicsWalesStar WarsS4CRhys IfansTelevisionScience fiction and fantasy filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Calls for UK bank tax to fund cost of living help as HSBC profits hit £7.5bn | Banking | The Guardian
description: Levy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaigners
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Levy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaigners
Content: HSBC profits rose 60% year on year in the three months to the end of June.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAView image in fullscreenHSBC profits rose 60% year on year in the three months to the end of June.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PABankingCalls for UK bank tax to fund cost of living help as HSBC profits hit £7.5bnLevy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaignersKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 06.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCampaigners have renewed calls for a windfall tax on UK banks that could raise £19bn towards Andy Burnham’s cost of living agenda, afterHSBCraked in $10.1bn (£7.5bn) worth of profits in the second quarter of the year.Bosses at HSBC reported on Tuesday that profits rose 60% year on year in the three months to the end of June, helped by fees from wealth management and insurance business, as well as higher interest rates, which allow the bank to charge more for loans and mortgages.The HSBC chief executive, Georges Elhedery, said he would consider increasing banker bonuses on the back of the strong results and planned to restart a share buy-back programme that had been on pause since last year.HSBC to close all branches and pull out of Australian retail banking marketRead moreIt brings collective profits for the four largest banks – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – to £29.2bn over the first six months of the year, putting lendersback in the crosshairs of campaigners, including Positive Money and the Trades Union Congress, who are calling for a fresh tax on the lucrative industry.The campaign group Positive Money said bank bosses had pledged nearly half of their profits – a total of £13.7bn – to shareholders through dividends and share buy-backs, proving they could easily shoulder a tax that they calculated could ultimately raise £19bn towards the government’sspending plans at the October budget.Positive Money said the government could replicate Spain’s levy, targeting any UK revenues above £800m with a 38% tax, in line with the energy profits levy introduced for oil and gas companiesannounced by the Tory government in 2022.They said the resulting £19bn would be enough to cover the cost of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut from electricity bills (worth £850m), the £2 cap on bus fares (worth £500m) and the business rates cut for pubs, clubs and music venues (worth £100m) more than 13 times over.“Previous governments have allowed the powerful banking lobby to persuade them against taxing these record-breaking profits in recent years, despite overwhelming public support for the policy,” said the co-director of Positive Money, Sara Hall.“We’re calling on Andy Burnham to break with his predecessors by resisting the demands of City lobbyists and reclaiming these lost billions with a windfall tax on bank profits, the proceeds of which could be used to fund truly life-changing support for the households and businesses struggling to pay their bills right now.”Banking bosses have been cautious when asked about their views on a fresh tax rise. They told journalists over the past week that they were encouraged by Burnham’s economic vision, but stressed that their ability to lend money to businesses was crucial for the new prime minister’s growth ambitions. “UK growth requires strong banks,” Elhedery said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut advocates of a tax remain undeterred, and the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “There is now a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can easily afford to pay more tax. While higher interest rates have meant mortgage misery and bigger bills for the rest of us, the big banks have been rolling in it.”Joanne O’Neill, the co-director of advocacy and influencing at ActionAid UK, said the government should also take “meaningful action” to hold UK banks to account for their impact on the climate and human rights.“ActionAid research has shownhow HSBC funnelled billions into fossil fuels and industrial agriculture companies between 2021 and 2023, helping to fuel environmental destruction. And since then it has watered down its climate commitments, further shirking its responsibility to help bring about the just transition we need,” O’Neill said, adding that banks should face a “polluters pay tax” that fairly reflected their responsibility for financing and causing climate harm.Metro Bank followed its big four competitors in reporting bumper profits for the first half of the year.
