The challenger bank reported a 38% jump in pre-tax profits on Tuesday morning to £60.7m over the first six months of 2026, after a jump in corporate, SME and specialist mortgage lending, as Metro tried to corner “underserved markets” to boost profits.While the strong rise in profits will add weight to calls for a UK windfall tax, Metro would probably escape Positive Money’s proposals.The bank reported about £241.5m in underlying net interest income for the first six months of the year, and if repeated, would keep its full-year figure below the campaigner’s £800m threshold.Explore more on these topicsBankingHSBCTax and spendingUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests | India | The Guardian
description: Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
Content: Nationwide protests erupted after exam paper leaks and have encompassed growing anger at the India government and the prospects for young people in the country.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAView image in fullscreenNationwide protests erupted after exam paper leaks and have encompassed growing anger at the India government and the prospects for young people in the country.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAIndiaIndia’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protestsOpposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP supportPenelope MacRaein DelhiTue 4 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks thatforced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure.Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs.The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state.Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment.View image in fullscreenPrashant Kishor won the byelection for his fledgling Jan Suraaj party. He said he win was a wake-up call for Modi.Photograph: Hindustan Times/Getty ImagesDeepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.”The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of WorkingIndiareport by Azim Premji University.The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined.The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign.India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiRead moreAfter he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds.A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests.The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook.The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content.The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status.“The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said.Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.”But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: New York deputy police commissioner fired after attempted murder arrest | New York | The Guardian
description: Mount Vernon official is accused of driving getaway car after son allegedly opened fire outside Bronx court
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Mount Vernon official is accused of driving getaway car after son allegedly opened fire outside Bronx court
Content: The city of Mount Vernon said in an Instagram post that it had terminated Jennifer Lackard.Photograph: Google MapsView image in fullscreenThe city of Mount Vernon said in an Instagram post that it had terminated Jennifer Lackard.Photograph: Google MapsNew YorkNew York deputy police commissioner fired after attempted murder arrestMount Vernon official is accused of driving getaway car after son allegedly opened fire outside Bronx courtRichard LuscombeTue 4 Aug 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 20.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleANew Yorkstate police department fired its deputy commissioner on Tuesday after she allegedly acted as a getaway driver for her son in what is being investigated as an attempted murder.The city of Mount Vernon said in anInstagram postthat it had terminated Jennifer Lackard, deputy police commissioner for safety, for conduct “unrelated to her duties”.Lackard, 49, and her 20-year-old son Chase were arrested in an early morning raid on Tuesday at their home in New York City’s Bronx borough, according to theNew York Daily News, citing “police sources”.The newspaper said the pair were charged with attempted murder, attempted assault, gun possession, conspiracy and reckless endangerment, in connection with shots that were fired at a group of people outside Bronx criminal court on 29 June.Chase Lackard was the alleged gunman, according to the Daily News – and jumped into a car that was driven from the scene at speed by his mother.Nobody was struck or injured during the shooting.The Mount Vernon statement referenced the charges against Lackard in its announcement of her firing. The announcement described her as the city’s former deputy police commissioner of wellness.“The Mount Vernon police department is aware of the criminal charges filed by the Bronx county district attorney’s office against former deputy commissioner of wellness, Jennifer Lackard,” the statement said.“Effective immediately, the city of Mount Vernon has terminated Jennifer Lackard’s employment. The allegations are unrelated to her duties with the Mount Vernon [police] and do not stem from any conduct associated with the department or the performance of her official responsibilities.”According to theSee Through NYgovernment transparency website, Lackard’s salary was $138,219 in 2025.Chase Lackard had previously been shot multiple times, according to reports. In January 2023, when he was 17, he was reportedlyshot in the cheston a bus in a reported dispute over gang signs with three other boys. A 14-year-old member of a rival gang was later arrested and charged with attempted murder.At the time, Mount Vernon’s mayor, Shawyn Patterson-Howard, called Jennifer Lackard “a valuable member of our leadership team” – and said the city was praying for her son’s recovery.Then, in November 2024, police in the Bronx responded to reports of a large fight and ended up shooting Chase Lackard, then 19, after he was alleged to have pointed a 9mm pistol at an officer’s car. Lackard was taken to hospital with two gunshot wounds to a leg and later criminally charged.TheNew YorkCity police department’s chief of patrol, John Chell, told reporters that Lackard was also arrested in September 2024 on a gun charge. In a statement following that episode, the Mount Vernon mayor called it “a personal matter and we are praying for the family”.No lawyer was immediately listed for Lackards on Tuesday. The city of Mount Vernon said it “will not comment on the underlying allegations”.The Guardian sent a request for comment to the Bronx county district attorney’s office.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption when killed, jury told | Malta | The Guardian
description: Journalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trial
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Journalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trial
Content: Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing in October 2017.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing in October 2017.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersMaltaDaphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption when killed, jury toldJournalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trialJuliette GarsideTue 4 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption by the businessman Yorgen Fenech and members of Malta’s government when she was killed, a jury has heard.The heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes, Fenech is on trial for murder, accused of commissioning and paying for Caruana Galizia’s killing in a car bombing in October 2017.The journalist’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia, a software engineer who was part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers investigation into offshore companies, took the stand on Monday.He described being drawn in to helping his mother with her work, saying that as more facts came to light, it seemed to him a “portal” had opened and he could “see into hell”.View image in fullscreenMatthew Caruana GaliziaPhotograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesIn 2015, Matthew said, he was working on the Panama Papers leak, uploading millions of files into a database that reporters were using to investigate tax havens.While processing the files, he said, he found information directly relevant to Malta. “I had to share what I was seeing with my mother. I believed it was too important.”Over time, material from the leak and Daphne’s own sources produced evidence that Malta’s then energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies soon after entering office. A firm of accountants was helping them to open bank accounts in the name of those companies, Matthew said.The jury was shown a comment left by Daphne in early 2017 under a newspaper article about the minister and the chief of staff. She wrote: “How unbelievably corrupt they are – and worse still, they were not tempted into corruption when they were already jaded in power, but actually got into power with the express purpose of being corrupt. It was their roadmap.”View image in fullscreenThe Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersAt the time of her death in 2017, Matthew said, he had been helping his mother process another leak, consisting of thousands of emails stored in the servers of a company called Electrogas, partly owned by Fenech. One of the Muscat government’s flagship projects after winning the 2013 general election had been to privatise a key part of Malta’s electricity infrastructure. The contract had been won by Electrogas.“I was receiving this info, I couldn’t believe it, it was like a portal opened up and I could see into hell,” Matthew said. The defence objected, saying the witness was offering an opinion.Asked if Daphne had discussed the tendering process with him, Matthew said she had.“Factually, what did your mother tell you about the tendering process?” the prosecutor asked. Matthew replied: “That it was corrupt.” The judge interjected to remind the witness that this was an opinion, not a fact.Asked what he had seen in the emails, Matthew said: “When I started receiving the data and put it in a system to make it searchable, I could see that Yorgen Fenech was at the centre of everything. He was featured in countless emails.”Matthew said the Electrogas leak was ongoing the day his mother was killed. He said she had wanted to gather a group of journalists together to examine the data, in a collaboration similar to the one that had produced the Panama Papers. He had contacted the Guardian to begin work on the project, but his mother was killed a few months later.“We never got to do it, and in fact when I see these emails my heart beats fast because I’m taken back to that time when I was with my mother planning on what to do,” he told the court.After the murder, Matthew set up the Daphne Project, working with a wider group of publications, including the Guardian and Reuters, to continue investigating Electrogas and try to uncover who was behind his mother’s killing.The reporting uncovered evidence that suggested Fenech had intended to pay bribes in order to secure the power station concession, provoking international condemnation and a European parliament investigation. Fenech, Mizzi and Schembri reject any suggestion of corruption.The allegations were not repeated on Monday, after the judge ordered the testimony to focus only on what could be supported by documents shown in court.The prosecution’s questioning ended with a description by Matthew of the day his mother died. They were working together at home and she had prepared a mozzarella and tomato salad. She then left in her car to go to the bank.“I was working on some software and I heard an explosion. I opened the door, I felt the blood drain away … I started walking faster and faster towards the tower of smoke,” he said.“First I saw fire on the road – the road was on fire. I saw pieces of metal and flesh. My eyes followed the smoke and I saw a huge ball of fire. I ran towards it. The horn was going off, it wouldn’t stop. I saw a shadow in the car and I remember saying ‘that’s my mum’.”He told the court he had set aside everything to ensure those responsible were held to account, leaving his job, ending his career and returning to Malta. “We had to make it our mission, which we did. It came at enormous personal cost.”Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues.Transcript and translation by Amphora MediaExplore more on these topicsMaltaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Refuse collectors help Italian woman recover binned €1m lottery ticket | Italy | The Guardian
description: Winner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown away
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Winner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown away
Content: The instant win ticket was ‘miraculously still in one piece’ after it was found in a rubbish truck.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe instant win ticket was ‘miraculously still in one piece’ after it was found in a rubbish truck.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesItalyRefuse collectors help Italian woman recover binned €1m lottery ticketWinner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown awayAgence France-Presse in RomeTue 4 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA €1m lottery ticket has been recovered from the rubbish inItalyafter the frantic winner called on refuse collectors to help her retrieve it, according to the waste management company.The instant win ticket was “miraculously still in one piece” after garbage workers combed through mounds of rubbish on their truck, said Roberto Nicola Toscano, the administrator of the SANB company in Italy’s southern Puglia region.Toscano explained how when the winner went on Sunday to check her ticket at her local shop after the draw, the machine indicated it was “non-payable”. That was because smaller retailers can only redeem small wins.But the woman – who remains anonymous – didn’t realise she had won the big jackpot.“The winner always played the same numbers, as they were associated with a loved one,” Toscano said.When she returned home from the store, a family member told her that her regular numbers had won. They immediately ran back to the shop, only to discover the ticket had already been thrown away and the rubbish collected.She called Toscano.“We reconstructed the journey of the ticket, without much hope of finding it, as it had already been picked up by a garbage truck,” Toscano saidWith a stroke of luck, however, they managed to identify the correct lorry and stopped it.Given the risk posed by potentially dangerous material in the waste, they took the vehicle to a specialist company equipped to do the search, he said.The workers searched for over a day, finding various tickets and ticket stubs.“Among them was the stub we were looking for, which was miraculously still in one piece,” Toscano said.When he told the winner they had found it, “she cried with emotion”, he said. “I would have hugged her, but we were on the phone.”However, averting the disaster came at a price. SANB, located in Bitonto outside Bari, is a public agency, meaning that the cost of the search would have been borne by taxpayers.Toscano said the woman had to sign a promise to “cover all of the additional costs” incurred – a gamble that paid off.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: SpaceX beats revenue expectations in first earnings report after IPO crash | SpaceX | The Guardian
description: Company beat analysts’ predictions to post $7.81bn in revenue, following stock plummet after IPO
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Company beat analysts’ predictions to post $7.81bn in revenue, following stock plummet after IPO
Content: The SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy v3 Booster lift off from the launch complex in Starbase, Texas, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Steve Nesius/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy v3 Booster lift off from the launch complex in Starbase, Texas, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Steve Nesius/ReutersSpaceXSpaceX beats revenue expectations in first earnings report after IPO crashCompany posts $7.81bn in revenue, a jump of 92%, after share prices crashed following IPO debutDara KerrTue 4 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the first time sinceSpaceXwent public, the world is getting a first-hand look into the trillion-dollar corporation’s financials. TheElon Musk-run business reported its second-quarter earnings on Tuesday, saying that its revenue jumped 92% since June.SpaceX beat Wall Street expectations, reporting $7.81bn in revenue, versus analysts’ predictions of $6.93bn. While expansive, the company is not profitable. The company reported a loss of $541m, down from a $1bn loss in the same quarter last year.During a call with investors, Musk called it “another milestone year” for the company. “The SpaceX team is solving some of the hardest engineering problems in the history of humanity,” he said.The spike in revenue is likely to quell fears from nervous investors who have been waiting for more insight into the company’s potential for profit.SpaceX had ablockbuster initial public offeringin June with the largest stock market debut in history. The IPO transformed SpaceX into a $2tn company and briefly crowned Musk the world’s first trillionaire. But since then, the company’s stock has plummeted by 24%, erasing nearly $500bn in market cap.Even after the better-than-expected earnings, SpaceX’s stock still ticked down more than 8% in after hours trading on Tuesday, likely due to the company’s massive capital expenditures.Elon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technologyRead more“This report comes at an important time, the share price crashed and burned in recent weeks, it is down 50% from its peak and is trading below its IPO price,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at global brokerage firm XTB.“Unsurprisingly, investors are jittery leading up to this report as it may determine the long-term direction for the stock.”SpaceX is a conglomeration of several of Musk’s businesses, including the satellite maker and internet service provider Starlink, the artificial intelligence platform xAI, the social media company X and the SpaceX rocket business.Last year, SpaceX pulled in a revenue of $18.7bn, while recording anoperating loss of $4.3bn. The only profitable portion of the company is its connectivity arm, Starlink. For comparison, the social media company Meta generated revenue of more than $200bn last year with a net income upwards of $60bn.Breaking out the revenue for SpaceX’s three main businesses, the company reported $962m for space, $4.29bn for connectivity and $2.56bn for AI, which beat analysts’ forecasts of $835m for space, $3.38bn for connectivity and $2.18bn for AI, according to XTB.During the earnings call, Musk and other SpaceX executives touted the progress the company has made in launching its massive Starship rockets into orbit and sending even more Starlink satellites into space. They also discussed SpaceX’s ambition to build a city on the moon.“It sounds like super sci-fi right now,” Musk said. “But it’s gonna happen.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHis top lieutenant and the president of SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, followed up saying: “We want to put boots on the moon by at least 2028.”Tuesday’s earnings come just before the first “lockup” shares in SpaceX will be free for public trading. Lockup shares are what employees and some insiders obtain before a company goes public, which they cannot trade for a set amount of time.The purpose of a lockup is to prevent a deluge of shares from hitting the market, which can depreciate the stock price.On Thursday, more than900m shares from SpaceXwill be open for trading – that’smore than double the current amount available and, despite the positive earnings report, could stillweaken the company’s share price.“The central question for SpaceX’s first quarter as a public company was whether the machine underneath the story actually works, and on that questionElon Muskand his team delivered a few positives,” said Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com.But he warned: “In a market already wary of heavy capex [capital expenditure] and negative free cash flow amid a shifting rates cycle, that profile may not sit well for the longer term.”Explore more on these topicsSpaceXQuarterly resultsElon MuskXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Secondhand EV leasing hits the fast lane as more UK drivers explore ways to cut motoring costs | Motor finance | The Guardian
description: Numbers using finance rises 170% in a year as leasing firms boom alongside leapin secondhand vehicle supply and surging fuel prices
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Numbers using finance rises 170% in a year as leasing firms boom alongside leapin secondhand vehicle supply and surging fuel prices
Content: Demand for secondhand electric cars has been helped by steep increases in petrol prices since the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in February.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemand for secondhand electric cars has been helped by steep increases in petrol prices since the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in February.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersMotor financeSecondhand EV leasing hits the fast lane as more UK drivers explore ways to cut motoring costsNumbers using finance rises 170% in a year as leasing firms boom alongside leapin secondhand vehicle supply and surging fuel pricesJasper JollyTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of people leasing used electric cars in the UK has more than doubled in the last year as drivers look for cheaper ways to avoid soaring petrol prices during Donald Trump’s war on Iran.Used electric car leasinghas risen by 170% in the last year across members of the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA), a lobby group whose members buy about half the UK’s new vehicles to lease them out to businesses and consumers every year.The supply of secondhand electric cars is rising rapidly, as cars bought new by early adopters feed through into the used market. The number of electric cars on British roads surpassed 2m earlier this year.Most new vehicles in the UK – about 85% – are bought with finance, with British drivers favouring a monthly cost rather than an upfront payment. However, the number of firms offering leasing for secondhand electric cars had been relatively small until recently, with providers waiting until there were more cars on offer, as well as better data on how long they would survive.Demand for secondhand electric cars has been helped bybig increases in petrol pricessince the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in February. Higher fuel prices have made owning an electric car cheaper relative to petrol for many people.View image in fullscreenThe number of EVs coming on to the secondhand market is rising as early adopters upgrade their vehicles.Photograph: John Walton/PAToby Poston, the chief executive of the BVRLA, said the biggest opportunity to convert drivers to electric vehicles was now via used cars.“Used leasing is giving consumers real choice: access to a well-maintained electric car with the latest technology, at a range of price points, without taking on the financial risk. Used [car] salary sacrifice, in particular, is opening electric driving to households that previously thought it was beyond their reach,” he said.Salary sacrifice in effect subsidiseselectric vehicle purchases by allowing people to deduct the cost of cars before tax is calculated. The number of secondhand EVs leased this way has risen fivefold in the last year, the BVRLA said.Personal contract hire for used cars has increased almost six times over. Under such contracts,people in effect rent a carfor a monthly fee. That minimises the risk of losing money on depreciation, although it also means the user does not own the car after the leasing period ends.Early growth in electric car sales came through businesses because of generous tax breaks on benefits in kind for employees. The BVRLA said business contract hire for used EVs rose 50% in the last year.The Electric Car Scheme, a salary sacrifice company, said its used EV leasing had more than tripled since its introduction in 2024. Thom Groot, its chief executive, said: “Affordability is driving that shift, as used vehicles bring EVs within reach of people who couldn’t justify a new one, and supply catching up with demand means we’re expecting growth of 80% to 120% over the next year.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGroot said one thing holding back secondhand leasing was that benefit in kind tax breaks were calculated on a car’s value as new, even when someone was buying secondhand.Octopus Electric Vehicles, the car arm of the UK’s largest retail energy provider, said it had recorded 122% year-on-year growth to June in secondhand leasing.Gurjeet Grewal, Octopus EV’s chief executive, said: “Used EVs are one of the best-value ways to go electric. Drivers are catching on fast – they’re selling quicker than the rest of the used-car market because the savings are simply too good to ignore.“You get the same cutting-edge tech, the same low-cost electric driving, but for around £60-70 less on average a month than leasing a new EV – with some models offering savings of up to £200. It’s no surprise demand is accelerating.”Explore more on these topicsMotor financeAutomotive industryElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsMotoringnewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honesty | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Gill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a director
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: Gill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a director
Content: Highest standards … Peter Gill in 2008.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/the GuardianView image in fullscreenHighest standards … Peter Gill in 2008.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/the GuardianTheatrePeter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honestyGill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a directorPeter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86Michael BillingtonTue 4 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Gill, who has died aged 86, was one of the unsung heroes of British theatre. As both director and playwright his work was characterised by its uncompromising honesty and unflinching integrity. Much admired by his fellow artists, he at last achieved a degree of public fame inhis annus mirabilis of 2002when his terrific playThe York Realistwon a number of awards and the Sheffield Crucible staged a month-long retrospective of his work as well as a brand-new play,Original Sin.Few remember that Gill, born into a Welsh, working class Catholic family, began life as an actor: look closely and you can spot him in the film of Zulu. But it was at London’s Royal Court, where he began work as an associate director in 1964, that he learned his craft and acquired the values that were to shape his whole career: a belief in the sanctity of text, the purity of design and a respect for actors.His first play The Sleepers Den, showing three generations of women all in bed next to each other, was a meticulous re-creation of working-class life. But it was his rediscovery of three neglected plays of DH Lawrence – A Collier’s Friday Night, The Daughter-in-Law and The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd – staged as a trilogy in 1968, that marked him out as a first-rate director: as Irving Wardle wrote, “the ordinary processes of living became not only interesting but objects of respect and something beautiful.”View image in fullscreenPeter Gill at the Royal Court theatre, London, with a photograph of George Devine on the wall.Photograph: Sarah Lee/the GuardianGill’s work as a playwright and director were ultimately inseparable because they were linked by an unsparing honesty. In Small Change (1976), he recalled the unhealed emotional scars left by an adolescent sexual relationship. In Kick for Touch (1983) he wrote with equal truth about a Welsh world of male bonding, rugby-as-religion and women as outsiders. Gill invariably directed his own work but he approached classic texts in the same rigorous, investigative spirit. One of his finest achievements was to turn a former TV studio into a performance space at the Riverside Studios in Hammersmith, London, and to stage a number of productions, including The Cherry Orchard, The Duchess of Malfi and Measure for Measure, of glittering clarity there. If the Riverside is still a going concern, it is because of Gill’s visionary enterprise.He also worked extensively at the NationalTheatre, where his many productions included a brilliantly hard-edged version of Christopher Hampton’s Tales from Hollywood and an astonishing revival of Otway’s Venice Preserv’d, where Ian McKellen, Michael Pennington and Jane Lapotaire achieved a heroic acting style that perfectly matched the tone of Otway’s verse-tragedy. Gill’s tenure as director of the National Theatre Studio, which he founded in 1984 to develop new work, ended less happily. But during his time there he tirelessly championed new writers and ensured their work reached the stages of the Royal Court and the Bush.Peter Gill: ‘Nothing happens unless the middle classes do it’Read moreIf I had to seize on one play that shows Gill as both writer and director at his best it would be The York Realist. Its involves a farm labourer, George, who has an affair with a London-based director, John, while working on a production of the York Mystery Plays in the early 1960s. It owes an obvious debt to DH Lawrence in its emotional intelligence, raw honesty and fascination with the intersection of class and sex. For John, the Yorkshire countryside has an exotic otherness of which he can never fully be a part while his lover, George, relishes the intellectual excitements of London but is wedded irrevocably to the land. It was as if much of what Gill had learned during his early years at the Court had been not just absorbed but miraculously enhanced.Gill carried on working as both dramatist and director but in later years became increasingly detached from the British theatre. Periodically my phone would ring and he would be on the line, often talking volubly for half an hour, about something that had caught his attention. He cared passionately about the theatre and his occasional gripes were dictated by his adherence to the highest standards and his belief in the sacrifice of personal ambition to the primacy of the work itself.Explore more on these topicsTheatrePeter GillRoyal Court theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was a death row lawyer. Here’s why I now joke about capital punishment | Comedy | The Guardian
description: In my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortable
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortable
Content: Josh Pickar: ‘What excited me most [about standup] was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Steve UllathorneView image in fullscreenJosh Pickar: ‘What excited me most [about standup] was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Steve UllathorneComedyI was a death row lawyer. Here’s why I now joke about capital punishmentIn my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortableJosh PickarTue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTShareThe first time I came out as gay to a client on death row, he said: “Josh, I don’t care what you do with your ass, as long as you’re helping mine.” That joke did something legal arguments and moral philosophy rarely could: it made him impossible to keep at a distance.I spent seven years working as a lawyer for men on both Alabama and federal death rows. I stumbled my way into it. I was only 24, fresh out of law school and working at a big corporate law firm in Manhattan. A friend from law school asked if I wanted to join two pro bono death-penalty cases. I had no relevant experience and knew nothing about capital punishment.I was, after all, a fresh-faced gay Jewish kid from the Boston suburbs. What did I have to offer a man awaiting execution?double quotation markIt was often my clients’ humor that made them impossible to flattenMy friend wouldn’t hear it. She told me the clients were really nice, there were interesting legal issues, and I would have the opportunity to work with an important partner at the firm. Those seemed like pretty good reasons to join the team.One of my first taskswas to review the evidence the prosecution presented at trial. One piece of evidence demanded my attention: a 30-second surveillance video. I spent hours studying those 30 seconds. I knew every damn frame. Something was just off. Then it clicked: it was not a video. It was a slideshow. The surveillance camera had captured a series of still images, which the prosecution presented as continuous footage. That footage had huge gaps that the jurors unconsciously filled in.The “video” was extraordinarily misleading. The government’s conduct was unconscionable. I was hooked.During one of my first visits, after some light panicking and a full-body pat-down at the prison entrance, I sat down across from a strongly built, baby-faced Black man in his mid-30s.Before the visit, the prison had told me not to wear khaki. Now I understood why. He wore a khaki prison jumpsuit over a white undershirt. The guards did not want to mistake a lawyer for a prisoner. He was covered in tattoos, including one of a woman’s name stretched across his neck.I introduced myself and asked how he was doing.“I’m blessed, I can’t complain. Doing better than Muammar Gaddafi,” he replied.I wasdelighted. Five minutes earlier, I had been terrified of saying the wrong thing. Now, we were laughing about whether it was worse to be on death row or to be a slain Libyan dictator.Climate anxiety was consuming me. Then I learned to laugh about itRead moreThat instinct for humor in an unspeakably harsh context was not unique to him. Another client of mine had made several attempts to take his own life. After one such attempt, a correctional officer gave him a pamphlet of yoga poses and mindfulness exercises. He mailed me the pamphlet and wrote across the top in all caps: “NOT WORKING! :P” Even in despair, he wanted me to see the joke.The death penalty depends, in part, on keeping the people it condemns abstract. Knowing them, and laughing with them, made that distance impossible to maintain.It was often my clients’ humor that made them impossible to flatten. They were people convicted of terrible crimes, but no verdict could account for the whole person. Many of them had spent more than 20 years on death row accumulating friendships, frustrations and routines. They could be funny, perceptive and infuriating all in the same conversation.One of my former clients has spent decades in solitary confinement. Locked away in a tiny cell whose narrow window is frosted over, he has become a prolific artist. He makes abstract, distorted figures he calls his “Sassy Boys”. They have tiny hats, canes and earrings. They’re always late and unbothered.He says they’re like jazz: either you get it or you don’t.Watching him make work that strange and alive from his cell made it harder for me to justify postponing the life I claimed I wanted.I began performing standup and improv around New York City. Public speaking did not bother me much, but I was no theater kid. I made friends laugh in conversation, but doing it intentionally was different. What excited me most was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.During the day I was fighting to get people off death row. At night, I was improvising a scene in a firehouse where the firefighters greeted one other by saying “lesbians”.Comedyoffered an outlet, a community, and a place where the stakes were low.Bryan Stevenson’s book Just Mercyin particular had shown me how storytelling could bring audiences closer to the people the legal system reduced to verdicts. As I spent more time performing, I began to wonder what comedy might do differently – not by making the subject lighter, but by helping audiences remain engaged when the subject became uncomfortable. I started telling jokes about the death penalty, wondering whether humor could bring audiences even a fraction as close as my clients’ jokes had brought me.double quotation markI do not know whether laughter can change someone’s mind. But a joke can unsettle an assumptionMy clients’ jokes revealed the people inside the system. My own jokes often revealed the system’s grotesque logic. I began telling a joke about mitigation evidence: the information that defense lawyers present to help a judge or jury see a life larger than the crime.The uncomfortable truth was that the more horrific the information we uncovered about a client’s life, the more useful it became for his case. After an interview with a client’s cousin, I called another lawyer on my team: “I have amazing news. He was molested! The dad AND the uncle.”In ordinary conversation, talking about the death penalty often made people shut down. But even in noisy comedy rooms, audiences listened. After shows, people came up to me with questions about the cases and the system. The laughter did not trivialize the subject. It gave me permission to keep talking about it, and seemed to give them permission to keep listening.I eventually decided to leave the law. I was burned out. When the stakes of work are literally life and death, it becomes hard to keep the rest of life in proportion.Still, leaving felt like a betrayal of my clients. I dreaded telling them. But the goodbyes were anticlimactic. They had seen lawyers come and go before. I have stayed in touch with several of them, and I think about them all the time.After years of treating control and expertise as the highest virtues, I wanted to learn how to fail. So I left for France to study at École Philippe Gaulier, the clown school where Sacha Baron Cohen and Emma Thompson studied. The school taught that a performer’s cleverness is not enough. Audiences respond to the pleasure a performer takes in being on stage, especially when things go wrong.The teachers were ruthless in their criticism. “Change completely!” they would yell. “Do you hear anybody laughing? Why do you keep doing the same fucking thing over and over if nobody is laughing?”‘It turned out I had a brain tumour …’ Six standup comics on what spurred them to get on stageRead moreAs a lawyer, I had spent years making sure I had a plan for every contingency. At Gaulier, I began to see how the instinct that had served me as a lawyer could stand between me and an audience. Uncertainty, it turned out, was not a weakness. It was an invitation.Legal advocacy is essential. A single filing could be the difference between life and death. But after years of working case by case, I became increasingly interested in reaching people for whom the death penalty could remain safely abstract. A court can overturn a sentence. But a legal ruling cannot dissolve the emotional distance that allows executions to remain politically possible.Comedy offers another way to lessen that distance. Not by lecturing an audience toward a conclusion that took me years to reach, but by letting them watch me stumble toward it through the contradictions, jokes and relationships that changed me.I do not know whether laughter can change someone’s mind. But a joke can unsettle an assumption and make indifference harder to sustain.A few weeks ago, the former client who makes the Sassy Boys called and suggested we make a musical. Not to make a political point. Just because it sounded fun to make something with another person. With me.I can’t sing. But you may see a death penalty musical coming to a theater near you.Josh Pickar’s debut standup showGetting Offwill be running at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe at the Assembly Roxy (Snug) on 5-30 August

title: Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy review – Mo Gilligan ruffles feathers in battle against ultra-processed foods | Movies | The Guardian
description: The ultra-likable comedian decides to go on a chicken shop diet for 28 days, but like a gen-Z Super Size Me uncovers some dark truths behind this billion-dollar industry
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The ultra-likable comedian decides to go on a chicken shop diet for 28 days, but like a gen-Z Super Size Me uncovers some dark truths behind this billion-dollar industry
Content: Finger lickin’ … Mo Gilligan in Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy.Photograph: 2026 Netflix. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenFinger lickin’ … Mo Gilligan in Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy.Photograph: 2026 Netflix. All Rights ReservedMoviesReviewBig Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy review – Mo Gilligan ruffles feathers in battle against ultra-processed foodsThe ultra-likable comedian decides to go on a chicken shop diet for 28 days, but like a gen-Z Super Size Me uncovers some dark truths behind this billion-dollar industryCath ClarkeTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ithink you’re going to die,” says a teenager bluntly to comedianMo Gilliganwhen he tells her about his plan to eat only from chicken shops for one month. Spoiler: he lives. But after 84 fried chicken meals, Gilligan is heavier, unhealthier and starting to feel depressed. In this funny, slick and accessible Netflix documentary he takes on “Big Chicken”, the industrialised poultry farming industry. Flavouring doc-journalism with his brand of ultra-likable humour, he’s gen Z’s answer to Michael Moore or Morgan Spurlock (who pulled a similar trick 20 years ago, eating nothing but McDonald’s for one month in his 2004 documentary Super Size Me).At the start of the film, there is no guilt in Gilligan’s pleasure walking into a chicken shop (“Bring on the wings!”). Growing up in a low-income household in London, a bucket of KFC was a family treat. He’s even done voiceover work for a Nando’s advert; “It’s just chickens, right?”. What works so well in the film is that Gilligan’s shock as he digs deeper into the industry doesn’t look manufactured for the camera. The UK rears one billion chickens a year and, in Lincolnshire, Gilligan meets animal welfare activists in balaclavas (“This is like Call of Duty. I’m scared!”). He learns about the environmental harm to rivers that chicken farming causes, and explores racist ideas around black people and fried chicken.In America, he investigates employment conditions in factories, workers denied toilet breaks forced to wear nappies. Back at his hotel, he bursts into tears; eating fried chicken for breakfast, lunch and dinner isn’t helping his mood. Gilligan speaks to a psychologist who explains how ultra-processed foods hook us, making us feel great – and then comes the crash. You can see the difference in Gilligan, who is lethargic and grumpy. It might not kill him, but his chicken diet is doing harm.The obvious objection to all this is that of course you’re not meant to eat fried chicken every day. But, as he finds out, half the calories in people’s diets in the UK come from ultra-processed foods and globally, there are now more obese children than hungry children. It’s probably fair to say Gilligan doesn’t uncover anything new in his film, but what he might succeed in is speaking to a new audience. At the very least it’s likely to encourage viewers to go cold chicken.Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy is onNetflixfrom 5 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMo GilliganChickenFast foodRaceFarmingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and serial killers: inside Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis’s lurid TV thriller | US television | The Guardian
description: The Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleaze
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleaze
Content: Homer Gere as Robert Mallory and Igby Rigney as Bret Ellis in The Shards.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreenHomer Gere as Robert Mallory and Igby Rigney as Bret Ellis in The Shards.Photograph: FXUS televisionSex, drugs and serial killers: inside Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis’s lurid TV thrillerThe Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleazeEmma MaddenTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the first thingsRyan Murphy’s TV adaptation ofBret Easton Ellis’sThe Shardswill make you ask is: where the hell are these kids’ parents? The answer is simple. This is Los Angeles in 1981, and these fabulously benumbed kids aren’t being helicopter-parented. They’re going to parties, drinking whiskey, listening toUltravox’s Viennaon repeat and doing copious amounts of cocaine. It’s a complete vision of Ellis’s dully hedonistic America.The FX series follows a character named Bret Ellis – a thinly coded version of the author – in senior year at an exclusive Los Angeles prep school whose controlled, Joan Didion-coded world begins to unravel with the arrival of enigmatic transfer student Robert Mallory. At the same time, in the post-Charles Mansonand Jeffrey Dahmer era, a serial killer known as The Trawler draws ever closer to Ellis and his increasingly paranoid circle of friends. Ellis (the real one) first released his autofictional story The Shards as a serialized podcast between 2020 and 2021 before expanding it into a novel in 2023.Gregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’Read moreOriginally, the novel seemed destined to be adapted byLuca Guadagnino. Instead, in a twist of fate (and professional conflict), Guadagnino’s more measured style gave way to Murphy’s unashamed extravagance, as he came onboard in February 2025. On paper, Murphy and Ellis might seem like opposites, but in The Shards, they find everything they have in common. Both are “obsessed with moments in their youth of hidden identities”, said Brad Simpson, The Shards’ executive producer, and both came of age in the time of Aids. “That’s affected gay artists more than most people think.“This story is about a group of young, beautiful people who are about to embark on the world, and there is a killer that hunts them. There’s an obvious metaphor to Aids in the 1980s for that,” says Simpson, speaking on Zoom along with the cast a week before the show’s release.For Murphy’s interpretation of The Shards, he assembled a combination of seasoned actors and the next wave of young Hollywood. The cast includes Kaia Gerber, returning to Murphy’s world after appearances in the American Horror Story franchise, as the reluctantly perfect Susan Reynolds. Igby Rigney, television’s future Evan Peters, plays Ellis. Meanwhile, the seven-time Tony award-winning producer Jordan Roth plays personal assistant Steven Reinhardt, a kind of Lynchian version of Andy Warhol who Murphy says he modeled around Roth. “He sent me a DM saying, ‘I have a part for you. Call me,’” says Roth.Homer Gere steps into what feels like a role poised to launch a career overnight as Robert Mallory, the irritatingly self-assured object of Ellis’s obsession. “Gen Z wants to have new stars, they want fresh faces,” explains Simpson.The cast hadn’t met before, but Gere and Gerber had certainly heard of one another. There was some air that Gere (son ofRichard) and Gerber (daughter of Cindy Crawford) felt they had to clear. Their parents were one of the defining star couples of the 90s, so when they first met two weeks before filming: “I think one of the first things we said was, ‘Should we address it?’” says Gere. They ended up laughing about it, and got the inevitable conversation out of the way before they went to set. “So it’s not like we ended up talking about it every day.”View image in fullscreenKaia Gerber as Susan, Rigney as Bret, Hayes Warner as Debbie Schaffer, Gere as Robert Mallory and Graham Campbell as Thom Wright in The Shards.Photograph: FXOne of Murphy’s main casting criteria for selecting this cast was their aspirationalism: namely, would you want to go to a party, drink whiskey and do mounds of coke with them? Probably. But also, please don’t do that. WhileLove Story, Simpson and Murphy’s previous series, helped make smoking cool again. “We regretted that,” Simpson says, laughing. He hopes this one won’t inspire kids to “have drug-fueled parties and drive quickly on the PCH”.Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’Read moreRight now, a week out from the season premiere, life is much the same for the acting newcomers. “I’m just hanging out, seeing friends, reading books,” says Gere. Upon release, that will all be turned on its head. Entering Hollywood through one of its biggest doors, the cast are suddenly staring down the possibility of overnight fame. The closest glimpse of what’s to come is seeing themselves plastered across billboards all overLos Angeles. How do you prepare for something like this? “You can’t,” says Campbell, who’s kept the blond perm that he sports as character Thom Wright, whose jock archetype devolves throughout the season.In The Shards, each of the characters is desperate to be seen, no more explicitly than Debbie Schaffer, a seethingly insecure teen played by Hayes Warner, primarily known as a musician somewhere in the vein ofAvril Lavigne. Those feelings were easy to access, she says. “I was in the music industry, and it’s so oversaturated, and there’s so much desperation to get your music out there, like, how do you get people to listen and care and hear about it?”View image in fullscreenRigney and Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXThe Shards clearly demands attention with its classic cocktail of sex, drugs and rock’n’roll, though it leans heaviest towards the drugs. Throughout filming, the cast consumed a staggering amount of “terrible cigarettes and iced tea [standing in] for whiskey”, says Campbell, who only landed his first professional role three years ago on Broadway. Then there were the cocaine re-creation experiments, as the actors went through a series of milk and coconut powders. Out of everyone, Warner’s character had by far the most coke. That first trial with coconut powder “was too sticky”, she says. Eventually, they traded it for milk powder, which Warner snorted in large quantities while reshooting her many coke-sniffing scenes. “The powder would begin to liquefy in my nose,” she says, grimacing.The Shards is billed as an erotic thriller, though it’s a surprisingly chaste entry in the genre. In the era ofHeated Rivalry, expectations have been heightened for graphic man-on-man sex, but The Shards instead thrives on tension and suspense. There’s nary a dick shot to be seen. No blowjobs and not even a measly handjob. There’s some aggressive making out, but that’s as far as it goes.“I think it’s deeply erotic, and I think it’s deeply beautiful. I think there is a lot of sex, drugs and rock’n’roll, but it’s done in a way that’s much more elevated than people are accustomed to these days,” says Campbell.View image in fullscreenRigney and Warner in The Shards.Photograph: Ray Mickshaw/FXFor the sexy scenes there are, Rigney says: “The intimacy coordinator gave us an ungodly amount of Listerine strips, and you have to watch what you eat for lunch,” although he was tempted to find out how good his fellow actors really were by “going the pickle, onion, tuna route”, he says. “But in the end, I just love them too much to do that.”Rigney plays the leading role with keenly observed physical code-switching, veering between his real (gay) and fake (straight) selves. In Ellis’s straight romances, Rigney plays the rigidity of a straight teenage boy. In his homosexual encounters, his entire body shifts. He’s suddenly sylph-like and coy, eyebrow arched, smarmy, crotch forward. Rigney said it’s not something he had to be directed to do. “That was all natural, baby.”As the next generation of actors, they’re desperately hoping for a second season. “Is the cash coming in?” Rigney pauses. “Well, what I will say is it’s amazing to have a stable job as an actor, regardless of what the income is.” He taps the wooden table next to him. “If we get a second season,” teases Simpson, “we promise there’ll be more sex.”The Shards premieres on 5 August on FX/Hulu in the US and on 6 August in the UK and Australia on Disney+Explore more on these topicsUS televisionRyan MurphyBret Easton EllisTelevisionLos AngelesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Web of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in Hollywood | Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day | The Guardian
description: Tom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Tom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?
Content: Tom Holland in a scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony Pictures via APView image in fullscreenTom Holland in a scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony Pictures via APSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayWeb of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in HollywoodTom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?Jesse HassengerTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAyear ago, the superhero-industrial complex looked like it was on the wane. All three of Marvel’s big movies for 2025 underperformed to some degree or another, outgrossed by DC’s newest reboot of Superman – which itself made less than any number of previous-regime DC movies, and was followed up by this summer’sSupergirl, a costly bomb. It looked as if the age of heroes might be coming to an end, and only seemed fitting that the next big Avengers movie was subtitledDoomsday(and had resigned itself to sharing a release date with the Imax-grabbing release ofa third Dune movie).But look out, as the song goes: here comesSpider-Man.Spider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilersRead moreSpider-Man: Brand New Day, the fourth solo film starring Tom Holland as the third live-action iteration of the character in the past 25 years, was always expected to do well at the box office this summer. Its predecessor, 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home, was the first movie since Covid to post 2010s-style numbers. At the same time, it seemed like an anomaly, given its advantage of two additional Spider-Men, as previous stars Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield returned for an unexpectedly moving curtain call to their versions of Peter Parker. Still: the (relatively) lower-grossing movies that sent those past Peters packing made a substantial amount of money, too, so there was a general understanding that Spider-Man would be a perennial favorite and Brand New Day would do accordingly well.Yet a few months ago, hardly anyone predicted that it would swoop so far asthe all-time opening weekend record in North America, outgrossing Avengers: Endgame with $360m, and coming in a strong second worldwide, making nearly a billion dollars within four days. What’s more, Brand New Day is keeping pace with a movie that was an all-in team-up event, also sold as a de facto finale. Most of it focuses on the six core Avengers who first assembled in the 2012 smash (plus Ant-Man, Captain Marvel and Rocket Raccoon) but its climax features appearances from just about every major MCU character brought back from the dead, including Holland’s Spidey.Brand New Day certainly takes advantage of that same wide cinematic universe, with supporting parts for the Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), the new Black Widow (Florence Pugh), the Punisher (Jon Bernthal), and one major figure fromMarvelcomics. But that mystery character’s identity wasn’t part of the ad campaign in order to keep the movie’s surprise intact, and the Punisher is from a few Marvel TV shows – not exactly a blockbuster-level draw. No, it’s safe to say that Brand New Day is breaking records – it will become the biggest movie of the year in a matter of days – because of Spider-Man himself.That means the character, not Holland (though his version is obviously popular). Spidey has been posting numbers like this longer than any single movie star: back in 2002, the Spider-Man film starring Maguire and directed by Sam Raimi was the first movie to ever open with over $100m at the North American box office, and it sure didn’t have any other marquee heroes helping it along. Combined with the surprise success of an X-Men movie two years earlier, Spider-Man 02 kicked off a superhero-movie craze – and due respect to Professor X and his noble mission of mutant-human brotherhood, but the Raimi film pulled in well over twice as much. It was a sign that he was attracting audiences beyond the comics-fan faithful, even – cue the nerd sweats – girls!It’s probably an oversimplification to chalk Spider-Man’s enduring cinematic appeal to a female audience, not least because all three live-action Spider-Man series center a male point of view, unswervingly make the female lead a love interest for Peter Parker, and ignore all of the super-powered women in this corner of comics lore; only the animated Spider-Verse movies get into Ghost Spider, Spider-Woman and so on. (It would also be unfair to deny the existence of female comics fans, excited to see Spider-Man on screen.) But while Kirsten Dunst’s Mary Jane from the Raimi films does play like a damsel frequently in distress – she’s climactically endangered for three movies in a row, and Raimi’s take on gender roles is not exactly forward-thinking – she does have her own hopes, dreams and disappointments.Her feelings are a big part of what drives the emotional core of the much-maligned, underrated Spider-Man 3, just as Peter’s feelings for her drive the action for the first film. In the new movies, the evolving relationship between Peter and MJ (Zendaya, Holland’s real-life spouse) is rarely far from the center of the film. Hell, the obvious affection between Garfield’s Spider-Man and Emma Stone’s Gwen Stacy is just about the only thing that makes the abruptly curtailed Amazing Spider-Man movies watchable (and the comics-accurate death of Gwen at the end of the second film probably helped doom it with audiences; it’s a colossal and unearned-feeling downer to kill off your superstar female lead in just the second film).View image in fullscreenTom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Courtesy of Sony Pictures/Sony PicturesIt doesn’t feel like a coincidence that all three live-action Spider-Man actors dated their co-stars at some point; these are superhero movies that reboot and reconfigure and recast, but never fully dispense with romance. At first, that was very much part of MCU at large; the first two Iron Man movies run on screwball-adjacent byplay between Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr) and Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow). But as romance leached out of the MCU following Phase One, replaced with weirdly businesslike allusions to off-screen hookups and breakups, Spider-Man remained at least a little bit lovelorn, perhaps reminding audiences of a crucial human angle missing from big-scale smash-em-ups.Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superheroRead moreIt’s not just the love stories that continually draw audiences to Spider-Man, of course. The character has long resonated as a keen fusion of longtime DC titans Superman and Batman: he’s got the diverse (and potentially playful) power set like Superman, paired with a Clark Kent-like humble-nerd identity; and the relatable angst of Batman, who of course has no fantastical powers and, as such, bumps up against his human limitations. He wasn’t the first Marvel hero, but he’s probably the archetypal one, mixing in more overt teen melodrama in an era where Superman was flying further into sci-fi territory.Adapting Spider-Man into other media has only increased his cachet; toddlers are now routinely shown Spidey and His Amazing Friends, a sort of Marvel version of Paw Patrol that gets them hooked on a version of that mythos early, via Disney+. Yet another Spider-Man advantage, though, is very much the opposite of Disney-umbrella synergy: the movie rights for the character have stayed with Sony since the first film. That’s a big part of why there have been three different Spider-Man actors; Sony has to keep making movies to hang on to the characters. (That’s also why a whole bunch of negligible movies about tertiary Spider-verse characters like Madame Web exist.)Disney’s Marvel Studios still deserves credit for the recent successes; they produce the Holland movies, which are in continuity with their other projects. But there’s still probably some manner of negotiation in terms of their timing and, at least with Brand New Day, maybe their creative direction. Holland has told the press that his experience making The Odyssey inspired him to push for a more disciplined approach to Marvel’s assembly line. For her part, Zendaya seems to have brought in Justin Kuritzkes, screenwriter for her film Challengers, to punch up some of the character work. (He receives an “additional literary material” credit.)The stars and film-makers working to make Brand New Day feel more like its own movie with some fun Marvel tie-ins, rather than the latest Marvel homework assignment, may have put it over the top in terms of good buzz and a huge opening in the wake of The Odyssey. (The promotion of having three of its main actors – Holland, Zendaya and Bernthal all appear in both! – shared with the second-biggest movie of the summer couldn’t have hurt, either.) But Spider-Man movies are also notable for their consistency. The series’ biggest disaster, The Amazing Spider-Man 2, still pulled in $700m worldwide. (As far as low points go, that actually beats Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman, Iron Man, Captain America … pretty much everyone.) The first film premiered less than a year after the 9/11 attacks on the US – an early trailer was pulled because it consisted of a visual-effects sight gag where a bad guys’ helicopter got caught in a Spidey web spun between the two towers of the World Trade Center – and while the world has changed plenty in the past quarter-century, it does feel as if Spider-Man is the most enduring film character of the new millennium so far.View image in fullscreenTom Holland and ZendayaPhotograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockIt might be a little trite to suggest that a movie in production well before 9/11, featuring a character that had been beloved for decades and earmarked for a big-screen debut for ages (James Cameron wrote a detailed treatment in the 1990s in preparation for a version that never came to pass), received such a franchise-long boost from a single historical event. But in retrospect, it is difficult to picture these Spider-Man movies working quite so well in the 1970s/80s of the original Superman movies (which clearly influenced Raimi’s films) or the 1980s/90s of the early Batman cycle, with their ornate, almost otherworldly spectacle. It’s as if Spider-Man needed to accumulate some eras to throw back to while also moving past those previous icons.The forward progress has always been subdued; the first movie is the only one to really make much of post-9/11 New York, and only obliquely, in a scene where citizens rise up and help Spider-Man, declaring “you mess with one of us, you mess with all of us!” (This protective togetherness is further echoed in the sequel’s subway rescue sequence, though there it takes on more of a pseudo-religious aura that’s surprisingly touching all these many years later.) Well into the 2020s, Spidey is still foiling old-timey bank robberies; there may not be sacks of money with dollar signs on them, but there might as well be. That he’s doing this casually using invasive, illegal surveillance equipment marks him as a truly well-integrated post-9/11 superhero, while Marvel mutes real-world allegory elsewhere in their increasingly insular universe.Even if his nominal co-parent is just another flavor of multinational corporation, the current Spidey being of the MCU but not Disney-exclusive sets him ever-so-slightly apart from his many famous co-stars. Worlds end and new phases begin for the original Avengers; two appear to be actually-for-real-dead, while others threaten to age out of their costumes (or, worse, age back in when they don’t know what else to do).This should be a bigger problem for Spider-Man, a character who, despite the second part of his moniker and a whole lot of comics stories where he’s an adult, is largely thought of as a perpetual teenager. Yet as often as he’s been recast back to high school in the movies, he stays in the culture’s good graces and captures a range of demographics. Maybe it’s because that endless cycle that’s supposed to be the sign of a soulless, deathless franchise actually (however accidentally) has come to resemble the kind of endless struggle that made the character so refreshing in the first place. Even when he’s making billions in days, he’s a superhero who remains an unambiguous work in progress.Explore more on these topicsSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandMarvelSuperhero moviesZendayaSpider-ManfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Liberated from its ludicrous libretto: how the magnificence of Oberon can be properly heard at last | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Full of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brilliance
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Full of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brilliance
Content: Blowing the dust off the original … Jennifer Davis as Reiza and Rachael Wilson as Fatima in rehearsals for Oberon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBlowing the dust off the original … Jennifer Davis as Reiza and Rachael Wilson as Fatima in rehearsals for Oberon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianClassical musicLiberated from its ludicrous libretto: how the magnificence of Oberon can be properly heard at lastFull of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brillianceMark ElderTue 4 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarl Maria von Weber was a great opera composer with a minimal ability to find the right libretto writers. He never made a good choice in any of the three pieces for which he’s still known.View image in fullscreenCarl Maria von Weber, by Caroline BarduaOberon was his final work. He wrote it in London 200 years ago for Covent Garden theatre and died of tuberculosis shortly after its premiere in 1826, aged only 39. He was buried in the cemetery just north of the Barbican, although his grave today is in Dresden. Some 18 years after his death, Wagner – who adored, and was inspired by, the older composer (there could not have been Lohengrin without Weber’s earlier opera Euryanthe) – raised the money to repatriate his body. A large crowd met the coach at the gates of Dresden and processed through the rain to the city’s old Catholic cemetery where a second funeral was held and Wagner’s specially composed fantasia for wind band based on themes from Euryanthe was performed.German audiences did not doubt Weber’s worth, but only in the past few years have Weber’s three great operas – Der Freischütz, Euryanthe and Oberon – begun to be treasured more widely. I conductedEuryanthe at Glyndebournein 2002 and loved every minute. It’s the most wonderful piece of dramatic music, saddled with a terrible libretto. Der Freischütz was a sensation on its Berlin premiere in 1821: Weber had written a new kind of German national romantic opera, an everyday story of country folk (with apologies to the Archers) but it’s hard to get a staging right today and it is little performed outside Germany – everybody just laughs at the plot’s daft mix of supernatural and silly. Yet its music is exuberantly inventive, full of colour and beauty, and – as with Weber’s other two grand operas – deserves to be heard.View image in fullscreen‘Wonderful dramatic music, saddled with a terrible libretto’: Clive Bayley in Glyndebourne’s 2002 staging of Weber’s Euryanthe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOberon’s libretto is best described as a phantasmagoria. It’s by James Robinson Planché, a prolific commercial dramatist who wrote well over 100 theatre shows involving exuberant opulence and fantastical stories. The work’s sprawling tale of fairyland, desert islands, pirates, crusaders and an imaginary Arabia would have been completely acceptable in the 1820s, but now seems very far away. There are elements of Mozart’s Magic Flute (two couples, trials, magic) and James Bond movies (escapism, effortless flitting between exotic locations), while Ivor Novello is a useful comparison point. Novello’s musicals are full of wonderful tunes. However, the shows themselves – King’s Rhapsody, Glamorous Night and such like – are wild extravaganzas that haven’t aged well.To stage, or even semi-stage Oberon, its text needs to be rewritten, and for our Proms performance, author Timothy Knapman has created a new single narrative that respects the original but blows the dust off it. His witty version, narrated byTamsin Greig, will entertain today’s audiences just as Londoners were entertained in 1826.The music needs not a jot of revision: it has an immediacy and daring that still startles. Full of panache and confidence, this is the work of a showman at the top of his powers. Weber’s heart lay in the theatre and he understood how to write for it.From the first notes ofthe overtureyou know you’re in the hands of a master. It begins with stillness and a sense of something coming. Perhaps we’re in a forest on a summer afternoon. The harmony is gentle and serene, leading us into a dreamy world where anything can happen. There are three notes, long-short-long, on a horn. These, we later learn, are the call Oberon gives to one of his mortal charges: if you’re in trouble, blast those three notes and I will save you. And then, suddenly, some manic fairy energy breaks in and you don’t quite know what’s hit you. You hear lots of different characters and tunes; it’s brilliant and fast.double quotation markOberon’s music is full of panache and confidence: the work of a showman at the top of his powers.Nobody had really done anything quite like this before. Mendelssohn had that same lightness of spirit in his A Midsummer Night’s Dream concert overture, written in the same year as Oberon.The period instruments of theOrchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, with the players so expert in this kind of repertoire, will bring a suitable litheness. There might be three trombones but the sound has to be lively, not ever fat. Weber’s orchestral palette is full of colours and reflects the characters on stage and the different settings; he writes particularly beautifully for woodwind. You can almost feel him thinking:“Ah, this moment has got a bit of melancholy … we need to make sure this is clear. Let’s bring the clarinet in as well as the strings, to give another yearning quality.”View image in fullscreenMark Elder rehearses with John Findon (Sir Huon of Bordeaux) and Jennifer Davis (Reiza) and the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe overture aside, the act one finale is also a great favourite of mine. It’s a substantial piece in different sections. We’re just getting to know Reiza, the heroine. She has been told in a dream that Sir Huon will rescue her from a forced marriage, and she calls out to him, saying please don’t delay. She and her servant Fatima sing this brilliant little duet, and then, suddenly, we hear a march that represents the harem guard closing things up for the night. There’s a tiny extra wind orchestra and percussion, which I’m going to put at the top of the stage, separate from the other musicians. This is my last chance, Reiza says, I’ve got to escape before they close the gates…Skilled in understanding the voice, Weber gives his singers amazing opportunities to shine. The leading role of Sir Huon needs an Olympic heldentenor: nimble and athletic. We’ve got John Findon, a really terrific tenor who is going to make a big impact. (And I always say it’s like Wimbledon. You have to get your first serve in when you sing this sort of music.) The chorus, the superb Monteverdi Choir, also have their work cut out – they’ve got to be fairies, elves, slaves, courtiers and even mermaids.View image in fullscreenNicky Spence (Oberon) rehearses at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianListen out too for Reiza’s showstopper aria Ocean, Thou Mighty Monster in act two. By now she and Huon have been shipwrecked on a desert island. Despairing, she spots a sail and waves like mad hoping to be rescued – but it’s pirates, who kidnap her and leave Huon tied up on the shore. Luckily, he’s still just able to sound his magic horn to summon help.
