title: Post your questions for Imelda Staunton | Movies | The Guardian
description: She’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: She’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?
Content: Warm and calm, but won’t stand for any nonsense … Imelda Staunton.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APView image in fullscreenWarm and calm, but won’t stand for any nonsense … Imelda Staunton.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Imelda StauntonShe’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?Rich PelleyTue 4 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is perhaps fitting that Imelda Staunton ended up playing Queen Elizabeth II in the last two series of The Crown, considering she has been acting royalty for years. Her film career has seen her voice champion egg-layer Bunty in 2000’s Chicken Run, followed by roles in Mike Leigh’s 2004 drama Vera Drake and the 2005 comedy Nanny McPhee. In 2014, she played the formidable Welsh miners’ strike campaigner Hefina inPride. She also plays Lady Maud Bagshaw in the first two Downton Abbey films, and voices Paddington’s beloved Aunt Lucy in all three Paddington films. For a whole generation, however, she will always be Dolores Umbridge in two of the later Harry Potter films, where she somehow made a pink cardigan almost as frightening as Voldemort.View image in fullscreenBafta-winning role … Imelda Staunton, left, with Daniel Mays in Vera Drake.Photograph: Moviestore collection Ltd/AlamyOn TV, she has cropped up in everything from Little Britain and Doctor Who to Psychoville, Brassic and a memorable guest appearance in the fourth series of A Bit of Fry & Laurie, where – for reasons known only to F&L – she was introduced as “Snutty”. Whether she’s playing a chicken, a bear or the head of state, there is always something unmistakably Imelda about her performances: warm and calm but with the distinct impression that she won’t stand for any nonsense.After training at Rada, Staunton spent six years in repertory theatre before making her film debut in Bill Douglas’s 1986 historical epic Comrades. She went on to appear in 1992’s Peter’s Friends, 1993’s Much Ado About Nothing, 1995’s Sense and Sensibility and 1998’s Shakespeare in Love. Then came Leigh’sVera Drake, in which she plays a warm-hearted cleaner who secretly carries out illegal abortions in 1950s London. Her performance won her a Bafta and the best actress prize at the Venice film festival, as well as earning her an Oscar nomination.In addition, Staunton has had a garlanded career in musicals, beginning in 1982 with The Beggar’s Opera. Her performances in Follies, Guys and Dolls, The Wizard of Oz, Gypsy, Sweeney Todd and Hello Dolly! have been widely acclaimed. She has received 15 Olivier award nominations, winning five of them. In 2024, she was awarded a DBE.View image in fullscreenA terrifying pink cardigan … Staunton as Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter: Order of the Phoenix.Photograph: Warner Bros/AllstarHer latest film,& Sons, reunites her with her Pride co-star Bill Nighy, who plays a famously difficult novelist who summons his family together to make a startling announcement; Staunton plays his estranged wife.Now Staunton is here to answer your questions so please post them below by 6pm on Wednesday 5 August, we’ll put the best to Snutty and publish her answers in Film & Music.& Sons is in cinemas from 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewImelda StauntonHarry PotterMike LeighVera DrakeTelevisionMusicalscalloutShareReuse this content

title: ‘A 99 with a Flake? That will be £7, please’: what’s behind the surge in ice-cream van prices? | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: From the cost of milk and chocolate to diesel and electricity, every part of producing the summer treat has been hit by the climate crisis and other shocks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the cost of milk and chocolate to diesel and electricity, every part of producing the summer treat has been hit by the climate crisis and other shocks
Content: Flake news … families are spending an average of £50 a child on ice-cream this summer.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlake news … families are spending an average of £50 a child on ice-cream this summer.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesPass notesIce-cream and sorbet‘A 99 with a Flake? That will be £7, please’: what’s behind the surge in ice-cream van prices?From the cost of milk and chocolate to diesel and electricity, every part of producing the summer treat has been hit by the climate crisis and other shocksTue 4 Aug 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Iceflation.Appearance:An ice-cold rip-off, with a Flake on top.Ah, here we go – expensive ice-creams. It seems like only yesterday thetwo eight-year-olds who went viral on TikTokwere complaining about having to pay £9 for two screwballs from an ice cream van.It was 2024 – and the cost of licking has only risen since then.Wow,gross expression, but go on.According to asurvey of 2,000 British parents commissioned by Aldi, they are spending £50 a kid on ice-cream over the six-week summer holidays this year. The average cost of a 99 is £2.65, but one vendor outside the British Museum in Londonis reportedlycharging £7 for one scoop with a flake. A survey of 33 seaside resorts by the credit card company Zable found a single-scoop cone in Porthmadog in north Wales cost £3.85.Any cheaper spots?It would cost you a more reasonable £1.95 for one scoop at Barton-on-Sea in Hampshire.I guess that’s where we’re heading on holiday then. What’s causing this round of iceflation?Exactly what you’d expect. As an Ice Cream Alliance spokespersontold the Daily Mail: “Almost every part of serving a 99 has become more expensive.” Milk and chocolate are among the five most climate-impacted foods, according to arecent report from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, and ice-cream vans need to keep products cool and travel around at a time of rising diesel and electricity prices.A sorry state of affairs. But hasn’t ice-cream always been pricey?Not everywhere: in Naples, it was apopular treat for all classes in the 18th century. “Penny licks” – reusable glasses filled with ice-creamcustomers licked and returned – democratised it as a street treat in Britain in Victorian times, though you might get a free cholera topping, according toan 1879 medical report.Yuck! You’re putting me off ice-cream altogether.It may actually be good for you – a mysterious, seemingly beneficial “ice-cream effect” has been observed in diet-related research multiple times. One Harvard study in 2005 found men who ate two or more servings of ice-cream a week had a 22% lower risk of diabetes; a 2016 meta-analysis of multiple studies also found that eating as little as half a cup was associated with a 19% lower risk.Ice-cream vans should broadcast those findingsinstead of catchy jingles.Unfortunately,many scientists are sceptical that the ice-cream effect is real.Unlike the wallet effect, which definitely is real.Is it too late to tell the kids the van only plays a tune when it’s out of ice-cream?Do say:“I got 99 problems but a Flake ain’t one.”Don’t say:“I scream, you scream, we all scream for high ice-cream prices caused by acute and sustained climate and energy shocks!”Explore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetPass notesFoodUK cost of living crisisConsumer affairsFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The ultimate guide to travel etiquette: how to handle 36 tricky situations, from manspreaders to smelly armpits | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: It’s easy to lose your cool when you’re crammed into a train, bus or plane with a bunch of strangers and one of them is playing music without headphones or fighting you for the armrest. Here are the rules everyone should be following
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: It’s easy to lose your cool when you’re crammed into a train, bus or plane with a bunch of strangers and one of them is playing music without headphones or fighting you for the armrest. Here are the rules everyone should be following
Content: ‘It’s not an extension of your sitting room. It’s just inappropriate behaviour in a public place.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s not an extension of your sitting room. It’s just inappropriate behaviour in a public place.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianSocial etiquetteThe ultimate guide to travel etiquette: how to handle 36 tricky situations, from manspreaders to smelly armpitsIt’s easy to lose your cool when you’re crammed into a train, bus or plane with a bunch of strangers and one of them is playing music without headphones or fighting you for the armrest. Here are the rules everyone should be followingEmine SanerTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePublic transport can be a hot, noisy, cramped and stressful environment – and that’s before you add in people with pungent food, questionable hygiene and giant backpacks. Most of us know the general rules – though we don’t all follow them – about letting people off first, not putting bags on seats, where to stand on escalators and offering your seat to others. But what about the vaguer conventions? How can you avoid chatty passengers? Or manspreaders? Is it sometimes OK to put your feet on the seats? (Spoiler: it’s not.) Here, three etiquette experts show us the way to public transport propriety.How to use a seatWhoshould I offer my seat to?In principle, the answer is simple: anyone who needs it more than you do. “The reality is harder,” says Rupert Wesson, director of etiquette advisers Debrett’s, when trying to ascertain who that might be. If it’s a harassed parent with a baby or toddler, that’s obvious. But is that woman over there actually pregnant? Might that older person be appalled to be considered too frail to stand? “Nobody should be offended by being offered a seat – it’s a nice thing to do – but nevertheless you need to exercise a little caution,” says Wesson. Weigh it up, and offer discreetly. “Don’t make a big show about it – just try to catch somebody’s eye. You can do it without speaking.”If you’re not sure, should you stand up, as if you’re pretending to get off, and hope the person takes your seat? “The danger is that somebody who doesn’t need it jumps in, so I try to be a bit more targeted,” says Wesson. “I’ll stand up, but not move out of the way straight away, just so that I know the person who might need it has caught my eye or my movement.” The idea of offering women a seat, mainly because of the assumption they are too delicate to stand, is “an old-fashioned concept. I know some people who will always do it, but the world has moved on from doing that by default.”The most important step in ascertaining whether someone might need a seat, though, is getting off your phone and looking around at your fellow humans. “Checking in as people are getting on board is the critical thing,” says Wesson.Can I put my feet on the seat?Absolutely not, says Laura Akano, etiquette coach and founder of Polished Manners. “It’s a public space you’re sharing with other people, and you really should treat it with respect. You think that’s OK – to put [your shoes] on a seat that somebody else is going to sit on?” What if you think your shoes are clean enough? “They won’t be because you’ve been walking around,” says Akano, adding that it’s just as bad when people take their shoes off and put stockinged or bare feet on seats. “It’s not an extension of your sitting room. It’s just inappropriate behaviour in a public place.”Can I always take the aisle seat?Yes, but be alert and prepared to move to allow someone else to get to the window seat. “It’s an awful lot easier for you to jump into the window seat, rather than have people scramble over you,” says Wesson. But he points out that if the bus or train isn’t busy, and you’re making a short journey, then there is no real issue.Can I sit at a four-seat train table if I’m on my own?Of course. But if a group gets on, it would be considerate to offer to move. “You don’t have to, but it’s a nice thing to do,” says Wesson. Otherwise, “If you need to work and have your laptop out [on the table], then so be it.”Can I ask someone to move so that I can sit next to my friend/partner?“If you really can’t cope without sitting next to them, then yes, that would be fine,” says William Hanson, etiquette expert and director of the English Manner. “Although it depends on how busy it is. You also need to be aware that they may say no, and that’s their right.” If you’re aware of a couple being separated by your seat choice, should you move? “If there is a comparable seat, and they ask nicely, then yes,” says Hanson. “But sometimes I’ve had it where people come over and go, ‘Sorry, I want to sit next to my girlfriend’, rather than, ‘Would you consider moving?’ I think it would depend on how they ask.”If I’m sitting in one of the prime front seats at the top of a doubledecker bus, do I have to give it up for children?How generous are you feeling? “If they were to come to me politely and say, ‘Could we maybe swap seats with you?’ then I would,” says Akano. But beware of making assumptions. “I wouldn’t automatically think: ‘Because they’re children, they would prefer to sit here.’”View image in fullscreen‘Many people would consider dogs on seats unacceptable.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianIs it unforgivably rude to move away from a stranger once more seats become available?No, says Wesson. “It feels a bit weird when a train suddenly empties and everybody gets off, and then there’s just the two of you sat together. It’s always nice to spread out, and no, you don’t need to explain what you’re doing.”Can I recline my seat on a plane?If the seat reclines then it’s fair game, even on a short daytime flight, and even if the person behind you is silently seething. Don’t do it during food or drinks service, though. And if you do it, do it slowly. “It’s worth checking who’s behind you and what’s going on before you dip the seat back,” says Wesson. “Make sure you’re not going to skittle somebody’s drinks all over their lap.”Is it acceptable to take up two seats on a bus or train if you have ahuge suitcase and there’s nowhere else to put it?“Sometimes there’s no choice, sadly,” says Wesson. “You’ve got to block something, and it’s either an aisle or a seat, so better to block a seat.” But he adds that the scenario is rare – there’s usually something you can do, and other people who can help you lift luggage on to a rack. “We can usually find ways of making things work, with a bit of polite collaboration.”Travelling with children and petsIs itOK to letmy dog sit on a seat?No, says Hanson. It is potentially tolerable if the dog sits on a mat or blanket on a seat, but “not during busy periods”. And many people, including those with severe allergies, would consider this unacceptable.View image in fullscreen‘Nobody thinks your child is as adorable as you do.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianHow much should children be allowed to roam on a plane or a train?This is tricky, says Wesson. Some people may think it’s sweet, “as a child goes around talking to everybody in the train carriage. I have seen that, and it’s delightful, and shakes everybody out of whichever world they’re in.” And sometimes an energetic preschooler allowed to go on a walkabout is better for everyone than a bored and screeching one confined to their seat. But remember: nobody thinks your child is as adorable as you do. “People are often trying to work or relax on a train, so do try to keep your child from disturbing them,” says Wesson. Wandering around occasionally is fine but be mindful of “the noise and chaos that accompanies it”.On personal space and other bodily mattersCan I lean, louchely, on a pole on a bus or train?“It’s not very elegant, but it’s fine,” says Hanson. That is, if the bus or train is relatively empty; otherwise, move out of the way so people can use it to hold on to.View image in fullscreen‘Leaning on the pole is not very elegant, but it’s fine.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianWhat if I accidentally make skin contact with a stranger?Obviously immediately move back. “Say sorry to the person that you have inadvertently touched, whether you know them or not,” says Hanson. Could you just ignore it? Yes, he says. “If it was fleeting and they don’t seem to have noticed, I think you could probably get away with it, but even just a hand gesture to say sorry is better than nothing.”Who gets the armrest?On a plane, the general rule seems to be the person in a middle seat of three gets both armrests. On a bus or train, Hanson advises to view it as “an elbow rest, not an armrest”. That way, both of you could probably use it.If somebody in the next seat is snoring and dribbling onme, canI wake them up?View image in fullscreen‘Touch their shoulder and say: “I’m so sorry, but you were dribbling on me.” Laugh it off if needs be.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianDribbling, yes; snoring, no. Neither are deliberate, hopefully, but only one really adversely affects you. Hanson advises: “I would touch their elbow or their shoulder and say: ‘I’m so sorry, but you were dribbling on me.’ Keep it factual. Laugh it off if needs be. They’ll probably be absolutely mortified. Say: ‘Oh, it’s not a problem. I just thought I’d step in now before I’m drenched.’” With snoring, he says, “there’s not a lot you can do”.Can you ever be too sweaty to use public transport?Look, it’s not illegal but this comes under consideration for others and context. We all need to get around. Drenched with club sweat on a night bus? Probably fine, given the potential state of the other passengers. Travelling at rush hour after your morning gym session? Not ideal. “If there is a place for you to shower or freshen up before you get on public transport, I think that is a courtesy for others, particularly at busy periods,” says Hanson.How do I deal with manspreading?View image in fullscreen‘The general leg aperture rule is nothing bigger than a tennis ball in between your knees.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianDon’t manspread back, says Hanson, “because two wrongs don’t make a right, whether you are a man, or however you identify. But if you need to adjust yourself slightly pointedly, then that normally does the trick.” He adds: “Obviously, don’t use your hands to touch somebody’s leg but you could slightly push against it [with your knee] if you feel emboldened. If you feel comfortable enough, you could always be quite passive aggressive and say something like: ‘Oh, I’m so sorry – am I taking up too much space?’” The general leg aperture rule is “nothing bigger than a tennis ball in between your knees”.Can I apply makeup on public transport?Hanson used to say absolutely not, but he’s softened. A quick lipstick refresh, or an elegant pat with a powder compact is “probably OK but starting-from-scratch makeup, I would say not – and this is not exclusive to women”. Akano is in agreement about the full face of makeup. “Ideally, you shouldn’t be doing that in a public space, whether on public transport or anywhere else in public,” she says. “I know some people say: ‘I don’t have the time before I leave home.’ Why don’t you wake up 10 or 15 minutes earlier to give yourself time?”What about doingmy hair?No, says Hanson. “General grooming in public is to be kept to an absolute minimum, and I think brushing hair is too much.”Ormy nails?“No, you shouldn’t be doing that in public,” says Akano. “These are private things and not something that other people should have to witness. You should have done them before you left home.” As for people who clip their toenails on public transport: “They deserve to be sent to a different planet,” says Hanson.Can Iapply sunscreen?If you really have to – and even then, it should be the minimum amount you need, and ideally not a whole-body dose. It’s fine, says Akano, if “it is a cream or lotion that you can just put a little bit of in your hands, but if it’s a spray, then you’re most likely going to affect other people. It’s really about consideration and awareness of your environment and the people around you.”Can I get changed in a train carriage?“Absolutely not,” says Hanson. “You can remove some clothes – you could take off a hat, scarf, gloves or even a jumper. But beyond that, no. Small modifications, fine, but not big modifications.” Taking shoes or sandals off is also “a complete no”.What should I do if I think I’m about to be sick?Easy (in theory). “Go to the loo as quickly as possible,” says Hanson, “and hope that you are not sick anywhere other than the loo.”Can I hold on to the overhead bar or strap if I’m wearing a sleeveless top?How is your underarm hygiene? “If you know that it’s not good, then it’s not advisable,” says Akano. Even if you are impeccably clean and fragrant, bare armpits at eye level on busy trains and buses is not particularly pleasant, she adds. “If you’re quite tall, and there are shorter people around you, then that would not be a good experience for them. If you don’t have a choice, then I guess there’s nothing to do because safety is more important. But it’s not something I would necessarily do.”Eating and drinkingCan I drink alcohol, even discreetly?It depends, says Wesson. In some places, such as London and New York, drinking alcohol on public transport is forbidden. “But on the train I catch to London, they come round with a trolley full of the stuff.” If you are going to enjoy your can of beer or mini bottle of wine, make sure you’re not inconveniencing anyone. “Be conscious that if you’re travelling with somebody else, and you’re both having a drink, the chances are you’re going to be a bit louder because that’s what booze does to us all,” says Wesson.Can I eat?On a packed commuter train: “Nothing bigger than a Polo mint,” says Hanson. “Most public transport is riddled with germs, so why do you want to be eating anything in that environment?” On a longer train or coach journey, food is acceptable but nothing “that you’re going to be able to smell halfway down the carriage”. Hot food, and especially the aromas from fast food, can be particularly offensive, but so can a salad nicoise. “An orange or a tangerine is one of the most antisocial things to eat,” points out Hanson.The social contractView image in fullscreen‘The bus comes, and that’s when some people start rummaging in their bag to get their card.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianShouldI havemy ticket/passport/payment method ready?You know the bus is coming, or you’re about to have your passport checked, so make sure whatever it is you need is in your hand. “That way, you don’t hold up a queue of people,” says Akano. “The bus comes, and that’s when some people start rummaging in their bag to get their card, or whatever it is they’re going to use. It’s the same thing with the barriers at the train stations.” Worse still is when you don’t move out of the way while you search for what you need. “Then we all stand there waiting for you.”Is it acceptable to have loud conversations on your phone, or on speakerphone?“Speakerphone, absolutely not,” says Wesson. “Nobody needs to hear both sides of the conversation.” A loud phone conversation is inconsiderate, but sometimes unavoidable. On a train, says Wesson, “You can always stand up and go into the bit between the carriages if needs be.” Ideally, phone calls should be quiet and quick.Can I open the window?Yes, but it’s polite to ask first, says Wesson. “Nine times out of 10, everyone will say: ‘Thank goodness for that.’” It also establishes some communality, he says, “so that if it becomes a problem for somebody, they can say: ‘Look, I’m absolutely perishing. Would it be possible to close it for a bit? What does everybody else think?’ It then doesn’t become about one person.” He adds: “Just doing it unilaterally is rarely the right thing to do.” It’s the same with anything else that affects others, such as blinds.How can I ask someone to use headphones?Hanson has a new way he’s so far only tried once. “You say: ‘Excuse me – I don’t think your headphones are connecting.’ When they go: ‘Oh no, I don’t have headphones’, you go, ‘Ah, that’ll be why.’ It’s so passive aggressive, which a lot of British etiquette is.” If they’re using headphones and it’s still so loud you can hear it, you might just have to try to ignore it. “I probably would move,” says Hanson.ShouldI give money to people begging on trains?As long as it’s not illegal in whichever country you’re in, “and if you feel comfortable doing it and you’d like to do it, then yes”, says Hanson. If you don’t want to, it’s rude to pretend to be engrossed in your phone. “Smile at them. They’re a human being.”Can I sing football songs in a big drunken pack? I’ll take out all the bad languageAkano isn’t a fan of this behaviour. “It can be quite rowdy, especially if people have been drinking, and it gets uncomfortable,” she says. “I have experienced it enough times, and usually I move carriages, or sometimes I’ve decided to alight and wait for another train.” People chatting about the match is fine, “but you start singing, and there’s a whole element of chaos and unrest. I feel that is inappropriate because you’re not the only ones there. Show some consideration for other passengers.”Can I peruse the book/paper/phone screen of someone next to me?View image in fullscreen‘They are minding their own business and you should mind your own business as well.’Illustration: Viki Mladenovski/The GuardianThat one is never OK, says Wesson. “We have such private information on our devices these days, and also you might end up seeing or reading something you didn’t want to.” How about givingsomeone the answer to the crossword they’re doing? Absolutely not, says Akano. “They are minding their own business and you should mind your own business as well,” she says. “You never know who you’re dealing with. Someone might say: ‘Did I ask for your help?’ I would make a conscious effort to not look.”My train is cancelled andeveryone’s stranded. ShouldI offer to share a taxi with fellow passengers?Consider vulnerability, including your own. “Personally, I wouldn’t,” says Akano. “My take on that is to do with safety, being a woman. It’s happened to me before – I got stuck, in the evening, and we didn’t know when the train tracks might be clear. There were a few people trying to book taxis, and one or two offered me a ride, and I thought, ‘No, I don’t know these people – they’re strangers’, so I didn’t take it.” It does depend on the situation, though, she says – if there is someone you feel more comfortable sharing with, perhaps a mother with small children, things might be different.ShouldI wake a stranger up ifI think they’re about to miss their stop?This one takes some judgment, says Wesson. But if you absolutely know that it’s their stop – you had a chat earlier, or you overheard them buying their ticket – you should probably wake them up. “I have friends who fall asleep on trains quite regularly,” he adds, “and the cost of their taxi journeys is enormous and far exceeds the train tickets. I think my advice would be yes.” A gentle nudge in good time should be enough.And finally, how do I get out of talking to a chatty stranger on a long journey?Respond politely at first, says Akano. “Then, if you really don’t want to chat, we all have our phones now, or you might have a book on you. Get it out so they can see that’s the end of the conversation. I think when you do that, most people will tend to hold back on chatting.” If they’re oblivious to all hints, you may just have to pretend it’s your stop and move to another carriage.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The best suitcases in the UK for your next holiday, rigorously tested | Travel | The Guardian
description: Most suitcases look hardwearing, but which ones actually are? We dropped bestselling brands’ luggage from a ladder to find out …
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Most suitcases look hardwearing, but which ones actually are? We dropped bestselling brands’ luggage from a ladder to find out …
Content: Bags of fun! Our writer puts the suitcases through some serious stress-testing.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBags of fun! Our writer puts the suitcases through some serious stress-testing.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianThe FilterTravelReviewThe best suitcases in the UK for your next holiday, rigorously testedMost suitcases look hardwearing, but which ones actually are? We dropped bestselling brands’ luggage from a ladder to find out …The best carry-on luggagePete WiseTue 4 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Asuitcase is like the portrait in the traveller’s attic, accumulating more than its fair share of knocks and scrapes while we refresh ourselves on the road. We trundle them over cobbles, see them tumble from luggage racks on the train – and if we choose to fly, there’s a fair chance they’ll be mishandled before we reunite at the carousel.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.For our testing, we pushed 11 suitcases to the limit by dropping them on to a hard surface, as if they’d been fumbled by a baggage handler. Air travel is especially tough on suitcases, so you might get away with choosing a less-resilient case if you make the climate-conscious choice to travel by rail or sea.According to one Gatwick worker interviewed by the Guardian, the average baggage handler has to load about 150 bags within 40 minutes to facilitate every landing or takeoff – and that’s one of several stints of intense effort during a shift. It’s only natural, then, that some suitcases are roughly handled or dropped. Sita, a service provider to the civil aviation industry, reports that more than 24m items of hold luggage worldwide – or just under five per 1,000 passengers – were mishandled in 2025. Clearly, dings, scratches, and even breakages are a distinct possibility.The good news is that many of today’s suitcases are extremely tough. Some of the best are made with highly durable plastics such as polycarbonates, which are also used in hard-wearing items such as safety goggles and windscreens.There’s more to being a suitcase than getting bashed about, of course. Most travellers want something that looks appealing, provides useful internal organisation, such as storage compartments and pockets, and is easy to manoeuvre with components such as casters and a telescopic handle. I tested 11 models – diverse in shape, size, material, style and price – to help you find the best suitcase to be your trusty travel companion.At a glanceBest suitcase overallAwayThe Large£348 at AwayBest budget suitcaseTrippHoliday 8 Large£69.50 at AmazonBest lightweight suitcaseJulyChecked£275 at JulyBest small suitcaseHorizn StudiosH6 Pro£450 at Horizn StudiosBest for a luxurious lookCarl FriedrikThe Trunk£645 at John LewisBest suitcase for teenagersMiffyCabin trolley spinner suitcase£190 at CaseWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing products since the mid-2010s – long enough to know you can’t assess a product superficially. I’ve tested them rigorously, from the waterproof jackets I’ve worn in the pouring rain tothe sunrise alarm clocks that woke me up every day one winter. But luggage has felt like a special case – to test them to the same degree of rigour, I had to consider the suitcase’s experience when out of the owner’s hands, too.How I testedA man stands on a ladder and drops a suitcase from the top‘Among the hardiest performers during drop testing’: the July Checked suitcase. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianWhether they’re being dropped at the train station or tumbling from the hold of an Airbus A320, suitcases must prove their mettle. So I stress-tested each case by filling it and dropping it, several times, from a ladder on my driveway. As we’ll see, some cases sustained significant damage as a result of the drop tests, while others emerged with just a few scuffs.I also assessed each model’s everyday functionality by packing it, carrying and wheeling it, and testing features such as TSA combination locks and telescopic handles. The most impressive models offered durability and travel-ready convenience in equal measure.Perhaps unsurprisingly, given my testing methodology, none of the brands wanted their suitcases back after testing. Review units in saleable condition have been donated for fundraising to theCat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats. This charity is close to my heart: I’ve fostered over a dozen of their cats and kittens, and some of their cats helped me to reviewthe best cat toys.The best suitcases in 2026A man stands on a ladder and drops a suitcase from the top‘Held up impressively’: Carl Friedrik’s the Trunk. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianBest suitcase overall:Away the LargeAwayThe Large£348£348 at AwayWhat we loveSuperb finishing and toughnessWhat we don’t loveStorage capacity is good, not greatView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£348 at AwayIf you’re happy to shell out for a very well-made suitcase, this would be a good pick. It was one of the best performers in my drop tests, emerging with just a few scuff marks on the sides and scratches on the corners. Using the special “eraser” sponge included with the case, I was able to remove most of these marks after testing.Why we love itIt’s very nicely finished, with an understated pattern of horizontal grooves on the slightly rough-textured shell, and a silky-soft lining and mesh on the inside. I particularly admired fine details, such as the rubbery trim around the main zip, and a recessed handle on the underside that comes in handy when the case is packed with heavy items.The Large is a lovely suitcase to use in every respect, from adjusting its glossy compression straps to wheeling it around on its nimble casters. This wasn’t an official part of testing, but it also proved more than capable of supporting a person’s weight during an impromptu joyride around the spare room.It’s a shame that …considering its imposing size, this suitcase has a middling storage capacity.Carry-on version available:yes,the Carry-On 39.8l (£258)Capacity:99.2lWeight:5.5kgDimensions:52.1 x 31.8 x 73.6cm (WDH)Outer material:polycarbonateClosure:zipper with TSA combination lockStorage:main compartment with two compression straps, a zippered flap pocket, a mesh storage insert with two zippered pockets, and a laundry bag; lid compartment with two zippered pockets in the mesh coverAwayThe Large£348£348 at AwayWhat we loveSuperb finishing and toughnessWhat we don’t loveStorage capacity is good, not greatBest budget suitcase:Tripp Holiday 8 LargeTrippHoliday 8 Largefrom£69.50£75 at Next£69.50 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent quality for the priceWhat we don’t loveEasier to scuff than some swankier rivalsView image in fullscreen£75 at Next£69.50 at AmazonWhat sort of suitcase can you get for less than £100? A very good one, it turns out. The Tripp Holiday 8 is an exceptional case for the price you pay, with an expandable design (using a secondary zipper) that bumps its internal storage up to a generous 102l.Why we love itChoosing an affordable suitcase does come with some trade-offs. There’s no doubt this Tripp case is made with coarser materials than some of its costlier competitors, and it takes a little extra effort to click the telescopic handle into its one and only height position. For the most part, though, the case is a pleasure to handle. The casters manoeuvre fluidly, and the textured outer material should minimise any sliding during transit.Most of all, the Holiday 8 stands out among affordable suitcases for its durability. While hurling the case from a ladder, I noticed that the material has plenty of give, which may have helped it to stay intact. On a less glowing note, scratches and scuff marks stood out prominently on the case’s shiny material.It’s a shame that …there aren’t any small storage compartments or pockets to help with organisation.Carry-on version available:yes,Holiday 8 Cabin 35l suitcase (£55)Capacity:102lWeight:4.2kgDimensions:50 x 32 x 76cm (WDH)Outer material:polypropyleneClosure:zipper with TSA combination lockStorage:main compartment with compression straps; zippered lid compartment with mesh coverTrippHoliday 8 Largefrom£69.50£75 at Next£69.50 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent quality for the priceWhat we don’t loveEasier to scuff than some swankier rivalsBest lightweight suitcase:July CheckedJulyCheckedfrom£275£275 at July£305 at John LewisWhat we loveBuilt (and styled) like a tankWhat we don’t loveSlightly rougher handling than a few competitorsView image in fullscreenFrom £275 at July£305 at John LewisThis cool, minimalist case from Aussie brand July ticks all the boxes for couples on a weekend break or solo travellers taking a slightly longer trip. It has a reasonable weight relative to its toughness and abundant internal storage options. I appreciated the internal mesh pockets and removable laundry bag, which make it simple to keep particular items separate from the bulk of your clothing.Why we love itJuly produces this case in a jaunty array of colours, including eye-catching clay and shadow lavender versions. Taking hue out of the picture, the luggage has a utilitarian, almost military aesthetic, with a textured surface that holds up well to scuffs and scrapes.And I should know, as this suitcase proved to be among the hardiest performers during drop testing. Scuffing occurred mostly around the anodised aluminium protective corners, which actually looked pretty good with the extra wear.It’s simple to move around, with a good telescopic handle for wheeled use and a side handle providing an extra option for hoicking it off the luggage carousel.The same case is available with an integrated ‘CaseSafe’ tracking system (compatible with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub) for £30 extra.It’s a shame that …the casters don’t run quite as smoothly as they might – but that’s me splitting hairs.Carry-on version available:yes,Carry On 42l (from £245)Capacity:80lWeight:3.8kgDimensions:47 x 29 x 66cm (WDH)Outer material:aerospace-grade polycarbonate; anodised aluminium corner bumpersClosure:Japanese YKK zippers with TSA combination lockStorage:main compartment with Y-shaped compression strap, large zippered mesh sleeve, zippered pocket and removable laundry bag; lid compartment with two mesh pocketsJulyCheckedfrom£275£275 at July£305 at John LewisWhat we loveBuilt (and styled) like a tankWhat we don’t loveSlightly rougher handling than a few competitorsBest small suitcase:Horizn Studios H6 ProHorizn StudiosH6 Pro£450£450 at Horizn StudiosWhat we loveSuperior protectiveness and smart looksWhat we don’t loveThe smaller size and high price won’t suit everyoneView image in fullscreen£450 at Horizn StudiosGiven its jet-set pricing, I fully expected the H6 Pro to be something special – and so it proved during my rough-and-tumble testing. Simply put, this case came away with less damage than any other. For the most part, there were just a few light marks, and many of these wiped away easily (except at the corners, which were more deeply scratched). This was a relief, as it’s a fine suitcase, from its weighty casters and abundant internal storage options to the two-position telescopic handle.Why we love itThe polycarbonate outer shell is light, hardy and lovely-looking. Much like the internal organisation, it’s delightfully smooth to the touch – and there are tough plastic rests on one side of the case to help you keep it that way. The TSA lock and locking zippers feel extremely robust.One potential downside to this case is that it’s on the smaller side. You wouldn’t be able to use it for a week-long couple’s holiday, but the H6 Pro is a great fit (both practically and aesthetically) for work trips and weekends away. The largerH7 Pro (£540)provides more baggage capacity at a marginally higher price.It’s a shame that …the price will be off-putting, even for frequent flyers.Carry-on version available:yes, M5 Pro 37l (£470)Capacity:61lWeight:4.1kgDimensions:46 x 24 x 64cm (WDH)Outer material:aerospace-grade polycarbonateClosure:zipper with TSA combination lockStorage:main compartment with two compression straps, two very small mesh pockets, one large mesh sleeve, and a removable clear toiletries pouch; lid compartment with a mesh cover, long zippered pocket, and a removable laundry bagHorizn StudiosH6 Pro£450£450 at Horizn StudiosWhat we loveSuperior protectiveness and smart looksWhat we don’t loveThe smaller size and high price won’t suit everyoneBest for a luxurious look:Carl Friedrik the TrunkCarl FriedrikThe Trunkfrom£645£645 at John Lewis£645 at Carl FriedrikWhat we loveFabulous materials and standout styleWhat we don’t loveSome may consider it OTT and unaffordableView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£645 at John Lewis£645 at Carl FriedrikThis suitcase oozes luxury, from its riveted hinges to the satisfying, thumb-wound number dials on the combination locks. It’s fairly heavy but does plenty to make handling easier, with excellent casters that truly glide across hard surfaces, and a height-adjustable telescopic handle with a nicely moulded grip that doesn’t dig into your hand while you pull the case.Why we love itOpen up the case, and you’ll find ample internal storage options, including three removable zippered bags that are ideal for stashing items such as beauty products. The lid compartment is surprisingly deep, thanks to the case’s distinctively cuboidal shape, which could make it an ideal choice for packing a couple’s belongings in separate sections.The Trunk sustained some scratches and dents (especially on the corners) during drop-testing, perhaps more so than some of the other polycarbonate cases we’ve featured, but it held up impressively overall. If anything, I think a little wear and tear has made it look better.It’s a shame that …the polycarbonate shell, although strong and lightweight, is a bit of a magnet for dust and finger marks. And of course, the eye-watering price of this suitcase will rule it out for a large proportion of holidaymakers.Carry-on version available:not an exact match, but Carl Friedrik sellsthe Carry-on (£345)Capacity:90lWeight:6.2kgDimensions:39.3 x 36.6 x 72.5cm (WDH)Outer material:polycarbonateClosure:buckle and two TSA combination locksStorage:three removable storage cubes; zippered lid compartment; two compression strapsCarl FriedrikThe Trunkfrom£645£645 at John Lewis£645 at Carl FriedrikWhat we loveFabulous materials and standout styleWhat we don’t loveSome may consider it OTT and unaffordableBest suitcase for teenagers:Miffy cabin trolley spinner suitcaseMiffyCabin trolley spinner suitcasefrom£190£190 at Case£190 at VeryWhat we loveCute and surprisingly high qualityWhat we don’t loveQuite sturdy, but not the toughestView image in fullscreen£190 at Case£190 at VeryIn the 2026 luggage launch we didn’t realise we needed, the Miffy brand has released a collection of suitcases adorned with Dick Bruna’s darling bunny. The range includes an even smaller (and orange!)case specifically for kids, while the small cabin option I’ve tested is perfect for younger teens and light-packing grownups. There arelarger hold luggage variantsfor bulkier loads.Why we love itThis is surely the cutest thing I’ve ever thrown from a ladder. Behind the lovely, debossed Miffy face on the front of the case, this is a practical, high-quality piece of luggage. The case is a fairly tough polycarbonate, the casters glide smoothly, and the zipper and TSA lock are robust. Make no mistake: this is not a piece of tatty merchandise.Inside, there’s a beautiful Miffy and aeroplane-print lining, a main compartment with compression straps, and a roomy lid compartment with two pockets on its flap cover – including a transparent one that’s handy for storing easily misplaced essentials, such as currency and travel documents.It’s worth noting that the case I reviewed is on the smaller side, and while there are good storage solutions inside, there’s enough space for only one or two nights’ worth of belongings. For longer trips, choose one of the larger models.I was distraught to see that this case was dented after my stepladder drop test. Thankfully, I was able to pop the material back out from the inside, leaving only a slight mark on the outer.It’s a shame that …you can get tougher suitcases for a similar price.Hold version available:yes, theMiffy large four-wheel trolley case (£275)Capacity:37.9lWeight:2.34kgDimensions:34.8 x 20 x 54.5cm (WDH)Outer material:polycarbonateClosure:zipper with TSA combination lockStorage:main compartment with two compression straps; lid compartment with a zippered cover and two zippered pocketsMiffyCabin trolley spinner suitcasefrom£190£190 at Case£190 at VeryWhat we loveCute and surprisingly high qualityWhat we don’t loveQuite sturdy, but not the toughest***The best of the restA man stands on a ladder and drops a suitcase from the top‘This case split at one of the corners’: the It Legion Medium. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianM&S Pisa 4-wheel hard shell medium suitcaseM&SPisa 4-wheel hard shell medium suitcase£40£40 at M&SWhat we loveStraightforward design and budget priceWhat we don’t loveNo TSA lock and limited organisationView image in fullscreen£40 at M&SBest for:a simple suitcaseThis Marks & Spencer case is a good budget option for those of us who are content to travel without fancy luggage. I’d describe the internal organisation as “no nonsense”: there’s a main compartment with compression straps, and a similarly sized zippered compartment in the lid. It’s an arrangement that maximises usable space, but also risks a jumble of clothes. I used packing cubes inside it to limit movement.The ABS material feels soft, flexible and undeniably flimsier than the polycarbonates often used in premium hard-shell suitcases. It came out of drop-testing a little scratched and scuffed. On the plus side, the case is 1-2kg lighter than some of the tougher models featured here. That’s a big difference in the hand, or on a set of scales.It didn’t make the final cut because …it lacks some commonplace features that many travellers find useful, such as a lock and internal pockets. Still, it’s £40.Carry-on version available:yes, thePisa 4-wheel hard shell cabin suitcase (£30; currently out of stock);capacity:64l;weight:3.4kg;dimensions:44 x 26 x 66cm (WDH);outer material:ABS;closure:zipper (no combination lock);storage:main compartment with two compression straps; lid compartment with a zippered coverM&SPisa 4-wheel hard shell medium suitcase£40£40 at M&SWhat we loveStraightforward design and budget priceWhat we don’t loveNo TSA lock and limited organisationDelsey Paris Chatelet Air 2.0 check-in suitcaseDelseyChatelet Air 2.0 check-in suitcasefrom£395£395 at Delsey£399 at John LewisWhat we loveCombines function with fancy finishingWhat we don’t loveIt’s a little OTT for some tastesView image in fullscreen£395 at Delsey£399 at John LewisBest for:high-capacity luxuryHigh storage and high fashion tend to be awkward travelling companions, but this case from luxury brand Delsey Paris is a good mix of the two. It has an impressive capacity relative to its dimensions, and the internal space can be boosted further by unzipping the expansion gusset at its centre. I had no trouble fitting a week’s worth of clothing inside and was able to separate toiletries and worn items into the various pockets and pouches.I was impressed with this case’s sturdiness during drop-testing. The corner guards bore the brunt of the fall, sustaining a few scuffs, while the rest of the case was unaffected.Aesthetically, this case is “Marmite”, but there’s no doubt that the textured outer shell and chunky gold zippers have a luxurious look and feel, nor that the stitching throughout is immaculate. The case is also available in a new-for-2026,light blue colour.It didn’t make the cut because …it’s prohibitively expensive for most travellers.Carry-on version available:yes, theDelsey Paris Chatelet Air 2.0 cabin suitcase (£276);capacity:73l;weight:4.5kg;dimensions:45 x 30-33 x 66.5cm (WDH);outer material:polycarbonate;closure:zipper with TSA combination lock;storage:main compartment with two compression straps, a zippered flap cover and two zippered mesh pockets in the cover; lid compartment with two compression straps, a zippered flap cover and one zippered mesh pocket in the cover, plus two drawstring storage pouchesDelseyChatelet Air 2.0 check-in suitcasefrom£395£395 at Delsey£399 at John LewisWhat we loveCombines function with fancy finishingWhat we don’t loveIt’s a little OTT for some tastes****skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt Luggage Legion Medium PlusIt LuggageLegion Medium Plus£60£60 at It LuggageWhat we loveIt’s easy to carry and looks charmingWhat we don’t loveStruggled with our stepladder testView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£60 at It LuggageBest for:a lighter-duty suitcaseThis case eschews the trending shell material of the moment, polycarbonate, in favour of good, old-fashioned ABS. You might not know what that material is, but you’ll know how it feels – lightweight and comfortingly familiar.Unfortunately, when it came to drop-testing, this case split at one of the corners. So, if you want a really hardy suitcase, this wouldn’t be our recommendation. If you’re only travelling a few times a year, though, and don’t fly regularly, this might be less of an issue.In all other respects, it was one of my very favourite suitcases. Inside the case, storage options are good, if not dazzling, and the materials feel luxurious relative to the modest price. The casters, telescopic handle and combination lock work perfectly.It didn’t make the final cut because …other cases proved more durable.Carry-on version available:yes,expandable cabin case 47l (£45);capacity:104l;weight:4.2kg;dimensions:48.5 x 30 x 70cm (WDH);outer material:ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene);closure:zipper with TSA combination lock;storage:main compartment with two compression straps; lid compartment with one large zippered compartment and two stuff pockets in the coverIt LuggageLegion Medium Plus£60£60 at It LuggageWhat we loveIt’s easy to carry and looks charmingWhat we don’t loveStruggled with our stepladder testAntler Icon Stripe LargeAntlerIcon Stripe Largefrom£204£204 at Antler£245 at John LewisWhat we loveFamily-sized storage capacityWhat we don’t loveA little less sturdy than our top performersView image in fullscreen£204 at AntlerFrom £245 at John LewisBest for:family tripsPity the plucky parent who has to haul a family-sized suitcase through a busy airport or train station. It’ll never be easy, but really good high-capacity luggage will help. This is just such a suitcase from time-honoured label Antler, with a whopping volume of 135l.On the outside, this suitcase looks and feels quite similar to some of the other polycarbonate cases I’ve tested for this feature: lightweight, subtly detailed and soft to the touch. The inside is more traditional, with a dark cream lining and accent colour zippers. Dare I say it feels a little more special?When fully packed, this suitcase will be very heavy. It’s a good job that the telescopic handle (which doesn’t have far to telescope, given the case’s stature) feels very robust, and the casters manoeuvre serenely.It didn’t make the final cut because …some models proved tougher during drop testing. This case didn’t break, but it accumulated relatively deep scuffs and scratches, especially around the corners. There was also damage to the plastic around the casters.Carry-on version available:yes,four-wheel cabin case 38l (from £185);capacity:135l;weight:4.9kg;dimensions:51.7 x 33.6 x 78cm (WDH);outer material:polycarbonate;closure:zipper with TSA combination lock;storage:main compartment with X-shaped compression straps and a long, zippered flap pocket; large lid compartment with two zippered mesh pockets in the coverAntlerIcon Stripe Largefrom£204£204 at Antler£245 at John LewisWhat we loveFamily-sized storage capacityWhat we don’t loveA little less sturdy than our top performersWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianWhat makes some suitcases more durable than others?Among the various factors that play into a suitcase’s durability, its materials, design and construction are particularly important.Most modern hard-shell suitcases are made of plastic, but this shouldn’t be taken as an indication that their material has similar durability. Some plastics, such as polycarbonates, are particularly tough and lightweight, and you’ll find these types used in some of the hardiest luggage.Suitcase design also affects durability and the level of protection given to the items inside. Corners are especially vulnerable to splitting, so in some cases they’re shored up with a hard-wearing guard over the suitcase shell. Joins between the parts of a suitcase can also prove to be weak points.If you don’t have the luxury of being able to drop several suitcases from a ladder, you might have a hard time determining which suitcases are well constructed with secure joins. Tightly fitting parts and premium fixings such as rivets often bode well, but above all, a generous guarantee should put your mind at ease. Some suitcase brands offer lifetime coverage against manufacturing faults, and we’d recommend seeking a multi-year guarantee at minimum.Are all suitcases suitable to fly as hold luggage?The maximum permitted dimensions (and weight) of your suitcase will depend on the airline and options you choose when booking a flight. Bear in mind that budget airlines and short-haul operators sometimes apply tight size limits, so choose a case to suit the stingiest airlines you use. There are often options to pay extra for an increased hold luggage size allocation when booking your flight.If a suitcase has one or more locks – and most good ones do – then these must be TSA locks, with a special keyhole that will allow customs officials to open the case using a master key. Most large suitcases have these TSA locks, which are denoted by a red diamond symbol. If your suitcase doesn’t have locks and you wish to keep it locked, you can use a TSA padlock such asthis Master Lock model (£12.16).For this article, we’ve focused on large suitcases that would be placed in the hold of an aircraft, rather than the cabin. Smaller cabin bags can stay with the passenger on certain flights – although restrictions apply, and you should always check the flight operator’s policy.The best way to pack a suitcaseThis depends on your objectives, and to some extent, on the suitcase you’re using.For thebest use of space, rolling up items of clothing is generally considered ideal. This allows each sausage-shaped item to be squeezed into a well-suited gap inside the suitcase’s storage compartments. A nice side benefit is that this method will prevent irregular wrinkles from forming in the fabric.When packing smarter clothing, such as your best dresses or shirts, you may prefer to fold these items neatly, rather than rolling them up. It’s usually good practice to fold them at seams or at natural pivot points on the body, such as where the sleeves join the main body of a shirt, or at the waist of a dress. You can usepacking cubesto keep items in their neatly folded shapes within a suitcase.Make good use of your case’sinternal storage optionsto compartmentalise your things. For instance, zipped pockets or sections are handy for storing worn clothing (on your journey home) or toiletries.If travelling by air, pop your packed case on to some weighing scales before you leave for the airport.It’s easy to overpack, and if your case is found to be over the weight limit at check-in, you may face a costly surcharge. Also consider that the weight of your luggage directly affects your carbon footprint. The lighter you pack, the less fuel the plane will use on your journey.For more, check outthe best travel packing hacks to save you space and moneyWhat to do with your old suitcaseThe easiest way to repurpose an old suitcase is for storage at home. My family’s Christmas decorations lived in a tattered suitcase for much of my childhood, and there are surely countless other examples of these containers spending their semi-retirements in cupboards, loft spaces, garden sheds and so on.A suitcase is good for keeping groups of items together and reasonably well protected (depending on the case’s condition), so you might consider using one to store things such as spare bedding, old documents or seasonal items. However, if these things have sentimental value, then storing them inside an airtight, watertight storage box would be a safer bet.One good use for old suitcases in good condition is to donate them to a charity working with young people in precarious housing situations. A serviceable case could be useful to a young person who doesn’t own a dependable bag and must carry their belongings between locations. Often, refugee charities and adult homelessness charities will also make good use of a well-looked-after, preloved suitcase. If there are no charities in your area that can make direct use of your suitcase, you might be able to donate it to a local charity shop for resale.For more, read thebest carry-on luggageand thebest travel pillowsPete Wise is ajournalist with more than a decade’s experience covering everything from global development and social causes to technology and music. He’s had some interesting experiences as a product reviewer – setting up a plethora of pet water fountains to discover which one his cat liked best; squinting at severed plant stems to see which secateurs cut the most cleanly – but dropping suitcases from a ladder might take the biscuitThis article was originally published on 18 May 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. title: What’s the best vegetarian alternative to gelatine? | Vegetarian food and drink | The Guardian
description: There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatine
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatine
Content: Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Benjamina Ebuehi. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Julia Aden.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Benjamina Ebuehi. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Julia Aden.Kitchen aideVegetarian food and drinkWhat’s the best vegetarian alternative to gelatine?There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatineAnna BerrillTue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do I go about substituting gelatine sheets for a vegetarian setting agent?Sarah, Aberdeen“The truth is, there’s no exact substitute for gelatine, because it has an incredibly unique texture,” says Richard Phillips, head of pastry atTimberyardin Edinburgh. Sure, there are plenty of plant-based gelling agents out there – “agar-agar [or just agar], gellan gum, pectin, carrageenan, locust bean gum, vege-gel… the list goes on,” says Phillips – but the result will never quite be the same.“The temperature you have to use them at is different [to gelatine],” says Philip Khoury, author ofBeyond Baking, so his usual workaround is to simply formulate recipes that don’t use gelling agents. Now, that’s all well and good when you’re a pastry chef, but what about the rest of us? “If, for example, I’m making a thick, pipeable cream, then I’ll use cornflour,” says Khoury, and just manipulate it to get different textures. Let’s take the panna cotta and creme brulee recipes in his first book,A New Way to Bake, as an example: “You get two very different textures from essentially the same recipe. The only difference being that if you pour the custard into a tray and chill it, it will set, whereas if you beat it with a whisk, it will turn into this luscious, creamy texture that’sjustset.”But one gelatine substitute doesn’t fit all. “There are specific alternatives for specific things,” says Phillips: “Reversible pectin for glazes; kuzu [root starch] to thicken sauces; pectin to make jellies, using different dosages for different sets.” Khoury, meanwhile, prefers agar for the latter, and the seaweed-derived gelling agent has become something of a poster child here. But again, don’t expect exactly the same result as you’d get with gelatine. And that’s not a subjective statement, as Harold McGee explains in his bibleOn Food and Cooking: “Agar forms gels at even lower concentrations than gelatine does, less than 1% by weight. An agar jelly is somewhat opaque and has a more crumbly texture than a gelatine jelly.” Where gelatine sets and remelts at around the same temperature, an agar gel “only melts again when its temperature reaches 85C [185F]”, which is to say, a jelly made with agar won’t have that joyous melt-in-the-mouth texture.Even so, Reece Kallah, head pastry chef atMount St Restaurantin London, uses agar in fruit puree gels, which feature in her set vanilla custard. “As a general guide, use 0.5% agar by weight of your liquid – for example, 5g agar per 1 litre of liquid.” Kallah mixes the agar with a little sugar “to help it disperse evenly, as it doesn’t dissolve particularly well on its own”, before whisking it into the boiling liquid, pouring into a tray or ramekin, and leaving to set. “I still prefer gelatine, though – it has a softer, more delicate texture because of that lower melting point.”Stars don’t always live up to their hype, after all, and Khoury adds another word of caution. “If Sarah goes about this by saying: ‘I want to swap gelatine for something else’, then it won’t work; if she wants success, then follow a recipe that doesn’t contain gelatine.” It’ll likely be less faff, too.Got a culinary dilemma?
