title: Herby feta frittata and a knockout fruit and rocket salad: Sami Tamimi’s Arabic summer recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Levantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket salad
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: Levantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket salad
Content: Sami Tamimi's courgette and feta cheese Ijeh-Aravic frittata with a fruit, red onion and rocket salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi's courgette and feta cheese Ijeh-Aravic frittata with a fruit, red onion and rocket salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodHerby feta frittata and a knockout fruit and rocket salad: Sami Tamimi’s Arabic summer recipesLevantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket saladSami TamimiTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve always loved food that can be enjoyed at room temperature, or even cold the next day. As the UK, along with many other parts of the world, swelters through another hot summer, these are exactly the kinds of dishes I want to cook and eat. Fresh, light and unfussy, they require little effort, yet never compromise on flavour. This herb-packed courgette and fetaijehpaired with a lush fruit, red onion and rocket salad alongside makes the perfect meal for warm days and relaxed summer gatherings.Courgette and fetaijeh(Arabic frittata)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIjeh is a much-loved Palestinian herb frittata-like omelette that perfectly captures the freshness and simplicity of everyday home cooking. Made with eggs, generous handfuls of fresh herbs, onions and fragrant spices, it is crisp around the edges and soft in the centre and can be enjoyed at any time of day. Together, with some cool mint yoghurt and a salad of fruit and caramelised onions, they celebrate the generosity at the heart of any table.Prep20 minCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4-62 large courgettes(about 700g),trimmed and coarsely gratedSalt and black pepper1 red pepper (about 120g),pith and seeds discarded, flesh finely choppedOlive oil1 small onion (80g),peeled and finely chopped3 spring onions (45g),trimmed and finely chopped3 garlic cloves,peeled and crushed25g flat-leaf parsley,finely chopped20g fresh dill,finely chopped4 large eggs,lightly beaten200g feta,crumbled100g plain flour1 tsp baking powderFor the mint yoghurt300g Greek-style yoghurt2 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp lemon juice1 small garlic clove,peeled and crushed¼ tspdried mint¼ tsp aleppo chilli flakes⅓ tsp saltHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and line the base and sides of a 26cm round baking dish with parchment paper.Put the grated courgette in a colander, sprinkle with one teaspoon of salt and leave for 10 minutes. Using a clean tea towel, squeeze out as much moisture from the courgettes as you can, then put them in a large mixing bowl. Squeeze out the excess moisture from the red pepper, too, then add them to the bowl. Add all the remaining ingredients, along with three quarters of a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper, and combine well using your hands. Transfer the mixture to the prepared dish and smooth the top with the back of the spoon. Bake for 50 minutes, until golden brown, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.To make the mint yoghurt, mix the yoghurt in a medium bowl with the rest of the ingredients, until well combined. Set aside.Once theijehhas cooled, cut it into slices and serve warm or at room temperature with the mint yoghurt and fruit, red onion and rocket salad (below).Fruit, red onion and rocket saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenWhile I like to make loquats the star here, peaches, nectarines, or apricots make excellent alternatives. Serve as a light starter or alongside the ijeh, grilled meats or hearty, nutty grain dishes.Prep15 minCook40 minServes4, as a starter or side1 red onion (150g),peeled and cut into 8 wedges3 tbsp olive oil6 large loquats, peaches, nectarines or apricots (350g),peeled and sliced in half lengthways100g rocket leaves5g coriander leaves,picked5g mint leaves,picked40g pecan kernels,toasted and roughly choppedFor the dressing2½ tbsp balsamic vinegar1½ tbsp pomegranate molasses1½ tsp runny honey1 small garlic clove,peeled and crushedFlaked sea salt and black pepper3 tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/gas 6. First, make the dressing by mixing the balsamic, molasses, honey, garlic, a quarter teaspoon of flaked salt and a grind of black pepper. Slowly pour in the oil, whisking constantly, until combined and smooth.Put the onion wedges into a medium bowl and add one and a half tablespoons of the dressing, along with an eighth of a teaspoon of salt. Toss well to combine, then transfer to a parchment-lined baking tray and roast, tossing once, until softened and slightly caramelised – about 20 minutes. Set aside to cool.Heat one and a half tablespoons of olive oil in a medium frying pan. Add the halved fruit cut side down and fry for two to three minutes, then flip and cook for two minutes more, or until slightly caramelised. Remove from the pan and set aside.Put half the roast onion in a large mixing bowl along with the rocket, herbs, half the pecans, a half-teaspoon of flaked salt, a good grind of black pepper, and half the remaining dressing. Toss well to combine, then transfer to a serving dish, layering the salad and fruit cut side up. Repeat with the remaining salad, onions and fruit, and finish with the remaining toasted nuts.The headline of this article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version referred to a “herby frittata and a fruit and feta salad”; this should have said herby feta frittata and a fruit and rocket salad.Explore more on these topicsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkSaladMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: The Scottish explorer who fancied an adventure closer to home: hiking the Highlands’ Affric Kintail Way | Highlands holidays | The Guardian
description: Globetrotter and TV presenter Alice Morrison trades in her camels and backup team for wild camping in one of Scotland’s most beautiful glens
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Globetrotter and TV presenter Alice Morrison trades in her camels and backup team for wild camping in one of Scotland’s most beautiful glens
Content: River Affric at the west end of Loch Affric in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: Paul Glendell/AlamyView image in fullscreenRiver Affric at the west end of Loch Affric in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: Paul Glendell/AlamyHighlands holidaysThe Scottish explorer who fancied an adventure closer to home: hiking the Highlands’ Affric Kintail WayGlobetrotter and TV presenter Alice Morrison trades in her camels and backup team for wild camping in one of Scotland’s most beautiful glensAlice MorrisonTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.‘Imiss my camels. I miss the sun. I miss the vast emptiness of the desert plains …” These are my thoughts as I trudge through thick conifer plantations and my fifth consecutive hour of rain at the start of the Affric Kintail Way in the Scottish Highlands.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.My last big adventure was a world first. I became the first recorded person to walk the full length of Saudi Arabia, north to south, from Jordan to Yemen. It took three years to organise, then 112 days of walking half a marathon a day, and I had a backup team plus Juicy and Lulu, my naughty but nice camels.It was a fantastic, life-enhancing, often brutal, endeavour but it is over. Adventurers have got to adventure though, and I was looking for something cheap in my own country that needed little organisation or backup. I am a proud Scot and, even though I spend so much time away, I feel a strong emotional pull to my homeland, an almost physical attachment to the landscape and the thousands of ancestors who have walked it before me.There are an abundance of long-distance walking trails in Scotland, and after many happy hours checking out the options onWalk Highlands, I settle on the Affric Kintail Way. It’s a doable distance – 44 miles (71km) in four days; easy to get to and from by bus from Edinburgh; and according to my brother, Robbie, Glen Affric is one of the most beautiful areas of the country.View image in fullscreenAlice Morrison and a guide crossing the Saudi desert.Photograph: Alice MorrisonPreparations are simple. I buy a map, read all the information on the dedicatedwebsite, download the route on the AllTrails app and pack my rucksack. I’m doing it solo, self-supported and wild camping, so need to take everything with me but also keep my pack as light as possible. In the end it weighs around 12kg, which is not bad. My luxury is four Ferrero Rocher chocolates given to me by my mum – one for each evening.The bus drops me off at Drumnadrochit and I walk straight up into the forests. The rain is constant, but I enjoy the sharp smell of the conifers and the sound of the cuckoos. There’s plenty of up, but the way is easy to follow along the Forestry Commission tracks. I keep checking my weather app, which promises a half-hour break in the rain, as it is so much better to pitch a tent in the dry. It comes to 6pm and I get my tent up just before the rain starts again. I’ve done a respectable 5 miles or so since the bus dropped me off, in about four hours.double quotation markOne of the great pleasures of walking in wild places, whether in Scotland or the Arabian peninsula, is finding echoes of the past and wondering what life was like thenThe next morning, I drop down into Cannich and history is waiting for me after a long pull up out of the village. My plan is to walk about 11 miles today. Comar Wood Dun is about 250m off the path. It is a jumble of stones perched at a lookout point over the strath. Once, it was a drystone fortified house and home to a family and their animals between 400BCE and 200AD. Life must have been so hard. It is cold and wet even in June. Barley was the main crop, grown in small clearances in the wood, augmented with meat and milk from the livestock.One of the great pleasures for me of walking in these wild places, whether it is the Highlands of Scotland or the deserts of the Arabian peninsula, is finding these echoes from the past and wondering what life was like then. Were the people happy? Were there compensations for this hard life? How did they deal with all the extremes of nature that we have managed to smooth out with our air conditioning and heating? By hiking and camping, I am trying to get closer to them in some way.View image in fullscreenThe writer on the Affric Kintail Way.Photograph: Alice MorrisonI spend the night beside Dog Falls and the morning is another haul through the forests. Sitting in my midge net at the Glen Affric car park overlooking the inlet to Loch Beinn a’Mheadhoin, hunger kicks in and I wolf down a roll, a big bag of Revels and my emergency veggie sausage rolls – a large chunk of my provisions.I’ve been walking steadily up and down through woodlands, interspersed with farmland. This area is one of the UK’s most ancient natural woodlands – more than 10,000 years old – and is dominated by gnarly Scots pines and silvery birch.My heart yearns for the open spaces, though, and I’m glad when it starts to open up and I see the hills rise on either side of Loch Affric. I’m alone almost all of the time: in four days, I meet just eight people. It’s just me and the green of the hills and the deep black of the loch between them. My heavy pack hurts my shoulders, and my feet are sore from the hard tracks, but I feel so alive. I relish the adventure of being on my own, self-reliant and with no one to worry about or answer to.double quotation markI relish the adventure of being on my own, self-reliant and with no one to worry about or answer toWhen the rain stops and the sun comes out, the grassy uplands glow almost neon-bright. I stop to drink peaty water from a burn and fantasise about living in the tiny wooden hut on the sandy shores of the loch. It’s my third night of camping and the best so far, just me and the geese, but I feel completely safe and relaxed within nature.The next day, my fourth on the trail, I’m on a mission. I need to get some provisions from the Glen Affric hostel and do a solid 10 miles so that I only have a shortish walk the day after to catch the bus. I hike as fast as I can until I finally see the hostel ahead – this tiny outpost is among Scotland’s most remote hostels. I put out my tent to dry on their fence and get to the door. “Shut between 10.00 and 17.00”.View image in fullscreenWild camping above Loch Affric.Photograph: Alice MorrisonDisconsolate, I sit at the side and contemplate my life choices. Then, a woman shrieks as she sees me unexpectedly – Chrissie, who runs the hostel and kindly lets me in to buy chocolate, crisps and a fizzy drink. Sugar and fat consumed, I feel whole again and happily share a story of camels and Saudi hospitality for the sound art project she is doing. She is recording poems, stories and songs from people who stay in the hostel for an exhibition.I continue onwards, struggling on the ups. With a couple of miles to go, my pack feels as if it’s full of rocks. I try to focus on the waterfalls all around me, dashing loudly down the rocks to meet the rivers Affric and Croe.I walk down to a small, flat clearing beside one of them. It’s the perfect camp spot, but if I stop now I’ve failed to reach my 10-mile goal. The sun comes out and I see there’s even a flat rock to sit on. I throw my manufactured goals and failure guilt to the wind and pitch my tent.No billionaire is richer than I am that night in that place. I sit on my rock looking out over the peaks and listening to the music of the water. Tomorrow, I will eat my porridge and walk out by the river to the bus and everyday life. But for tonight I am queen of the world.For more information visit:Walk Highlands, the Affric Kintail Waywebsiteandalltrails.com. The bus from Invernessgoes to Drumnadrochit and picks up atThe Pit Stop cafeat Kintail(citylink.co.uk)Alice’s website isalicemorrison.co.uk; she is also onInstagramExplore more on these topicsHighlands holidaysScotland holidaysWalking holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Acrobatic, goofy and super-fast: the biama battles redefining Ivorian dance culture | Côte d’Ivoire | The Guardian
description: Fuelled by TikTok and street dance battles, the coupé-décalé offshoot is latest expression of Côte d’Ivoire’s pop culture
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Fuelled by TikTok and street dance battles, the coupé-décalé offshoot is latest expression of Côte d’Ivoire’s pop culture
Content: A biama dancer performing in Abidjan. Photograph: Miléquêm DiarassoubaFuelled by TikTok and street dance battles, the coupé-décalé offshoot is latest expression of Côte d’Ivoire’s pop cultureByEromo Egbejulein AbidjanTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 400-strong crowd, perched on plastic chairs and wooden benches in Abidjan’s Yopougon-Selmer neighbourhood, roared with approval as Sauce Graine twisted and turned on the spot with breathtaking speed and dexterity.The dancer, named after the Ivorian palm nut delicacy, was competing in a series of street dance battles set to biama, a frenetic offshoot of coupé-décalé, a type of percussive dance music popular across west Africa that originated inCôte d’Ivoirearound the turn of the century.View image in fullscreenThe genre exploded in popularity after the Covid-19 pandemic.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The GuardianA neighbourhood square in Yopougon-Selmer had been transformed into a dance arena for the event, which got under way about six hours after its advertised midday start. The performers were all under 25, with some as young as five. Audience members, some munching on skewered meat or drinking from beer bottles or plastic cups, periodically joined in as one competitor after another showcased intricate footwork and dramatic chest pops.“This [is a] small ceremony so that people can see the talent we have … a talent that God has given to each of us to share with the whole world,” says Sauce Graine, a 15-year-old whose real name is Arnold and who began dancing to biama six years ago.“Since many people aren’t very familiar with the dance yet, they think it’s just a neighbourhood thing. All we have to do is create the dance so that more people can see it and love it.”Abidjan dancers showcase their talent in Ivorian pop music street battlesAlongside the local strain of hip-hop known as maïmouna – a new fusion of coupé-décalé and rap Ivoire – biama has become emblematic of the resurgence of Ivorian pop culture over the past decade.There is some debate over exactly when biama emerged, but it exploded in popularity after the coronavirus pandemic as young people turned to TikTok to post and respond to dance challenges that fused acrobatics with goofiness that pushed bodies to their limits.“Biama is basically coupé-décalé 2.0, like at 200% speed,” says Cédric Kouamé, a music producer and chief archivist atBaoulecore Archive Centerin the Angrè district of Abidjan. “Like maïmouna,it comes from Yopougon . Most trends start [in] Yopougon. It is basically where a lot of artists started their career.”View image in fullscreenA dancer shows off his moves. ‘Biama is basically coupé-décalé 2.0, like at 200% speed,’ says Cédric Kouamé.Photograph: Miléquêm DiarassoubaFor decades, this working-class district has dictated the cultural zeitgeist of both Abidjan and Côte d’Ivoire. Stéphane Doukouré, better known as Douk Saga, grew up there before founding coupé-décalé with his Jet 7 crew after returning from Paris in the early 2000s. There, he had made a name for himself in a nightclub frequented by wealthy young partygoers bysetting light to thousands of euros.Their genre championed the philosophy ofsagacité– the shrewdness needed to outwit authority – alongsidefarotement, the flamboyant display of wealth. Its free-spending hedonism offered escapism from many Ivorians living through the country’s civil war.Doukouré’s career was short-lived. He died from lung disease in 2006 at the age of 32.The genre was propelled to new heights by Ange Didier Houon, who was born in Yopougon to an icon of the Ivorian sound engineering industry. In his teens, his Lebanese friends gave him the stage name DJ Arafat, after the Palestinian political leader.View image in fullscreenBiama is a frenetic subgenre of coupé-décalé.Photograph: Miléquêm DiarassoubaOne of his earliest breakthrough hits as a teenager was 2003’s Jonathan, a homage to a DJ friend killed in a motorbike crash. Over time, he increased the tempo of his music to match the high-energy, acrobatic roukaskas routines devised by his dancers, drawing on traditional Ivorian dance.Their feet shuffling quickly in lêkê – the ubiquitous Ivorian water-resistant plastic sandals – the dancers performing Arafat’s roukaskas continued a long tradition of audience participation in Ivorian popular music.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArafat’s following grew so large that fans referred to themselves as “the Chinese”. But after his death in another motorbike collision in August 2019, many believed the genre, already showing signs of decline, was nearing its end.View image in fullscreenThe singer Davido (centre) leaves after paying his respects at the funeral of DJ Arafat at the Félix Houphouët-Boigny stadium in Abidjan in 2019.Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/GettyToday, a new generation of artists is vying to be the next megastar of Ivorian pop. Among those hoisting the flag for maïmouna are Didi B, who has gained international recognition, and the more street-famous Himra. The rappers’ rivalry entered a new phase last year when both filled stadiums just weeks apart in different parts of the country.Biama remains the more popular of the two subgeres, particularly among children and young people, who proudly call themselves biamaseursand eagerly accept dance challenges shared across social media. “Biama is, first of all, a dance for the immature,” the popular dancer Kalomamansaidin a recent interview.Kouamé argues that dance has always been inseparable form Ivorian music. “Since the beginning of Ivorian music, as artists were creating their sounds, they were also thinking of the dance moves,” he says.Ernesto Djédjé performing Assouna.He cited the example of Ernesto Djédjé, a superstar of Ivorian music who emerged in the 1970s, who created ziglibithy, a music and dance style whose name comes from a Bété phrase meaning “delicious rhythm”.“Since we were very young, each six months there was a new dance move that we had to learn,” Kouamé syas.Midway through the event in Yopougon,Kehou Mousso– a biama dancer and one of the genre’s few female musicians – took to the stage to loud cheers. Wearing a waist-length orange wig and frilled green outfit, she and four of her dancers came as special guests.View image in fullscreenSauce Graine, one of the Goodofwar biama dancers, predicts the genre ‘will take off’.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The GuardianKnown to her 2.6 million TikTok followers as the “queen of coupé-décalé”, she says the frenetic biama choreography demands constant improvisation. “You have to be improvising every second.”Some cultural observers in Côte d’Ivoire dismiss the genre as little more than “street music”, but biamaseurs remain undeterred. “People will love us,” Sauce Graine says. “They will dance [and] little by little, they will spread the word through their social networks. Then it will take off.”Explore more on these topicsCôte d’IvoireAfricaDanceHip-hopRapfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tell us: has Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey stoked your interest in classics and poetry?  | Classics | The Guardian
description: We would like to hear from people for whom the film has increased their interest in poetry or classics in general

title: Guatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of people | Guatemala | The Guardian
description: Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert
Content: The Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes.Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes.Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty ImagesGuatemalaGuatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of peopleEruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alertAgence France-Presse in San Juan AlotenangoTue 4 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people living on the slopes ofGuatemala’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning.By Tuesday, rivers of lava were streaming down the 3,763-metre (12,346-foot) volcano, which is located less than 100 kilometres (62 miles) fromGuatemalaCity. Ash rose six kilometres (3.73 miles) into the red sky.“Since early morning it was active. That night, the alarm was raised that we needed to evacuate,” a local resident, Alejandro Garcia, 68, told AFP.Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, Garcia said, describing terrifying scenes of lava tumbling down the mountainside.Firefighters said they transported at least 350 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality.Evacuees are staying in a community hall, where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown.“If there were any chance of moving to a different house, it would be better, because you’re always afraid since the volcano doesn’t give any warning,” Lidia Ortiz, 40, said at the shelter.Escuintla, to the south, was sheltering dozens more families, including children, local authorities reported.“If an evacuation is ordered or conditions pose a risk to your life, follow the principle of self-evacuation,” Conred spokesperson Valeria Urizar said in a video posted on social media.The country’s Institute of Volcanology warned of hot volcanic debris flows down Fuego’s slopes, with communities on the western and southern flanks at the greatest risk.Fuego had been erupting for 23 hours straight by Tuesday morning, it said, although the intensity was easing.“We’ve already gotten used to having the volcano constantly active, but this time it was really too much,” 50-year-old resident Sonia Vasquez said.Guatemalan authorities urged “precautions with air traffic”, but there has so far been no impact on the capital’s international airport.The education ministry ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes in communities within two municipalities near the volcano.Guatemala volcano: rescuers battle boiling ash to recover Fuego’s deadRead moreTraffic police also closed a road encircling the mountain range that connects the south coast with the colonial city of Antigua, the country’s main tourist destination and a Unesco World Heritage site.Guatemala lies on the Pacific ‘ring of fire’ and experiences frequent seismic and volcanic activity.There have been several such mass evacuations in recent years because Fuego erupted.Authorities evacuated more than 500 people last year after Fuego spurted gas and ash, with residents moved to shelters from communities near the crater.Another eruption in 2023 pushed around 1,200 people to evacuate.In 2018,215 people were killed and a similar number left missing when rivers of lava poured down Fuego’s slopesand destroyed a village.Explore more on these topicsGuatemalaVolcanoesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: White elephant in the room: Colombia swears in costumed anti-corruption activist as senator | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Luis Carlos Rúa revealed himself to be Elefante blanco just three days before election for ‘his own safety’. Now he is tackling graft from senate floor
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Luis Carlos Rúa revealed himself to be Elefante blanco just three days before election for ‘his own safety’. Now he is tackling graft from senate floor
Content: Luis Carlos Rúa: ‘The inauguration day was spectacular because nothing like it had ever happened anywhere in the world.’Photograph: Elefante BlancoView image in fullscreenLuis Carlos Rúa: ‘The inauguration day was spectacular because nothing like it had ever happened anywhere in the world.’Photograph: Elefante BlancoColombiaWhite elephant in the room: Colombia swears in costumed anti-corruption activist as senatorLuis Carlos Rúa revealed himself to be Elefante blanco just three days before election for ‘his own safety’. Now he is tackling graft from senate floorTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen 102 senators were sworn in for Colombia’s latest parliamentary session, they included 32 women, 69 men – and one cartoon elephant.He had some difficulty making his way down the narrow central aisle of Congress’s ceremonial chamber, weaving past fellow senators in sharply tailored suits and dresses, before taking the oath in his pot-bellied white plush costume.Blending in was never an option for the new senator, who ran almost his entire campaign without revealing his identity.It was only three days before the election that Luis Carlos Rúa, 34, revealed himself as the person behind Elefante blanco, the White Elephant, a reference to the term used to describe overpriced, abandoned or ultimately useless public works, which he had spent the previous five years exposing on social media.Hisvideosattracted hundreds of thousands of views,someprojects were resumed, and Rúa became one of Colombia’smost votedfor senators, with about 124,000 votes.View image in fullscreenLuis Carlos Rúa only revealed himself as Elefante blanco three days before the election.Photograph: Elefante Blanco“The inauguration day was spectacular because nothing like it had ever happened anywhere in the world,” said Rúa, whotook offthe head of his costume only occasionally during the swearing-in ceremony.“No senator had ever taken office like that,” Rúa said during a video call from the Congress corridors, showing his face and dressed in formal attire. “I’m about to go into a plenary session, but I’m not wearing the costume because it’s for specific occasions and not every debate is that significant,” he added.The character’s origins can be traced back to 2019, when Rúa was working for the mayor’s office in Pereira, a city of almost 500,000 people about 205 miles from the capital, Bogotá. He said it was during that time he witnessed the administration pressuring employees to secure votes for a candidate. Rúa recorded a conversation andleaked itto the press.“I had to leave the city because I received death threats,” he said.Rúa moved to Medellín and decided to continue exposing wrongdoing, but anonymously because “here in Colombia, if you don’t do things the way the crooked people want, you’re not welcome”.He commissioned the elephant design from an illustrator and later had the costume made by a seamstress, and posted hisfirst videoin November 2021, about an unfinished road.View image in fullscreenLuis Carlos Rúa exposes a road to nowhere.Photograph: Elefante BlancoSince then, there have beendozensmore about bridges, schools, tunnels and hospitals, all narrated in a distorted voice and sometimes showing Elefante blancotrudging through mudor wading through murky water that stains the white plush costume – Rúa keeps a spare.“It’s extremely hot inside it, but it still has to be done because I’ll go to places the state doesn’t go,” he said.Rúa funded his trips through freelance work, the sale of Elefante blanco plush toys and crowdfunding campaigns, but said it was not sustainable and decided to run for office so that, with a senator’s salary, he could continue his oversight work.He announced his candidacy in December, but remained anonymous. “Revealing my facejust three days before the election gave me enough time to protect my own safety,” Rúa said.He received at least one vote in almost all of Colombia’s approximately 1,100 municipalities.View image in fullscreen‘It’s extremely hot inside it, but it still has to be done because I’ll go to places the state doesn’t go,’ Luis Carlos Rúa says of his costume.Photograph: Carlos Ortega/EPAFor the political analyst Gabriel Cifuentes, Elefante blanco’s election says as much about the growing influence of social media on elections as it does about “a growing weariness with traditional politics”.“Politics is seen as a corrupt exercise and, in that sense, activists like him, who are not tied to political parties, tend to attract the attention of a public that is increasingly connected through social media,” Cifuentes said.One of Rúa’s proposals is a law requiring municipalities to allocate dedicated budgets for repairing potholes. It would be named afterhis father, Darío Rúa, who was 85 when he fell on a potholed street and died in 2024.The senator said he cast a blank vote in the presidential runoff between the leftwing senator Iván Cepeda and the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella,who won. “I’m not from the left, the right or the centre. I’m independent,” Rúa said.Even so, the new senator has faced criticism for voting in favour of De la Espriella’s proposal to move this Friday’s presidential inauguration ceremony from Bogotá to 280 miles away in Cali. The proposalpassedthe senate by 58 votes to 30.Criticsarguedthat Rúa had campaigned against wasting public money,only to backmoving the entire inauguration, with its hundreds of guests and staff, for a single day.He said he wanted to send “a signal of state presence in a region that has historically been neglected” and that, even with the venue change, the inauguration would cost less than the one held when the leftist president Gustavo Petro took office in 2022.Rúa said he would attend De la Espriella’s inauguration dressed as Elefante blanco. “My relationship with him will basically be one of political oversight, and it would have been exactly the same if the other candidate [Cepeda] had won,” he said.Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Three lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan swelters | Japan | The Guardian
description: Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer
Content: One of the Tama Zoological Park lions that has died of suspected heatstroke.Photograph: Tama Zoological ParkView image in fullscreenOne of the Tama Zoological Park lions that has died of suspected heatstroke.Photograph: Tama Zoological ParkJapanThree lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan sweltersMost of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summerAgence France-PresseTue 4 Aug 2026 01.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, as the big cats struggle in Japan’s high levels of humidity.Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year andparts of the country have hit 40Cin recent weeks, qualifying for thenew “cruelly hot day” designation.Since mid-July, 10 of the 16 lions in Tama zoological park have suffered from “loss of appetite and decreased activity”, and three lionesses had died, the zoo said in a statement. One lioness died on Tuesday, another Friday, and the third on Sunday, it said.Japan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperaturesRead moreThe cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke, as dehydration and multiple organ failure were observed by a veterinarian, the zoo said.“Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zoo keepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan’s summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity; that is different from heat with dry air in Africa,” a zoo spokesperson said.“But this summer, heat arrived suddenly after the rainy season was over” in late July, they added.View image in fullscreenThe exterior of Tama Zoological Park.Photograph: Syced/Wikimedia Commons“We are strengthening measures against the heat, sprinkling water, improving ventilation and installing spot air conditioners.”The zoo said several lions are still being treated.About 18,600 people in Japan were taken to hospital for heatstroke between 20 and 26 July, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the fire and disaster management agency.Authorities have adjusted the timings of a string of cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat, including the World Cosplay Summit in Nagoya, which held its last summer edition last weekend.Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually and is aiming to halve that number by 2030. The country’s highest recorded temperature was registered in August last year: 41.8C in Isesaki, north of Tokyo.Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events in Japan and elsewhere.South Korea is currently engulfed by a heatwave, with the rising summer temperatures linked to at least 16 deaths.Explore more on these topicsJapanExtreme heatExtreme weatherAsia PacificWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour
Content: Nine Lives, the feral cat that devastated a rare duck population in New Zealand for years, pictured in February 2024.Photograph: Pest Free PureruaView image in fullscreenNine Lives, the feral cat that devastated a rare duck population in New Zealand for years, pictured in February 2024.Photograph: Pest Free PureruaNew ZealandNine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three yearsLarge tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviourEva Corlettin WellingtonTue 4 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed inNew Zealand, ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations.The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host ofkiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island.“We don’t take for granted that we’ve had this success because it had us baffled for so long,” said Andy Mentor, the project manager for Pest Free Purerua, a conservation project.‘Coming home’: kiwi enter parliament for first time as New Zealand marks conservation winRead moreNew Zealand has one of the highest rates of cat ownership in the world, and the impact of feral and domestic cats on biodiversity ignites fierce debate. Some on social media were horrified Nine Lives had been shot, believing it deserved to live, while others said its capture was “a fantastic result”.Nine Lives will form part of that debate long after its death, with its body set to be taxidermied for use as a tool to educate the community about the devastating impact of feral cats on native species.Nine Lives was first spotted on the Purerua peninsula in Northland in 2023. What ensued was a frustrating and twisted game of cat and mouse.View image in fullscreenNine Lives ate dozens of pāteke, or brown teal, that were being introduced back into the wild.Photograph: Pest Free PureruaPest Free Purerua had just introduced 20 pāteke, or brown teal – the country’s rarest mainland duck – to the peninsula, believing it had control over the feral cat population.“But within a week we had our first death. We put up some cameras and we identified a particular cat with specific markings,” Mentor said. Another 15 pāteke were killed, with the same cat turning up.“It was a really stressful time. So we brought in more traps, gear, night cameras to try and get to the root cause of the problem.”The project managed to catch other feral cats over the next year, but Nine Lives remained elusive. They decided to release more pāteke in 2024 but the same cat appeared, killing another 15 of the 20 birds.“This particular cat would be very erratic. It would show up in a particular place and then not show up for another two or three months. It would show up in the dusk, midnight, early morning, through the day, so it was never a predictable pattern, which made it very, very difficult to track,” Mentor said.The team came close to catching it on a number of occasions, but each time it slipped their grasp, earning it the name Nine Lives.At the end of July, Mentor and his team noticed the cat had turned up to a quarry three nights in a row, which was “quite unusual”. They laid out salmon, fried chicken and rabbit to attract the animal, and deployed cages and traps.On 30 July, a notification on a cellphone camera showed a cat in one of the cages.“We dispatched our trappers to check it out and there it was. So it was humanely shot,” Mentor said.The animal will have its stomach contents examined to see what it was feeding on before being taxidermied. Mentor said it has likely also fed on kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife.More than 2.5m feral cats roam New Zealand’s bush and on offshore islands, where they can grow up to a metre long, including their tail. They have destroyed native wildlife and hunted some bird species to the brink of extinction.In November, the government announcedferal cats would be addedto the country’s world-leading Predator-Free 2050 strategy. Mentor said moving from the suppression of cats to an elimination strategy will be a “real step up” for the peninsula and the team may restart introducing pāteke once more.But for now, conservationists will celebrate the capture of Nine Lives, as well as honour their most evasive adversary. “Nine Lives needs to be given a certain amount of dignity and respect,” said Mentor.Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandWildlifeAnimalsAsia PacificInvasive speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperatures | Japan | The Guardian
description: Prime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 people
Content: Haruto Kubo holds his pet dog Miku, outside a house that collapsed in an earthquake with a magnitude of 7.1 that struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenHaruto Kubo holds his pet dog Miku, outside a house that collapsed in an earthquake with a magnitude of 7.1 that struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersJapanJapan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperaturesPrime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 peopleAssociated PressMon 3 Aug 2026 20.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 22.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has visited the south-western prefecture of Kumamoto, where recovery efforts are being hampered by heat and a lack of water supplies, almost a weekafter a magnitude 7.1 earthquakekilled dozens and caused widespread damage.Thirty-eight peopledied during the quake, including one person who died of apparent heatstroke while taking shelter in a car in hot weather, officials said on Monday.‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquakeRead moreResidents put out heaps of debris, broken furniture and damaged appliances for collection, while in the towns of Uki and Hikawa, construction of temporary housing began. Some hotels and inns were offering their rooms for evacuees.More than 46,000 households remain without water and many also face fuel shortages as the region suffers sweltering heat, stoking fears of heat-related illness. Temperatures were as high as 40C in the country’s south on Monday.More than 8,500 people remain at crowded emergency shelters in converted community centres, school gyms and classrooms, many of which lack airconditioning. Others are sleeping in cars at town hall parking lots and parks, or outside their homes.View image in fullscreenSanae Takaichi greets evacuees in Hikawa in the southern Kumamoto prefecture after a major earthquake hit.Photograph: undefined/Japan Pool/Kyodo News/APTakaichi on Monday flew over the affected areas from an army helicopter and visited one of the area’s best-equipped shelters, with cardboard beds, partitions and airconditioning, triggering criticism on social media that her visit distorted reality.The governor of Kumamoto, Takashi Kimura, in his meeting with Takaichi, stressed the “abnormal heat” over recent days. He said he sought further government support to improve the conditions at evacuation centres, saying many of them lacked clean water and medical care.“While taking into consideration the governor’s requests, we will quickly examine what the government can do for the disaster-hit region and affected people and move proactively,” Takaichi said.View image in fullscreenA house is seen collapsed onto a car in Hikawa.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, a company that owned a general store in the shopping mall thatcollapsed during last weeks earthquake, acknowledged that it had instructed two employees to return to the building to put sales proceeds into a safe, where they were killed in an explosion that followed the quake.Two executives of Habita, a local general store operator that had a shop inside the collapsed Aeon mall in the town of Kashima, attended the wake on Sunday of one of the two victims, 22-year-old Kurumi Otake, and apologised to her parents for the death.View image in fullscreenVehicles wait in line to transport disaster debris to a temporary storage site in Hikawa, amid sweltering temperatures.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPACompany sales manager Goji Yuse acknowledged that the company instructed the two to put sales proceeds into the safe if it was possible.“I wish someone had stopped her,” Otake’s tearful mother told them. “My daughter is not coming back.”The mall’s operator said it believes the explosion was due to a gas leak and occurred after about 3,000 shoppers had been evacuated to a parking lot after the quake, but some employees remained inside. Rescuers recovered five people and the bodies of seven others from the mall.Explore more on these topicsJapanSanae TakaichiEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Did you send that report?’ The Icac bombshell that came late for Damien Tudehope | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: The former Liberal finance minister was questioned by Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, on Tuesday
Author: Anne Davies
Headline: The former Liberal finance minister was questioned by Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, on Tuesday
Content: Damien Tudehope (right) has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenDamien Tudehope (right) has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPIndependent Commission Against CorruptionAnalysis‘Did you send that report?’ The Icac bombshell that came late for Damien TudehopeAnne DaviesThe former Liberal finance minister was questioned by Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, on TuesdayFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 4 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTShareThe bombshell came in the last five minutes of former finance minister and rightwing powerbroker Damien Tudehope’s examination before theIndependent Commission Against Corruption(Icac).At 3.30pm on Tuesday, Tudehope was shown an email which he sent in February 2023, attaching a leaked draft parliamentary report into branch stacking in the Hills area by the Reformers, the shadowy group at the centre of Icac’s Operation Rosny.It has probably imperilled his parliamentary career.“Would you regard yourself … as being bound by keeping it confidential?” asked counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC. Tudehope visibly tensed.“Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?” she asked, showing him the email. “It appears that I did,” Tudehope replied quietly.Jeremy Greenwood is one of the group of conservative Catholic men who set up the Reformers, recruiting like-minded conservatives to theLiberal partyin order to take over branches from the moderate and centre-right factions.In 2023, during the parliamentary inquiry, the key Reformers and associates – Christian Ellis, the then premier’s brothers Jean-Claude Perrottet and Charles Perrottet, and Greenwood – had left NSW to avoid being called to the parliamentary inquiry.NSW Liberal admits to leaking confidential report to young conservative powerbrokers, inquiry hearsRead moreTudehope told Icac he had had a conversation with the premier, Dom Perrottet, who said he knew his brother had gone to Fiji.Leaking a draft parliamentary report is a serious breach of parliamentary rules and contempt of parliament. It may even constitute corrupt conduct depending on the motivation of the leak.Tudehope has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general.Wednesday’s evidence, however, raised questions of just how tightly Tudehope was tied into the activities of the Reformers and the donations they are alleged to have taken to fund their branch takeover activities.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe day started well enough. A politician for 20 years, Tudehope was happy to talk expansively about his alignment with the Reformers’ causes on conservative social issues.He’d been happy to be a speaker at events advocating for safe schools and opposing gender fluidity and marriage equality.But when it came to questions about whether funds flowing into the Reformers were political in nature, the lawyer in Tudehope emerged.“I don’t necessarily accept the premise that every event where someone signs up to a party as a result of attending the event is necessarily a contribution for the benefit of a party, and I think I identified to you that there are people who may sign up to a party to provide no benefit to a party,” Tudehope said.“So, to the extent that you identify for the benefit of a party, I think that’s a very moot point about the definition of a benefit to the Liberal party.”Dwyer wasn’t letting him off the hook so easily. In painstaking detail, she ran him through text messages and WhatsApp groups that she alleged showed knowledge of the secret money trail.Tudehope’s close friend and former law partner Michael O’Hara, who became a successful hotelier, became a major donor to the Reformers, giving $165,000 to a number of entities after introductions at a function at Tudehope’s home where the News Corp columnist Miranda Devine was the speaker.Tudehope agreed he might have introduced Ellis to O’Hara, but denied he had encouraged illegal donations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“If you think that I would expose a friend of mine to that level of scrutiny that he was exposed to, 83 years of age with stage three/four cancer, you think that I would have done that in circumstances where I knew that he would be a prohibited donor for the purposes of the Electoral Funding Act, not on your life!” he said.Under sustained questioning, Tudehope agreed that using invoices to public relations firms to channel payments was “concealment” as the commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, phrased it.The other major backer of the Reformers was Catholic Schools NSW and here Tudehope has several connections. He was friends with the CEO, Dallas McInerney, also a powerful key figure in the right, while his son James worked in communications at Catholic Schools NSW.Icac heard on Wednesday that at a Sunday lunch, James Tudehope told his father he was being pressured to pay an invoice from Ellis. He was “very agitated” because he didn’t think they were getting value for money, Damien Tudehope said.Tudehope said he recommended his son take it up with McInerney, his boss.In Dwyer’s opening address we learned that Ellis, who has moved to London and declined to appear, had used his public relations firm, Beckington, to take donations for Reformer work.Tudehope was also an employer of key Reformers in his ministerial office.In August 2019, the federal member for Berowra, Julian Leeser, who was unaligned to a faction, went public with his concerns about the branch stacking in the Hills in theSydneyMorning Herald.Icac heard that Ellis had said publicly at a Reformers event that “Leeser was a lefty and had to go”, drawing the ire of several in the party.Dwyer tabled an article by Tom Rabe written in 2019 about the factional war and the involvement of two of the Reformers, Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, who were employed in Tudehope’s office. He suggested Liberals were concerned the pair spent most of their time on branch stacking.By October 2019, Tudehope’s office let Ellis go, concerned about the adverse publicity his activities were drawing. Tudehope said it was the chief of staff who made the call.Tudehope was on Tuesday also shown messages from 2018 between members of the Reformers in which they said MPs “were getting scared about ICAC,” and that “Scott and Damien are afraid”.Tudehope denied knowing what they were about. But by the end of the day, he could have little doubt he now had reasons to fear Icac.This article was amended on 5 August 2026 to state that the messages between members of the Reformers that were shown to Damien Tudehope in the hearing dated from 2018. An earlier version said they came from 2020.Explore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionLiberal partyNew South WalesSydneyAustralian politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review finds | MI6 | The Guardian
description: UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
Content: MI6 headquarters at Vauxhall Cross, London. The service was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenMI6 headquarters at Vauxhall Cross, London. The service was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants.Photograph: ReutersMI6MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review findsUK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’Nadeem BadshahTue 4 Aug 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMI6 has been ranked as the most powerful foreign intelligence service inEuropeahead of France and the Netherlands, according to a peer review.The British intelligence agency scored 251 points in the research and was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants and penetrating the ruling elites in Russia, China, Iran and Turkey, according to the review by 60 professionals from 25 countries.France’s General Directorate for External Security (DGSE) finished in second place with 169 points for its global reach and operational capability, the Times reported.The Netherlands, Ukraine and Germany complete the top five, while Slovakia’s service was rated the worst.The review was conducted by French magazine L’Express, which contacted people in stateservices de renseignements(intelligence services) to rate their counterparts in the western-allied countries.Britain caught in ‘space between peace and war’, says new head of MI6Read moreBritain was the first to warn Ukraine about the likelihood of the Russian invasion that began in February 2022, and has been a staunch ally of Kyiv.Ralph Goff, a former chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia at the CIA, told the magazine: “The British are in the lead on the Ukrainian file. We are right behind them.”Robert Gorelick, a former CIA station chief, added: “The United Kingdom has by far the strongest secret services in Europe.MI6is extraordinary.”Last year,Blaise Metreweli became the first woman to lead MI6, taking over from Sir Richard Moore.A former head of the DGSE said: “The British have the ability to play the long game, investing in sources over a 10-year horizon, somewhat like the Russians. And they have a taste for dirty tricks.”The DGSE, which was depicted in the French series The Bureau, was rated as one of the world’s best in counter-terrorism.The service is renowned for its clandestine operations to “eliminate” people deemed a threat to French security. François Hollande, the former French president, spoke publicly about ordering at least 40 operations to assassinate “high value” targets in the Middle East and Africa, according to a 2017 book.A Polish intelligence executive told L’Express: “It is the only service in continental Europe with near-global reach.“They combine technical collection, human intelligence and operational action capabilities.”Explore more on these topicsMI6EspionageUK security and counter-terrorismFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meeting | European Union | The Guardian
description: Migration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for Europe
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Migration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for Europe
Content: People wait on the beach in Ceuta for food provided by the Red Cross on Monday after arriving from Morocco.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople wait on the beach in Ceuta for food provided by the Red Cross on Monday after arriving from Morocco.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersEuropean UnionEU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meetingMigration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for EuropeExplainer: Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?Jennifer Rankinin BrusselsTue 4 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU’s top official on migration has criticisedSpain’s plan to regularise undocumented migrantsas “not a good signal” for Europe, after an emergency meeting intended to draw a line under divisions on theCeuta crisis.Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for migration, said that while the EU could not currently see a direct link between events in Ceuta and Spain’s regularisation plan, the policy was “definitely not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.It was a rare note of discord as the EU sought to move on from an acrimonious row, caused after tens of thousands of migrants arrived – and mostly left – the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged video conference on Tuesday, intended to learn lessons from the politically divisive Ceuta crisis and chart next steps.Spain’s government saidat least 75 people had diedtrying to reach the territory last week, although Ceuta authorities on Monday put the death toll at 88, with at least 11 more on the Moroccan side of the border.About 70,000 of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta had left, Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, told reporters on Tuesday. He described the EU meeting as constructive, saying ⁠member states had ​recognised Madrid’s “immediate and efficient” response.View image in fullscreen‘A test of our resilience’: Magnus Brunner speaking on Wednesday.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPABrunner said the past few days had been “a test of our resilience” and the EU’s external border. The situation, he said, was under control; no one had moved to mainland Spain and the EU’s border-free Schengen zone had not been affected.The message of unity came after several EU member states heavily criticised Spain. Twenty two signed a letter, organised by Italy and Denmark, that implicitly criticisedMadrid’s plan to regularise 500,000 undocumented migrants and asylum seekersas a “pull factor” for “illegal migration”. Nearly 1.2 million people have applied for the scheme.Asked about Spain’s regularisation policy, Brunner said it was not discussed on Tuesday, but added: “I always say to this regularisation discussion … it’s not a good signal, definitely not a good signal for the rest of Europe.”He went on: “I do understand that it is a member state’s competence. And I do understand that Spain did it because it’s mainly about Latin Americans speaking the same language, having the same culture, but the signal for the rest of Europe is not a good one, definitely not.”Brunner declined to criticise Italy’s decision to reintroduce air and sea border checks with Spain for one month, afterthe Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said such moves were informed by “prejudice, fake news, ignorance and political interest”.Brunner said any suspension of Schengen rules had to be proportionate and temporary, adding: “I have some understanding of this reaction of the Italians, because the citizens are concerned.”France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said EU ministers had agreed the Schengen zone was “not the problem”. France was one of the few member states not to sign the letter of 22 EU leaders indicating readiness to reintroduce border checks, although it did step up its own controls.Denmark’s interior minister, Morten Bødsko, said he was “very satisfied” with Spain’s handling of the crisis, but doubled down on the message that the EU needed tougher border controls, adding: “Uncontrolled immigration is a threat to Europe and Denmark.”10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestMinisters broadly endorsed a five-point plan set out by European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, who proposedfurther action to strengthen Europe’s external borders, including an early-warning system and better cooperation with non-EU countries on migration.A statement published by the EU council after the meeting said there was “a common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight”.Ministers emphasised the need to improve “situational awareness, which could be achieved by further developing early-warning systems such as pre-frontier intelligence and social media monitoring” and efforts to “counter malicious external actors engaged in foreign information manipulation and interference”, the statement said.The EU’s foreign policy service was investigating the possible role played by Russian disinformation, but it was too early to reach conclusions, Brunner said.Migration has been a deeply divisive issue for the EU since the 2015-16 crisis, when more than a million people sought asylum in the union. As far-right and nationalist parties seek to outflank mainstream rivals on the issue, tensions remain high, despite fewer people making irregular crossings.The EU’s border agency, Frontex, reported 178,000 irregular border crossings in 2025, down 26% on the previous year and the lowest since 2021, when much of Europe was in Covid lockdown.Irregular arrivals in Spain (36,683) were significantly lower than inItaly(66,328) and Greece (51, 399), as well as attempted and successful crossings to the UK (65,891), according to Frontex.The 2015-16 crisis paved the wayfor a sweeping overhaul of the EU’s asylum and migration rules, which came into force in June.Brunner emphasised the need to implement the EU’s migration pact, playing down a suggestion from Greece that further emergency measures were required.The Greek prime minister, Kyriákos Mitsotákis, inan article for Politico, said countries should be able to suspend asylum applications for newly arrived people when facing “exceptional situations of extreme and disproportionate pressure”. Europe was facing the “deliberate instrumentalisation of migration by state and non-state actors”, he wrote, saying the pact did not provide the tools for these scenarios.Brunner disagreed – “the pact does offer solutions for this” – while not ruling out changes, saying EU leaders would discuss a “strategic way forward”.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionSpainItalyMigrationImmigration and asylumEuropePedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: Refuse collectors help Italian woman recover binned €1m lottery ticket | Italy | The Guardian
description: Winner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown away
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Winner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown away
Content: The instant win ticket was ‘miraculously still in one piece’ after it was found in a rubbish truck.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe instant win ticket was ‘miraculously still in one piece’ after it was found in a rubbish truck.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesItalyRefuse collectors help Italian woman recover binned €1m lottery ticketWinner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown awayAgence France-Presse in RomeTue 4 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA €1m lottery ticket has been recovered from the rubbish inItalyafter the frantic winner called on refuse collectors to help her retrieve it, according to the waste management company.The instant win ticket was “miraculously still in one piece” after garbage workers combed through mounds of rubbish on their truck, said Roberto Nicola Toscano, the administrator of the SANB company in Italy’s southern Puglia region.Toscano explained how when the winner went on Sunday to check her ticket at her local shop after the draw, the machine indicated it was “non-payable”. That was because smaller retailers can only redeem small wins.But the woman – who remains anonymous – didn’t realise she had won the big jackpot.“The winner always played the same numbers, as they were associated with a loved one,” Toscano said.When she returned home from the store, a family member told her that her regular numbers had won. They immediately ran back to the shop, only to discover the ticket had already been thrown away and the rubbish collected.She called Toscano.“We reconstructed the journey of the ticket, without much hope of finding it, as it had already been picked up by a garbage truck,” Toscano saidWith a stroke of luck, however, they managed to identify the correct lorry and stopped it.Given the risk posed by potentially dangerous material in the waste, they took the vehicle to a specialist company equipped to do the search, he said.The workers searched for over a day, finding various tickets and ticket stubs.“Among them was the stub we were looking for, which was miraculously still in one piece,” Toscano said.When he told the winner they had found it, “she cried with emotion”, he said. “I would have hugged her, but we were on the phone.”However, averting the disaster came at a price. SANB, located in Bitonto outside Bari, is a public agency, meaning that the cost of the search would have been borne by taxpayers.Toscano said the woman had to sign a promise to “cover all of the additional costs” incurred – a gamble that paid off.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain says 70,000 out of 72,000 migrants that entered Ceuta in mass border crossing have returned to Morocco – as it happened | Hungary | The Guardian
description: Minister tells reporters least 75 people died after EU ministers meet to discuss response to the crisis
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Minister tells reporters least 75 people died after EU ministers meet to discuss response to the crisis
Content: 08.06 EDT70,000 out of 72,000 migrants in Ceuta returned to Morocco, Spanish minister saysSpain’s interior ministerFernando Grande-Marlaskais also briefing the press right now.He says all countries were “constructive” and acknowledged Spain’s immediate response.He tells reporters that70,000 of the estimated 72,000 that crossed in Cueta have now returned toMorocco.Spain is “in the process of resolving” the status of the remaining individuals,and those who do not have the right to remain in the country will be returned to Morocco, he says.But he goes out of his way tomake it very clear that the EU’s Schengen area “was in no way compromised” by the crisis,with “no secondary movement, nor even the possibility of any.”As we explained on Europe Live on Friday,Ceuta has a special status under the Schengen rules, meaning that all entries and exits to mainland Spain or the EU still require full border and document checks.He says today’s meeting was “satisfactory” in recognising Spain’s work on irregular migration.Share

title: UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland | Plastics | The Guardian
description: A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
Content: Plastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenPlastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersSeascape: the state of our oceansPlasticsUK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartlandA Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problemSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighand Ayça Aldatmaz in AdanaTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub inTurkeysupplied with plastic waste by British companies.The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey.The findings from a Guardian investigation reignite concerns over Britain’s continuing role in “waste colonialism” – a term used to describe the export of plastic waste by rich nations to poorer countries with less regulated waste management.The UK government pledged to reduce plastic pollution and eliminate harmful plastics duringtalks to reach a global plastics treaty, which collapsed last year, but it has not committed to a ban on exports.Treaty negotiations are expected to resume in 2027.Britain, one of the world’s largest exporters of plastic waste, exported 675,000 tonnes in 2025, its largest amount in eight years, of which139,000 tonnes was shipped to Turkey. The EU’s plastic waste exports to Turkey that yearrose 19% on the year before to more than 500,000 tonnes.Environmental campaigners in the UK and Turkey say that British and EU plastic waste exports are driving the operations responsible for the pollution, leaving the city’s poorer residents to pay the price.About 13% of UK plastic waste to Turkey was shipped to eight facilities within the recycling zone in Adana between May 2021 and July 2024, according to an analysis of import and export data carried out for the Guardian by an international NGO, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA).Thirteen British companies sent 545 shipments, totalling 52,000 tonnes, of plastic waste to the hub during the three-year period. There is no suggestion that the companies exporting plastic waste are acting illegally. British exporters of plastic waste do, however, have a duty under various regulations to ensure that the plastic they export is recycled in an environmentally sound manner.View image in fullscreenA plastic waste recycling plant near Adana. Samples taken from a canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites.Photograph: Ayça AldatmazSedat Gündoğdu, a Turkish marine biologist at Sabancı University’s Istanbul Policy Center, who conducted the microplastic sampling, has called for a ban on all plastic imports to Turkey. “The discharge of microplastic-laden wastewater into irrigation canals raises critical concerns about agricultural contamination and food safety,” he said.Plastic pollution from recycling centres that contaminates canals ultimately ends up in the Mediterranean Sea, he added, which “exacerbates marine plastic accumulation” and undermines efforts to protect the sea from contamination.Samples taken from the canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites, according to Gündoğdu’s research,published in Environment Monitoring and Assessment. He also found pellets, films and fragments “highly characteristic of [waste] recycling processing”, he said.He has called for mandatory installation of microplastic filtration at all facilities and independent monitoring of all wastewater discharges in agricultural zones.Amy Youngman, a legal specialist at the EIA, said that, by its continued reliance on exporting rather than investing in reduction or domestic recycling, the UK had failed to “keep pace with the EU” and had created a “structural imbalance”.“This results in pollution occurring overseas in ways that would not be tolerated within the UK itself and passes the devastating human health, economic and environmental harm to communities in Turkey,” she said.The findings added to an “expanding body of irrefutable evidence exposing waste colonialism in the UK’s waste-export system”, she said.We need to talk about plastic: five everyday items choking the planetRead moreA Greenpeace investigation in 2021 found plastic waste from British supermarkets wastedumped and burned in Adana. The same year, the Turkish government announced aban on certain waste, including polyethylene, which is used in 94% of UK plastic waste exports including yoghurt pots, salad bags and plastic film, but revoked the ban afterpressure from the recycling industry.The EU has recently imposedstrict controls on plastic waste exports. From November, exports other than to mostly rich OECD countries will be banned. Environmentalists fear this could lead to more exports to Turkey, an OECD country and already the main importer of EU waste.A spokesperson for the UK’sDepartment for Environment, Food & Rural Affairssaid: “There are already strict controls in place on the export of waste set out in UK legislation. Businesses involved in the export of waste from the UK are required to ensure that the waste they ship is managed in an environmentally sound manner, and we have already taken action to further reduce our need to export plastic waste.”The Turkish government was approached for comment but did not respond.Explore more on these topicsPlasticsSeascape: the state of our oceansRecyclingTurkeyPollutionEuropeEuropean UnionWastenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rubio hopes US can reach Hormuz deal with Iran ‘very shortly’ as officials say progress has been made – as it happened  | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: US secretary of state comments come after treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Washington could reach a deal ‘by tomorrow’
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: US secretary of state comments come after treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Washington could reach a deal ‘by tomorrow’
Content: 12.23 EDTIran and Oman make progress on a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz, officials sayIran andOmanhave made progress toward a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz, a potential breakthrough that could help end the war in the Middle East, regional officials have said.Under the emerging agreement, ships would enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman, with service fees charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment, two regional officials told the Associated Press.They said negotiations are still underway and that the final agreement could take a different form. They said any deal would be linked to lifting the US blockade on Iran’s ports.The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive negotiations unfolding behind closed doors.Share

title: Iran’s president denies threatening to resign during talks over strait of Hormuz | Iran | The Guardian
description: Masoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Masoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’
Content: The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has rejected the idea he and the country’s supreme leader cannot work together.Photograph: Iranian Presidential Office Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has rejected the idea he and the country’s supreme leader cannot work together.Photograph: Iranian Presidential Office Handout/EPAIranIran’s president denies threatening to resign during talks over strait of HormuzMasoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’Middle East crisis live – latest updatesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorTue 4 Aug 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMasoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been forced to deny claims that he has repeatedly threatened to resign as he battles hardline factions opposed to reaching a settlement with the US over the strait of Hormuz.The US and Europe hope a deal is imminent to reopen the strait and they are putting pressure on Oman to accept a temporary agreement that officials in Muscat fear will leave Iran retaining near permanent dominance of the vital oil shipping channel.
