Ships would enter the strait in a route close to Iran, but leave on a route that passes through Iranian and Omani waters.But far from being feted over an imminent diplomatic victory, Pezeshkian was instead forced to deny that he had repeatedly offered to resign, verbally and in writing, during a television interview marking his second anniversary in the job.Pezeshkian accused some of wishing to create a rift inside Iran and said: “If I want to resign, I will officially announce that I have resigned. I will not resign, I will stand.”View image in fullscreenAn anti-US billboard at Enghelab Square in central Tehran, Iran.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAThe resignation claims, which have been front page news in Iran, were made by Mohammad Bagher Kharazi, who is linked by marriage toMojtaba Khamenei, the new supreme leader.He said Pezeshkian had become frustrated at being excluded from decision making, made worse by the supreme leader’s reluctance to reveal his whereabouts for fear of foreign intelligence agencies. Khamenei wasbadly injured in the Israeli bombingon the first day of the war that killed his father and has not been seen or heard in public since.Trump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regimeRead moreKharazi claimed Pezeshkian had threatened to quit so many times that Khamenei warned him he would accept the next resignation threat, a claim Khamenei’s office eventually said on Tuesday was “fundamentally false and untrue”.Pezeshkian insisted in the interview that he was in complete harmony with the military and said those that claimed30,000 people had been killed in the January protestsnever took up the offer to provide proof.The interview, marking the halfway point of his turbulent presidency, appeared to be an attempt to dispel the impression that his belief in consensus was a weakness, or that he had been sidelined by hardline war leaders.Kharazi is the brother-in-law of Massoud Khamenei, the younger brother of the supreme leader. Critics say he has a record of making unsubstantiated allegations and despite his family connections to the supreme leader, it is not clear if he has seen him since hiselevation to the post in March.However, the row has highlighted the deep strategic and tactical differences inside Iran over the wisdom of talks with the US.Mehdi Tabatabaei, a senior member of the Iranian president’s office, described the reports as “complete nonsense and lies”.In a post on social media, he condemned a “sinister coalition of lying, deceitful and reckless extremism”whose members could not accept democratic outcomes. He said: “Two years have passed since their failure in the arena of national elections, yet they are still seeking revenge against the will of the nation. They have become puppets of Iran’s enemies.”Ahmad Zeidabadi, a reformist reporter, said the claims were inflammatory and served only to exacerbate tensions.Pezeshkian on Sunday suggested that the memorandum of understanding, negotiated with the US in June and reviled by some hardliners, would serve as a cornerstone for Iranian foreign relations in the future, saying that Iran “must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed”.On Monday, the conservative-dominated Assembly of Experts issued a statement describing hopes for an agreement or understanding with the US as “futile” and labelled what it termed “whispers of capitulation in the name of defending peace” an “unforgivable betrayal”. It added that trusting this arrogant government was nothing more than a mirage.Khamenei himself had said in April he was opposed to talks with the US in principle, but in deference to Pezeshkian had allowed them to go ahead.Explore more on these topicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaMojtaba KhameneiStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: Mass funeral held in Gaza for victims of 2023 Israeli strike | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Remains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyed
Author: William Christou
Headline: Remains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyed
Content: 1:04Mourners hold funeral for 112 people killed in 2023 by Israeli strike in Gaza – videoGazaMass funeral held in Gaza for victims of 2023 Israeli strikeRemains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyedWilliam ChristouTue 4 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMourners gathered in central Gaza on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, including 40 children, who were killed in 2023 in one of the deadliest Israeli strikes of the Gaza war.Their bodies could not be recovered until now because of Israel’s continuing strikes, which have slowed, though not halted, since the ceasefire in October.Hundreds of people gathered around more than 100 coffins wrapped in Palestinian flags and arranged in rows on the ground in Deir al-Balah. Mourners prayed for the victims before carrying the bodies through rubble-lined streets and past destroyed buildings for burial in a nearby cemetery.The victims had been among more than 300 people killed on 22 November 2023, when Israeli warplanes demolished a residential block inGazaCity. The bodies of only about 40 people could be recovered by people at the scene, who dug through smouldering rubble with their bare hands and basic tools.Last weekend, Gaza’s civil defence dug through the levelled apartment block and recovered the remains of a further 112 victims, including women and children. It said 157 people were still missing after the attack.The ceasefire that was established in October – which has not stopped Israeli bombing of Gaza – has allowed first responders to dig through the rubble where thousands of remains are still buried across the territory.View image in fullscreenPalestinians carry the bodies through the rubble-lined streets of Deir al-Balah for burial in a nearby cemetery.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAAt least 7,400 people have been reported by relatives as still buried under the rubble, Zaher al-Waheidi, head of the Gaza health ministry’s records department, told the Associated Press. He added that the true number was probably thousands higher because some strikes had killed entire families, leaving no loved ones to report them missing.A UN commission, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. In June, a UN commission found that Israel wascontinuing to commit genocide in Gazaand that its security forces “deliberately targeted and killed” Palestinian children.At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes over the weekend, despite the announcement of a deal intended to solidify the second phase of the October ceasefire. The killings happened just a few days after the US president, Donald Trump, hailed the latest deal – intended to lead to Hamas disarming and Israeli troops withdrawing from Gaza – as a “historic agreement”.More than 73,000 people in Gaza have been killed by Israel since 7 October 2023, including more than 1,250 people since the October ceasefire.Israel launched the war in Gaza after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the October ceasefire.Ceasefire talks intended to move the agreement into a second phase have largely stalled. Senior Hamas officials said that the group’s disarmament is conditional on Israel withdrawing from the strip. Israel said that it had “serious security concerns” about last week’s agreement.Most of the Gaza Strip remains in ruins, with the vast majority of its 2 million population displaced and living through a humanitarian crisis in unsanitary, overcrowded tent cities.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait | Iran | The Guardian
description: Optimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposals
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Optimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposals
Content: The US, Europe and Saudi Arabia are reportedly putting pressure on Oman to accept an arrangement on reopening the strait of Hormuz with a temporary shipping route.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US, Europe and Saudi Arabia are reportedly putting pressure on Oman to accept an arrangement on reopening the strait of Hormuz with a temporary shipping route.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersIranUS and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz straitOptimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposalsMiddle East crisis live – latest updatesJulian BorgerandPatrick WintourTue 4 Aug 2026 13.19 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS and Qatari officials have said progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz.The optimistic speculation on Tuesday brought oil prices down 2%, but the strait remained closed to shipping and a cargo vessel was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast close to the strait.Britain’s maritime security agency, UKMTO,reported the strikeon Monday night but did not name the vessel.The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said the US andIranwere negotiating and told CNBC television: “I think there is a chance we may have a deal today ​or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised ​position in this conflict.”His remarks echo similarlyupbeat comments on Monday from Donald Trump, who claimed that a breakthrough was imminent, though Tehran quickly denied it was involved in any direct talks with the US.Qatari and Pakistani mediators said they were talking to both sides in an effort to close gaps, restore the ceasefire deal from thememorandum of understanding(MoU) signed in mid-June and reopen the Hormuz strait, which was the portal for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquified natural gas.Qatar’s ‌foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, said Qatar, Pakistan and Oman were mediating in close coordination and exchanging draft proposals between Washington and Tehran. He said the diplomatic contacts had reached “very progressive stages”.A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters news agency: “A lot is happening in the ‌background … We are talking to both sides. Our sole goal at this moment is to make both parties at least agree to start talking.”However, neither Qatar nor Pakistan are directly involved in the focus of negotiations in recent days, which has been betweenIran and Oman on a temporary transit schemethat would allow ships to enter and leave the Gulf. The MoU broke down in July when vessels tried to cross the strait along the Omani coast without seeking Iranian approval, and Iran attacked them.On Tuesday, the crew of an Indian-flagged commercial ship that sank in the Red Sea after an attack was rescued, a local Yemeni official said, with Delhi condemning the “unprovoked” aggression.Yemen’s internationally recognised government blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the attack, according to the official Saba news agency.Last month, the Houthis declared a Red Sea maritime blockade ofSaudi Arabia, and have since claimed several attacks on oil tankers and infrastructure.All the crew of MSV Faize Noore Oliya, comprising 13 Indian nationals and one Yemeni, were rescued after the vessel came under attack south of the port city of Hodeida, the Yemeni official said.India’s shipping minister, Sarbananda Sonowal, said on X: “India strongly condemns this unprovoked attack”, saying the vessel was “hit by a projectile near Yemeni waters”.Regional diplomats involved in the talks about the strait of Hormuz said Oman was under concerted US, European and Saudi pressure to accept a temporary scheme that would allow shipping to enter the Gulf via a route through the strait close to Iran, and then leave on a southern route along the Omani coast, which would be jointly controlled with Iran.The contentious issue of Iran’s demand to charge transiting vessels tolls or other fees would be left to be decided during a 60-day negotiating period, during which time Iran’s nuclear programme would also be addressed.The Omani government has been resisting the Hormuz proposal out of fear it could become permanent and give Tehran an enduring say over sea routes in Omani waters, the regional diplomats said.The Iranian state-run broadcaster IRIB reported on Tuesday evening: “These negotiations, taking place between the two coastal countries of the strait of Hormuz, are focused on determining safe routes for ships to transit. The talks have so far been assessed as positive at both the technical and political levels, and Iran is working with Oman to develop the necessary mechanisms for future arrangements to manage shipping traffic in this strategic waterway.”The talks are complicated by splits in Tehran, according to the diplomats, with the foreign ministry keen to do a deal and fearing Iranian control of the Hormuz strait could prove to be a wasting asset over time as sea traffic finds alternative routes. Regime hardliners, on the other hand, oppose the deal on the grounds that the US administration cannot be trusted to deliver the financial benefits promised in return for opening the strait.“I think the regime understands the magnitude of the hold Iran has over the strait, and they smell the desperation coming from the US in terms of [trying to] strike a deal,” a diplomat from the region said.Another diplomat said Riyadh was putting particularly heavy pressure on Oman because the Saudis thought “we may be on the brink of a regional war because there is a big faction in Iran that does not want a deal under any circumstances”.Explore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranQatarSaudi ArabiaOmanMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdom | X | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook
Content: Yahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist, is one of those affected by the account blocking.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist, is one of those affected by the account blocking.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianXElon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdomExclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and FacebookGeneva AbdulTue 4 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk’s X has become the latest major US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi Arabian dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.Earlier this year, the Guardian reported that platforms includingSnapchat and Meta’s Facebook and Instagramhad blocked dissidents’ accounts over allegations by Saudi authorities that they were violating local law.At the time,X, formerly Twitter, said it had notified users that it had not taken any action following requests by Saudi authorities, and it “strongly believes in defending and respecting the voice of our users”.However, since mid-July more than 60 accounts on the platform have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia through geoblocking, which prevents users inside the kingdom from viewing the content, according to the London-based human rights organisation ALQST.Those affected includeYahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist who runs ALQST, and Abdullah Alaoudh, a US-based activist and vocal critic of Saudi human rights violations. Others affected include exiled activists, Saudi academics and independent media.Alaoudh, a senior policy adviser for Gulf issues at the American Committee for Middle East Rights, said: “I think it’s horrible because we were fighting tyrants back home and now we’re fighting tyrants and their cronies here where we are in exile.“It’s censorship – and what’s even worse is that they did not say we violated X’s rules or Meta’s rules.”Account holders received emails from X informing them that their content had been withheld in the kingdom “in order to comply with X’s obligations under Saudi Arabia’s local laws”.A Saudi decree attached to the letters and seen by the Guardian said the accounts had transmitted material that “infringes on public order, religious values, public morals or the sanctity of private life”.Abdullah Aljuraywi, a monitoring and campaigns officer at ALQST, whose X account was also blocked inside the kingdom, said: “The news was sadly not very surprising, given that the authorities have a long history of silencing criticism at home and treating Saudis who speak out from abroad, especially those still connected to people inside the country, as a threat.“What is even more concerning is that technology companies have helped enable this suppression, instead of protecting the freedom of speech they often say they support.”ALQST has called on X, Meta,Snapchatand YouTube to restore access to the accounts and provide transparency over how the decisions were reached.Meta previously told the Guardian that when it received reports of content violating local law but not the company’s own community standards, the company may restrict the content’s availability in the country where it was alleged to be unlawful.X and the Saudi embassy in London have been approached for comment.Other accounts targeted include those of Ghanem al-Masarir, a prominent Saudi satirist. Earlier this year a British court ordered Saudi Arabia topay him £3m in damagesafter his iPhones were hacked and he was physically attacked outside Harrods in central London.In May, al-Masarir was notified by YouTube that two of his accounts, with more than 800,000 subscribers combined, would be blocked in the kingdom after legal complaints made from a “government entity”. YouTube did not respond to a request for comment.The same month, X emailed al-Masarir informing him of the request from Saudi authorities alleging that his account violated Saudi law, with an attached decree. By July, the company had notified al-Masarir that his content had been withheld in the kingdom to comply with local laws.“I’m not surprised that Saudi has asked to block, but I’m surprised Elon Musk has listened,” al-Masarir said. He predicted “other authoritarian countries around the world” would follow suit.Explore more on these topicsXSaudi ArabiaSnapchatFacebookInstagramMetaInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests | India | The Guardian
description: Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
Content: Nationwide protests erupted after exam paper leaks and have encompassed growing anger at the India government and the prospects for young people in the country.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAView image in fullscreenNationwide protests erupted after exam paper leaks and have encompassed growing anger at the India government and the prospects for young people in the country.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAIndiaIndia’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protestsOpposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP supportPenelope MacRaein DelhiTue 4 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks thatforced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure.Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs.The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state.Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment.View image in fullscreenPrashant Kishor won the byelection for his fledgling Jan Suraaj party. He said he win was a wake-up call for Modi.Photograph: Hindustan Times/Getty ImagesDeepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.”The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of WorkingIndiareport by Azim Premji University.The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined.The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign.India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiRead moreAfter he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds.A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests.The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook.The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content.The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status.“The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said.Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.”But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: UN experts urge Canada to protect Sikh activist amid credible threats to his life | Sikhism | The Guardian
description: Special rapporteurs say ‘transnational repression by Indian authorities’ has put Moninder Singh in danger
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Special rapporteurs say ‘transnational repression by Indian authorities’ has put Moninder Singh in danger
Content: Moninder Singh, centre, speaks to the media in September 2023 after Hardeep Singh Nijjar was killed outside a gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia.Photograph: The Canadian Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenMoninder Singh, centre, speaks to the media in September 2023 after Hardeep Singh Nijjar was killed outside a gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia.Photograph: The Canadian Press/AlamySikhismUN experts urge Canada to protect Sikh activist amid credible threats to his lifeSpecial rapporteurs say ‘transnational repression by Indian authorities’ has put Moninder Singh in dangerAgence France-Press in GenevaTue 4 Aug 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUN rights experts have urged Canada to take all feasible measures to protectthe Sikh activist Moninder Singh, who has been repeatedly warned by the Canadian authorities of credible threats to his life.Sign up for This Is India: our free weekly newsletter on life in the subcontinentRead moreIn a letter to the Canadian government, the five UN experts raised “concerning allegations of foreign intimidation and reprisals” against Singh, a Canadian national.The letter recalled that since 2022, Singh has received four “duty to warn” notices from the Canadian authorities about credible and imminent threats to his life. It urgedCanadato “take all feasible measures at its disposal to protect Mr Moninder Singh and his family, as well as similarly situated individuals on Canadian soil”.It went on to say: “We also urge the authorities to accelerate the investigations into these allegations, hold perpetrators accountable, ensure adequate remedy to victims and take all steps to prevent reoccurrence.”The letter, dated 3 June and made public two months later, was written by the special rapporteurs on: protecting rights while countering terrorism; freedom of peaceful assembly; human rights defenders; freedom of religion; and the expert on promoting a democratic international order.UN special rapporteurs and experts are independent figures appointed by the Human Rights Council to report their findings. They do not, therefore, speak for the UN itself. A copy of the letter was also sent to the Indian government.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Sikh community in Peshawar, Pakistan, stage a protest in 2023 after the killing Hardeep Singh Nijjar.Photograph: Muhammad Sajjad/APSingh visited the UN in Geneva earlier this year to appeal for international action against India’s alleged targeting of Sikh activists abroad and against transnational repression more broadly. Sikh activists accuse India of targeting members of their community around the world, including alleged killings using organised crime groups – charges that India denies.The best-known case was the 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a friend of Singh’s who was shot dead near the Sikh temple he led in a Vancouver suburb. Canada’s then-prime minister, Justin Trudeau,publicly accused India of involvement in that assassination, a charge later repeated by Canadian intelligence.India denied the allegations but the row chilled ties between the two nations, both of which expelled a string of diplomats in 2024.Canadian intelligence accuses India over Sikh’s killing as Carney meets ModiRead moreRelations improved after the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, took office last year, culminating with an India visit in March to sign a string of trade deals, as Canadian authorities downplayed their previous threat assessment.Like Nijjar, Singh, 44, is part of a fringe groupadvocating for an independent Sikh state called Khalistan. The Khalistan campaign dates to India’s 1947 independence and has been blamed for the assassination of a prime minister and the bombing of a passenger jet. It has been a contentious issue between India and several western nations with large Sikh populations.In their letter, the experts said they were concerned that the threats against Singh “fall within a broader pattern of transnational repression by Indian authorities against Sikh activists in different countries, including Canada”.Singh said the letter was “a stark reminder of how far the Indian state is willing to go to silence Sikh voices advocating for self-determination”.“When a foreign state feels empowered to commit violence in Canada to silence dissent, it signals a profound failure to protect the rights and safety of targeted communities,” he said.“I refuse to be intimidated into silence. My leadership and advocacy for Khalistan are rooted in international law, human rights principles and most importantly the lived experiences of my community,” Singh added.Explore more on these topicsSikhismCanadaIndiaReligionSouth and central AsiaUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Campaign warns of perils UK waters can pose for dogs and owners | Dogs | The Guardian
description: Dogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or people
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Dogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or people
Content: Emma-Jane Thomas with Bruno: ‘We’ve had all this hot weather … and it’s easy to not realise the dangers.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma-Jane Thomas with Bruno: ‘We’ve had all this hot weather … and it’s easy to not realise the dangers.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDogsCampaign warns of perils UK waters can pose for dogs and ownersDogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or peopleNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith its gentle rippling water, tall purple flowers and rustling trees, Earlswood Lakes near Solihull in the West Midlands seems the perfect spot for dogs to paddle. But their owners have been warned that the otherwise idyllic open water could prove perilous to pets.“We’ve had all this hot weather and millions of families are now spending time around open bodies of water, and it’s easy to not realise the dangers,” said Emma-Jane Thomas, rehoming manager atDogsTrust Kenilworth during a walk around Earlswood.“Dogs love water and it’s great exercise and enrichment for them. However, not all dogs are natural swimmers,” she added. “Even strong swimmers can get into difficulties in the water.”Accompanying Thomas is Bruno the dalmatian who is clearly eager to go for a dip. But he’s been kept on a short lead. Dogs Trust has launched a new campaign with the catchline “If in doubt, keep your dog out”, in an attempt to reduce the injuries and fatalities that can occur among dogs and their owners around lakes, canals, rivers and the sea.Data from the Royal National Lifeboat Institute obtained by Dogs Trust shows that 308 dog-related incidents in open water in the UK were recorded between 2021 and 2025, almost all taking place on the coast. About a third occurred between June and September of those years.Separate figures from the National Water Safety Forum show there were 10 accidental deaths due to drowning in England between 2019 and 2025 linked to animal rescue, and 12 linked to dog walking.Data from the Canal & River Trust shows that dog-related incidents in the UK reached a five-year high in 2025, increasing by 39% compared with the previous year.Dogs Trust notes that many cases were related to dogs – or people attempting to rescue them – needing help after entering the water. Strong currents and fatigue can pose a risk, too.“When you’re thinking about open bodies of water, it’s always stop, check and think about what could be the dangers,” said Thomas, noting many are not clearly visible on first sight. “Steep banks could be an issue if a dog gets in and then swims around, [and] can’t find a way out again,” she said. “Hidden debris under the water – trolleys, broken glass, lots of weeds or branches. Blue-green algae is a danger to dogs.”View image in fullscreenSign alerting walkers at Earlswood to dangers of blue-green algae.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThomas also cautioned against attempting a rescue should a dog get into trouble.“If your dog’s in difficulty, it could then be two emergencies, not just one,” she said. “If you can see a safe place where your dog can exit the water, call your dog there with their recall. If you can’t do that, call emergency services and they will come and assist with dog emergencies.”Even on a picturesque summer’s day Earlswood is far from hazard-free, with a small yellow sign alerting walkers to dangers of blue-green algae.Such cyanobacteria thrive in warmer weather, forming blooms and scums – and some release toxins.“Not all blue-green algae blooms and scums are toxic, but you can’t tell just by looking at them, so it’s best to assume they are,” theEnvironment Agency notes.Emily Mills, veterinary projects manager at Dogs Trust, said: “Dogs can become unwell from drinking contaminated water or simply cleaning it from their fur after swimming. Symptoms can be seen as little as 15 minutes after exposure and may progress rapidly to become fatal.”Walking her rescue border collie Billy, local resident Sally said the blue-green algae was a concern – adding that Billy was always kept on a lead.View image in fullscreenBlue-green algae can contain toxins.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“But there’s more dogs off the lead than on the lead when you walk around here. And it is a worry that there isn’t enough signage around,” she said.An online Dogs Trust survey of 2,000 owners in the UK, conducted in June, revealed that many may be unaware of such risks, with 33% reporting they did not believe blue-green algae posed a serious risk to dogs.The survey also found 19% of dog owners were unaware calm-looking water can still pose serious risks, and 80% said they’d enter water to rescue their dog, despite the risk to themselves.“Dogs love the water, we know that, and we absolutely don’t want to stop that,” said Thomas. “The reason that we’ve put the campaign out is so that owners and dogs can continue to enjoy these types of areas safely, so that when they do come here, they are aware of the risks.”Explore more on these topicsDogsAnimalsPetsHealth & wellbeingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charity Commission to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlements | Charities | The Guardian
description: Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint made by Labour MP about the funds
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint made by Labour MP about the funds
Content: Israeli settlers look at nearby Palestinian towns from an outpost in Yitzhar, Occupied West Bank.Photograph: Marcus Yam/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers look at nearby Palestinian towns from an outpost in Yitzhar, Occupied West Bank.Photograph: Marcus Yam/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesCharitiesCharity Commission to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlementsOfficial action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint   made by Labour MP about the fundsHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn official investigation has been launched into charities in England and Wales donating funds to illegal Israeli settlements inPalestine.The Charity Commission will aim to establish the amount of charitable funds going to illegal settlements, whether the spending was in furtherance of their purposes and any regulatory action that may be necessary.The investigation follows the Guardian’s reporting about the issue. Last year, it revealed thattwo UK charities had transferred approximately £5.7mto the Bnei Akiva Yeshiva high school in Susya, in the Israeli-occupied territory.In June, the Guardian published details of a formal complaint made by the Labour MP, Melanie Ward, to the regulator in which she said that32 charities in England and Wales had donated at least £28mto Israeli settlements that are illegal under international law. The Guardian understands that the inquiry is a direct response to Ward’s complaint.Announcing the investigation, which will initially focus on eight unnamed charities, Stephen Roake, assistant director, high risk compliance at the commission, said: “Serious allegations have been made about UK charities operating in illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine, so our first step is to establish the facts. Only then can we determine if regulatory action is required, based on our findings and the evidence we see.“Our fact-finding will also help us develop regulatory guidance for charities, which will to help ensure public trust and confidence in charities.”In June, the then foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper,said in parliamentthat she had asked the regulator to investigate the issue, telling MPs that “charity systems are abused to funnel support to illegal settlements” and “some evidence suggests that rules are being broken”. She expressed concern about “UK gift aid [tax relief] being funnelled to illegal settlements”.Responding to Cooper, Ward said her and 140 Labour colleagues wanted to see a ban rather than an inquiry. She told MPs that the commission appeared to have been made aware of the issue of donations to settlements in July last year – when the Guardian published its first story on the matter – but “has done nothing so far”.The regulator said the eight charities are among those that have been identified in concerns recently raised with it and that it would look at the location of their respective partners and how recently alleged activity occurred. It said it would consider naming them when it publishes its findings.The commission added that it planned to extend the number of charities under investigation over time.It said it has shared information about the scope of its inquiry with the police and HMRC. The Metropolitan police’s war crimes unit has said that it is not currently investigating any charities in relation to donations to illegal settlements.Last month, the Guardian revealed that a British charitywas funding a religious school at the heart of expansion plansfor the illegal Israeli settlement in the Palestinian city of Hebron.Friends of Yeshivat Shavei Hevron, which was approached for comment at the time, sent nearly £200,000 to the school between 2019 and 2024.Construction of a new dormitory for the school was approved in June, after the far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, unilaterally broke a decades-old international agreement on control of Hebron to give Israel planning authority.Abtisam Mohamed, a Labour MP and member of the foreign affairs committee, said that while she and other parliamentarians welcomed news of the investigation, “we know there is evidence of at least 32 charities engaging in this abhorrent practice. The Charity Commission must investigate them as well and move quickly to stamp out this behaviour altogether.“Funding illegal Israeli settlements is extremist activity linked to the violence and dispossession of Palestinians and bears no relation to charitable activity.”Explore more on these topicsCharitiesCharitable givingEnglandWalesIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Government contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rules | Unemployment | The Guardian
description: Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Content: The first secretary of state, Louise Haigh (left), says new rules will ensure £90bn spent annually on government contracts can help ease unemployment.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe first secretary of state, Louise Haigh (left), says new rules will ensure £90bn spent annually on government contracts can help ease unemployment.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAUnemploymentGovernment contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rulesLouise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groupsAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.As part of a government push to reduce the number of peoplenot in education, employment or training (Neets)in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, said the move would help small businesses who often find themselves locked out of contracts because of the requirements, which big businesses know how to get around.“Every pound of taxpayer money should be spent in a way that benefits local communities – creating good jobs and giving young people the skills they need for the future,” said Haigh. “For too long, securing government contracts has been a tick-box exercise that fails to deliver the positive change that people feel in their pocket and see in the places they live.“We are doing things differently. These new rules will ensure the £90bn that is spent each year through government contracts supports British jobs, skills and people in every postcode.”Central government departments are required to weigh up the social value of government contracts, which counts for 10% of the decision. Under new measures this will be increased to 20%, but instead of considering social good, government buyers will be pushed to secure contracts with companies creating local jobs that pay above the minimum wage, offer training, work experience or plug local skills gaps.Contracts worth less than £1m will be exempt from the requirement, which ministers hope will make it easier for smaller companies to compete.The plans were criticised by environmental and green campaign groups, which said that job creation should not be a trade-off with protecting the environment.“Protecting the environment and helping young people into good work are mutually beneficial and one shouldn’t come at a cost to the other,” said Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy. “Companies should be held to account with environmental targets to help achieve a better future without leaving young workers behind.”‘They’re anxious about everything’: life for young people seeking work in Dudley and LewishamRead moreFriends of the Earth’s head of campaigns, Rosie Downes, said: “Encouraging companies to create good local jobs is crucial, but it shouldn’t be an either/or with efforts to safeguard our environment.“Communities are already paying the price of environmental inaction, with the UK on course for record levels of heat-related deaths this summer and our natural world in sharp decline.”Sarah Williams, the director of strategic partnerships at Green Alliance, said: “The UK is facing a growing youth unemployment crisis, so businesses should be encouraged to create good jobs and opportunities for young people. But scrapping requirements on climate and sustainability is simply not the answer. It’s not an either/or choice.”The move is also likely to spark concern among anti-trafficking and equality campaigners. ALaboursource said the government knew it would face criticism for scrapping some of the current social value indicators.“What companies have to do at the moment feels too much like a box-ticking exercise and it’s just red tape instead of being useful,” they said. “We are trying to make sure that the government pound is being used to invest in companies that want to invest directly in young people in their areas, and it brings real results and doesn’t just look good on paper.”Suppliers will be assessed on their commitment to backing British jobs and developing skills, and specifically targeting support for young Neets, care leavers and people with long-term health conditions.Explore more on these topicsUnemploymentLabourLouise HaighnewsShareReuse this content

title: BP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North Sea | BP | The Guardian
description: Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double
Content: Meg O'Neill says the North Sea investments are ‘not competitive’ within BP’s portfolio.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenMeg O'Neill says the North Sea investments are ‘not competitive’ within BP’s portfolio.Photograph: Darren England/AAPBPBP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North SeaMeg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than doubleRevealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisisNils Pratley: BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to BurnhamJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBP’s chief executive has urgedAndy Burnhamto make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even as the oil company prepares to sell its North Sea business after 60 years in the ageing basin.In a conversation with the new prime minister, Meg O’Neill said the country should prioritise using energy produced in the UK, “where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts”.BP’s endorsement of UK oil production came days after the 117-year-old companysignalled a plan to exit the North Seaafter six decades, as part of a wider plan to streamline its business.BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for saleRead moreO’Neill said North Sea investments were “not competitive” within BP’s portfolio, while the company reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine because of rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis.BP’s quarterly profits more than doubled to $5.73bn (£4.27bn) in the three months to the end of June, as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt energy exports from the Gulf.O’Neill added that BP had already received several unsolicited approaches to buy its North Sea fields and she was “very optimistic” that the assets would “continue to be profitable in the hands of a future owner”.Burnham’s government is expected to make a decision on whether to allow two controversial North Sea oil and gas projects – the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields – to move ahead despite growing outrage over oil company profits and evidence of a deepening global climate crisis.The new ministers are also facing calls to reform the North Sea tax regime. The industry has consistently argued that the UK government’s high taxes on oil and gas accelerate its natural decline.In an interview with CNBC News, O’Neill said Burnham had “reinforced his desire to work closely with business” and “be pragmatic”.She said: “The UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas. The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.“The UK is still using a huge amount of oil and natural gas every single day, and we ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party.“You know, I think the new prime minister has come in with a focus on being pragmatic, and with a focus on understanding how communities around the nation can benefit from developing local economic outcomes.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drillingRead moreBurnham was warned last week he could face the first revolt of his premiership over his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas.BP revealed its climbing profits days after Shell posted its second highest quarterly earnings on record after months of market volatility caused by the Middle East crisis.Europe’s largest oil companydoubled its net profit to almost $10bnin the three months to June, the highest since its record earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.The Middle East crisis has helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in ​net profits to $32.69bn in ​the three ​months ​ending on ​30 June, despite disruption in ‌the strait of Hormuz, owing to higher ​sales revenue for refined and chemical products and crude oil.The windfall profits for the world’s biggest oil and gas companies have faced criticism. Households and businesses are struggling with rising energy bills, and millions have been affected by severe heatwaves across Europe, which are made more likely and more severe by the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis.Donald Trump has said Chevron and ExxonMobil, which also reported sharp profit increases this week, are “making too much money” and should return some of their profits to the public.Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “Clearly not everyone is feeling the pain of the energy crisis. While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control with increasingly severe heatwaves, wildfires and droughts.”Explore more on these topicsBPOil and gas companiesAndy BurnhamEnergy industryOilGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire  | UK news | The Guardian
description: All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after large air and sea rescue operation by France and UK
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after large air and sea rescue operation by France and UK
Content: People disembark from a French rescue ship after their boat caught fire during an attempt to cross the Channel from France.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople disembark from a French rescue ship after their boat caught fire during an attempt to cross the Channel from France.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsDinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fireAll passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after large air and sea rescue operation by France and UKDiane TaylorTue 4 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 06.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dinghy carrying 173 people has capsized after its engine caught fire as it attempted to cross the Channel fromFrance.The people onboard were rescued from the water after a large air and sea operation was launched using UK border security and French vessels along with an RNLI boat.According to French authorities there were initially 173 people onboard but five were rescued overnight in an earlier incident and taken back to Boulogne. The rest of the passengers said they wanted to continue their journey.The dingy was carrying the highest number of people so far this year. A boat that arrived on 23 July was carrying 165 passengers.A coastguard spokesperson said: “A vessel caught fire earlier this morning whilst in the French search and rescue region. UK vessels and a lifeboat are assisting.”An RNLI spokesperson said Eastbourne’s all-weather lifeboat launched at 6am on Tuesday.View image in fullscreenThe people rescued from the dinghy board a bus after disembarking from the French rescue ship.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Calais préfet said 40 firefighters and a specialised medical team were involved in the incident. Eleven people suffered minor injuries and three were taken to hospital in Boulogne.On Monday, Reform UKproposed using the Royal Navyto return people to France or Belgium under a plan they called “operation fortress”. The party has described the scheme as a humanitarian response.Last week,four people died on overcrowded boatstrying to cross the Channel. Smugglers are using increasingly dangerous techniques in response to successive UK government clampdowns to stop crossings.They are also launching boats from parts of the French coast that are farther away from the UK in the hope of evading French police interceptions. The boat on Tuesday reportedly left from Dieppe, about 70 miles (112km) from the UK compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles.The new prime minister,Andy Burnham, has promised to continue working to stop the crossings, although more than 2,000 people have crossed the Channel since he became prime minister. The government has put a number of deterrents in place to stop crossings, but desperate people continue to get into increasingly dangerous dinghies.1:22Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – videoAccording to a statement issued by French authorities on Tuesday, the people in the boat initially refused an offer of assistance. “Given the structural fragility of the overcrowded boats, the decision was made not to force the migrants to board state rescue vessels, to avoid endangering their lives in the event of a shipwreck,” the statement read.All 173 people have now been returned to Boulogne.Explore more on these topicsUK newsMigrationFranceAndy BurnhamImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: US stock market hits record highs as AI profits pile and oil prices ease | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: S&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months ago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: S&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months ago
Content: A screen displays stock market index data as traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenA screen displays stock market index data as traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersStock marketsUS stock market hits record highs as AI profits pile and oil prices easeS&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months agoAssociated PressTue 4 Aug 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US stock market rallied to records on Tuesday as profits kept piling up for companies and as oil prices eased.The S&P 500 shot up 1.8%, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a couple months ago. The Dow Jones industrial average added 907 points, or 1.7%, to its own record set the day before, while the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6%.Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and surged 29.5% after its CEO, Alex Karp, said its overall revenue leaped 93% in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026.Caterpillar climbed 5.6% after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $20bn in sales and revenue in a quarter, and its CEO, Joe Creed, said it was seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power datacenters, among other things.They are the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, after strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50% in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet.That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the Covid-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, when stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group.Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices.Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.3% to $79.36 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $72 and $102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.The yield on the 10-year treasury fell to 4.62% from 4.70% Monday and from 4.75% at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI datacenters.Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.6% for Nvidia, 6.6% for Broadcom and 7.6% for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.They more than offset a drop for Chipotle Mexican Group, which fell 9.7% on fears that future profits could be hurt after the chain removed jalapeños from some of its restaurants after a salmonella outbreak. Chipotle said Minnesota health officials had no ongoing concerns with it.All told, the S&P 500 rallied 136.02 points to 7,736.52. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 907.47 to 54,085.88, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 671.10 to 26,584.99.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsUS economyAI (artificial intelligence)DatacentersnewsShareReuse this content

title: David Ellison claims opposition to his mega-merger stems from potential CNN control | Business | The Guardian
description: With $111bn deal to acquire cable network’s parent company stalled in courts, Ellison courts public
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: With $111bn deal to acquire cable network’s parent company stalled in courts, Ellison courts public
Content: Paramount Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison looks on during Day 10 of the BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells Tennis Garden on 13 March 2026 in Indian Wells, California.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParamount Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison looks on during Day 10 of the BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells Tennis Garden on 13 March 2026 in Indian Wells, California.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesBusinessDavid Ellison claims opposition to his mega-merger stems from potential CNN controlWith $111bn deal to acquire cable network’s parent company stalled in courts, Ellison courts publicJeremy BarrTue 4 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpeaking out on the lawsuit against the big merger between Paramount Skydance andWarner BrosDiscovery (WBD),Paramount’s CEO, David Ellison, said that the legal backlash against the deal is “not really about market share” but rather stems from political motivations.Noting in a New York Timesguest essaypublished on Tuesday that the deal had “been reviewed and approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States”, Ellison played down the competitive concerns raised by the state coalition and Writers Guild of America West and Writers Guild of America East, which also sued to block the deal, and said he believed the reaction came from a “plainer worry”.“The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’sCNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions,” Ellison wrote. “Unfortunately, I can’t give anyone a view into my heart and mind, but I can share this: I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans.”Reporting has showedthat Ellisonandhis fatherhave made promises to theTrump administrationabout swaying the network in a more favorable direction, purportedly to encourage federal regulators to approve the merger, prompting backlash from Democrats such as Senator Elizabeth Warren.Backlash against Ellison, son of the tech mogul Larry Ellison, one of the wealthiest people in the world, as a media owner began last summer after after his company, Skydance Media, went through an $8.4bnmergerwith Paramount Global. As the deal was closing, CBS abruptly announced it was canceling The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, which aired its last episode in May.Once the merger was completed, Ellison appointed the heterodox opinion writerBari Weissto run CBS News, a controversial move that has led tolayoffsandeditorial tensionsat the network.Without directly addressing any of the controversies around CBS News, Ellison wrote that he was committed to the independence that is at the core of the “founding principles” ofCNNandCBSNews.“I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. “Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause.“These were founding principles for both CNN and CBS News,” Ellison continued. “For legends like Ted Turner and Edward R. Murrow, and it is exactly that kind of independence that has always fueled the greatness of ‘60 Minutes.’”Ellison’s essay (“The Critics Are Wrong About My Politics”) comes at a pivotal time for his $111bn merger agreement to buy WBD, which is currently held up in a California court after a 12-state coalition sued to block the deal on anti-competitive grounds.After district judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín agreed to temporarily block the deal, Paramount made the unusual decision to bypass the temporary injunction stage and hold up the merger until the case can go to trial – or until June 2027. The parties have both made proposals for when the case should reach trial, with Paramount asking for a November trial and the state coalition asking for a date in April 2027.Explore more on these topicsBusinessCNNTelevision industryWarner BrosParamount+newsShareReuse this content

title: Trump Fed chair’s inflation strategy: leave it to the market | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Kevin Warsh would rather stay out of the fray – and thus devalue the Fed’s credibility as an economic steward
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Kevin Warsh would rather stay out of the fray – and thus devalue the Fed’s credibility as an economic steward
Content: Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve chair.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve chair.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFederal ReserveTrump Fed chair’s inflation strategy: leave it to the marketEduardo PorterKevin Warsh would rather stay out of the fray – and thus devalue the Fed’s credibility as an economic stewardTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 16.31 EDTShareIt must feel strange to argue that government action is inevitably counter-productive – illegitimate even – when the government is you.For the last half century, the Republican party has been comfortable with the contradiction. It’s framed in that clever quote fromRonald Reagan’s 1981 inaugural speech: “Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.” Solutions, in this view, are delivered by free, unencumbered markets.The proposition can trip over its shoelaces, though. Last week, it wasDonald Trump’s new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, who found himself entangled in the oxymoron.Trump’s hypocritical new tariffs are a chance for the world to fight back | Joseph StiglitzRead moreAs financial markets expectantly awaited some hint of the Fed’s view of the nation’s obdurate inflation, some understanding of what the central bank’s strategy might look like if, as appears likely, prices get further out of hand, Warsh offered neither. Instead, he proposed that the market do its job, tightening financial conditions without the Fed’s intervention.The increase in long-term bond yields “has provided us some comfort”, he said, during his press conference following the split decision by the federal open markets committee not to raise interest rates despite inflation running at double its 2% goal. “The markets have done quite a bit,” he added. “Even while at some level we haven’t done much in 42 days.”The guardian of low inflation in the US, the steward of global financial stability since the second world war, would rather stay out of the fray.The markets didn’t like it, though. The price of US government bonds sank, sending long-term interest rates – which determine borrowing costs for businesses and households – much higher. The yield on 30-year US treasury bonds spiked to the highest in 19 years. Stock markets tumbled. Financiers openly worried about potential political motivations, given Trump’s demand that the Fed cut interest rates, not raise them.Warsh’s sunny description of the economic outlook, attributing rising bond yields to “solid” economic output, “strong” business investment and productivity, and “solid” labor markets – no mention of that irksome war in Iran – did little to convince investors that the chair has the guts to get out from under Trump’s shadow. His failure to provide guidance to the markets, other than to helpfully explain that he is “resolute” about doing his job, did little to temper misgivings.double quotation markWhen market participants have no idea what the central bank will do next, perhaps they will be more carefulWhat Warsh’s willingness to outsource monetary policy to the markets is most likely to achieve is to devalue the Fed’s credibility as an economic steward. Redefining it as a “referee”, calling fouls in some game inside the chairman’s head, won’t help. (Perhaps he views a quarter-point rate hike as a yellow card?)In this new configuration, markets will be left to their own devices not only to make sense of the gyrations of the economy – battered by war, tariffs, artificial intelligence and whatnot – but also to figure out what an opaque, lackadaisical central bank that refuses to explain itself might choose to do next.Warsh hasfloatedthat the Fed should hold fewer interest-rate-setting meetings and has mulled scaling back the press conferences held after every meeting. This wasa practice introducedby former chair Ben Bernanke, who for some reason believed that providing markets and the broad American public a sense of the thought processes guiding this opaque, unelected, massively powerful economic agent was probably good for financial stability and, perhaps, democracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is not to say that there is no sense to Warsh’s desire to keep the markets guessing. When market participants have no idea what the central bank will do next, perhaps they will be more careful. In a more uncertain world, the financial institutions that lead us into a crisis every few years will be even more wary of taking on risk and piling on debt, unsure of what the Fed might do or whether it will save them when the next disaster hits. A more volatile world will tame some of the exuberance that regularly takes hold of the stock market.Understood this way, Warsh’s vision of a Fed-light economy appears benign compared with other strands of the GOP’s project to remove the government from the American experiment. This is not “starve the beast”, as Republicans call their efforts to bankrupt the public sector.That strategy has done enormous damage to the republic. Its crowning moment may have been Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which delivered a colossal tax cut and eviscerated programs to provide healthcare and food for the poor. It has done away with the notion of shared prosperity, which is essential to sustain liberal democracy.While Warsh’s worldview doesn’t look quite so destructive, his vision also comes at a cost. What’s going to happen? Financial markets will experience a lot more volatility. Investors will have to price in a lot more uncertainty. Businesses will delay decisions to invest or hire more workers. Borrowing across the economy will thus become more expensive.And while we wait for the markets to do their magic, we will probably have to live with higher inflation.Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on SubstackExplore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS interest ratesUS economyEconomicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Price of olive oil expected to rise again as European crops feel the heat | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Farmers warn impact of high temperatures, drought and wildfires on range of foodstuffs means costs will increase
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Farmers warn impact of high temperatures, drought and wildfires on range of foodstuffs means costs will increase
Content: A farm worker uses olive branches to extinguish flames during a wildfire in the Megara valley, Greece on Sunday.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersView image in fullscreenA farm worker uses olive branches to extinguish flames during a wildfire in the Megara valley, Greece on Sunday.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersFood & drink industryPrice of olive oil expected to rise again as European crops feel the heatFarmers warn impact of high temperatures, drought and wildfires on range of foodstuffs means costs will increaseSarah ButlerTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarmers acrossEuropeare warning of a slump in food production and rising prices as crops from maize to salads suffer as a result of extreme heat, drought and wildfires.Olive groves have also been hit as the climate crisis drives temperatures across the continentto fresh record highs, meaning the cost of olive oil – already at elevated levels – is expected to start rising again.The vegetable growers association Légumes deFrancehas warned that thousands of tonnes of products worth tens of millions of euros had been lost – including salad leaves, carrots, leeks, garlic and onion with production on certain crops expected to be halved because of the lack of rain.The scorching French weather has also held back grape growth in wine regions including Champagne, Bordeaux and Burgundy, threatening a smaller crop and one of the earliest harvests on record.In Champagne, producers expect the earliest harvest ever, with picking likely to start around 15 August, about a month earlier than was typical a few decades ​ago. Growers now expect grape yields to be about 10% smaller than last year, Reuters reported.View image in fullscreenGrapes hang on vines in a drought-affected Muscadet vineyard in Saint-Fiacre-sur-Maine near Nantes.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersIn Spain, the ministry of agriculture predicts the country’s 2026-27 cereal crop will fall from last year’s 24m tonnes to little more than 18.5m tonnes – a forecast made beforewildfires took their toll.That is despite Spain’s farmers being more adapted to hot dry conditions, growing crop varieties that can cope with higher temperatures and drawing more on irrigation and water storage to manage periods of drought.TheEuropean Unionhas cut harvest predictions on a whole menu of crops with expectations for sunflowers, essential for cooking oils, down by 7%. Meanwhile, grain maize is down 6% on the previous forecast and expectations for potatoes and soya beans have been trimmed by 3%.However, some countries have been less badly hit than others with Romania, for example, seeing more rainfall and Italy’s wheat crop proving resilient.View image in fullscreenForest firefighters try to extinguish a wildfire in Sierra do Careon in Palas de Rei, Lugo, Spain.Photograph: Eliseo Trigo/EPAThe ASAJA agricultural trade body said direct damage from fire had hit orchards, vineyards, agricultural land and greenhouses – affecting citrus fruits, avocados, almonds, vineyards, vegetables and olive groves – while water stress and extreme temperatures had hit production of tomatoes and maize.“While local production losses may reduce export volumes for some products,” a spokesperson said, the main concern was “higher production costs” rather than restrictions on international trade.Olive oil producers said they expected another surge in prices this year as growers struggled with a combination of extreme heat, drought and, in some cases, fires.Groves have burned in Greece, Italy and Portugal this summer and even those nearby that were spared the flame have suffered blowing ash and poor air quality. The extreme hot weather has also prompted an increase in pests, disease and heavy storms as well as affecting fruit size.The price of olive oil around the world had drifted downfrom a spike two years agothat was driven by rising demand, hot and dry weather and the spread of pests and disease. However, the prices for a one-litre bottle of extra virgin oil in UK stores remain above £7 on average and have begun rising again in recent months.Sarah Vachon, founder of the Citizens of Soil olive oil group, said: “Unless the weather is under control soon, we should expect pricing to rise in the autumn since there will be less edible fruit to make olive oil from.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPrices for a one-litre bottle of extra virgin oil remain above £7 on average and have begun rising again in recent months.Photograph: Oramstock/AlamyWalter Zanre, head of the UK arm of olive oil brand Filippo Berio, said temperatures in Spain, Europe’s main olive oil producer, had been closer to normal than elsewhere in Europe but trees were suffering from drought, which can prompt them to shed their crop.“The combination of drought-induced fruit loss and an earlier harvest will be closely monitored over the coming weeks, as both factors have the potential to materially influence olive oil production volumes and market prices for [next year] he said.”The UK harvest has also been hit by ongoing droughts with wholesalers saying they are having toturn to Spain and elsewherefor mainstay items such as iceberg lettuce and broccoli whileBritish farmers have warned of shortages.Jason Bull, managing director of UK food importer Eurostar Commodities, said: “Repeated heatwaves have accelerated the ripening and harvesting of winter crops across much of Europe, shortening the critical grain-filling period and potentially reducing grain size, quality and overall yields.“Winter harvests are progressing rapidly and remain reasonable in many countries, but heat has reduced yield potential and may affect grain quality.View image in fullscreenThe Loire river in Langeais near Tours. Drought conditions have worsened amid heatwaves and water shortages across much of France.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters“Summer crops face a much more serious threat from drought, depleted soil moisture and heat during flowering. Irrigated crops are generally performing better than rain-fed crops, but rising water demand and possible irrigation restrictions create additional risk.”He said Turkey was the “major positive exception” as a cool and wet spring supported record-high winter crop yields, while prospects for summer crops were also favourable.Italy is also emerging as “one of the more positive stories” for the production of the kind of wheat for flour used in cakes and biscuits. The European Commission is forecasting a 10% increase in Italian output, supported by improved yields. Romania has also had a good year after several years of drought.Cezar Gheorghe of grain market consultancy Agricolumn predicted the maize harvest would hit 8.2m tonnes this year, which compared with an official estimate of 7.75m ​for 2025, according to Reuters.Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryFarmingExtreme weatherVegetablesEuropeFranceSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: BP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North Sea | BP | The Guardian
description: Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double
Content: Meg O'Neill says the North Sea investments are ‘not competitive’ within BP’s portfolio.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenMeg O'Neill says the North Sea investments are ‘not competitive’ within BP’s portfolio.Photograph: Darren England/AAPBPBP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North SeaMeg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we
