generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than doubleRevealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisisNils Pratley: BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to BurnhamJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentTue 4 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBP’s chief executive has urgedAndy Burnhamto make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even as the oil company prepares to sell its North Sea business after 60 years in the ageing basin.In a conversation with the new prime minister, Meg O’Neill said the country should prioritise using energy produced in the UK, “where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts”.BP’s endorsement of UK oil production came days after the 117-year-old companysignalled a plan to exit the North Seaafter six decades, as part of a wider plan to streamline its business.BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for saleRead moreO’Neill said North Sea investments were “not competitive” within BP’s portfolio, while the company reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine because of rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis.BP’s quarterly profits more than doubled to $5.73bn (£4.27bn) in the three months to the end of June, as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt energy exports from the Gulf.O’Neill added that BP had already received several unsolicited approaches to buy its North Sea fields and she was “very optimistic” that the assets would “continue to be profitable in the hands of a future owner”.Burnham’s government is expected to make a decision on whether to allow two controversial North Sea oil and gas projects – the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields – to move ahead despite growing outrage over oil company profits and evidence of a deepening global climate crisis.The new ministers are also facing calls to reform the North Sea tax regime. The industry has consistently argued that the UK government’s high taxes on oil and gas accelerate its natural decline.In an interview with CNBC News, O’Neill said Burnham had “reinforced his desire to work closely with business” and “be pragmatic”.She said: “The UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas. The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.“The UK is still using a huge amount of oil and natural gas every single day, and we ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party.“You know, I think the new prime minister has come in with a focus on being pragmatic, and with a focus on understanding how communities around the nation can benefit from developing local economic outcomes.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drillingRead moreBurnham was warned last week he could face the first revolt of his premiership over his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas.BP revealed its climbing profits days after Shell posted its second highest quarterly earnings on record after months of market volatility caused by the Middle East crisis.Europe’s largest oil companydoubled its net profit to almost $10bnin the three months to June, the highest since its record earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.The Middle East crisis has helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in ​net profits to $32.69bn in ​the three ​months ​ending on ​30 June, despite disruption in ‌the strait of Hormuz, owing to higher ​sales revenue for refined and chemical products and crude oil.The windfall profits for the world’s biggest oil and gas companies have faced criticism. Households and businesses are struggling with rising energy bills, and millions have been affected by severe heatwaves across Europe, which are made more likely and more severe by the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis.Donald Trump has said Chevron and ExxonMobil, which also reported sharp profit increases this week, are “making too much money” and should return some of their profits to the public.Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “Clearly not everyone is feeling the pain of the energy crisis. While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control with increasingly severe heatwaves, wildfires and droughts.”Explore more on these topicsBPOil and gas companiesAndy BurnhamEnergy industryOilGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland | Plastics | The Guardian
description: A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
Content: Plastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenPlastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersSeascape: the state of our oceansPlasticsUK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartlandA Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problemSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighand Ayça Aldatmaz in AdanaTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub inTurkeysupplied with plastic waste by British companies.The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey.The findings from a Guardian investigation reignite concerns over Britain’s continuing role in “waste colonialism” – a term used to describe the export of plastic waste by rich nations to poorer countries with less regulated waste management.The UK government pledged to reduce plastic pollution and eliminate harmful plastics duringtalks to reach a global plastics treaty, which collapsed last year, but it has not committed to a ban on exports.Treaty negotiations are expected to resume in 2027.Britain, one of the world’s largest exporters of plastic waste, exported 675,000 tonnes in 2025, its largest amount in eight years, of which139,000 tonnes was shipped to Turkey. The EU’s plastic waste exports to Turkey that yearrose 19% on the year before to more than 500,000 tonnes.Environmental campaigners in the UK and Turkey say that British and EU plastic waste exports are driving the operations responsible for the pollution, leaving the city’s poorer residents to pay the price.About 13% of UK plastic waste to Turkey was shipped to eight facilities within the recycling zone in Adana between May 2021 and July 2024, according to an analysis of import and export data carried out for the Guardian by an international NGO, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA).Thirteen British companies sent 545 shipments, totalling 52,000 tonnes, of plastic waste to the hub during the three-year period. There is no suggestion that the companies exporting plastic waste are acting illegally. British exporters of plastic waste do, however, have a duty under various regulations to ensure that the plastic they export is recycled in an environmentally sound manner.View image in fullscreenA plastic waste recycling plant near Adana. Samples taken from a canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites.Photograph: Ayça AldatmazSedat Gündoğdu, a Turkish marine biologist at Sabancı University’s Istanbul Policy Center, who conducted the microplastic sampling, has called for a ban on all plastic imports to Turkey. “The discharge of microplastic-laden wastewater into irrigation canals raises critical concerns about agricultural contamination and food safety,” he said.Plastic pollution from recycling centres that contaminates canals ultimately ends up in the Mediterranean Sea, he added, which “exacerbates marine plastic accumulation” and undermines efforts to protect the sea from contamination.Samples taken from the canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites, according to Gündoğdu’s research,published in Environment Monitoring and Assessment. He also found pellets, films and fragments “highly characteristic of [waste] recycling processing”, he said.He has called for mandatory installation of microplastic filtration at all facilities and independent monitoring of all wastewater discharges in agricultural zones.Amy Youngman, a legal specialist at the EIA, said that, by its continued reliance on exporting rather than investing in reduction or domestic recycling, the UK had failed to “keep pace with the EU” and had created a “structural imbalance”.“This results in pollution occurring overseas in ways that would not be tolerated within the UK itself and passes the devastating human health, economic and environmental harm to communities in Turkey,” she said.The findings added to an “expanding body of irrefutable evidence exposing waste colonialism in the UK’s waste-export system”, she said.We need to talk about plastic: five everyday items choking the planetRead moreA Greenpeace investigation in 2021 found plastic waste from British supermarkets wastedumped and burned in Adana. The same year, the Turkish government announced aban on certain waste, including polyethylene, which is used in 94% of UK plastic waste exports including yoghurt pots, salad bags and plastic film, but revoked the ban afterpressure from the recycling industry.The EU has recently imposedstrict controls on plastic waste exports. From November, exports other than to mostly rich OECD countries will be banned. Environmentalists fear this could lead to more exports to Turkey, an OECD country and already the main importer of EU waste.A spokesperson for the UK’sDepartment for Environment, Food & Rural Affairssaid: “There are already strict controls in place on the export of waste set out in UK legislation. Businesses involved in the export of waste from the UK are required to ensure that the waste they ship is managed in an environmentally sound manner, and we have already taken action to further reduce our need to export plastic waste.”The Turkish government was approached for comment but did not respond.Explore more on these topicsPlasticsSeascape: the state of our oceansRecyclingTurkeyPollutionEuropeEuropean UnionWastenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bid | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Jordan FA president has accused Fifa of “blackmail”, claiming it threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The Jordan FA president has accused Fifa of “blackmail”, claiming it threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election
Content: Prince Ali bin al-Hussein (left), the president of the Jordan Football Association, says players have not been paid for their appearance at last year’s Arab Cup.Photograph: Mike Nelson/EPAView image in fullscreenPrince Ali bin al-Hussein (left), the president of the Jordan Football Association, says players have not been paid for their appearance at last year’s Arab Cup.Photograph: Mike Nelson/EPAFifaFifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bidJordan FA president says Fifa threatened to block fundsSecretary general calls selloff plan ‘sad and reproachable’Nick AmesTue 4 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, has accused Gianni Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”, claiming that Fifa threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election.In a major intervention Prince Ali, who ran for theFifapresidency against Infantino in 2016 and finished third, listed a number of problems dogging the global governing body and said Jordan’s players have not yet been paid for appearing in the Arab Cup last year. Prince Ali is head of the West Asian Football Federation, which includes influential states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates that have thus far backed Infantino to stay on.Concacaf countries considering withdrawing support for under-fire Gianni InfantinoRead moreIt came on a day when Infantino’s authoritywas dealt a further blowas two more key allies distanced themselves from his failed World Cup private investment plan. His No 2, the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, was revealed to have called the botched Fifa Forward Enterprise a “sad and reproachable series of events” in an email to the organisation’s staff. Meanwhile the former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who is now Fifa’s chief of global development, said the project’s withdrawal was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”.Infantino is steadily losing backing from countries who previously had sent letters to endorse his continuation for a fourth term in charge. It is understood that Greece is the latest federation to have pulled its support, following the lead taken by countries such as England, Wales, Finland and Serbia. More European federations are expected to follow in the coming days, while a number of nations in Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – are also giving serious consideration to withdrawing their backing.Prince Ali’s statement, published on X, painted the picture of a small country facing a litany of roadblocks when it came to receiving help from the global governing body. Jordan competed in their first World Cup this year but he explained some of their fans had not received visas, despite purchasing tickets, and expressed anger at being taxed by the US for being based in the country.“We have been waiting for reward money for our players since December for the Arab Cup in Qatar, which is a Fifa event,” his statement read. “The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet, while at the same time Fifa brags about how many billions they have in reserve.View image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (centre), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström (right), with Arsène Wenger during the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock“It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, Fifa has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters – until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out.“We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that.”Other countries are understood to have been put under concerted pressure to formally back Infantino before the Fifa election in March, although details of how it was applied remain unclear in those cases.Grafstrom’s email had urged Fifa staff to keep morale high after what was perceived to be a successful World Cup. His message stopped short of criticising Infantino by name and promised to shield colleagues from the strife enveloping their organisation.“A sad and reproachable series of events – which were thankfully concluded with the FFE project permanently abandoned – for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality,” read a section of the email.11:54Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president? - The LatestHe referred to “a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept” and said: “Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure.”Wenger, who assumed his current position in November 2019, confirmed he had been among the many senior Fifa staffsidelined by Infantino’s plan. “I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports,” he said.“The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity.”Fifa was contacted for comment regarding Prince Ali’s accusations.According to reports, Infantino has called Fifa staff to a crisis meeting in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, today as he tries to cling to his position.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoArsène WengerFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UFC’s White House spectacle led to losses of around $30m, company reveals | UFC | The Guardian
description: TKO Group Holdings said the lavish, invitation-only Freedom 250 card cost the UFC about $30m despite attracting 8.2m viewers in the US
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: TKO Group Holdings said the lavish, invitation-only Freedom 250 card cost the UFC about $30m despite attracting 8.2m viewers in the US
Content: The UFC’s Freedom 250 card garnered 8.2m viewers domestically and around 34m views worldwide.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UFC’s Freedom 250 card garnered 8.2m viewers domestically and around 34m views worldwide.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesUFCUFC’s White House spectacle led to losses of around $30m, company revealsFreedom 250 staged on White House South LawnInvitation-only event cost an estimated $60m in allGaethje won title on night marred by Obama smearAgenciesTue 4 Aug 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUFCstaging its Freedom 250 card on the South Lawn of the White House in June led to losses of around $30m (roughly £22m), the company’s owners announced.US president Donald Trump, alongtime fan of the UFC, and vice-president JD Vancewere in attendance for the eventwhich marked celebrations for 250 years of American independence.UFC flyweight Allan Nascimento dies aged 34 after apparent heart attackRead moreApurpose-built structurewas constructed, holding about 4,300 seats, with none available to the public. Invitation-only tickets were reserved for political allies, financial sponsors and members of the military.Gate revenue contributes substantially to the earnings of an event and an estimated $60m (£44m) was spent on production and overall costs, which the UFC was unable to recoup via sponsorships.Parent company TKO Group Holdings saw an increase in revenue for the second quarter of 2026 but their financial results said a decrease in profit margin “was entirely due to the financial profile of the UFC Freedom 250 event. Absent Freedom 250, margins would have increased year-over-year.”Ariel Emanuel, executive chair and CEO of TKO said: “Despite a challenging global environment, TKO delivered solid results in Q2, with strong momentum heading into the back half of the year.”Freedom 250 garnered 8.2m viewers domestically and around 34m views worldwide, making it one of the most watched mixed martial events of all-time.The headliner for the UFC lightweight title saw America’s Justin Gaethjeproduce a stunning upsetto dethrone Spain’s Ilia Topuria.Explore more on these topicsUFCDonald TrumpMMAUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Falcons make Bijan Robinson highest-paid running back in NFL history with deal worth up to $75m | NFL | The Guardian
description: Atlanta agreed to a three-year contract extension that gives Robinson an average value of $22.25m, surpassing Saquon Barkley’s $20.6m
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Atlanta agreed to a three-year contract extension that gives Robinson an average value of $22.25m, surpassing Saquon Barkley’s $20.6m
Content: Bijan Robinson will be the highest-paid running back in NFL history.Photograph: Dale Zanine/USA Today SportsView image in fullscreenBijan Robinson will be the highest-paid running back in NFL history.Photograph: Dale Zanine/USA Today SportsNFLFalcons make Bijan Robinson highest-paid running back in NFL history with deal worth up to $75mTwo-time Pro Bowler expected to get $51m guaranteedAverage value surpasses that of Eagles’ Saquon BarkleyAgenciesTue 4 Aug 2026 15.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheAtlanta Falconshave agreed to a three-year contract extension with Bijan Robinson through the 2030 season that makes the fourth-year player the highest-paid running back in NFL history.Robinson reposted the NFL’s Instagram post detailing the extension on Tuesday morning, writing “God this is for you! Blessings. Love this team and this city!”The extension is worth up to $75m with incentives, with $51m guaranteed. The base value of $66.75m gives Robinson an average of $22.25m that makes him the league’s top-paid running back. Philadelphia running back Saquon Barkley’s average is $20.6m.“Obviously very excited for him, excited for us,” Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said Tuesday.NFL Network and ESPN first reported the extension. Robinson’s agent, Nicole Lynn of Klutch Sports, posted on X on Tuesday morning “Anyone have a brinks truck?” while the Falcons posted a photo of a smiling Robinson.The new deal comes after Robinson spent the first week of training camp, including Monday’s first day in pads, as a spectator. He attended the practices but did not participate in an apparent contract “hold-in” as he sought a new contract.“I just knew throughout this whole process that it would be a process and I felt good about where we were,” Stefanski said. “I think everybody understands how we feel about Bijan the person and Bijan the player.”Robinson joined practice on Tuesday as Stefanski and the Falcons no longer have to worry about their star running back’s status for the season.Robinson led the NFL with 2,298 yards from scrimmage and scored 11 touchdowns last season. He has been the focus of Atlanta’s productive ground game since he was the No 8 overall pick in the 2023 draft. The two-time Pro Bowl selection flourished as a dual-threat back last season, finishing fourth in the league with 1,478 rushing yards while adding 820 receiving yards. Steven Jackson in 2006 is the only other player ever with at least 1,400 rushing yards and 800 receiving yards in the same season.Explore more on these topicsNFLAtlanta FalconsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: USMNT to face Mexico and Canada in friendlies to kick off 2030 World Cup cycle | USA | The Guardian
description: The USMNT will face Peru and Chile in September before playing regional rivals Mexico and Canada to round out their fall schedule
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The USMNT will face Peru and Chile in September before playing regional rivals Mexico and Canada to round out their fall schedule
Content: The US men will play their first friendlies after the World Cup against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US men will play their first friendlies after the World Cup against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersUSAUSMNT to face Mexico and Canada in friendlies to kick off 2030 World Cup cycleFall opponents also include Peru and ChileMatches set for 26 September to 6 OctoberFirst games since Pochettino agreed to returnAssociated PressTue 4 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US men’s national team will kick off the next World Cup cycle with four matches over 11 days on home soil.The friendlies include games against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada in US cities that didn’t host World Cup action this summer.The Americans will face Peru on 26 September at Inter.co Stadium in Orlando, Florida. Three days later, they will host Chile at Energizer Park in St Louis. The US-Mexico rivalry resumes 3 October at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. And the finale against Canada follows three days later at Allianz Field in St Paul, Minnesota.Mauricio Pochettino’s US return is risky, expensive and probably unnecessary | Leander SchaerlaeckensRead moreAll four matches will be broadcast on TNT, HBO Max, Telemundo, Universo and Peacock.The games come on the heels of the US team’s run to the last 16 at the World Cup. They also will serve as the first action since US head coach Mauricio Pochettinoagreed to a new dealthat puts him under contract through 2030.“We are so excited to start this new phase of our journey with matches in front of our home fans,” Pochettino said in a statement. “Their amazing energy during the summer has set the standard.“Our objective is always to play the best opponents possible, and these matches provide a variety of experiences for this group of players as we begin this new chapter of the US Men’s National Team.”The 2030 World Cup will be held in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal target Vinícius says Mourinho ‘wants me to be happy’ at Real Madrid | Vinícius Júnior | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior said he is ‘getting to know’ new Real Madrid coach José Mourinho as speculation continues over a move to Arsenal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vinícius Júnior said he is ‘getting to know’ new Real Madrid coach José Mourinho as speculation continues over a move to Arsenal
Content: Vinícius Júnior has returned to pre-season training at Real Madrid after the World Cup.Photograph: Antonio Villalba/Real Madrid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior has returned to pre-season training at Real Madrid after the World Cup.Photograph: Antonio Villalba/Real Madrid/Getty ImagesVinícius JúniorArsenal target Vinícius says Mourinho ‘wants me to be happy’ at Real Madrid‘It has gone very well, getting to know the new coach’Brazil winger has one year left on contract at BernabéuReutersTue 4 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVinícius Júnior is settling into life under the new Real Madrid manager, José ⁠Mourinho, with a smile on his face even as uncertainty swirls around the Brazil forward’s future at the Bernabéu.The 26-year-old, who has ⁠been ​one of the linchpins of Real Madrid’s attack in recent years, gave an upbeat assessment of his second ⁠day of pre-season training under Mourinho despite speculation linking him witha possible move to Arsenal.Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may work | Jonathan WilsonRead more“It has ⁠gone very well, getting to know the new coach and the new ​players, and training very hard,” ‌Vinícius toldReal Madrid‌TV. “Mourinho wants me to be as I have always been: happy, cheerful ‌and playing my football.”Vinícius’s cheerful demeanour, however, masks a potentially thorny situation brewing behind the scenes. He is in the final year of his Real Madrid contract, with speculation that the club and player remain locked in negotiations whileArsenalexplore a potential transfer.Vinícius has scored 128 goals for Madrid and provided 100 assists, with the club reluctant to ​let one of their prized assets leave for free next year.He had a busy summer playing for Brazil at the World Cup, wherethey were knocked out in the last 16, and his focus now is ⁠on preparing for the new campaign.“We have to prepare physically ​so that during the ​season we have fewer ​injuries and can count on everyone,” said Vinícius, who was ​Brazil’s top scorer ‌at the ​World Cup with ​four goals.“It was a good training session and we all left very tired, but now it’s time to rest for tomorrow. That’s how pre-season is and we have to be ready.”Explore more on these topicsVinícius JúniorReal MadridArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Reusser aces stage four time trial to snatch yellow jersey | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Switzerland’s Marlen Reusser showed her time trial pedigree to win stage four of the Tour de France Femmes and take the yellow jersey
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Switzerland’s Marlen Reusser showed her time trial pedigree to win stage four of the Tour de France Femmes and take the yellow jersey
Content: Marlen Reusser shows her time trial pedigree on stage four.Photograph: Tim de Waele/GettyView image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser shows her time trial pedigree on stage four.Photograph: Tim de Waele/GettyTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Reusser aces stage four time trial to snatch yellow jerseySwiss rider leads Vollering by 14 seconds overallFerrand-Prévot toils up climbs and loses more groundJeremy Whittlein DijonTue 4 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world time-trial champion, Marlen Reusser, took the overall lead in theTour de France Femmesafter winning the fourth stage from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon.It was the 34-year-old Swiss rider’s third career win in the Tour and lifted her into a commanding lead over the defending champion, Pauline ­Ferrand-Prévot. Reusser, a specialist in racing against the clock, now leads the pre-race favourite Demi ­Vollering by 14 seconds, with the 2024 Tour winner, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, 1min 9sec further back.Tour de France Femmes cyclists face checks after claims that padded bras aid aerodynamicsRead moreBut in a performance that the French media labelled catastrophic, Ferrand‑Prévot is now 2min 13sec behind the race leader, Reusser. “It was our Project Dijon,” Reusser said after donning the yellow jersey.“This was the idea that we had for a long time and I saw the Tour as my goal for the year. I really targeted it. I am here as a leader, and I knew the Tour was going to start in Switzerland, on Swiss national day, and we would have a TT on the fourth day. So it was our Project Dijon.”Vollering said: “I knew I’d lose time to Marlen, but I’m happy with this time trial because I knew it was really one for the specialists. But keeping the gap so close makes me very happy.”While Reusser and the 2023 champion Vollering were at their best, Ferrand-Prévot toiled up the climbs and never mustered the form that hadtaken her to victory last summer. The anxiety she had felt about the stage proved well founded. Lacking power and seemingly purpose, she dropped to 14th overall, more than two ­minutes behind Reusser, winner this year of the Tour of Switzerland.Even before the stage, as she waited to roll off the start ramp, Ferrand-Prévot had looked ­nervous, clutching an ice cube in her hands and closing her eyes in concentration. “There’s ­nothing I can do,” she said after the stage. “I pushed as hard as I could. It was a lot of stress. I’m glad this day is over.”The French rider now faces a considerably harder task to defend her title, as the peloton heads into a series of stages peppered with climbs, culminating in the ascent of Mont Ventoux on Friday. While she outclimbed Vollering in the Tour Femmes last year, Ferrand-Prévot seems to be on the back foot in the race this year.Reusser and Vollering have laid down a marker, but Ferrand-Prévot remains optimistic. “Now I have to chase,” she said, “and I love that.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’re not alone’: Chris Hoy on his ambition to stop men dying of prostate cancer | Chris Hoy | The Guardian
description: Cycling legend tells Donald McRae about the reality of living with stage 4 cancer, fundraising with Miguel Induráin and why Andy Burnham could be key to his ambition of helping others with similar diagnoses
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Cycling legend tells Donald McRae about the reality of living with stage 4 cancer, fundraising with Miguel Induráin and why Andy Burnham could be key to his ambition of helping others with similar diagnoses
Content: Sir Chris Hoy: ‘It’s so isolating when you get a cancer diagnosis. You’re suddenly on borrowed time.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSir Chris Hoy: ‘It’s so isolating when you get a cancer diagnosis. You’re suddenly on borrowed time.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianChris HoyInterview‘They’re not alone’: Chris Hoy on his ambition to stop men dying of prostate cancerDonald McRaeCycling legend on living with a stage 4 diagnosis, fundraising with Miguel Induráin and why Andy Burnham could be key to his ambition of helping othersTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSir Chris Hoy arrives a couple of minutes late and the apologies roll from him. I don’t have a chance to tell thesix‑time Olympic sprint cycling championthat waiting an hour for a star interviewee is more common. Hoy is already deep into a story about how he and his wife, Sarra, were walking here when an unknown man stopped him on the street in Glasgow.The stranger had recently been diagnosed with prostate cancer and he wanted to share what had happened to him and, I suspect, find new strength by talking to a compassionate public figure. Hoy has lived a full life withstage 4 cancerfor nearly three years. He has also worked tirelessly to highlight the fact that prostate cancer affects more men in this country than any other cancer while, at the same time, to offer a tangible sense of hope when there is horror for men, and their families, after a terminal diagnosis.‘I still want to achieve’: people living with stage 4 cancer embrace Chris Hoy charity rideRead moreHearing a discreet account of this encounter, it sounds as if the 50‑year‑old Hoy helped the man at a raw and vulnerable moment. “It’s so isolating when you get a cancer diagnosis,” Hoy says. “You’re suddenly on borrowed time. You’re observing the world and not living in it – because it’s for other people. But then you realise you’re not special and it’s very common, sadly. I want to make sure that anyone in a similar situation will realise they’re not alone.“I also want to raise awareness that 10,000 men a year get the news that they have stage 4 prostate cancer. A lot of it comes down to a lack of awareness so we need to get men to understand the risk.”In September 2023, Hoy saw his physiotherapist about a nagging pain in his shoulder. Without any other symptoms he assumed he had strained a muscle while lifting weights. The physio sent him for a scan, which identified a tumour in his shoulder. Two days later, a second scan brought shattering news. The primary cancer was in his prostate and had spread to his pelvis, hip, spine, ribs and shoulder. “Just like that,” Hoy wrotein his memoir, “I learn how I die.”His life-expectancy was said to bebetween two and four years. I ask Hoy how he is feeling now. “I’m doing really well, thank you,” he says. “As well as can be expected, really.”How often is he tested? “On average, between every three and six months. But if there’s an area of activity you might have it more frequently. You have blood tests regularly and there’re periods where you’re in and out of the hospital. The regular blood tests are horrible because it’s like the clock is ticking. At some point that afternoon or the next day, you’ll get that email.View image in fullscreenSir Chris Hoy waves to the crowd after winning gold at the 2012 Olympics in London.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“I remember when I was about to walk on stage for a talk. It was one of these ‘An Evening With …’ events. It had sold out and I was just about to go out in front of a packed audience. I shouldn’t have done it, but I checked my phone and the results were there. The PSA [prostate-specific antigen] had gone back up. It was like: ‘Oh God.’ And then: ‘Put your phone down, put a smile on and do it.’”Hoy makes a grimace before smiling more wryly. “In a way the concentration of being on stage helped.”When did this happen? “Probably last summer. Even theTour de 4[the charity bike ride in Scotland which Hoy led for the first time in September last year] was difficult. The treatment at that point had started to fail so I was changing to a different treatment. Only with hindsight do you realise [the difficulties].“For me, the worst is when you walk into the consultant’s room. You’re immediately trying to read their body language. Is it good news? Is it bad news? Let’s get to the punchline. So it’s why I’ve switched to Zoom for these meetings about my results. You can switch it off and you’re in your sanctuary, your home. You don’t have to be in the hospital, walking past strangers, having that long drive home.”He seems able to live in the moment better than most people, but does the fact that he is approaching the end of his third year of a supposedly limited life‑expectancy play on his mind? “A little, but not really because these are average statistics you get in the very early days. You have to remember the people outliving those statistics can’t be added to the data yet.View image in fullscreenSir Chris Hoy and wife Sarra raised £3.1m for cancer research with their Tour de 4 charity ride last September.Photograph: Tour de 4“But not everybody is as lucky as me to respond to treatment. Sadly, you have people likeDermot Murnaghan[the television journalist who died from prostate cancer last month]. I’d been confident and hopeful he and I would do the Tour de 4 for many years to come. So that was a big blow, a huge shock when I got the message from his family saying the time was coming.”Hoy continues to live with real vitality – even if he endured a serious accident on his mountain bike in November. He was racing down a trail in south Wales when, at speed, he misjudged a steep jump. Hoy still shudders at the memory.He was warned that if surgery was unsuccessful his leg might have to be amputated, but Hoy plays down the situation now. “It’s shocking at the time, but they have to tell you what could happen from a legal perspective. It wasn’t a little fracture of the leg. It was a full reconstruction of the tibial plateau. A friend of mine who’s a doctor saw the X-rays and said: ‘Oh. That’s the kind of X-ray you’ll see when someone’s parachute hasn’t deployed.”Hoy describes his post-op recovery as “a miserable, incredibly difficult time”, saying: “I was keeping my head above water and everything was going OK and then you have this freak accident. You have a lot of time sat around thinking, which you don’t want to be doing.”View image in fullscreen‘It was a huge honour to be with him.’ Sir Chris Hoy joined his teenage hero Miguel Induráin on a charity bike ride across Spain.Photograph: Courtesy of LaureusHe looks down at his right leg and says: “It’s just metalwork from here [just below his knee] down to here [near the ankle]. It’s not what I needed and yet the irony is that mountain biking gives me so much physically, mentally and socially. Being out in the fresh air and being in the moment is so good for me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHoy was soon back on his bike and last month, despite another injury to his “good” leg, he cycled across Spain with riders including his teenage heroMiguel Induráin, a five-time Tour de France winner. “I was on holiday in Greece and feeling great. I had this big charity ride across Spain coming up, coast-to-coast, with Miguel and others. Amazing. I was sitting cross-legged on a paddle board with my son for quite a long time, just watching the sunrise.“When I stepped off the paddleboard, my weight shifted, and there was sharp pain: ‘Oh. That didn’t feel good.” It was a torn meniscus and there was this little piece floating about in the knee.“It was four days before I went out to Spain but so many people were coming I couldn’t say: ‘I’ve got a knee injury, I’m not coming.’ I thought I’ll take my bike and see what I can do. I was hobbling through the airport using my carry-on case as a crutch, thinking: ‘This is ridiculous, I can’t even walk.’ But on the bike you never fully extend your knee. So, tentatively, I was like: ‘This doesn’t feel too bad.’ And long story short, I managed to get through the week and we raised £200,000 and had an amazing experience.”He somehow rode alongside the mighty Induráin with a torn meniscus? “Yes. He’s not your average 62-year-old. He still does these crazy 10-hour rides and he’s as fit as a butcher’s dog. It was a huge honour to be with him.”Such drive, against all odds, stands in stark contrast to the laxity that epitomises the failure of successive governments to take coherent action against prostate cancer. “I can’t see how the government are not coming up with some form of proactive decision,” he says. “They say thatthe risk of testing every man, and the number of men who would have elevated PSA levels, would then lead to too many being unnecessarily treated, and then having to deal with the consequences of surgeryor treatment. To me, that’s a treatment issue, not a screening issue … I don’t know why we don’t [have a screening system]. It just doesn’t make sense.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t know why we don’t have a screening system. It just doesn’t make sense.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHoy has other pressing concerns. Sarra was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis two months after he heard he had stage 4 cancer. But, worrying about him, she kept the news from her husband for almost a month. “She’s incredible,” Hoy says. “She’s receiving treatment and doing really well. Sarra took up cycling to do the Tour de 4 and she’s physically fitter than she’s ever been. She’s adamant that [MS] won’t get in the way. She’s doing all she can to support me and the family.”How are their children, 11‑year‑old Callum and eight‑year‑old Chloe? “Kids’ concept of time is very different to ours and they know how to live in the moment. They were more concerned when I broke my leg than about my cancer diagnosis, because they could see me in pain. I was unable to get up.“Cancer is an abstract concept for kids and we’ve tried not to allow it to change family life too much. They understand the situation but, equally, they’re living in the here and now.”Next month, with Tour de 4, he and Sarra hope to raise even more than the £3.1m they made last year for cancer research. Hoy is inspired by the rapid progress being made in medical science in terms of treating, and potentially, finding a cure for the disease. “From what I’ve been told by people at the forefront of new treatments, this is the most exciting time for prostate cancer drug development in the last 25 years. They’ve seen a real upturn in new treatments and new therapies.”This additional source of hope means Hoy is still full of ambition. He has just completed work as a pundit for TNT at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where the cycling was held at the velodrome named after him.“I also have ambitions to help decision-makers do something proactive. A change of prime minister, with Andy Burnham, might help. I’ve met him a couple of times and he’s good friends with [the former GB cyclist] Chris Boardman. I would love to speak to Andy and see what he thinks we could do.“I have all kinds of goals and the biggest are raising as much money as we can for these amazing charities, changing perceptions of what is possible during a stage 4 diagnosis and also trying to one day have some proactive gateway to screen men – so less men die of prostate cancer as a result of my diagnosis. That would be quite something.”This article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version said prostate cancer had the highest mortality rate of any disease in the UK; in fact, it is the most common form of cancer in men. Also, France does not have a screening program as an earlier quote said. This reference has been removed.Explore more on these topicsChris HoyCyclingProstate cancerinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him? | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The president is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the governing body
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The president is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the governing body
Content: Gianni Infantino speaks at the podium during the 76th Fifa Congress in April.Photograph: Bob Frid/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino speaks at the podium during the 76th Fifa Congress in April.Photograph: Bob Frid/EPAFifaExplainerThe Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him?Gianni Infantino is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the presidentNick Ames,John Duerden,Alexander Abnos,Osasu ObayiuwanaandMarcela Mora y AraujoTue 4 Aug 2026 16.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pressure is growing on the Fifa president,Gianni Infantino, with many countries withdrawing their support following the bungled World Cup sell-off. However, how key is Infantino’s relationship with each confederation and is it likely that an election contest will actually happen? We look at the key considerations, confederation by confederation.1) How does each confederation view Infantino’s re-election?Uefa(Europe) has firmly led the moves under way to achieve Infantino’s removal. The threat last week to boycott all Fifa competitions if the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme was not scrapped contributed hugely to its failure. In a scathing statement on Saturday, Uefa said the current Fifa leadership had “not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family”, and pledged to push for change. Some Uefa member associations, including the English and Welsh FAs, havewithdrawn their letters of supportfor Infantino’s re‑election and efforts are continuing to ensure others follow suit in a bid to weaken his position irretrievably.Nick AmesReports ofAFC(Asia) support for Uefa are premature; the confederation is divided. The AFC has spoken out, strongly in relative terms compared to its usual pronouncements, against the proposed World Cup deal and has called for reform of Fifa. The AFC has been a staunch supporter in the past but if it looks as if Infantino is in trouble the AFC leadership, which was genuinely angry at how the proposal was made (probably more so than the actual details of the deal), could switch sides, which would probably confirm Infantino’s downfall if Uefa and Concacaf oppose but it is not a foregone conclusion – some in Asia are not convinced that Uefa has the numbers. The big problem is that, while the AFC leadership may want Infantino out, most individual Asian federations do not want him to be replaced. The AFC president, Sheikh Salman, has ambitions of his own and has been historically successful at preserving AFC unity but this will be tricky especially as west Asian nations such as Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia support Infantino and are influential in Asia. It could be that the only way to ensure Asian unity is to have an Asian candidate. Jordan’s Prince Ali bin Hussein’sclaim of “blackmail”could prove a significant moment, however.John DuerdenWenger and Infantino’s No 2 Grafström criticise ‘sad and reproachable’ World Cup planRead moreConcacaf(North and Central America, and the Caribbean) is among the confederations that have come out strongly against Infantino and his FFE proposal, first directly rejecting it and then releasing a statement after it was withdrawn that took direct aim at Infantino. A release speaking on behalf of Concacaf’s 41 member associations called the plan “a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first”, and a “unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership” and said that “a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative”.That is about as direct a call for no confidence in Infantino as you are likely to get outside of an election itself. It should be noted, of course, that the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is also aFifavice-president and would be a leading candidate to run for president should there be a united desire among confederations to oust Infantino. Montagliani has kept silent on the subject when asked in the past but this statement, which speaks for him, shows at the very least he is not immune to the idea of going against Infantino.Alexander AbnosView image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani, pictured consoling Lionel Messi after the World Cup final, is a potential successor to Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAPatrice Motsepe, president of theConfederation of African Football, has said the 54 member associations are in unanimous support of Infantino’s re-election in Morocco next year.Osasu ObayiuwanaSince the rumpus over Infantino’s proposed FFE brokeand died, the South American confederation,Conmebol,has been notably silent. Its president, Alejandro Domínguez, has been posting birthday wishes to individuals, clubs and institutions from Uruguay where he is visiting ahead of the 2030 centenary of the first World Cup. Unlike Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC, which publicly opposed Fifa’s aborted FFE proposal, Conmebol took several days before issuing a fence-sitting statement stressing football first, and requesting further information and clarification. That was the only official response at all, and there has been absolute silence since.“Conmebol’s current position is best described as cautious support rather than open confrontation,” says Marina Mendez, a director of AD Sporting Industry Professionals and a friend of Conmebol who consults on football in the region. “The distinction is politically significant. It suggests Conmebol wants to preserve its institutional relationship with Fifa and maintain room for negotiation, rather than join a public campaign against Infantino. This should not necessarily be interpreted as unconditional personal loyalty. Conmebol’s approach is pragmatic: it is protecting South American football’s access, influence and negotiating position within Fifa while assessing how the international balance of power develops.”Brazil and Argentina are the main countries, and Domínguez looks after the relationship with both, with most of the other countries expected to follow suit. “They are not federations likely to confront Infantino directly because they will always prefer to be on the right side of the non-Europeans,” says an industry insider who does not wish to be named.Marcela Mora y AraujoIt remains to be seen what the 11Oceania Football Confederationmember associations will do. New Zealand, the leading member of the confederation, was quick to come out against the World Cup proposal – though the reaction of the OFC itself was noncommittal – and there is still support for Infantino among the other federations.John Duerden2) What are the historical links to Infantino?UefaThe parties go back a long way. Infantino was Uefa’s secretary general from 2009 until 2016 and it backed him strongly when he first ran for the Fifa presidency. But there has long been push and pull between the global governing body and that of football’s most powerful continent. Relations have deteriorated in recent years, Uefa fending off Infantino-led initiatives such as abiennial staging of the World Cupand a proposed investment in 2018 by SoftBank. Things appeared to reach a head in May 2025 when delegates from several European federationswalked out of Fifa’s annual congress in protestat Infantino’s late arrival. They accused him of pursuing “private political interests”. That turned out to be the tip of the iceberg. The past year’s near-interminable list of Fifa-related controversies have further ensured that the differences between the two are irreconcilable.NAAFCIt has been a close relationship, Salman and AFC have backed Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election. It is not just about money either, though this is of course important. He is seen as approachable, available and open. Fifa has historically been seen as a European (and to a lesser extent South American) institution in Asia, and while Infantino is from Uefa, he is seen as a leader who gives equal weight to all. One president said to me that in the past, conversations with Fifa were like receiving decrees from above but now there is a genuine dialogue. World Cup expansion has gone down well,64 teamswould be welcomed too, and there are more tournaments held in Asia these days. Infantino has already been reminding Asia about this.JDView image in fullscreenSheikh Salman and the AFC have backed Gianni Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election.Photograph: Vincent Thian/APConcacafInfantino’s most direct relationship has been as the president under whom the World Cup was awarded to the US, Mexico and Canada, after a bid from the US lost out to Qatar for the 2022 hosting rights. Aside from that, there was not much of a direct, historic relationship between Infantino and Concacaf – at least, not until the letter released by the confederation over the weekend.AACAFInfantino’s association with African football began in 2016, when he backed Ahmad Ahmad of Madagascar totopple the late Issa Hayatou as CAF presidentin March 2017. Being an eyewitness to that election, at the African Union HQ in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, I recall the anger with which Hayatou confronted Infantino and Fatma Samoura, then Fifa secretary general, over their involvement in an election.Infantino, under Ahmad’s ill-fated four-year tenure between 2017 and 2021 – which ended in his untimely removal from office over ethics violations – got Fifa to take over the daily administration of the CAF from August to December 2019, with Samoura going to Egypt to take charge of the organisation. Many in African football saw this as a neo-colonial act and a direct violation of the CAF’s autonomy and independence. Infantino was involved in the ascension of Motsepe to the presidency in March 2021.OOConmebolAlong comes Infantino, the Uefa salvation who promises an anti-corruption ticket. After Julio Grondona’s death, an AFA (Argentina Football Association) election found more votes than members and Fifa intervened, naming a committee of industry insiders to oversee a cleansing of the house. Infantino was present in the AFA headquarters at its inaugural press conference. Imagine Infantino launching an English FA governance intervention.In 2018, in Buenos Aires for a Libertadores final to be played by two clubs from the same city for the first time in Argentina’s history (policing was a mess and fan violence before the second leg led to its suspension andeventual move to Madrid) Infantino was invited by the then president of Argentina, Mauricio Macri, to be guest of honour at the G20 held in the city later that week.Infantino, as we know him today is created then, photographed gifting football shirts to the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Donald Trump, POTUS at the time. “Yes, that G20 was key for Infantino, because he’d inherited a corruption scandal. He needed to instil the belief that football would cease to be a mafia, that he would achieve this. And he managed,” Macri, now president of the Fifa Foundation, told the Guardian: “From an ethical point of view he is impeccable. There is nothing odd in Fifa today, Fifa manages fortunes, more than ever, because Infantino is successful; he organises competitions that are more and more profitable, and it’s all above board. I should say the same applies to Conmebol.”The Conmebol president, Nicolás Leoz, fell in the same Fifagate swoop, although he had left office in 2013. A series of interim and short-lived presidencies ensued until January 2016 when current president Domínguez took his post. Unanimously voted in by the 10 member associations, he pushed for every professional club to have a female team and introduced “hydration” breaks before this World Cup, albeit less structured ones. Infantino has also maintained a functional and stable relationship with the AFA president, Claudio “Chiqu” Tapia. “This relationship is politically relevant because Macri has been an opponent of “Chiqui” Tapia,” Mendez says. “This demonstrates Infantino’s ability to maintain links with both sides of Argentine football’s internal power structure.” Tapia was approached for comment.MMAView image in fullscreenClaudio Tapia of Argentina’s FA has a stable relationship with the Fifa president.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersOFCLike Asia, Infantino has worked hard to build relationships both of the personal and financial kind. It is common to hear officials describe him as a friend. The expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams finally gave Oceania an automatic World Cup spot – something that Fifa had promised in the past but never delivered. And the idea of having more spots in a 64-team competition was also attractive. Under Infantino,New Zealand co-hosted the Women’s World Cupwith Australia. Fifa also supported the establishment of the Oceania Professional League that kicked off in January to provide much-needed pro club football for the region.JD3) How financially dependent is the confederation on Infantino and Fifa?UefaNot at all. While the World Cup is Fifa’s most essential driver of revenue, Uefa can lay claim, among other things, to the highly lucrative Champions League and the vast sums that it attracts on an annual basis. Expanding its tournaments and staging them more often is one of the only ways available for Fifa to keep pace. Private investment would not harm its cause, either. Uefa’s annual revenues have recently totalled around double those of Fifa; as things stand football’s powerhouse can cope perfectly well on its own.NAAFCLike always in Asia, it varies. There are rich federations on either side of the continent but in between there are some that are almost completely dependent on Fifa money. Bhutan, for example, gets $1.5m a year, which makes up the majority of its budget. Even Australia, which has reached the knockout stages of the past two World Cups, has lost around $17m over the past two years, which may explain its rather vague statement calling for more time when the plan was first heard.JDView image in fullscreenPaul Okon Engstler, Jackson Irvine and Harry Souttar after Australia’s World Cup exit; even their federation, one of AFC’s richest, loses money.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersConcacafThis is a very top‑heavy confederation, perhaps more so than any other in the world. The US and Mexico have been regional powers for most of the past 30‑40 years, and recently Canada has shown signs it can compete on the field and is addressing business issues off of it. Just below them is a middle class consisting of Panama, Jamaica, Costa Rica and Honduras. The remaining 33 Concacaf nations are fairly small by comparison, and thus naturally more reliant on funding from Fifa via the forward programme and other initiatives. The fact that smaller Caribbean nations feel empowered to join with the big dogs says a lot about how at risk they feel they may be without Infantino at Fifa’s helm.AACAFThe confederation funds activities from its own commercial revenue, so it is not dependent on Fifa and Infantino in that sense. But the majority of CAF’s 54 member associations are financially challenged and are dependent on the annual grants that the world governing body gives them to meet their operating costs.OOConmebolIt represents only 10 nation members. Variations among them notwithstanding, the federations are self-sufficient economically and their local leagues are attractive and profitable. Their national teams are the No 1 sporting attraction, pulling in vast numbers of fans who are emotionally attached to their heroes, who in turn love to play for their country. The main sources of revenue for clubs are TV rights, marketing and the sale of players. For this, the top market is the Premier League (which operates entirely outside the FA and therefore Fifa) and the other European leagues, which are also largely independent of their FAs. Montevideo has produced more World Cup players than any other city in history, so even a financially struggling association such as Uruguay’s continues to rely more on the income from the development of youth talent than Fifa aid. There were six Argentinian managers with extensive international trajectories at this World Cup. Exporting home‑grown talent, of which there is plenty, is a bigger source of revenue than Fifa project distribution funds. Two of the most colourful stories of the World Cup, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha and the New Zealand defender Tim Payne, transferred to Chilean and Paraguayan clubs respectively following their popularity during the tournament. Popularity due in no small part to the efforts of streamers and influencers from Argentina and Brazil.MMAOFCOceania is made up of small federations that tend to be reliant on what Fifa gives them. So the recent World Cup proposal would, had it gone through, have made a huge difference financially.JD4) Would a breakaway cause an existential threat?UefaEurope has the strongest club and international teams in the world. Parting ways from Infantino and Fifa would be unlikely to cause serious damage, although it could cause issues with clubs who have been looking to expand their global reach through the revamped Club World Cup. It is plausible that bigger teams from other continents would seek to join forces with Uefa and compete in new tournaments given the kudos and financial opportunities available when competing with the majority of the sport’s giants.NAView image in fullscreenEuropean clubs such as Chelsea have been looking to expand their global reach through Fifa’s revamped Club World Cup.Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAAFCIt is a generalisation but, in Asia, Fifa as an institution does not make the headlines that it does in western Europe. Usually, interest in a country comes when they are affected specifically by a decision, as when bidding for a tournament. In my experience, there just isn’t the same interest in the day‑to‑day running of the organisation. Breaking with Infantino would not be a massive threat to Asia but there is some concern about a return to a more Europe‑dominated Fifa, if that were to materialise. While pretty much everyone has supported Infantino from 2016 until the past few days, Asian federations that have done so are seen in some quarters as being corrupt and/or greedy but the Europeans, who did exactly the same, are now trying to paint themselves as the moral guardians of the sport.JDConcacafIf a breakaway would cause an existential threat, then Concacaf is living it right now. One could certainly read it as a principled stand, but it’s hard to separate the confederation’s statement with Montagliani’s current position as Infantino’s most likely successor, should the latter need to stand down.AACAFThe relationship between Infantino and Africa’s 54 national associations is largely seen as a “master-servant” one, in which he basically tells the FA/federation heads, through Fifa officials, to do his bidding. Those who do not toe the political line of Zurich, as decided by Infantino, may well end up having their books audited over how they have spent their Fifa grants. Many FA/federation presidents faced Fifa ethics proceedings and subsequent bans as a result.OOConmebol“There’s no morality involved, just politics,” the industry insider says. Mendez concurs: “It’s not a simple case of morality, it’s a power struggle and a rupture in perspectives about football in general and the business of football in particular. Today, Eurocentrism is dominating, and things like sponsored hydration breaks and Super Bowl-style half-time shows impose a North American regard hitherto unseen.”MMAOFCOceania welcomed the fact that Infantino had a “global” mentality and went out of his way to engage with smaller nations far from the centre of global football power. If the confederation does break away, it would want something similar in the opposition candidate and not a return to the old days when the confederation was an afterthought in the corridors of power.JD5) How important is the current and historical relationship?A strong relationship between Uefa and Fifa would make for a far more harmonious global football scene but, as described above, there is huge work to do before that can be repaired.NAIt’s very important – barring some new organisation stepping in to run world football in a better way, Fifa is Concacaf’s best link to the traditional power centres of world football. The US, Mexico and Canada derive a lot of their value as federations from how they’ve been able to perform at men’s and women’s World Cups – that’s not something they’ll want to give up lightly, which is perhaps why they did not threaten a boycott the way Uefa did.AACAFAfrica’s political power within Fifa began to rise in 1974, when João Havelange successfully courted the continent as a block and made it an important pillar of his electoral victory over Sir Stanley Rous in Germany, becoming the first and only non-European, to date, to be Fifa president. Sepp Blatter, Havelange’s successor in 1998, also leveraged Africa’s support in a similar fashion to defeat the Uefa president Lennart Johansson. Delivering on his promise to the continent that it would host a World Cup during his presidency, which South Africa did in 2010, bolstered his popularity and support base on the continent. But the last 10 years of the Infantino presidency have made many resent the undue influence of the world governing body in Africa’s affairs.OOView image in fullscreenSepp Blatter, pictured with the then South Africa president Jacob Zuma at the 2010 World Cup, cultivated support in African football.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianConmebolFifa as we know it was essentially invented, developed and moulded by the Brazil and Argentina federation presidents Havelange and Grondona respectively. They specifically wanted to break Europe’s stronghold. Initially, they started funding grassroots via “partnerships” with big brands, which benefited from reaching wider markets. A vivid example is the giant sign with a Coca-Cola bottle on every corner of the pitch, seen in places such as Russia and China where advertising was otherwise prohibited, every single time a corner kick was awarded. After Havelange’s time at the helm was up, Blatter took the lead. Blatter kept Grondona close by, his right-hand man, while the business venture grew and grew, and places for other confederations increased. When Fifagate blew up, most leaders close to the top faced trials and disgrace; Grondona was saved by death.Infantino’s reign was a continuation of keeping Conmebol as a key ally. The historic power derived from on-the-pitch success in the region, and the crown jewel that is Lionel Messi, have contributed to keeping the small confederation big. “The relationship is neither purely personal nor purely institutional. It is built on mutual strategic value,” says Mendez. “The coming election will be Uefa versus footballistic populism,” the industry source said. “Conmebol owns Fifa.”MMAExplore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Trabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talks | Mohamed Salah | The Guardian
description: The Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor have begun transfer ⁠negotiations with Mohamed Salah and hope to sign the former Liverpool player this week
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor have begun transfer ⁠negotiations with Mohamed Salah and hope to sign the former Liverpool player this week
Content: Mohamed Salah in action for Egypt against Iran at the World Cup in the US this summer.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenMohamed Salah in action for Egypt against Iran at the World Cup in the US this summer.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersMohamed SalahTrabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talksClub chair says forward will have medical on WednesdayEgypt international left Liverpool after nine yearsReutersTue 4 Aug 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor say they have begun transfer ⁠negotiations withMohamed Salah, with the club chair adding they hoped to sign the Egypt forward later this week.“Negotiations have been launched ⁠to transfer professional footballer ⁠Mohamed Salah, ​who is in a free status, to our club,” the club said in a statement.Frank Lampard hails ‘huge’ signing as Coventry seal record £22.5m Rushworth dealRead moreSpeaking to the broadcaster ⁠A Spor, the Trabzonspor chair Ertugrul Dogan said that while the transfer was not completed, Salah is expected to arrive ⁠in Istanbul for a medical on Wednesday and then go to Trabzon to sign with the ​Black Sea side.He did not confirm ‌when the contract would be ‌signed, but said it would likely be on Thursday.Salah left Liverpool this summerafter nine ‌years, having scored 257 goals in 442 appearances, where he won the Premier League twice and the Champions League once.In the 2024-25 season Salah scored 29 Premier League goals and provided 18 assists, equalling the league record for most goal involvements in a season andsetting the record for a 38-game campaign.He was named Premier League Player ‌of the Season and won the Golden Boot and the Playmaker Award, becoming the first player to take all three in one campaign.His output ​waned last season, with seven goals and seven assists in 27 league matches and he was left on the bench in Champions League games, leading to a public spat with Liverpool’s then-manager Arne Slot.The 34-year-old began his career in Europe at Swiss side Basel in 2012 and ⁠later joined Chelsea. He also had brief stints at Fiorentina and Roma between 2015 and 2017 ​before joining Liverpool.Trabzonspor – generally ​considered to be the fourth-biggest team in Turkey after Istanbul ​sides Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, and ‌Besiktas – finished third ​in the Super Lig ​last season and will enter the Europa League playoffs.Salah had been close to joining Istanbul club Besiktas, whose football director Onder Ozen said negotiations had stalled over financial and image-rights demands, according to local media.Explore more on these topicsMohamed SalahTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coach | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: Manchester United are closing in on their new head coach after the departure of Marc Skinner
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester United are closing in on their new head coach after the departure of Marc Skinner
Content: Manchester United are expected to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach.Photograph: Callum Landells/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United are expected to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach.Photograph: Callum Landells/Getty ImagesManchester United WomenManchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coachOlid expected to meet players on WednesdayUnited squad pays tribute to former head coach SkinnerTom GarryTue 4 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United are set to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach to replace Marc Skinner,following his exiton Monday, multiple sources have told the Guardian.Talks with the 40-year-old are understood to be very advanced and she is expected to be introduced to the United squad on Wednesday.United are confident that the Spanish coach is the right person to lead them into a new chapter, as first reported by the Telegraph, as the Women’s Super League club focuses on developing young, homegrown players.Marc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thin | Tom GarryRead moreOlid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last term on a dramatic final day of the season, but it had already been confirmed in April that she was to leave the Edinburgh club this summer by mutual agreement. She was in charge of Hearts for five years and also guided them to the 2024 Scottish Cup final, where they were beaten by Rangers.She has previously coached in the United States with Houston Dynamo, working with their women’s team and their under-19s men’s squad, before she had a spell with the Catalan Football Association.United are understood to be impressed by her playing style and her ability to develop and improve players, and they carried out extensive background checks on Olid prior to publicly announcing Skinner’s departure on Monday, with succession planning having already been well under way.Skinner left partly because of frustration at United’s transfer strategy. The club are understood to feel the current level of spending across the WSL is unsustainable and they want a different approach, focusing on their own younger talents and improving their academy to deliver longer-term success.View image in fullscreenMarc Skinner left Manchester United party because of frustration over the club’s transfer strategy.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersUnited finished fourth in the WSL last term. They start the new season away to big-spending London City Lionesses on 4 September.The news comes on the day that the United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will “stick together” and be ready for the new WSL season, despite Skinner departing.Le Tissier and the rest of the playing squad were informed bySkinner that he would be leaving, in a meeting on Monday morningshortly before the news was announced, and on Tuesday Le Tissier and her England teammate Ella Toone paid tribute to Skinner for his contribution to the club over five years in charge, which included winning the2024 Women’s FA Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLe Tissier said the “energy he brought to the club was amazing”, while Toone told reporters: “He wanted to tell the team before it came out. It was nice that he was able to tell us [and] he was able to say goodbye, because he’s done a lot for the club. We can’t thank him enough for everything he’s done, the hard work and the passion that he’s put into leading this team.”Le Tissier said that neither she nor Toone have been consulted on who the next head coach should be but added: “I think the club have been pretty clear with what they’ve said, bringing through the youth, that’s what something Manchester United has been kind of made for, and they’ve always done that historically. I think they’ve been pretty clear with that. When we speak to the new manager, the ambitions will be clear.“Me and Tooney are at Man United because we want to win and we’ll be doing everything we can to make that happen. We’ve got a great team, a great squad, great girls. I’m ready to do that.“No matter who comes and goes, we’ve always had that togetherness and that fight for each other and we stick together in tough moments. There’s been a few over the years and we’ve always come through as a team, and, yeah, this one might be difficult right now, we’re in the start of pre-season and we want to make sure that we’re 100% ready for the start of the season.“We spoke to the girls today, we’ll stick together, we always do. We’ve got to go out on the pitch, enjoy playing football and being with each other and we’ll get through it.”Explore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona sign Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City for club-record £1.25m | Barcelona Women | The Guardian
description: The transfer fee is the largest sum received for a sale by a WSL side, eclipsing Olivia Smith’s £1m move from Liverpool to Arsenal in 2025
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The transfer fee is the largest sum received for a sale by a WSL side, eclipsing Olivia Smith’s £1m move from Liverpool to Arsenal in 2025
Content: Kerolin was part of the Manchester City side that won the WSL title and the Women’s FA Cup last season.Photograph: Gary Oakley/PAView image in fullscreenKerolin was part of the Manchester City side that won the WSL title and the Women’s FA Cup last season.Photograph: Gary Oakley/PABarcelona WomenBarcelona sign Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City for club-record £1.25mTransfer fee largest sum received for a sale by WSL sideSigning eclipses Olivia Smith’s £1m move to ArsenalTom GarryTue 4 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona have signed the Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City for an undisclosed fee that sources say is in the region of £1.25m, which would represent the largest sum received for a sale by a Women’s Super League side.The deal is also a club-record for Barcelona, and in terms of a fee received by an English club it eclipses the £1m that Liverpool received for thesale of Olivia Smithin Arsenal in 2025 and Melvine Malard’s more recent£850,000 switchfrom Manchester United to Chelsea.Putellas, Batlle and León are gone: what will be left of Barcelona after latest exodus?Read moreKerolin, 26, was part of the City side that won the WSL title and the Women’s FA Cup last season and was with the club for 18 months, after arriving from North Carolina Courage in January 2025.City have already added the England forward Beth Mead to their squad this summer, on a free transfer from Arsenal.The defending European champions Barcelona are understood to see Kerolin as a player who can thrive in the Champions League and become a regular goalscorer in that competition with her pace and trickery on the ball.A statement from Barcelona, who saidgoodbye to the Spain internationalsAlexia Putellas, Mapi León, Ona Batlle and Salma Paralluelo this summer, read: “The signing of Kerolin Nicoli is another clear statement of FC Barcelona’s ambition.
