The club remains committed to bringing together the best players in world football with the aim of staying at the top of the game and continuing to set the standard for excellence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The Brazilian international arrives at one of the best moments of her career to strengthen a squad built to compete for every trophy. With her talent, creativity and ability to decide matches, Kerolin adds even more quality to a team whose ambition remains unchanged: to challenge for every title and, once again, strive to win it all.”Explore more on these topicsBarcelona WomenManchester City WomenTransfer windowWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Frank Lampard hails ‘huge’ signing as Coventry seal record £22.5m Rushworth deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: The 25-year-old excelled during promotion campaign and the Golden Glove winner moves from Brighton
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: The 25-year-old excelled during promotion campaign and the Golden Glove winner moves from Brighton
Content: Carl Rushworth played all 46 league games for Coventry as they won the Championship title last season.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenCarl Rushworth played all 46 league games for Coventry as they won the Championship title last season.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersTransfer windowFrank Lampard hails ‘huge’ signing as Coventry seal record £22.5m Rushworth dealThe 25-year-old excelled during promotion campaignBrighton goalkeeper completes permanent switchBen FisherTue 4 Aug 2026 08.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoventry have completed the club-record £22.5m signing of goalkeeper Carl Rushworth from Brighton as Frank Lampard’s side continue to prepare for their return to the Premier League after 25 years away.The 25-year-old excelled on loan at Coventry in the Championship last season, playing an instrumental role in their promotion as champions, starting all 46 league matches and earning the Golden Glove award for keeping 17 clean sheets.Football transfer rumours: Chelsea’s Mudryk to reunite with Lampard at Coventry?Read more“It’s great to have Carl back with us on a permanent basis,” said Lampard, whose side begin their season at Arsenal on 21 August. “He’s a top professional, a great character and he had a huge impact on the team to help us get promoted last season. I’m looking forward to working with him again and welcoming him back into the group.”Rushworth, who is also highly regarded within the Football Association and the England setup, joined Brighton from non-league Halifax in 2019 but departed the club without making a senior appearance. Before his season at Coventry he had enjoyed loans across the league pyramid with Walsall, Lincoln City, Swansea and Hull.Brighton’s sporting director, Mike Cave, said: “While we would have liked to keep Carl with the club for longer, we respect his decision to secure regular first-team football in the Premier League.” Brighton are thought to have negotiated a sell-on clause and a buy-back option as part of the sale, which could rise as high as £30m including add-ons.Rushworth represents Coventry’s fourth summer signing. Last month they eclipsed their previous transfer record when paying Eintracht Frankfurt £17m to sign the Switzerland defender Aurèle Amenda, and have also signed Loum Tchaouna and Frank Onyeka. Until Amenda’s arrival, their record outlay was £7.7m, to Antalyaspor, for Haji Wright in 2023.Elsewhere,Aston Villahave welcomed the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) upholding their appeal to register 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo. The teenager, who was born in London but raised in Luxembourg, joined Villa from Metz in January but had been ineligible to play owing to Fifa’s regulations on international transfers of minors. Madjo, who has scored four goals in pre-season, is now available to feature for Villa.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowCoventry CityBrighton & Hove AlbionAston VillanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t wait’: Dominik Szoboszlai hungry for Liverpool reset under Andoni Iraola | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola’s debut campaign at Anfield offers promise and the key midfielder wants to make amends for last season’s flop
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola’s debut campaign at Anfield offers promise and the key midfielder wants to make amends for last season’s flop
Content: Dominik Szoboszlai (left) has been a standout player for Liverpool for some time.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai (left) has been a standout player for Liverpool for some time.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesLiverpool‘I can’t wait’: Dominik Szoboszlai hungry for Liverpool reset under Andoni IraolaMidfielder adapting to life under new managerReds need ‘something special’ without further additionsAndy HunterTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDominik Szoboszlai believes last season’s frustration can pushLiverpoolto challenge for the title again but admits the squad must produce “something special” if no reinforcements arrive before the transfer deadline.The Liverpool midfielder upped his already impressive level last season, being named the club’s player of the year, but collectively the team went into reverse withArne Slot losing his jobas a consequence. The poor title defence from a team that won the Premier League comfortably in Slot’s debut season should, Szoboszlai insists, prompt a reaction in Andoni Iraola’s debut campaign as Liverpool head coach.Worn in the USA: Liverpool’s pre-season tour had highs but exposed glaring gaps in the squad | Andy HunterRead more“I can’t wait [for the new season], honestly,” said the Hungary captain following Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US. “I feel that we are ready to go again and take motivation from last season because it was not the best. We didn’t end up where we wanted to. So now we’re going to go for it again.“Everyone is motivated. I think I see in everybody’s eyes that he wants to play and, if you want to play, you have to give your best. And from there the manager is going to decide who is going to play. But everybody is on zero right now.”Liverpool have added the central defender Jérémy Jacquet and theversatile forward Victor Muñozthis summer but, while they remain in pursuit of Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola, a squad that has seen Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konaté depart as free agents remains light in several positions.Szoboszlai said of Liverpool’s transfer activity: “It’s not my job to tell you who we have to sign or if we have to sign someone. If the guys above and the manager decide to sign someone, then we are very happy and are going to welcome him – or them – well. If they decide not to, then we have to do something special with this squad.”View image in fullscreenLiverpool’s new head coach, Andoni Iraola, cuts a thoughtful figure during the US pre-season tour.Photograph: Geoff Stellfox/Getty ImagesThe Liverpool midfielder revealed Iraola prefers not to address his players in the immediate aftermath of a game, a trait he discovered after the pre-season friendlies againstSunderland,WrexhamandLeeds. “He doesn’t speak after the game,” Szoboszlai disclosed. “I think every manager is different in his own way. That’s how he is. He always would rather speak the day after the game, which is fine for everyone. We have to get used to this.”Iraola has also not spoken to Szoboszlai – or any other player for that matter – about filling one of the vice-captaincy positions vacated by Robertson and Salah. But the 25-year-old, who captained Liverpool on the US tour, says it would be a huge honour to be asked.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “There hasn’t been any conversation. We have Virgil [van Dijk] as the captain, we have Ali [Alisson], we have Joe Gomez [as vice-captains], so there was no conversation at all. Obviously Ali is not here and Joe is injured. Let’s see. It’s not fixed. If you get offered the vice-captain of Liverpool, you’re going to take it. It would be a proud moment for me but I respect everybody. Whoever it’s going to be, we’re going to follow them.”The captain’s armband became an issue for Curtis Jones when Szoboszlai passed it to Kostas Tsimikas during the win over Wrexham in New York. But Szoboszlai, who recently signed a new five-year contract at Anfield, insisted there was no problem with his fellow midfielder.“It was never a debate between us three,” he claimed. “We just discussed something on the pitch. After, you guys make it very big. But next time we will manage to do it in the changing room. Nobody was angry. It’s all cleared. We are cool, everybody.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tearful Jack Draper loses on comeback from injury at Canadian Open | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Jack Draper was in tears during his 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jack Draper was in tears during his 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open
Content: Jack Draper of Great Britain plays a backhand against Térence Atmane.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper of Great Britain plays a backhand against Térence Atmane.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesJack DraperTearful Jack Draper loses on comeback from injury at Canadian OpenBriton withdrew from Wimbledon with bruised boneDraper in tears during 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 loss to Térence AtmanePA MediaTue 4 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Draper was in tears during a first-round comeback defeat by Térence Atmane at the Canadian Open.The Briton was competing for the first time sincepulling out of Wimbledonwith a recurrence of a bruised bone in his left arm, and was beaten 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 in Montreal.Draper pulls out of Wimbledon with arm injury in fresh blow to British hopesRead moreThe 24-year-old was visibly upset during a changeover in the third set. His serve speed had significantly dropped, and he appeared concerned about his left arm.He has a wildcard entry for the Cincinnati Open, beginning next week, but there will be doubts about his involvement after this defeat, as well as regarding his fitness for the US Open.Draper pulled out of the DC Open in Washington last week, as well as missing Wimbledon.He reached a career-high ranking of No 4 in the world last summer, but has been plagued by injuries since and has spent the better part of a year on the sidelines.Draper’s fellow Briton Jacob Fearnley reached the second round in Montreal with a 7-6, 6-4 victory over Adrian Mannarino.Meanwhile, world No 2 Carlos Alcaraz has withdrawn from the Cincinnati Masters as he continues his recovery from a wrist injury that has sidelined him since April. The Spaniard had been slated to make his return in the tournament to prepare for the US Open, the final Grand Slam of the year, which starts on 30 August in New York.Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland risk ECB ire by agreeing to play five matches against Afghanistan | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Ireland’s decision to stage a full one-day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer could cost them lucrative future fixtures against England
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Ireland’s decision to stage a full one-day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer could cost them lucrative future fixtures against England
Content: Ireland, who beat India in a T20 series in June, are playing five one-day internationals against Afghanistan this month.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenIreland, who beat India in a T20 series in June, are playing five one-day internationals against Afghanistan this month.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PACricketIreland risk ECB ire by agreeing to play five matches against AfghanistanFirst ODI of series will take place in Bready on WednesdayEngland refuse to face Afghanistan due to Taliban regimeExclusive byMatt HughesTue 4 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland’s decision to stage a full one‑day international series for their men’s team against Afghanistan this summer couldcost them lucrative future fixtures against England.The England and WalesCricketBoard is understood to be unhappy about the series, which starts on Wednesday, ­taking place as England refuse to play Afghanistan outside ­International Cricket ­Council global events because of what the ECB chair, ­Richard Thompson, has described as the “gender apartheid” of the Taliban regime.Durham sitting pretty in One-Day Cup despite Ben Stokes’ golden duckRead moreThe ECB’s policy is backed by the UK government, but Cricket ­Ireland has taken a different view and has developed close relations with the Afghanistan Cricket Board, ­offering it five ODIs this month, all of which will take place in Northern Ireland. In a reciprocal arrangement Ireland will play Afghanistan in the UAE next March for one Test, three ODIs and three T20 fixtures.England played a one-off Test against Ireland at Lord’s as prepara­tion for both the 2019 and 2023 home series, but the ECB has opted for a warmup Test against Bangladesh instead next year.England’s men played ­Afghanistan in a Champions Trophy group game in Lahore last year after a specially convened ECB board meeting approved the fixture, which was criticised strongly by a cross‑party group of 160 MPs, who had urged them to withdraw in a joint letter.The ECB will not schedule any bilateral cricket against ­Afghanistan, however, and this summer organised a tour of England for the Afghan Refugee Women’s team, as well as ­inviting them to the T20 World Cup final at Lord’s. The Afghanistan women ­players fled the country with the majority relocating to Australia after the Taliban retook control in 2021 and enforced a ban on female sport.While Afghanistan are the only ICC full member not to operate a ­women’s cricket programme the world ­governing body has not banned them. Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand also refuse to play Afghanistan in ­bilateral series, however, with ­Ireland ­joining West Indies, ­Zimbabwe and the four Asian ICC full members in granting them fixtures.The ECB’s relationship with Cricket Ireland has been delicate for some time, as England have declined an invitation to join a proposed new Euro Nations Cup tournament also involving Scotland, the Netherlands and Italy next year because of their congested calendar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile England’s men played three T20 internationals in Ireland last September the ECB sent a second-string team and there are no more matches in the calendar. England’s women, however, will host Ireland in a three‑match ODI series next month.Explore more on these topicsCricketECBIreland Cricket TeamAfghanistan cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest padding | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Riders at the Tour de France Femmes were subject to extra clothing checks before Tuesday’s stage following claims some could be using extra padding to seek an aerodynamic advantage
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Riders at the Tour de France Femmes were subject to extra clothing checks before Tuesday’s stage following claims some could be using extra padding to seek an aerodynamic advantage
Content: The peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenThe peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest paddingChest fairings could smooth airflow around the bodyWarning came before time-trial stage to DijonJeremy Whittlein DijonTue 4 Aug 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRiders in theTour de France Femmeswere examined for hidden aerodynamic enhancements, or chest fairings, before the race’s time trial stage to Dijon on Tuesday, in a clampdown on the latest attempts to circumnavigate cycling’s rules.Changes to body morphology to improve aerodynamics are banned under InternationalCyclingUnion rules. The UCI’s commissaires were looking for padded chest fairings that would artificially improve airflow and reduce wind resistance.Tour de France Femmes: Reusser aces stage four time trial to snatch yellow jerseyRead moreIn June the male rider Jan-Willem van Schip was disqualified in a French race for inserting a water bottle into the front of his racing jersey on the basis that it enhanced his aerodynamics and speed.The UCI directive that selected riders have extra checks before the stage to Dijon came at the instigation of some teams who had noticed changes to rider physiques before time trials.Stijn Steels, director of the AG Insurance-Soudal team, said he first noticed suspicious padding at the Paris Olympics in 2024. “There was a rider who suddenly had huge breasts,” Steels told the Belgian newspaper Het Laatste News.“Last year, many riders filled their bust area completely with ice or other items to create a larger volume, which gives a much better aerodynamic effect. It’s only a few watts difference [in power], but a few watts matter a lot in a time trial. It’s possible and it does make a difference, but I wouldn’t risk it.”Stephen Delcourt, manager of the race favourite Demi Vollering’s FDJ United-Suez team, said: “We never play with the rules like this. If they want to have controls for this, it’s because someone is doing it. Every season everybody does more work in wind tunnels and looks at equipment from the handlebars, the bike, the helmet. But we don’t play with the rules, we are always transparent.”The former world champion Marianne Vos, teammate to the defending Tour de France champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, supported the clothing checks. “It’s good that they try to enforce the rules,” Vos said. “Everybody is looking for the best aerodynamics, so there are some games. But there are rules to live by.”In a statement to the teams taking part in the Tour Femmes, the UCI said “particular attention” would be paid to ensure cyclists complied with regulations over “non-essential items or other accessories worn by a rider that could alter their physique”.Vos said of the checks: “I don’t think it’s really body searching, so I don’t have a problem with it, as long as it’s not too invasive.”Rolf Aldag, team manager to Kasia Niewiadoma, winner of the Tour Femmes in 2024, saw little difference between the clothing inspections and standard doping controls. “You have to enforce the rules,” Aldag said. “Otherwise, don’t make them. If there’s something to check, then it should be checked. They do that every time they do a doping control. So do we question doping controls?“If we question it due to the privacy of an athlete, then you have to skip doping controls too, which we all agree that we should not do. It’s the same rule for the men and they would also be checked. I think there’s nothing wrong with that.”Bert Blocken, professor of aerodynamics, aerospace and mechanical engineering at Scotland’s Heriot‑Watt University, said a chest fairing can alter airflow around the body and reduce aerodynamic drag, allowing riders to conserve energy.“You don’t gain tens of seconds on a time trial, but over 20-30km, it can make a decisive difference,” Blocken said, adding that it could mean a gain of 0.78 seconds per kilometre.The UCI’s directive has led to accusations of sexism as no clothing checks were carried out either before, or after, the men’s Tour de France time trial, between Évian‑les‑Bains and Thonon-les-Bains on 21 July.Philip Roodhooft, manager of the Fenix-Premier Tech team that won three stages in the men’s Tour in July, said that he was “not surprised that people are exploring it”.Roodhooft said: “When you see that the men try things with water bottles placed in strategic spots, then I can imagine that women are thinking about it as well. Still, it’s not good that it happens because it’s still cheating.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: New MLS commissioner says promotion and relegation won’t be coming ‘anytime soon’ | MLS | The Guardian
description: Larry Berg was officially introduced to media and MLS staff on Tuesday, giving the first indications of his vision for the future of MLS
Author: Alexander Abnos
Headline: Larry Berg was officially introduced to media and MLS staff on Tuesday, giving the first indications of his vision for the future of MLS
Content: Larry Beg spoke with the press for the first time as incoming MLS commissioner on Tuesday.Photograph: Dustin Satloff/MLS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLarry Beg spoke with the press for the first time as incoming MLS commissioner on Tuesday.Photograph: Dustin Satloff/MLS/Getty ImagesMLSNew MLS commissioner says promotion and relegation won’t be coming ‘anytime soon’Larry Berg officially introduced to media and MLS staffBerg to take over for Don Garber on 1 January 2027Alexander Abnosin New YorkTue 4 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 16.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMLS will have a new commissioner starting in 2027, but don’t expect the league to adopt the promotion and relegation system seen in league systems throughout the world anytime soon.Larry Berg, a co-owner of MLS club Los Angeles FC and the league’s incoming boss, said in his introductory press conference on Tuesday that he doesn’t think that the long-mooted idea of bringing “pro/rel” to the North American league is “appropriate”.“I can understand the appeal for the fans, [but] I don’t think it’s a great way to build a league, I don’t think it’s a way to get stadiums built, get training facilities built, and to have owners invest in rosters and all the other things you need to do,” Berg said. “So the great thing about promotion/relegation for fans is that the jeopardy is quite severe. But I think there are other ways to create jeopardy during the regular season, [and] again in the playoffs, during the playoffs to get to the next round. That’s what we want to focus on.”How does MLS pick up the World Cup mantle? Casemiro helps, but it’ll take much moreRead moreMLS, which began play in 1996, is unique among global soccer leagues because of its single-entity structure, which see the central league office holds the ownership rights of all the teams and player contracts. This structure was a key role in reducing risk and attracting the league’s first investors. Promotion and relegation, too, was not implemented both because there were not enough teams to make it viable, and also because of the risk it posed to team owners, who not only controlled their own team’s operations but also acted as investor/operators for the league itself. The US has a second division league – the USL Championship – but the two organizations have not shown any inclination toward working together since MLS teams pulled their reserve teams out of the USL after the Covid-19 pandemic.MLS has grown from as little at 10 teams at the turn of the century to 30 in 2026 – a rapid period of expansion that has raised the possibility that the league may continue to expand and enact an internal version of pro/rel; an MLS1 and MLS2, if you will.“I don’t think it’s appropriate for our league,” Berg said. “I think [outgoing commissioner] Don Garber has said before, ‘never say never,’ but I just don’t see it happening anytime soon.”The comments stood as the most direct policy statement Berg made in his first public appearance as the commissioner-elect, which came in front of a small theater full of MLS employees and a handful of journalists. Garber, along with succession committee co-chairs Jimmy Haslam (co-owner of the Columbus Crew) and Bennett Rosenthal (co-owner of LAFC), also attended the press conference.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll 45 Major League Soccer players at the 2026 World Cup, rankedRead moreBerg was elected to the post in a meeting of MLS owners on Monday, concluding a process that Haslam said started with “125 different men and women”.“Some were in sports, some were in media, some were in technology, some were ‘just in business,’” Haslam said.That search eventually narrowed down to Berg and David Nathanson, a former Fox Sports executive. Berg, in addition to his co-ownership of LAFC, also holds a minority stake in Italian Serie A side Roma and Welsh side Swansea City, who competes in the English league system, last reaching the Premier League in the 2017-18 season.Berg also has a long history in private equity, working for 30 years at Apollo Global Management and last serving as a senior partner at 26North. Asked by the Guardian if his private equity background would influence is approach to the job of commissioner, Berg said he thinks it will be an advantage as he looks to speak to the “experts in the room”.“I do think there’s a lot of characteristics in private equity that apply to other things, which is not a surprise. It applies to everything,” Berg said. “It’s about a sense of urgency. It’s about rolling up the sleeves, being in terms of asking big questions, aligning people for a common goal … at the end of the day, this is a governance job with 30 owners and a lot of constituents.”Explore more on these topicsMLSUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fortnite on steroids’: the virtual gaming worlds transformed to train British soldiers | Military | The Guardian
description: Inside Skyral, part of a consortium that won a £2bn MoD contract to help forces game out complex decisions
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Inside Skyral, part of a consortium that won a £2bn MoD contract to help forces game out complex decisions
Content: Aisha Down taking part in a live VR demonstration of Skytral technology, which is to be used to train the British military.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAisha Down taking part in a live VR demonstration of Skytral technology, which is to be used to train the British military.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianMilitary‘Fortnite on steroids’: the virtual gaming worlds transformed to train British soldiersInside Skyral, part of a consortium that won a £2bn MoD contract to help forces game out complex decisionsAisha DownTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a sunny July day in Riga, Latvia, a Nato convoy drives down a street lined with kebab shops and a pharmacy. At a downtown intersection, there is the sound of an explosion and the lead tank bursts into flame.These are real streets in Riga – Lāčplēša iela and the downtown corridor of Tērbatas iela. The kebab shops and the pharmacy are on them. The pedestrians who flee after the tank explodes and huddle at a distance are modelled after the population of Riga: some old, some young, some friendly to Nato, others less so.But the entire thing is a simulation. It has been built by Skyral, a UK company that is part of a consortium that recently won a£2bn contractfrom the Ministry of Defence to train the British army.Modern armies have been training in virtual environments for decades. In 2002, the US army launched a video game called America’s Army, initially run on Windows, a multiplayer shooting scenario that aimed tomodelcombat situations but was criticised as being propaganda for the US military.A new generation of companies are trying to offer something different: intricate, layered models of systems or places that can capture the second-order consequences of events. Skyral aims to allow militaries to recreate cities and even entire countries. The purpose is less to familiarise a fighter pilot with how to handle an F-16, and more to train soldiers and tacticians on the consequences of a decision.View image in fullscreenAisha Down taking part in a live VR demonstration of Skyral’s platform, where a faithful and usable model of a real city and a real battlefield can be recreated.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianFor example, if a missile strike hits a crowded city street, the population will flee. But if that missile knocks out a power station on a cold winter’s day, the same people are likely to shelter in different areas.There’s limited research on how much a technology like Skyral’s might improve how soldiers are trained. Broadly, games work: earlier research hassuggestedthat service personnel who have trained on flight simulators perform far better in real-world scenarios. But there arelimitsto how effectively such scenarios model real-world environments, or how transferable they are to combat. That said, running a simulation is easier and cheaper than organising live combat drills – which is why militaries are spending billions on them. They may not perfectly replicate the real world, but they allow soldiers to train key skills on repeat.The ideas Skyral is offering have been in development for some time. But the UK will be one of the first militaries to integrate the technology deeply into training its forces. The contract comes amid a wider publicdebatearound how much money the UK is allocating to defence, and if this is sufficient to address changing and growing threats.How is it different than soldiers playing Call of Duty?View image in fullscreenNaomi Hulme of Skyral says: ‘If you swap, like, wizards for soldiers and dragons for tanks, it becomes really sort of defence applicable.’Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianIt’s “probably a bit more Fortnite on steroids,” says Naomi Hulme, Skyral’s co-chief executive, who co-founded the company with Jason Kennedy, formerly of the military tech company Raydon. Hulme joined the company after 20 years at BAE Systems, soon after the company was spun from Improbable Worlds Limited, a software company focused on gaming engines and the metaverse.They began with the virtual worlds that Improbable had developed, Hulme said. “If you swap, like, wizards for soldiers and dragons for tanks, it becomes really sort of defence applicable.” But over time, they built something else: a platform that integrates layers upon layers of information to build, as far as possible, a faithful and usable model of a real city and a real battlefield.Skyral calls this a “digital twin”. The term originally referred to virtual models of machines, such as cars, that enabled predictive maintenance – for example, by simulating how the brake pads might wear down after five years’ use. But it has widened out recently to refer to new, more ambitious efforts to model reality and allow armies – and humanitarian missions andsurgeons– to game out complex decisions.“It has become a buzzword,” says Wiktor Dotter, the chief executive of Power Size Technologies, a defence and automotive-tech company based in Royal Leamington Spa.Power Size Technologies is working with the UK military – as well as the US and a few others – on a separate set of simulations. The company builds virtual models of energy systems – everything from the batteries in a tank to the solar panels in a desert camp – and offers these to militaries to help them decide how to electrify their equipment.These technologies are particularly applicable to the military, he says, where procurement is expensive and decisions are political and take time. It is more challenging to trial a new tank than a new car.“In defence, you will see quickly that if the development of technology is not connected to usability, so everything’s driven by policy and rules,” he says. “What we try to do is say [to the] MoD: ‘You want to try solar panels in the desert? … You can just do that in simulation. You want to have a crazy idea to have a hybrid battle tank? You can just do it right here in simulation. We have enough data to do that.’”Skyral’s value proposal is to develop ways to train soldiers on the second-order consequences of battlefield decisions – how combat might affect logistics networks, critical infrastructure, and the behaviour of a human population. To do this, it builds extensive models of real cities, such as Riga.“In defence, you may well be making decisions without understanding the full consequences,” said Hulme. “What we do in a digital environment is you can test those decisions.”Meanwhile, a cluster of Natoresearchershave been working on digital twins, though often more limited setups, such as models of underwatersystems. The difference is in degree. Skyral is offering models that extend far beyond a single system, attempting to incorporate layer upon layer of information: the shape of the electrical grid, and the age and education levels of a real population, for example.“All of these things that up until now have been done in very siloed sort of modelling – you’re taking all of those models and bringing them all together,” said Hulme. “If you impact one, you see the cascading impact.”Explore more on these topicsMilitaryVirtual realityVirtual worldsGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US water facilities targeted by ‘malicious cyber actors’ – who’s to blame? | Hacking | The Guardian
description: Despite Trump’s efforts to blame Tim Walz and Minnesota, officials suspect Iran behind attacks on US infrastructure
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Despite Trump’s efforts to blame Tim Walz and Minnesota, officials suspect Iran behind attacks on US infrastructure
Content: A water tower in Plymouth, Minnesota, last week. At least 30 systems in the state have been targeted.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APView image in fullscreenA water tower in Plymouth, Minnesota, last week. At least 30 systems in the state have been targeted.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APHackingExplainerUS water facilities targeted by ‘malicious cyber actors’ – who’s to blame?Despite Trump’s efforts to blame Tim Walz and Minnesota, officials suspect Iran behind attacks on US infrastructureNick Robins-EarlyandDara KerrTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 20.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLate last week, federal authorities issued a stern warning saying “malicious cyber actors” were targeting water and wastewater facilities in at least seven states across the US.Minnesotaappeared to be the hardest hit with 30 of its water systems hit by cyber-attacks, leading to disruptions in the state’s water supply.The problems ranged from low-pressure water flow in people’s homes to some utilities announcing boil-water notices. But there have been no reports of drinking water contamination.“These threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes,” the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa) said in astatementlast Thursday.The agency highlighted the fact that critical infrastructure systems can be especially vulnerable to cyber-attacks in the digital age. Much of the problem stemmed from water facilities’ connection to the internet, which made it possible for hackers to infiltrate, change passwords and lock out operators. To mitigate continued disturbances, the agency advised utilities to take their systems offline and switch to manual mode.The culprit of the coordinated attack issuspected to be Iran, according to officials across the government who have spoken anonymously to various news outlets. Tehran has reportedly stepped up its cyber-attacks on the US since the war began nearly six months ago, but so far has only had nominal success. While the FBI announced that itopened an investigationinto the hack, it stopped short of putting the responsibility on Iran.Donald Trump, however, has said the attack is Minnesota’s fault.“I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” Trump said at acabinet meetinglast Friday at Camp David in Maryland, without providing evidence to support his claims. “I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota … Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”Tim Walz, the governor of Minnesota, fired back in apost on X: “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”Exact groups behind cyber-attacks still unclearLaw enforcement and cybersecurity agencies have not publicly identified which hacking group or groups are behind this past month’s attacks, nor have they directly accused the Iranian government of orchestrating them. But, several outlets, includingthe New York TimesandWashington Post, have detailed unnamed government officials claiming that Iran is likely behind the hacks.Cisa previouslyissued a warningin April about Iranian-backed cyber-attacks targeting critical infrastructure, specifically the programmable logic controllers that are used in water systems. The agency updated its advisory on 22 July to give additional guidance on how to secure systems against attacks and named which manufacturers could be vulnerable.“The authoring agencies urgently warn US organizations of ongoing Iranian-affiliated cybertargeting of internet-connected operational technology,” Cisa said in its advisory.Foreign-backed cyber-attacks have repeatedly targeted water infrastructure in recent years. In 2024, several rural Texas towns were hit withRussian-linked cyber-attacksthat briefly caused the tiny town of Muleshoe’s water system to overflow. In 2023 and 2024, a hacking group linked toIran targeted the industrial computersthat controlled some of Pennsylvania’s water systems. Lawmakers from thestate warned the federal governmentat the time that similar attacks could take place across the country.The incidents have also led to calls from cybersecurity experts and industry groups for the US government to address vulnerable infrastructure and invest into their defense.“This week we are facing a reckoning of the consequences of ignoring the importance of investing in our nation’s cybersecurity for our critical infrastructure,” Tatyana Bolton, executive director of the industry group Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition, said in a statement urging federal action on the matter.The coalition, which is made up of prominent infrastructure and cybersecurity companies, called on the government to reinstate and fund the state and local cybersecurity grant program, which is set to expire in September. The grant programwas established in 2021as a $1bn fund for shoring up critical infrastructure.“By not extending this grant program, Congress is leaving small towns to protect themselves from nation-state actors like Iran,” Bolton stated.In some cases, hacking groups have taken credit for their cyber-attacks or investigators have named alleged perpetrators, but often the provenance of hacks remains unclear.Explore more on these topicsHackingCybercrimeInternetMinnesotaIranUS foreign policyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: US stock market hits record highs as AI profits pile and oil prices ease | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: S&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months ago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: S&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months ago
Content: A screen displays stock market index data as traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenA screen displays stock market index data as traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersStock marketsUS stock market hits record highs as AI profits pile and oil prices easeS&P 500 shot up 1.8% and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a few months agoAssociated PressTue 4 Aug 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US stock market rallied to records on Tuesday as profits kept piling up for companies and as oil prices eased.The S&P 500 shot up 1.8%, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set a couple months ago. The Dow Jones industrial average added 907 points, or 1.7%, to its own record set the day before, while the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6%.Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and surged 29.5% after its CEO, Alex Karp, said its overall revenue leaped 93% in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026.Caterpillar climbed 5.6% after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $20bn in sales and revenue in a quarter, and its CEO, Joe Creed, said it was seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power datacenters, among other things.They are the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, after strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50% in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet.That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the Covid-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, when stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group.Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices.Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.3% to $79.36 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $72 and $102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.The yield on the 10-year treasury fell to 4.62% from 4.70% Monday and from 4.75% at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI datacenters.Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.6% for Nvidia, 6.6% for Broadcom and 7.6% for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.They more than offset a drop for Chipotle Mexican Group, which fell 9.7% on fears that future profits could be hurt after the chain removed jalapeños from some of its restaurants after a salmonella outbreak. Chipotle said Minnesota health officials had no ongoing concerns with it.All told, the S&P 500 rallied 136.02 points to 7,736.52. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 907.47 to 54,085.88, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 671.10 to 26,584.99.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsUS economyAI (artificial intelligence)DatacentersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration reportedly drafting ban on Chinese datacenter components | Datacenters | The Guardian
description: Trump’s FCC is developing a measure to bar US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter devices, sources say
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Trump’s FCC is developing a measure to bar US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter devices, sources say
Content: A Digital Realty datacenter in Oakland, California, on 18 July 2026.Photograph: Fred Greaves/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Digital Realty datacenter in Oakland, California, on 18 July 2026.Photograph: Fred Greaves/ReutersDatacentersTrump administration reportedly drafting ban on Chinese datacenter componentsTrump’s FCC is developing a measure to bar US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter devices, sources sayNick Robins-Earlyand agencyTue 4 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationis reportedly drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter components, in the latest sign US authorities are scrambling to respond to the rapid development ofAItechnology inChina.Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which oversees the US ⁠telecommunications industry, is developing a measure to bar imports of new ​Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within datacenters. Officials hope to publish the measure this year, according to Reuters.The FCC could still modify or shelve the restriction, Reuters reported. But the deliberations are the latest example that theTrump administrationis increasingly focused on limiting Chinese technological incursions into cutting-edge US industries.The US has long been at the forefront of the AI industry, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google driving the development of models, and chipmakers such as Nvidia commanding the chip supply chain.But advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond.Chinese companies are some of the biggest manufacturers of components necessary for datacenters, with the country’s optical transceiver industry controlling a majority of the global market for the technology. US tech companies have committed trillions of dollars to build out American AI infrastructure. Plans for that buildout are broadly falling behind schedule, however, while Chinaattempts to catch upwith its own massive development of datacenters.Chinese datacenter components are of concern because they could allow Chinese firms to steal ⁠data, install malware or disrupt service in the US if they are embedded in US infrastructure, experts say.Last month, the FCC announced a ban on China’s advanced humanoid robots. The Trump administration is also reportedly mulling whether to restrict the use of Chinese open-source AI models.US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as rationale for those measures. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.The White House and the FCC did not respond to requests for comment.The Chinese embassy in Washington told Reuters that Beijing ‌urges the US to “heed the objective and rational voices of the business communities in both countries” and “stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions”.“China will take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests,” it added.Some Trump administration officials have been citing the example of Huawei, a Chinese telecom company, to argue for the new restrictions. Huawei’s equipment was so deeply embedded in US infrastructure that efforts to remove it were difficult.A US ‌ban on new models of Chinese datacenter devices would probably hit China’s Zhongji Innolight, one of the biggest global sellers of transceivers, which was added to the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies in June.Explore more on these topicsDatacentersChinaTrump administrationAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Metro Bank customer fights for £14,000 refund after AI-linked fraud | Scams | The Guardian
description: Lender was told money was being taken without authorisation, with cash used to buy credits for Claude chatbot
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Lender was told money was being taken without authorisation, with cash used to buy credits for Claude chatbot
Content: The customer had been paying about £15 a month to use Claude for a few months when the scam happened.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe customer had been paying about £15 a month to use Claude for a few months when the scam happened.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyScamsMetro Bank customer fights for £14,000 refund after AI-linked fraudLender was told money was being taken without authorisation, with cash used to buy credits for Claude chatbotShane HickeyTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAMetro Bankcustomer has told of his fight to get more than £14,000 back after its systems failed to stop a fraud involving the AI chatbot Claude.Zoli Rutter, a businessman from Sussex, had a total of £14,244 taken from his bank account. The scam involved fraudsters buying credits to use Claude.When Metro Bank messaged Rutter to ask whether an attempted transaction was legitimate, he replied “no”, but the criminals were able to make a series of subsequent transactions of between £90 and £200.The fraud is the latest to be linked toAnthropic, the company behind the Claude family of AI tools.In May,a Claude user based in the US told Guardian Moneyabout how gift cards to use the chatbot had been bought using his financial details. Other users shared similar stories onReddit.Claude has been in the news a lot lately. Last week, theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA) appeared to endorse Claude when it said Anthropic would provide access to the tool for firms taking part in a hi-tech FCA initiative (which lets financial companies safely experiment with advanced AI) in order “to help speed up their development work”.However, this week it was revealed that some people’s conversations with Claude werepublicly available online.Rutter had been paying about £15 a month to use the chatbot for a few months when the scam happened.View image in fullscreenThe fraudsters used the Metro Bank debit card linked to the customer’s Anthropic account to make the payments and buy credits to use on the platform.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHe had been using the new technology to track and analyse business invoices.The fraudsters used the Metro Bank debit card linked to his Anthropic account to make the payments and buy credits for the platform.On 19 June, Metro Bank spotted a suspicious transaction for £90.90 and texted Rutter to ask whether he had authorised it. When he texted back to say that he had not, he received another text to say his account would be frozen. However, just the suspect transaction was blocked and not his account.Fraudulent transactions then continued. While some were blocked, says the bank, many were not. Metro eventually froze his card the day after the scam started, but by then, more than £14,000 worth of payments had gone through.A spokesperson for the bank says that owing to the “complex nature of the fraud, regretfully some payments were processed” before it blocked the card fully.After Guardian Money got in touch, Metro Bank temporarily refunded Rutter while a chargeback refund was sought from Anthropic.In a statement, the bank said: “This is a concerning case involving a third party that the customer had made previous genuine payments to and provided card details [to], which were then used to make a series of purchases without Mr Rutter’s knowledge.“We recognise how worrying and frustrating [the] experience has been for Mr Rutter. Metro Bank has refunded Mr Rutter while we progress a chargeback dispute request with Anthropic to refund the money that had been taken.”It added: “We would encourage customers to contact their bank as soon as they notice any unusual transactions or are aware of any compromise to accounts where their financial details are stored.”Anthropic says a coordinated gang had used Rutter’s cards to buy credits to use Claude. It says it has no evidence that the compromised card details had come from its own systems. The user behind the fraud has been banned, it adds.Anthropic says anyone who has been charged for a fraudulent purchase shouldcontact its supportsite and the charges will be refunded.Rutter has since been refunded by Anthropic, and the temporary refund from Metro Bank is due to be taken back by the bank.Metro Bank told him in a letter that he had not received the service it expected its customers to get, and it offered him £300 by way of compensation.Rutter says he intends to make a complaint about what happened to the Financial Ombudsman Service.The bank says it has taken steps to prevent delays in cards being blocked.Anyone who has been affected by an unauthorised card fraud is advised to contact their bank immediately and ask for a refund. They may then be asked to fill out forms detailing what happened.The FCA says the refund should be in a customer’s account by the end of the next business day.Explore more on these topicsScamsAI (artificial intelligence)Metro BankChatbotsAnthropicConsumer affairsBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: The best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – tested | Life and style | The Guardian
description: They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterLife and styleReviewThe best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – testedThey’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommendsThe best air fryersCaramel QuinTue 4 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.If you’re at a restaurant and hear a ping a couple of minutes before your meal arrives at your table, it’s unlikely to be a good sign. But microwave ovens are a brilliant tool in the home kitchen. They’re fearsomely fast at heating up – or even cooking – food when you’re time-poor and lacking the energy to make something wholesome after a hard day at work. And in hot weather, cooking by microwave isn’t just quick: it also won’t warm your home.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Microwaves work best for heating food with a high water content (they make the water molecules in food vibrate to create heat). However, before testing, I asked around to find out what people use theirs for most, with a view to using this information to shape my tests. I learned a few things – like lots of people eatmug cakes. Who knew? And that wheat bags are a popular alternative to hot-water bottles. But the majority of folk use their microwave for reheating cold cuppas, defrosting frozen batch-cooked meals, warming food, popping microwave popcorn – and, of course, cooking jacket potatoes more quickly. I used these insights to shape my testing.Ease of use is important, too. Most of us only ever use a few buttons on repeat, often having to reach for the instructions if we want to use some of the smarter functionality these appliances now come with – some can even air-fry.Microwaving can be healthy and fast, and it uses less energy than an oven. So, if you want to discover the best microwaves for your needs, read on.At a glanceBest microwave overallPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fry£379 at AmazonBest budget microwaveSalterDuoWave 2-in-1£184 at CurrysBest microwave for controlsLGMH6565CPS NeoChef£148.98 at LGWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist who’s been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with my children and several pets, meaning there were plenty of mouths for the extra food I was making while testing these microwaves. The humans got a lot of jacket potatoes and beans; the animals helped with the rest … which is how I discovered that hens love poppadoms!How I testedView image in fullscreenMicrowave magic … every model was put through the same tests, from jacket potatoes and baked beans to defrosting and popcorn.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI selected 10 microwave ovens from leading brands at various price points. The models differed in capacity and features but were similar in other ways. They all had a dial and buttons for control on a panel on the right-hand side. They all opened to the left, other than the Samsung Combi microwave, where the door opens downwards. And they all had a one-metre power cable at the rear that came from the top right (looking front on).I used each model to prepare the same set of foods. I made microwave popcorn, cooked jacket potatoes (200 to 250g each), and heated up 150g of baked beans.Next, I used each microwave to heat 250ml of chilled (starting at 9C) tap water for two minutes, using a digital thermometer to check its temperature after heating. I also used the defrost settings on a 500g block of ice in each microwave for 10 minutes, weighing how much ice was left. Finally, I cooked poppadoms to evaluate a microwave oven’s ability to cook evenly, and frozen oven chips in those models that come with an air-frying feature.None of the food I made went to waste, with the chickens happily eating any leftover popcorn and – surprisingly – the poppadoms, and the dog eating everything else.With testing done and dusted, any models that weren’t collected by the manufacturers were donated toFurnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes social housing for survivors of domestic abuse.The best microwaves in 2026View image in fullscreenHot competition … the microwaves battling it out for a place on your worktop.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest microwave overall:Panasonic NN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryfrom£379£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonWhat we loveHuge capacity; proper jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveBulky; greasy fingerprints show up on itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonThis microwave is huge, arriving with the biggest capacity on test. The turntable sits on a roller with six wheels, rather than the usual three, and the controls are a dial with a button at its centre, plus six clearly labelled buttons. Helpfully, the display features scrolling text, so you always know what you’re doing, and you’ll find a list of all the programmes inside the door, so you never need to consult the instructions to make full use of it.Why we love itPerformance was excellent: the microwave cooked popcorn fast, the poppadoms evenly, heated my mug of water to 75C and defrosted the ice well. I used a special programme to cook the jacket potato, which took 15 minutes but was well worth the wait. In fact, the Panasonic was the only microwave on test to produce a jacket potato that could have passed for oven-baked.This model also offers grill, convection oven and air-fryer cooking – personally, I think those last two are the same thing. Again, though, performance impressed. It comes with a circular rack, a crisper tray and a wire basket, which I used to air-fry frozen chips to perfection.If you want a microwave that does it all and gives you extra cooking capacity – essentially, an extra shelf’s worth of oven – this is the one to buy.It’s a shame that …fingerprints show on the brushed stainless steel finish.Dimensions:56 x 45 x 34cm (WDH)Power:1,000W (1,300W grill)Capacity:34lTurntable diameter:36cmOther cooking options:oven, grill, air fryerPanasonicNN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fryfrom£379£379 at Argos£379 at AmazonWhat we loveHuge capacity; proper jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveBulky; greasy fingerprints show up on itBest budget microwave:Salter DuoWave 2-in-1SalterDuoWave 2-in-1from£184£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterWhat we loveGood value; a whole shelf for air fryingWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need the instructions for some functionsView image in fullscreen£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterThe “duo” in the name refers to the fact that this microwave doubles as an air fryer. And it performed brilliantly on all fronts. If you don’t have the worktop space or the budget for the Panasonic, the Salter is a great buy.Microwaving is on a standard glass turntable, but you air-fry on a full-width, rectangular roasting tray that slides into the unit like a shelf, with a rectangular mesh basket that sits on top of this tray.Why we love itIt’s clever. Most microwaves have a jacket potato programme that takes five minutes, but that’s never quite enough: I experimented and found 5mins 20secs was the optimum time. The Salter automatically went for 5mins 20secs and cooked it perfectly.It’s quick, too, heating my mug of water to an impressive 73C and cooking two poppadoms quickly and evenly. I used the basket to air-fry frozen oven chips, and they were ready within 15 minutes.Controls are intuitive, with a button in the middle of the dial. It was easy to figure out how to defrost, and I could do so by time or weight.It’s a shame that …there isn’t a list of all the programmes inside the door.Dimensions:45 x 52 x 30cm (WDH)Power:900WCapacity:26lTurntable diameter:31cmOther cooking options:air fryerSalterDuoWave 2-in-1from£184£184 at Currys£187.99 at SalterWhat we loveGood value; a whole shelf for air fryingWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need the instructions for some functionsBest microwave for controls:LG MH6565CPS NeoChefLGMH6565CPS NeoCheffrom£148.98£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks classy and packs a good grillWhat we don’t loveThe musical alerts are an acquired tasteView image in fullscreen£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonThis feels like a high-end microwave for a mid-market price. The design is sleek, with a full-width door and a control dial that you can push in to sit flush when not in use. Inside the door is a list of all the programmes.The cooking area is impressive, too: the turntable sits on a roller ring with six wheels, rather than the usual three, so it doesn’t wobble. It comes with a circular rack and a crisper tray, too.Why we love itThe look is high-end and performance impressed, too. My mug of water was heated to 72C, and the 14-minute programme for the jacket potato gave decent results. The “healthy fry” setting did a great job of frozen oven chips as well – cooking them to perfection in 15mins 30secs, without the need to turn them midway.It’s a shame that …I couldn’t find a setting to defrost by time, so I had to do it by weight. Nevertheless, it worked well, defrosting more than half my ice in 10 minutes. Also, its alerts are a bit musical, which you’ll either love or loathe.Dimensions:48 x 39 x 27cm (WDH)Power:1,000W (900W grill)Capacity:25lTurntable diameter:29cmOther cooking options:grillLGMH6565CPS NeoCheffrom£148.98£148.98 at LG£149 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks classy and packs a good grillWhat we don’t loveThe musical alerts are an acquired tasteFor more, read our guide tothe best air fryersskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox.
