We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best of the restSamsung Combi All-In-One 32L MC32DB7746KCE3SamsungCombi All-In-One 32L MC32DB7746KCE3from£298.99£349 at AO£298.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLarge capacity and app controlWhat we don’t loveNot the best, nor the fastest, on testView image in fullscreen£349 at AO£298.99 at AmazonBest for:app controlOne of the priciest microwaves on test at RRP, although it’s worth keeping an eye out for discounts. It has a generous capacity and plenty of cooking options, including oven, grill, air fryer and steam. It comes with two circular racks (so you can cook on two levels at once), a crisper tray and a plastic steamer. Unusually, the door opens downwards like an oven.It’s also smart: the SmartThings app lets you view cooking progress, get notifications, and even control the microwave from your phone. You can connect it to voice assistants, too, but I didn’t find this especially useful.It didn’t make the final cut because …cooking performance was so-so. My water heated to only 66C; it was slow to cook a jacket potato, and air-frying chips was a 19-minute programme – slower than most dedicated air fryers and closer to an oven.Dimensions:52 x 52 x 33cm (WDH);power:900W (1,500W grill);capacity:32l;turntable diameter:34cm;other cooking options:grill, oven, air fryer, steamSamsungCombi All-In-One 32L MC32DB7746KCE3from£298.99£349 at AO£298.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLarge capacity and app controlWhat we don’t loveNot the best, nor the fastest, on testCaso MCG 25 Ceramic ChefCasoMCG 25 Ceramic Cheffrom£159£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoWhat we loveIts flatbed design means more cooking capacityWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsView image in fullscreen£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoBest for:a larger flatbedThe flatbed design means this model has more usable space than a microwave with a turntable. For example, I could fit in three poppadoms without any overlapping, which is good for a mid-size microwave. However, they cooked unevenly: I had to flip them over and give them another minute.It did a good job of heating baked beans, but it was slow to cook the jacket potato and the popcorn.It didn’t make the final cut because …I hated the controls. It is a truth universally acknowledged that all microwaves should have a button you can bash for 30-second increments. But this one does 30 seconds, a minute, then goes up in minutes (to a maximum of 10 minutes).Dimensions:49 x 48 x 29cm (WDH);power:900W (1,200W grill, 2,050W oven);capacity:25l;turntable:31 x 32cm (flatbed);other cooking options:grill, ovenCasoMCG 25 Ceramic Cheffrom£159£159 at Homebase£159 at WilkoWhat we loveIts flatbed design means more cooking capacityWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsBeko MCF25310BekoMCF25310from£179£179 at Very£179 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat controls and good jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveIt didn’t defrost well enoughView image in fullscreen£179 at Very£179 at AmazonBest for:amid-price combi microwaveThis is a combi: a microwave, grill and oven that can combine cooking styles. However, performance was a mixed bag. It turned out a jacket potato in 6mins 30secs – which, although no replacement for an oven-cooked spud, was better than a microwaved one. It heated my mug of water to 76C, but defrosted less than 20% of my ice.I was a fan of its controls, though: a dial with a button in the middle, plus six clearly labelled buttons.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found it confusing; sometimes it would keep cooking, but the timer didn’t go down. Plus, defrosting yielded disappointing results.Dimensions:48 x 44 x 28cm (WDH);power:900W (1,950W grill, 1,950W oven);capacity:25l;turntable diameter:27cm;other cooking options:grill, ovenBekoMCF25310from£179£179 at Very£179 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat controls and good jacket potatoesWhat we don’t loveIt didn’t defrost well enoughRussell Hobbs RHFM2365BRussell HobbsRHFM2365Bfrom£119£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesWhat we lovePowerful microwavingWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesBest for:a flatbed microwave on a budgetDoing away with a turntable means flatbed microwaves can fit in more food. For example, this one is compact but can accommodate a large 30cm dinner plate. On the downside, flatbed microwaves often struggle to cook evenly, and this model was no exception in my tests. I could fit two (and even three at a squeeze) poppadoms at a time, but while they were fully cooked at the centre, the sides were underdone.The microwave was powerful, though, heating my mug of water to an impressive 72C.It didn’t make the final cut because …it looks classy but the controls proved annoying. There’s no button in the middle of the dial and I had to read the manual to look up programmes.Dimensions:47 x 38 x 30cm (WDH);power:800W;capacity:23l;turntable:33 x 31cm (flatbed) ;other cooking options:noneRussell HobbsRHFM2365Bfrom£119£119 at Appliances Direct£119 at HughesWhat we lovePowerful microwavingWhat we don’t loveUneven cooking; annoying controlsTower T24041BLKTowerT24041BLKfrom£79.99£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmWhat we loveIt’s cheap and fairly powerfulWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for a big dinner plateView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmBest for:priceAt RRP, this was the cheapest microwave tested – but you get what you pay for. The styling is simple but old-fashioned. Overall, it looks pretty basic.When it comes to performance, while my mug of water was heated to only 64C, more than 60% of the ice was defrosted in just 10 minutes.Capacity is small, though: it could cope with only one poppadom and couldn’t accommodate my 30cm dinner plates. Also, it has eight preset programmes, but they’re not listed conveniently on the appliance itself, so you’ll be reaching for the instructions.It didn’t make the final cut because …I liked it, but I think it’s worth spending a bit more on the Salter.Dimensions:45 x 35 x 26cm (WDH);power:800W;capacity:20l;turntable diameter:26cm;other cooking options:noneTowerT24041BLKfrom£79.99£79.99 at Tower£80 at DunelmWhat we loveIt’s cheap and fairly powerfulWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for a big dinner plateWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenChoosing the purrfect microwave … think about capacity, cooking modes and available space before you buy.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianWhat microwave capacity is right for me?The room inside a microwave is usually measured in litres, but that’s the total volume, right up to the corners. I’ve included turntable diameter, so you can measure your dinner plates to see if they’ll fit. Some microwaves have a flatbed design, with no turntable. While you can fit more into these models, cooking can be uneven.Do I need a microwave?A microwave is a valuable tool in the kitchen, if you have the worktop space for it. If space is tight, look for one that’s shallow enough that you can make good use of the space in front of it to prepare food.Microwaves are best at heating, reheating and defrosting food with a high water content. They’re great for reheating everything from batch-cooked meals to a forgotten cuppa.Models that feature oven capabilities or air frying are great because they offer valuable extra cooking space, but only if you have the worktop space. It’s like having an extra shelf’s worth of oven – perfect when you’re cooking for lots of people.What microwave wattage do I need?Microwave power is measured in watts – this is a measure of cooking power, rather than electrical draw. The models on test range from 800W to 1,000W. They will all cook your dinner, but the higher-power appliances will do it faster. This shouldn’t use more electricity overall (and, therefore, money and carbon) as they use more per minute but take less time.Other features to look out forLarger microwaves sometimes offer grill, oven and air fryer modes – or all three. I considerair fryersand small convection (fan) ovens to be the same thing: they cook food by circulating hot air, and they’re faster than ovens thanks to their small size.Combi cooking is when one of these styles and microwave cooking are combined for the best of both worlds. For example, you can cook a crispy-skinned jacket potato in less than 20 minutes.Some microwaves also come with a set of plastic dishes for steam cooking. This works well, but do remember that you’ll need to find space in your kitchen to stow any accessories. Some people also prefer to avoid microwaving in plastic where possible.For more:The best toasters for toast, bagels and crumpetsThe best slow cookers for effortless homemade mealsThe best rice cookers for gloriously fluffy grains at homeThe best soup makers for healthy, thrifty mealsCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotmentExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterFoodGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s tiny, dumpy and funny – so his BMX tricks are hilarious’: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, an adorable slice-of-life adventure | Games | The Guardian
description: Denkiworks’ debut lets players pull off tricks and pull pints in a stunning, Japan-inspired setting
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Denkiworks’ debut lets players pull off tricks and pull pints in a stunning, Japan-inspired setting
Content: Move over, Tom Nook … Tanuki: Pon’s Summer.Illustration: Critical ReflexView image in fullscreenMove over, Tom Nook … Tanuki: Pon’s Summer.Illustration: Critical ReflexSummer games previewsGames‘He’s tiny, dumpy and funny – so his BMX tricks are hilarious’: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, an adorable slice-of-life adventureDenkiworks’ debut lets players pull off tricks and pull pints in a stunning, Japan-inspired settingSarah ThwaitesTue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfreeloading tanuki, mounting debt, and a town full of possibilities will sound familiar to fans ofAnimal Crossing. Alas, while you won’t find accountability from Tom Nook, Kyoto-based studio Denkiworks has stepped in to heal your financial trauma with a BMX-filled adventure in which a mammal finally pays the price for their years of bad behaviour. “Even Japanese people ask why it’s a tanuki,” jokes Liam Edwards, a game designer at Denkiworks. “They have such a mythological background to them; they’re almost like dragons in terms of their mythology.”In Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, you play as an adorable but irresponsible critter named Pon, who’s bled the coffers of the local shrine – his home – dry by buying video games and snack food instead of preparing for its semicentennial matsuri. As a result, the shrine is in total disrepair, and important architecture and cultural artefacts – such as the ema stand and the chōzuya – are left cracked and broken, unbefitting a festival half a century in the making.‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie is corvid carnage with a side of existential angstRead moreWith a forceful push from his ancestor, Pon takes a job at the local post office, delivering parcels on a tiny bike for cash to pay for repairs and buy event finery. “A key aspect of this project is that we check everything,” says Edwards. Although the development team included local Japanese people, Edwards and co were keen to ensure that all cultural details were accurate. “Can we create a shrine or a festival about a tanuki?” Edwards notes. “We did extensive research,” he continues, adding: “We have a whole internal encyclopedia of shrines and related items.”View image in fullscreen‘Pon is the vessel through which everything can exist’ … Tanuki: Pon’s Summer.Illustration: Critical ReflexAs a tanuki, your responses are limited to emojis – which Edwards sees as a metaphor for his early years in rural Japan, when he was unable to fully communicate with neighbours. “You can understand what people are saying to you, but the ability and depth of response is stunted,” Edwards says. “The flip side is, it doesn’t stop any character in the game from helping you, and I think that’s true of Japan as well,” he adds. “I’ve always found in my time here that no matter how hard things are and how much you’re struggling, when you try to communicate, people still want to help you.”While you motor through sunflower fields and suburban streets to complete delivery jobs, townsfolk will prod you to engage with their fixations by completing pint-sized activities. “A bit like a mini Yakuza game, you’re going to get involved,” Edwards says. There are all manner of extracurriculars to try out, from sumo to pulling pints in a local izakaya – modelled after the team’s real Kyoto watering hole – baseball and fishing. “It became a funny joke that every time you deliver a package, there’s going to be an activity there,” Edwards says. “Which was a nightmare for us because we basically developed 20 different mini-games inside of one game.”At the core of Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is the BMXing, with Edwards citing the likes ofTony Hawk’s Pro Skater,SSXandBomb Rush Cyberfunkas inspiration. Using a mixture of button presses and joystick flicks, you can shred down handrails and pull off a surprising number of tricks, from backflips to bunny hops and beyond. “Pon is the vessel through which everything can exist,” says Edwards. “And because he’s tiny, dumpy and he’s funny, the juxtaposition of him doing BMX tricks is just hilarious.”‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s taleRead moreTo pull off this ambitious style, Edwards sought support fromRollerdromedeveloper Jacob Mills, who helped ensure the world is primed for trick freestylers with responsive physics and plenty of themed stunt obstacles, such as bamboo half-pipes. And while players won’t need to flex intense finger dexterity to progress through the story, Edwards did want to ensure that making your way from point A to B is as fun as possible. “Even if 90% of people don’t know anything about BMXing and they just want to have fun, for that 10% of people who really like BMXing, you don’t want to let them down.”Tanuki: Pon’s Summer races on to PC, Xbox Series X\S, and Nintendo Switch soonExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAdventure gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artform | Games | The Guardian
description: The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Content: Designed to foster connections and playfulness … Big Walk.Illustration: PanicView image in fullscreenDesigned to foster connections and playfulness … Big Walk.Illustration: PanicGamesReviewBig Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artformSwitch 2, PlayStation 5, PC; House HouseThe creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measureLewis GordonTue 4 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRadiant sunsets glinting on lapping waves; bushland valleys that beckon with secrets; modernist buildings sat atop craggy ridges: Big Walk’s setting is as arresting as it is beguiling – a kind of architectural fever dream transplanted to a handsome Australian wilderness – but it is the images created by players that lodge deepest in the mind. Here’s one that has stuck with me: in the black of night, cicadas kicking up an almighty din, I had lost my partner. Panic. Despair. Fear. Then, there in the far distance, I saw him signalling in my direction. He was relentlessly spamming a gigantic, ball-shaped lamp on and off, the ground around him flicking from inky dark to warm pastel pink and back again, like a single Christmas light blinking from afar.This kind of encounter is common in Big Walk, the brilliant and whimsical new online co-op puzzler from House House, the Melbourne-based studio behind the 2019 viral hit,Untitled Goose Game. Rather than playing as a honking, mischief-making goose as you do in that game, you are a bug-eyed, gangly limbed kind of bird person (think Pingu as drawn by Mondrian) for whom getting separated from your mates is all part of the fun. That’s somewhat because this rugged terrain is dense with vegetation and cliffs to fall down, and also because the game makes ingenious use of proximity and direction-based voice audio. Step out of earshot of your party and you will find it difficult to call for one another (unless, of course, you’ve picked up a Fisher-Price-like walkie-talkie).View image in fullscreenStep into the wilderness … Big Walk.Photograph: PanicSo you and up to 12 players step out into this somewhat eerily photorealistic open world to uncover its mysteries. Quickly, you come across challenges which veer from the straightforward to the brain-scrambling: shoot the aforementioned ball-shaped lamp into a hoop; arrange wooden pegs decorated with odd, nature-themed symbols into some kind of shape. For each successfully completed task, you win what looks like a large red peanut. Get enough of these red peanuts and you score a key which in turn unlocks some important piece of infrastructure: for example, a slow-moving, toy-like train whose parping horns are a joy to obnoxiously blare across the otherwise bucolic landscape.This structure naturally sustains its own rhythm: moments of intense cooperative concentration followed by longer stretches of ambulatory downtime. Such is the layout of this world, you end up doing a lot of backtracking. This is when a little of the game’s quirky lustre wears off since the actual walking is the least interesting part of Big Walk (and you’re also liable to get stuck on bits of rock). Frustration builds as you traipse through the same patch of scrub for the umpteenth time.Still, Big Walk’s less action-packed moments can be gratifying in their own way: I never tired of watching the twinkling night sky segue with impossible speed into the warm, orange glow of a new day, or stopping to enjoy the sounds of a softly gurgling creak.The beauty of Big Walk lies in how it tasks you with working together, conversing verbally and physically, to access its most enchanting sights. It stands out in an era when so much of online communication, be that in video games or on social media, has been distorted by a kind of attention-holding logic – for instance, the serotonin-releasing kerching of notifications or the relentless rewards of levelling up. Yet Big Walk eschews these pernicious aspects of digital life for a gentler, less overbearing experience that seems expressly designed to foster enriching connections and childlike playfulness.Here’s another moment that has stuck with me: wiping away tears of laughter after my brother and I clumsily dropped one of those essential red peanuts to the bottom of the devilishly constructed, practically “masocore” 100ft shaft that we had painstakingly platformed our way out of. We nattered about it until we found the next thing that piqued our interest: wobbly rave tunes blaring from deep inside the belly of a mountain. I shan’t say any more: you and your pals will want to discover these delights for yourselves.Big Walk is out now; £15.99, A$29.50Explore more on these topicsGamesPuzzle gamesPlayStationPCNintendo Switch 2reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Beast of Reincarnation review – a taxing reflection of human-made damage | Games | The Guardian
description: Game Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holding
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Game Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holding
Content: A taxing and often monotonous journey … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakView image in fullscreenA taxing and often monotonous journey … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakGamesReviewBeast of Reincarnation review – a taxing reflection of human-made damagePC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Game Freak/FictionsGame Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holdingDiego ArgüelloMon 3 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of your time in Beast of Reincarnation is spent collecting last words. You cross paths with robots lying on the ground, who muster whatever energy they have left to provide guidance. These interactions are fleeting. Attempt to talk to them a second time, and protagonist Emma makes their fates painfully clear: “They’ve already passed on.”The latest detour by Game Freak, the studio best known as the primary developer of Pokémon games, is an action RPG set in a post-apocalyptic Japan. Taking cues from Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Final Fantasy VII Remake, and NieR: Automata, you wield the sword of an outcast accompanied by an ever-loyal canine. The pair embark on a taxing and often monotonous journey to defeat the titular beast, which nonetheless serves a thematic purpose to bolster a decaying reality, while reflecting a possible future for ours.View image in fullscreenA decaying reality … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakGame Freak hasn’t marketed Beast of Reincarnation as a Soulslike – the video game subgenre fostered by FromSoftware’s Dark Souls series – but there are many similarities. Smackdowns are challenging, boss encounters are frequent, and you rest at campsites scattered across each zone. However, as director Kota Furushima told Famitsu (translated by GamesRadar+), the team aims for the experience to be “enjoyable for even those who aren’t good at action games”.That design ethos is clear from start, as you’re able to select the difficulty level. My 20 hours with Beast of Reincarnation were spent in normal difficulty, with quite a few retries at first. As time passed, I realised just how much the mechanics want you to succeed – veering into hand-holding territory.View image in fullscreenAiming to be ‘enjoyable for even those who aren’t good at action games’ … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakTake Koo as an example. The pup is an invaluable combat companion for Emma. Yet, he is also a four-legged wiki. He sniffs out nearby enemies, valuable materials, chests, and characters – even before they’re in view. Despite exploration being encouraged and often rewarded, Koo’s actions ensure virtually no sense of discovery. Even forgetting to pick up an item from the ground is done for you, as he fetches it before you can even turn around.This streamlining extends to pretty much everything. Both Emma and Koo have robust skill trees to unlock abilities, which progressively turn the pair into a powerhouse. Yet mechanics such as cooking and harvesting are automated in the background as you fight. There are campsites aplenty, often with a merchant nearby, and returning to them after a defeat doesn’t have any consequences. You quickly repurpose yourself and try again, your body still drenched in blood from the previous attempt.View image in fullscreenThere are campsites aplenty, often with a merchant nearby … Beast of Reincarnation.These decisions aptly correlate to Emma as a character. She is, by design, a person devoid of memories and emotions – oblivious to the grief of the robots she encounters (referred to as golems), who carry human souls inside, trapped in machines designed to serve a single purpose, before shutting down. By learning about feelings from the characters around her and what drives them, Emma’s purpose in the world is questioned. Yet, she, and by extension you, is not offered any alternative.The senseless cycle of violence is even more pronounced in the second half, with enemies and boss encounters being largely recycled. Again, this feels like an attempt to placate you, by presenting obstacles you’ve already overcome. Almost every mechanic is designed to grant you what you need, exactly when you need it.When you’re approaching a boss’s lair, the environment around you morphs. Flora transforms, and the sky turns orange, clouds obscure the sunshine. It’s a striking vista, and one similar to reality, aswildfireshave affected air quality in North America and Canada, and their damage isyet to be calculated. A similar anxiety prevails when learning about the origins of golems, with the idea of human souls being digitised in the face of imminent calamity. There are many parallels to current reality, in a time when we are encouraged to lease ourcreativity,emotions, andautonomyto machines, as we’re algorithmically encouraged to stay oblivious to theactionandinactionof those in power in the face ofhuman-made disasters.Every time Emma defeats a boss, she obtains its power, depicted as a flower added to her braided hair. Using said power in combat creates an inflorescence out of thin air. It’s almost ironic to use a sword to re-establish colour to a world that is actively in a state of erosion. Despite being rooted in conflict and grief, Beast of Reincarnation doesn’t culminate in a nihilistic afterthought. Rather, it uses whichever energy it has left to muster a glimmer of hope – like the sight of a flower blooming on an empty, barraged field.Beast of Reincarnation is out nowExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesRole playing gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite  | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Feigning friendship? Katie Miller at the White House on 30 May 2025.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFeigning friendship? Katie Miller at the White House on 30 May 2025.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesOpinionAnthony FauciAsking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocriteArwa MahdawiThe vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning planTue 4 Aug 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.12 EDTShareYou should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy andMuslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics tostart a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich?While I may not need to inform you that the Millers arebad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, wasforced to appearat a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Bidenpreemptively pardonedFauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration.While the Millers were not directly involved in the Fauci hearing, they did make an interesting cameo.Paul releasedmore than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary from 2019 to 2022, which revealed that Fauci regularly talked to Katie, then a communications aide to vice-president Mike Pence, about her health concerns.“I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day,” Fauci wrote in notes dated 9 May 2020. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone.”View image in fullscreenTarget of vitriol … Dr Anthony Fauci at a Senate hearing in Washington on 29 July.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFauci seemed to like Katie, who he described as “tough, smart, but great”, and she seemed on good terms with him. Fauci also sent the Millers a baby gift and, per his diary, the couple called him to say thank you. “We had a nice discussion about life after Trump,” he wrote in December 2020.I don’t think any more gifts are going to be exchanged, however, because Katie has thrown Fauci under the bus. It’s very embarrassing for a Maga bigwig like her – someone who hasamplified vaccine-sceptic viewsand publicly called forFauci to be jailed– to be revealed as having privately asked him for medical advice. Katie has tried to explain away the relationship by insisting that she had simply been feigning friendship as part of a cunning plan.Katie toldthe political news website Notus that she’d been cordial with Fauci so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”. She added that she understood “how to manage somebody like him”. Some of the information about her seems to have been redacted. Notus reports that the original Fauci journal entries released “mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times”.After the diary entries became public, Katie attacked Fauci on social media and accused him of being fame-hungry. “Every man who has a journal is a narcissist,” she wrote onX on Thursday. “Dr Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponised my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandise himself. As they say, keep your friends close and your enemies closer … this man should be in prison.”Katie isn’t entirely wrong about Fauci enjoying fame. His journal entries contain cringeworthy details about flattering press coverage and celebs fawning over him. Julia Roberts, he wrote, “said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous”. Barbra Streisand apparently also chatted to Fauci about vaccines. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” he wrote in February 2021. “I told her that I work listening to her songs on Alexa. She really did not know what Alexa was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening …”Still, this was a private journal, and we’ve all been embarrassing in private haven’t we? Plus, if Roberts was gasping over me, you best believe I’d be telling dear diary. Fauci getting carried away by his sudden fame is understandable; there is no vaccine for being cringe. One day, however, I hope there will be a cure for the harm people like the Millers have inflicted on the body politic.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsAnthony FauciOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: My son has cancer. Kalshi wants you to be able to bet on his medical future | Joshua Pederson | The Guardian
description: The predictions market is planning to allow betting on clinical trial results and regulatory decisions as our family fights for his survival
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The predictions market is planning to allow betting on clinical trial results and regulatory decisions as our family fights for his survival
Content: ‘The idea that our family would turn to a prediction market to help us make these decisions – rather than to our extremely qualified team of oncologists – is preposterous.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The idea that our family would turn to a prediction market to help us make these decisions – rather than to our extremely qualified team of oncologists – is preposterous.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpinionPrediction marketsMy son has cancer. Kalshi wants you to be able to bet on his medical futureJoshua PedersonThe predictions market is planning to allow betting on clinical trial results and regulatory decisions as our family fights for his survivalTue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTShareMy son is 12 years old. No matter how many Legos we get him, he will only build robotic mechs. He draws haunting pictures in pen and ink but refuses to take an art class. He was devastated to learn that Chuck E Cheese is phasing out its animatronics. His guidance counselor says he’s so kind, he’s really hard to say no to. He sneezes when he steps out into the sunlight. And he also has a very aggressive tumor growing inches below his heart.Further, if Kalshi has its way, you could soon be able to bet on health treatments that could be essential to his survival.That’s because my son is part of a clinical trial for a novel cancer treatment. A shade under two years ago, we got word that he had mass growing around three of his ribs. The prognosis was scary, but early efforts to treat the disease were promising, and he was declared disease-free last summer. A couple of months ago, though, the cancer roared back. We didn’t have lots of good options, but the best of them was a clinical trial featuring a novel combination of chemo and immunotherapy. We signed up almost immediately. Early results have been mixed, but we press on, one teeth-grinding cycle at a time.Kalshi to offer betting on drug trial results and FDA regulatory decisionsRead moreThen out of the blue this summer, word broke that the prediction market Kalshi wouldlaunch a pilot programthat allows users to bet on pending FDA decisions and the results of clinical trials. The first raft of offerings includes a contract onwhether an anti-cancer drugwill be approved and another onwhether a trialfor an Alzheimer’s drug will meet its goals.In other words, cancer and Alzheimer’s patients are praying that these treatments will succeed. But Kalshi is about to permit outside speculators to place ghastly bets that they won’t. Why?Representatives from the company say that this isn’t about betting on the success or failure of potentially life-saving treatments. It’s about “surfacing information”, the company’s CEOsaid in a statement, via what the company describes as a “continuously updated, public probability that reflects the weight of the evidence, rather than the preferred message of the trial sponsor”.The CEO, Tarek Mansour,said: “Drug development is one of the most important and most information-constrained industries on earth […] The data that determines which drugs advance and which don’t is largely locked away from the people who need it most.”To some extent, I agree. When my son’s cancer returned, our doctors informed us of a number of different trials for which he was eligible. But picking among them was and continues to be a terrifying experiment for which we feel ill-prepared.That being said, the idea that our family would turn to a prediction market to help us make these decisions – rather than to our extremely qualified team of oncologists – is preposterous, even if we set aside the possibility that such marketsaremuch less accurate than their CEOs would lead us to believe. (All this is to say nothing of experts’ realfearsthat betting on trials and approvals will hinder or harm potentially life-saving research.)And yet for me, whether or not Kalshi is actually good at “surfacing” such data is beside the point. Having our child participate in a clinical trial has been at times a staggering burden. The treatment has some very challenging present side-effects – and others that may show up years in the future. And while we are hopeful that our trial succeeds, we are painfully aware that the heavymajoritydo not.To add to these things, the possibility that somebody out there might be wagering against my son, hoping that the treatment fails so they can make money, is enraging. How is this not just another type of “death market” – like markets for war or assassination – that even Kalshi says it won’t abide?It must be said that Kalshi is not currently allowing bets on treatments for children. But Mansour has been very insistent in imagining a world in which “any difference in opinion” is a wagerable event. Further, the Trump administration is going to remarkablelengthsto keep the sector from being regulated. So it feels possible that my son’s trial will be one of those “differences in opinion” all too soon. Maybe that won’t happen. But I wouldn’t bet on it.Joshua Pederson is professor of humanities at Boston University and the author of Sin Sick: Moral Injury in War and LiteratureExplore more on these topicsPrediction marketsOpinionUS healthcarecommentShareReuse this content

title: The US government’s mislabelled map of Africa at a global Aids conference shows again a failure to understand the continent | Kenneth Ngure | The Guardian
description: This crude lack of thought is influencing crucial budget decisions on HIV programmes, which were cut by 25% worldwide in 2025, writes Kenneth Ngure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This crude lack of thought is influencing crucial budget decisions on HIV programmes, which were cut by 25% worldwide in 2025, writes Kenneth Ngure
Content: The US government map, that clearly misrepresents each of the African countries, shown at an IAS conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.Photograph: Picture obtained by Reuters/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US government map, that clearly misrepresents each of the African countries, shown at an IAS conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.Photograph: Picture obtained by Reuters/ReutersOpinionGlobal healthThe US government’s mislabelled map of Africa at a global Aids conference shows again a failure to understand the continentKenneth NgureThis crude lack of thought is influencing crucial budget decisions on HIV programmes, which were cut by 25% worldwide in 2025Supported byAbout this contentTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTShareAt the end of July, thousands of scientists, advocates and policymakers gathered at Aids 2026, the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro, to advance the global HIV response. But during one high-profile session, a jarring moment threatened to derail our focus: a slide presented by a senior US state department official displayed a map of Africa with country names glaringly scrambled and mislabelled.While the mistake apparently occurred due to an over-reliance on AI tools, it carried a painful symbolic weight for many of us. It reinforced a longstanding frustration: that too many political leaders treat Africa as a monolithic abstraction rather than a continent of 54 distinct sovereign nations.A cartographic blunder is embarrassing, but far greater harm comes when that same lack of thought and care influences budget decisions. Today, global political resolve to address HIV continues to waver and the funding that has kept millions of people alive has plunged.Areport from UNAids and KFF, a health non-profit, released at Aids 2026 revealed that donor government funding for the global HIV response fell 25% in 2025 from the previous year, putting decades of hard-won progress at risk. And this shift was entirely due to a steep decline in US support.Due in part to these cuts, many African countries are already stepping up their own HIV investments. But hard-hit countries have extremely limited resources, often because they remain crippled by debt. And no single country can replace the sheer scale of international financing and partnerships that have sustained the global HIV response for decades.The most important of those partnerships is Pepfar, the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief, which hassaved more than 26 million lives since 2003and changed the trajectory of the HIV pandemic. During President Trump’s first term, the programme continued to expand and contributed to substantial progress towards global HIV targets. Since the start of his second administration, however, Pepfar has undergonesignificant disruptions.Two studiespresented at Aids 2026shed light on the real-world consequences of these disruptions. In the first, amfAR, the Aids research foundation, surveyedPepfar implementing partners in 46 countries. More than half reported that they had at least one terminated award, and these terminations led to more than 1,700 closed HIV service sites. Disturbingly, partners were most likely to have permanently stopped providing services for the very groups most vulnerable to HIV.HIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say expertsRead moreThesecond studydrew on a rapid analysis of newly released Pepfar data. It showed that, globally, more than 77,000 fewer children living with HIV received Pepfar-supported treatment in the fiscal year 2025 than in 2024, a decline of 14%. South Africa alone recorded a 45% drop, with more than 30,000 fewer children receiving treatment support from the programme.The maths of the HIV pandemic is unforgiving. If we retreat now, new HIV acquisitions will spike, more lives will be lost and the ultimate cost will increase massively.Sustaining donor funding for the HIV response is a shared global security imperative and a moral responsibility. We cannot end HIV as a threat to public health and individual wellbeing if donor countries treat Africans as disposable.It is time for political leaders to look at Africa clearly: as an essential partner deserving of mutual respect, serious engagement and sustained support. Getting our geography right is the bare minimum. Getting our priorities right will save millions of lives.Kenneth Ngure is the president of the International Aids Society and an associate professor of global health at the School of Public Health, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, KenyaExplore more on these topicsGlobal healthOpinionAids and HIVUSAIDDonald TrumpUS foreign policyTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: We are US civil rights lawyers. Trump’s policies have driven us to seek justice internationally | Thomas Becker and Antonio Romanucci | The Guardian
description: On Tuesday, a human rights commission will hold an extraordinary hearing over the administration’s alleged attacks on protesters, journalists and others
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: On Tuesday, a human rights commission will hold an extraordinary hearing over the administration’s alleged attacks on protesters, journalists and others
Content: ‘A body that has historically held the hemisphere’s most authoritarian governments to account will now scrutinize the United States.’Photograph: Seth Herald/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘A body that has historically held the hemisphere’s most authoritarian governments to account will now scrutinize the United States.’Photograph: Seth Herald/ReutersOpinionTrump administrationWe are US civil rights lawyers. Trump’s policies have driven us to seek justice internationallyThomas Becker and Antonio RomanucciOn Tuesday, a human rights commission will hold an extraordinary hearing over the administration’s alleged attacks on protesters, journalists and othersTue 4 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.37 EDTShareWe are constitutional law, civil rights and human rights scholars and practitioners who have spent decades litigating government abuse cases in the United States. Despite the US legal system’s flaws, our work – from securing a record civil settlement for George Floyd’s family to holding Bolivia’s ex-president accountable in US federal court for the massacre of Indigenous protesters – has demonstrated that US courts can rein in state power and provide a path to accountability. But this pathway is narrowing.As Donald Trump attacks the courts, weaponizes the Department of Justice, and targets attorneys who challenge his administration, we have been forced to seek justice beyond our borders.McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous | Judith LevineRead moreEarlier this year, we requested a thematic hearing at the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) on the United States’s violent suppression of protests against federal immigration policies. Never before had the commission granted such a hearing, but the extraordinary nature of the Trump administration’s actions – including allegations of excessive and lethal force against peaceful protesters, attacks on journalists and legal observers, and racial profiling and surveillance – warrants international scrutiny. On 4 August, the commission will hold that hearing.The IACHR is unfamiliar to most Americans. Together with the inter-American court of human rights, the commission is the bedrock of the hemisphere’s human rights system. For decades, it has served as a safeguard against authoritarianism and state repression in the region, providing an avenue for victims when domestic institutions have failed. While the United States claims it is not bound by the inter-American system’s norms, it remains subject to the commission’s oversight under the American declaration of the rights and duties of man. Condemnation by the commission has directly led to policy changes by countries, including the United States.The IACHR typically convenes sessions of hearings three times a year, rotating the location between countries in the region. Fittingly, ours will be held in Washington DC, just two blocks from the White House.Among those participating will be counsel for the family of Renee Good, who was shot and killed in her car by an ICE agent during a Minneapolis demonstration. Following the tragic killing of Good, the then Department of Homeland Security secretary, Kristi Noem,characterized Good’s actionsas “domestic terrorism”. Good’s counsel will also speak on behalf of the dozens of victims in Chicago he represents injured at protests and denied basic rights in detention – including access to food, medicine and lawyers. Also testifying will be the Rev David Black, who wasshot in the headwith a pepper ball by a federal agent at a protest outside Chicago. In response, Gregory Bovino, who was serving as US Customs and Border Protection’s “commander-at-large”,said the shooting“was absolutely in line with policy, and I applaud [the agents]”.Renee Good and the Rev Black are only two of the hundreds of protesters and bystanders who have been injured amid demonstrations against Trump’s remarkably cruel immigration policies. On his inauguration day, Trump signed a series of xenophobic executive orders, including the “Protecting the American People Against Invasion” order. Within days, he deployed federal agents to carry out paramilitary-style raids across US cities. Families have been torn apart and thrown into detention centers or sent to third countries. Everyday Americans watched agentsabduct,beatandshootunarmed migrants. Only weeks ago, separate violent ICE operationsresulted inthree more deaths.When Maga’s power fades, we cannot abandon those ICE killed | Moira DoneganRead moreThe international community has sharply criticized the United States’ treatment of immigrants. The United Nations high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk,saidhe was “astounded by the now-routine abuse and denigration of migrants and refugees”, while the United Nations committee on the elimination of racial discrimination expressed alarm overwhat it calledthe “systematic use of racial profiling” by ICE and “[r]acist hate speech by political leaders, including the President”.Such condemnation is entirely justified, but even those who support the administration’s immigration agenda should be deeply concerned by attacks on those who protest against it. Today’s target may be anti-ICE protesters. Tomorrow it could be advocates for climate justice, gun rights, abortion or labor rights. Freedom of assembly and freedom of speech are cornerstones of any functioning democracy. When they are under attack, other freedoms quickly fall.The upcoming hearing before the commission is both extraordinary and symbolic. A body that has historically held the hemisphere’s most authoritarian governments to account will now scrutinize the United States. As the Trump administration weakens domestic checks on power, international oversight has become not only relevant. It may be our last chance to stop the backsliding that threatens our democracy.Thomas Becker serves as the legal and policy director at the University Network for Human Rights and teaches human rights at Columbia Law SchoolAntonio Romanucci is a founding partner at Romanucci & Blandin, LLC and serves as counsel for Renee Good’s familyExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationMinnesota ICE shootingsLaw (US)United NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zone | Rebecca Solnit | The Guardian
description: Summer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joys
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Summer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joys
Content: ‘Summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianOpinionClimate crisisWe launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zoneRebecca SolnitSummer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joysTue 4 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTShareFar beyond the fires raging acrossEuropeand North America, the smoke, dangerous to breathe, hangs in the air, dimming the view, changing the very color of sunlight into something grimly unsettling.An estimated 20,000 are said to have died in the extreme heat in Europe earlier this year, and heat is climate change’s quiet killer, compared with the dramatic violence of death by fire or flood. In eastern Washington, 600 homes have just burned down, and in both Europe and North America, firefighters have died in the effort to contain the climate-fueled firestorms.Once, across much of the the world’s temperate zones, we looked forward to summer as a time of delights, from summer’s bounty of fruits, long days, warmth, school holidays, activities like camping and swimming, travel and adventure. Now many of us dread it.Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder | Bill McGuireRead moreSummer was the sweet season celebrated in poetry and song, often pictured as a gentle goddess; now it is too often a threat and a misery. All this makes me think of Bill McKibben’s 2011 book Eaarth, a proposal that we can understand climate change as equivalent to moving to a more perilous, unwelcoming planet than the gentle, stable one we evolved over the 12,000 years since the last ice age.I know that there are parts of the world where summer was already harsh, intense – 20 years ago, my friend Mark Klett, a photographer living near Phoenix, Arizona, joked: “Phoenix has two seasons: summer and hell,” summer being January and February; hell being the rest of the year.But even in Phoenix, summer is now more intense; there, people get severe burns from falling down on superheated asphalt. It’s changed everywhere.I’ve driven toNew Mexicoalmost every summer since 1989. A few years ago, I found that I feared heat for the first time: the temperature in Needles, a California desert town on the Colorado River near the Arizona border, was going to be 116F (46.6C). I didn’t know if my car could survive temperatures like that, and I feared what survival would look like for me if the air-conditioned car broke down on the highway. (I managed it by staying on the edge of the Mojave Desert the night before and darting across the low desert to Flagstaff, which at 7,000ft elevation stays cooler, and pressing on to New Mexico the next day.)I’m in New Mexico now, as I write, enjoying the beauties of its incomparable skies and summer thunderstorms, but 37 summers since I started coming, summer is not what it used to be. It’s hotter.The monsoon rains are less reliable and often more violent when they come; one New Mexico town,Ruidoso,has over the past few years been beaten up repeatedly by flood and fire. Like so many westerners, I have too often breathed in the toxic smoke of burning forests, have followed the news of forests and towns being consumed by flames, have friends whose homes have been reduced to ash and rubble, have seen brick chimneys standing above the blackened ruins of a neighborhood.As I hear about summer tourists sweltering miserably from Japan to Spain, I wonder if, going forward, travelers will shift peak vacation times to spring and fall, if schools will change when students have their holidays.Keeping them indoors in air-conditioned spaces may be even a safety measure for those who lack such protection at home. Summer has too often, in too many places, become something to brace against, prepare for, and dread: the season of danger, heat, fire, misery. The New Yorkerreports: “ A conflagration west of Bordeaux, described as four times the size of Paris, prompted the largest peacetime evacuation in the country’s history: 220,000 people.”I study the boreal forest. This summer wildfires came for my home | Julee BoanRead moreIt’s as if we launched a war against nature, and that has turned place after place into something that resembles a war zone. The climate movement is a peace movement, a movement to end this war and its casualties.We often talk about what climate change has wrecked in terms of what’s material, tangible, structures lost to fire, flood, or sea level rise, trees dying, species threatened, glaciers melting in warmer weather. But summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.There have been youth-led lawsuits against the producers of climate chaos and the governments who’ve refused to act adequately – essentially for robbing them of their future. Robbing us all of the immeasurable joys of summer as it was is part of that theft. It’s not the main reason that climate action matters so much, but it’s a reminder that what we’re losing is not only the terms of our survival and our safety, but our freedom and pleasure.Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. Her newest book is The Beginning Comes After the End: Notes on a World of ChangeExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionNew MexicoEuropeExtreme weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: Rise in adulterated sexual enhancement supplements could mean users are getting stiffed | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz | The Guardian
description: Often sold as ‘herbal’ solutions for sexual prowess, research has found many supplements are cut with prescription medications that could harm the people who take them
Author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Headline: Often sold as ‘herbal’ solutions for sexual prowess, research has found many supplements are cut with prescription medications that could harm the people who take them
Content: Therapeutic Goods Administration testing has revealed some sexual enhancement supplements have been adulterated with prescription medication like Viagra and Cialis.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTherapeutic Goods Administration testing has revealed some sexual enhancement supplements have been adulterated with prescription medication like Viagra and Cialis.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralHealthRise in adulterated sexual enhancement supplements could mean users are getting stiffedGideon Meyerowitz-KatzOften sold as ‘herbal’ solutions for sexual prowess, research has found many supplements are cut with prescription medications that could harm the people who take themRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.20 EDTShareSexual enhancement supplements have always been a bit of a joke: you walk into a supplement store (or chuck a search into Google) and voilà – hilariously titled drugs that supposedly give you the sexual prowess of a god await you. All you have to do is pop a little pill and your flagging stamina or general lack of desire will disappear.But like all things that sound too good to be true, is there any evidence these supplements work – and could they be doing more harm than good?What are sexual enhancement supplements?Sexual enhancement supplements are usually sold as “natural” products containing various herbal ingredients.Ads call ovarian cancer a ‘silent killer’. But does urging women to undergo early detection testing do more harm than good? | AntiviralRead moreThere are horny goat weed pills, touted as a way to support sexual function and energy because the plant contains a protein which may increase blood flow to your genitals. There are various pun-titled candies with everything from royal jelly – a product of bees created to feed the queen – to various types of honey, coffee, ginseng and more in them. And there are supplements that appear almost identical to normal multivitamins, presumably because vitamins are generally important to good health and therefore must improve your sex life as well.But asrecent Therapeutic Goods Administration testing reveals, many of the products available to buy in retail stores and online have been found to be adulterated with prescription medications such as sildenafil, commonly sold as Viagra, and tadalafil, sold under the brand name Cialis. These are common erectile dysfunction medications that require a prescription from a GP to avoid harmful side effects.How dangerous are the supplements?As a general rule, there is no evidence to support the fact that ingredients like goat weed or royal jelly can improve sexual performance. But the problem is, when supplements are adulterated with prescription medications, the products can become quite dangerous. In 2007, Cialis was discovered in a herbal supplement for men in Australia and was ordered to bewithdrawn from the market, with the TGA warning the product could have “serious health consequences, especially for patients with existing medical conditions such as heart problems, or persons at risk of stroke”.And it’s not just a problem in Australia – there areworldwide concernsthat prescription medications are readily being added to supplements. This problem is only getting bigger due to the proliferation of the online supplements hidden market thanks to influencers spruiking the products on social media.Why are they being adulterated?Dr Ian Musgrave, a molecular pharmacologist from the University of Adelaide, says the products are being adulterated because people want an effective supplement and “prescription drugs work”.“Adding pharmaceutical drugs to herbal preparations with marginal efficacy … provides for a readily marketable product” that can be illicitly sold as effective “herbal” or “natural” remedies.But these prescription drugs carry significant risks when taken without the advice of a doctor. Many of them work by influencing how blood flows around your body, which means that when combined with other medications they can cause extreme low blood pressure and other heart issues.A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?Read moreThis isn’t an issue if you’re prescribed the pills by your doctor, who will carefully go through the potential problems with you before you use the medication, but can be a huge problem if you don’t know that you’re taking it. For example, combining Viagra and chest pain medications can causereally serious health problems.The fact that there are supplements being sold on our shelves and online with potential hidden ingredients decades after the problem first emerged is concerning. Dr Musgrave says that part of the problem is that it is very hard to regulate the online illicit supplements market.“Border Force is vigilant for unapproved medical products, along with illicit drugs, but the supplement market is very fluid, and the types and forms of supplements vary continuously”. He said it would require a “significant expansion” in both monitoring and personnel to ensure that we are safe from adulterated products.What can you do to protect yourself?Buying supplements online without a prescription can be potentially dangerous. Purchasing products in a chemist reduces the risk of adulteration, especially if products carry an AUST L number on them, which means they are registered with the TGA. But the best advice is to always see your doctor first before taking supplements – even if they claim to be “natural”.Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of WollongongAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Pauline Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky political system. It’s not good for anybody | Peter Greste | The Guardian
description: By deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, the One Nation leader is upending the democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupy
Author: Peter Greste
Headline: By deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, the One Nation leader is upending the democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupy
Content: In an instant, Pauline Hanson has wiped out the neutral position that journalists so jealously guard, Peter Greste writes.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenIn an instant, Pauline Hanson has wiped out the neutral position that journalists so jealously guard, Peter Greste writes.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpinionPauline HansonPauline Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky political system. It’s not good for anybodyPeter GresteBy deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, the One Nation leader is upending the democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupyGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.37 EDTShareDemocracy’s lifeblood is information. But like any bloodstream, the more gunk that flows through it, the less healthy the system. For public debate to work, we all need reliable information grounded in facts and ethics, and the way we’ve done that for almost two centuries is through good journalism.The system isn’t always perfect – and sometimes it can look downright unedifying – but it has generally helped deliver one of the world’s most stable and successful political systems. We mess with it at our peril.For the most part, social media just doesn’t cut it. Nor do the media releases and videos published by our politicians. It is important that we hear from them, of course, but the whole point of having journalists in the room is to interrogate, challenge and question those statements.If that sounds obvious,Pauline Hansonseems to have missed the memo.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAt the event to launch her party’s campaign for the Victorian state election, reporters she deemed “unfriendly” were stopped from getting in.“The ABC were denied entry into here, and the Guardian,” she said.“I’m not putting up with their rubbish. I’m not putting up with their spin, their lies whatsoever.” Her staff also stopped a journalist from the Age.This should not come as a surprise. In her speech to the National Press Club in June, theOne Nationleader warned she would bar media outlets she didn’t like, and singled out the ABC, the Guardian and SBS. Earlier this year, ABC journalists were removed from a One Nation campaign event in the Farrer byelection.One Nation names eight Victorian election candidates as Hanson bars ABC and Guardian from press conferencesRead moreBut if she has a problem with the media, there are mechanisms for complaint. The Australian Press Council oversees print publications, while the Australian Media and Communications Authority handles broadcasters (both radio and TV). The ABC has its own ombudsman, and the Guardian has its own dedicated readers’ editor.All those institutions have clear sets of standards and ethics designed to hold news organisations within the bounds of responsible journalism. All have been criticised for being weak and ineffectual, but they remain the port of call for complaints about ethical breaches. In each case, the regulators measure complaints against their codes, and if a story has fallen short, they exercise their powers of sanction.Let the regulators do their job. By deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, Hanson is claiming that power for herself, and in a world already struggling with trust, that is indisputably bad for democracy.But there is an additional problem. Picking and choosing between news outlets and journalists also poses serious challenges for all the journalists covering One Nation. If Hanson is deciding between those she likes and those she doesn’t, between publications branded “friendly” and those marked “hostile”, between “good media” and “bad”, it risks tarnishing those who are allowed inside the One Nation tent as being on “their side”. In an instant, she has wiped out the neutral position that journalists so jealously guard.This is not to suggest those who remain “in the tent” are compromised, but it creates an awkward image for the media outlets who continue to cover her events. They are, after all, the ones permitted through the door.It also creates an incentive to keep delivering soft stories. That might have been Hanson’s intention, but it doesn’t make for robust scrutiny of her policies or her party, and it certainly doesn’t help public debate.As for those journalists who’ve been shut out, if they are ever allowed back in, there will always be questions around whether they got permission by ingratiating themselves, or whether One Nation recognised its mistake.Either way, by upending the independent democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupy, Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky system, and that can’t be good for anybody.Peter Greste is professor of journalism at Macquarie University and the executive director of the Alliance for Journalists’ FreedomExplore more on these topicsPauline HansonOpinionOne NationAustralian politicsAustralian mediaPress freedomcommentShareReuse this content

title: What if older people refuse help outside the family? This is the taboo that could wreck care reform | Emily Kenway | The Guardian
description: Many fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on board, says Emily Kenway, a social policy doctoral researcher
Author: Emily Kenway
Headline: Many fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on board, says Emily Kenway, a social policy doctoral researcher
Content: ‘People’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change.’Photograph: Phanie/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘People’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change.’Photograph: Phanie/AlamyOpinionCarersWhat if older people refuse help outside the family? This is the taboo that could wreck care reformEmily KenwayMany fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on boardEmily Kenway is the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve ItTue 4 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTShareLisa*has used her local glazier so many times that he gives her a discount. For months, when care workers arrived at her mum’s home, they would find the front door locked and the elderly woman – who has dementia – resolute in her determination to bar their entry. Often, the only solution was to break the glass in the front door. When I met Lisa, who was a participant in aresearch projectI ran, her mother had finally accepted help, but it had taken years of frustration and smashed glass. Unlike Lisa, Lily* never got to acceptance. After two years spent trying to persuade her elderly father to accept social care, she lied. He thinks the people who visit twice a day are nurses, legally required to dispense his dementia medication.Experiences like these are common among people caring for ageing parents. They present an uncomfortable challenge for those who, like our new prime minister, Andy Burnham, wish tofix our care system. Many people are like Lisa and Lily: they are providing eldercare notbecause of the lack of social care, but because their ageing relatives will not accept external help, or at least not without a years-long fight.Numerousstudies have shownthat people with dementia are prone to refuse medical and wider forms of care. More broadly, we know that people’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change: what your loved one thinks they’ll want in the future isn’t necessarily what they’ll accept when that future comes. There is a lag between ageing parents developing care needs and accepting external forms of help, and it’s in that lag that family members step in. There isn’t enough formal evidence of this problem – too few studies askwhypeople receive the type of care they do, rather than assume it’s due to absent alternatives. But in one of the few studies to pose this question, published in theJournal of Nursing Managementin 2007, “frail older people” attributed their reluctance to their fear of losing independence, and the humiliation and embarrassment they felt at the idea of being deemed needy.It is an understandable fear. In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence. You only need to look around at the paltry nods to accessibility in our public spaces or thedegrading assessmentsof people seeking to claim disability benefits. For people who have lived their lives independently and able-bodied, the slip into dependency can be hard to accept. This is why Lily’s father finds nurses more tolerable than care workers: he doesn’t want to needcare,butmedicine– with its connotations of formalisation and expertise – is more acceptable. My mother was the same; after a lifetime being able-bodied, cancer took her mobility. But the notion of a rota of workers trooping into her home was unconscionable; they would be a physical affirmation of her frailty. Nobody wants to need care, so why are we assuming everyone will take it up?There are more granular reasons for refusal too. In the same research in which I worked with Lisa and Lily, Malik*, a British Muslim, explained why his family would not use external care: “It’s a cultural thing, it’s also a religious thing … responsibility for the parents just lives within the family.” Numerous reports have shown that Black and minority ethnic people areless likely to useformal services – this appears to be partly because of community norms that locate responsibility for care within the family, and also because services may lack culturally appropriate options. And lest we forget, the state is not considered a friend by all: past experiences of discrimination may reduce the uptake of services.Last year, I raised this issue at an event packed with thinktankers and policy advisers working to fix our care system. In response, an attender asked, “What’s the risk of saying this?” She meant that talking about refusal of social care risks undermining the political case for its improvement. We may inadvertently strengthen rightwing arguments that care is a familial concern (by which they mean female family members should do it all for free), rather than something to be funded by government. In contrast, the political left locates care as a state responsibility, transferring it into the paid labour market (albeit still usually performed by women, for almost-free).My heart sank as the people around her concurred – the prevailing feeling in the room was that good progressives should not talk about this problem in case we undermine long-fought campaigns to make social care a political priority. And, of course, many thousands of peopleareabsolutely desperate for adult social care – according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services,at least 400,000 peopleare on waiting lists in England alone. But I saw in my mind the innumerable family carers I have met like Lisa, Lily and Malik. I saw the carers’ groups in which people have talked of their loved ones’ refusals. What does it mean if we allow political discomfort to get in the way of truth? And the truth of eldercare is that ageing parents will often refuse support even when they need it, at least for a while.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOur culture fears getting older. But there is a different way to think about the passing of time | Kelley SwainRead moreThere is some evidence that improving social care is actually part of the solution to its refusal: a studyexamining preferencesin countries in the OECD found that “older adults in countries with greater national expenditure on old age support … showed a stronger preference for formal care”. Nobody wants to deal with bad service, and social care is no different. This bodes well, but alone it will not be enough. We need to undo people’s view of dependency as a source of shame. This requires a culture shift. I don’t know how we achieve it, but centring the principles of the disability justice movement is a good place to start. This movement has worked indefatigably to show that people are worthy beyond their productivity, and that interdependence is a fundamental of existence rather than a personal failing. Too few of us have imbibed this wisdom, and the consequences are being played out in households everywhere; we must change that for future generations.Culture change takes time, time in which thousands of people like Lisa will continue to struggle with their ageing relatives’ refusals of support. Any realistic package of reforms must acknowledge this situation, providing improved rights and resources for family carers alongside reforms to social care. Time will tell if the government will face this reality, or whether some things remain too inconvenient to acknowledge.Emily Kenway is a social policy doctoral researcher at the University of Edinburgh and the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve It*All names have been changedExplore more on these topicsCarersOpinionCare workersSocial careAgeingcommentShareReuse this content
