title: The hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia Tait | The Guardian
description: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Author: Amelia Tait
Headline: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onWeddingsThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your weddingAmelia TaitSure, it’s about jealousy, infidelity and paranoia, but the Killers’ biggest hit is a dancefloor banger: any marriage that starts without it is guaranteed to end in divorceTue 4 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareI’ve been to two weddings where the bride and groom refused to play theKillers’ pop-rock hit Mr Brightside, and both ended in divorce. Well, not yet or anything – but I’m sure it’s coming. How happy can a couple really be if they’re not willing to play the biggest banger to ever bang moments after their hearts have been bound together as one? There are some things that should never be missing from a wedding unless you outright detest your guests. Canapes, yes. Cake, sure. And the opportunity to scream, “Comin’ out of my cage and I’ve been doin’ just fine” next to someone’s Auntie Debs? Undoubtedly.Why should a song about jealousy, paranoia and infidelity pump through the speakers on your special day? Because everyone knows it. Mr Brightside is thethird most sold and streamedsong in the UK, and it’s the longest-charting single in this country’s history, even though the Killers are (somehow) American. Unlike much else these days, the track transcends borders. In 2025, YouGov asked more than 1,000 Americans which songs they knew all the words to, and Mr Brightside came in15th place. The songs above it included The Star-Spangled Banner, Happy Birthday and Jingle Bells.Four years ago, my husband and I fought over our wedding playlist because he (I possibly unfairly believed) wanted to look cool and cultured, and I wanted to serve up a cheeseboard of belter after belter. In the end, our elderly Sicilian DJ forged his own path, playing The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air theme tune twice in quick succession, to my husband’s consternation and my utter delight. Was that DJ simply confused by our shared language barrier?No. He knew something, I think, that so many couples refuse to accept: your wedding playlist is not about you. Your wedding day is, sure. The dress, the venue, the food, the poems – they can all be a careful curation of your tastes. But the playlist belongs to the people. And the people demand to dance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Killers’ Mr Brightside becomes biggest song to never reach UK No 1Read moreDancing Queen. Come On Eileen. Jolene. Many failsafe wedding staples unite the generations by ending in an emotive “een”. But another way to be sure a song will set fire to the dancefloor is to ask yourself a very simple question: can my guests do a series of impassioned hand gestures as they scream-sing? Mr Brightside encourages listeners to not only touch their chests, but also take a drag of a phantom cigarette. The song allows us to bring a little finger-and-thumb-shaped phone to our earstwice– once to call an imaginary cab and once to answer the phone to destiny.This, in the end, is all that most of us come to a wedding to do. And as the track comes to a close, we can heed its final call to open up our eager eyes. Because in that moment, we’re all Mr Brightside.Amelia Tait is a freelance features writer and the author of Lily Tripp: Diary of an Accidental Time TravellerExplore more on these topicsWeddingsThe hill I will die onThe KillersPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left  | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Migrants being escorted in Ceuta, Spain, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenMigrants being escorted in Ceuta, Spain, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersOpinionMigrationCeuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the leftJonathan LiewIt was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment tooTue 4 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.07 EDTShareThe live streams are still running, training their cameras on the beach at Ceuta, where nothing is happening. The self-styled citizen journalists are still pounding the streets, capturing their shaky smartphone footage.Zia Yusufof Reform UK was out there at the weekend, wearing a crisp white shirt and smart tailored trousers, lest anyone confuse him with the other brown people there. The bad brown people.Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world? How did it manage to pique the interest ofDonald Trump and Elon Musk, to feature on NBC’s Nightly News, not – shall we say – a programme massively predisposed to spotlighting news stories from continental Africa? What about it so exercised Europe’s heads of government? What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph?Certainly not any kind of urgent or imminent threat to our own borders, much less the borders of the United States. The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla operate under special exemptions from the Schengen area, rendering it almost impossible for an undocumented migrant to reach mainlandSpain, about 12 miles away across the Mediterranean. Once many of the migrants realised this, they duly left.Nor any kind of humanitarian concern for those who drowned or were killed in the crowd crush. “About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day. Still, the sudden influx created a crisis for Spain’s pro-immigration government. Nearly three dozen died.” So read aNew York Times subheadingon Friday. And once you fight your way past the tortured syntax, did you notice anything unusual there? First the integrity of the border, then the political ramifications, then the people who died: the hierarchy of rightwing immigration discourse expressed in three perfect sentences. The death toll has since risen toeither 72 or 88– authorities disagree on the number – and nobody seems over-fussed either way.Rather, Ceuta functions as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies. If the historian Mike Davis once described the US-Mexico border wall as“a political stage set”, then in the age of the deepfake and the troll-farm, Ceuta has proved a similarly fertile source of content: the border interface reimagined as digital theatre, mass migration as primetime television.View image in fullscreenMigrants who entered the Spanish enclave by swimming or on foot from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Reduan/EPAThe rich irony here is that from a securitisation standpoint, Ceuta functions almost exactly as it was intended. A six metre-high barbed-wire fence, reinforced by watchtowers and a network of video cameras, separates it fromMorocco. From Ceuta, an internal checkpoint guards the only ferry route to mainland Spain. The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management.None of which seemed to matter in the slightest as European leaders queued up to give the Pedro Sánchez government a ritual horse-whipping. Italyreintroduced air and sea border controlswith Spain. Emmanuel Macrondeployed mobile unitsto the Spanish border to strengthen controls. Giorgia Meloni – backed by Finland, Denmark and Czechia – has argued that Spain’s membership of the Schengen areashould be suspended.And of course these are primarily domestic politicians catering to a domestic market, ahead of an electoral cycle in which incumbents in France, Italy and Poland are being outflanked by nativist insurgents to their right. Sánchez himself faces the ballot box in 2027, an election in which his government can boast strong economic growth and which his rightwing opponents will therefore be desperate to turn into a referendum on immigration.So that’s the political angle. But really the spectacle of Ceuta represents a more primal and guttural need, particularly in the English-speaking world, for the inflammatory anti-immigration crusade to beseenas well as spoken. The photos and footage coming out of the enclave in recent days, all shot from distance and almost never in closeup, are all geared towards a single end: to encourage the viewer to see these brown bodies as a single mass, each indistinguishable from the other, the accountants and surgeons from the bomb-makers and rapists, the living from the dead.And so, by small degrees, the line between nationalism and pure-blood white supremacy blurs a little more. Indeed, the very idea that a single border crossing 1,000 miles and two seas away from us is somehow our urgent problem, only really makes sense in a worldview whose real distinction is not between “Britain” and “abroad” but between an imagined white ChristianEuropeand a savage brown other.For all this, the right does not act alone. The palpable relief on many parts of the left as most of the original 60,000 migrants returned to Morocco spoke of a worrying acquiescence: a tacit acceptance of the dangerous trope of migration as a prima facie problem. Here’s a radical thought: what if migration is only a problem to those who want it to be? What if we started seeing the mass movement of people less as an existential threat and more as a simple inevitability of human existence? Nine years ago the great Gary Younge set out in the Guardiana utopian vision of open bordersand no immigration controls. What happened to that sense of vision and idealism? When did border discourse, the conversation on why and how we move, become something to be feared and not embraced?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen saysRead moreWhether Ceuta was an accidental security lapse or a deliberately engineered event is actually beside the point. The point is that as the global right grows in confidence, as the migration industrial complex thirsts for new content, new border porn, there will be more Ceutas in the future. People will keep migrating and die trying, and because this is good telly it will keep happening. “Today more than ever,” writes the sociologist Mimi Sheller in her bookMobility Justice, “these borderlands are soaked in the blood of white nationalism, ethnic profiling, and enforced death in the no man’s land.”The endgame here is massacres, vigilante violence, not “stop the boats” but shoot the boats, the border reimagined as a computer-game war zone. The endgame is what the likes of Musk and his far-right meat puppets are already depicting: a world where zombie armies of “military-age males” invade our virgin turf, and the problem is not the forces that drove them from their homes, but your“suicidal empathy”, because these are not equal humans deserving equal treatment. These are the stakes. And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: Even in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help them, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Schoolgirls read the Qur’an inside a traditional classroom in Salihan, Kandahar, 8 July 2026.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSchoolgirls read the Qur’an inside a traditional classroom in Salihan, Kandahar, 8 July 2026.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAfghanistanAfter five brutal years of Taliban rule, Afghan women and girls need our help – and I have a planGordon BrownEven in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help themTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTShareNext weekmarks the fifth anniversary of the takeover of Afghanistan by the Taliban asUS coalition troops were evacuatedfrom the country. That’s five years for the terrorists to have consolidated their grip, so now is a good time to reflect on what the “coalition of the willing” left behind.Through vindictive edict after edict, these five years have broughtan ever-escalating repression of Afghan girls and women– with far too little done by any outside authority to speak up or stand up against the most egregious denial of girls’ rights in the world today.Barely reported was the shocking massacre in June by troops whofired on a group of women’s rights protestersas they demonstrated against girls’ exclusion from education and the enforcement of strict dress codes. They were marching under the banner “Azadi”, meaning “freedom”. Two people, including a young boy,were shot deadand several were injured.In the most medieval of ways, the Taliban are also imposing even harsher lawsto legitimise child marriageand provide legal exemption for domestic violence perpetrated by husbands, including against school-age girls.‘When she turns eight they will take her’: rising number of Afghan girls being sold into child marriageRead moreAccording to UN observers, these girls, often sold into marriage or forced to become child brides, are victims of a new form of crime:gender apartheid. Historians will look back and ask why it is that, after landing more than 1 million coalition troops, suffering more than3,500 deaths and 23,000 injuriesand spendingin excess of $1tn, we have been unable to prevent the Taliban destroying the most basic of rights. But perhaps more important, and with the Taliban entrenched in Kabul and religious leaders regularly sending out instructions from Kandahar, the question for now is: what can we do immediately to improve the lives of girls and women?Can we help them fulfil their potential? Globally, the proportion of women aged 20-24 who were married before 18 hasdeclined over the past decade, and Unicef suggestsat least 25m child marriagesthat could have involved school-age brides have been prevented. Yet an estimated12 million girlsunder 18 are still married off each year when they could be at school.The issue is acute in the Afghanistan the coalition left behind, where girls are banned from secondary schooling and Afghan women are bannedfrom university, public sector employment and even workwith NGOsand charities. They are forbidden to travel or to enter many public places, from parks to restaurants, unless accompanied. And with the Taliban confident that they can act with impunity, a dozen recent anti-girl, anti-women injunctions are tightening their grip. In one recent case, a 15-year-old Afghan girl isreported to have been killed, along with her mother, by a Taliban official after he tried to abduct her for a forced marriage.It is appalling, and it does speak to the particular brutality of the Taliban. Pakistan’s Sindh province, by contrast,has enactedone of the strongest legal frameworks in the developing world against child marriage, criminalising marriage under 18 and introducing penalties for those who facilitate it.Bangladesh, too,has enacted new laws. A stronger birth registration system has made it harder to conceal a girl’s age, closing off a common pathway into early marriage. At the same time, programmes providing small-scale financial support to poor families have enabled girls to remain in education. Save the Children reports that inone programme in Bangladesh, the offer of financial support helped more than 1,000 girls stay in school and avoid early marriage. Child marriage is not simply a cultural practice, as often portrayed. It is also driven by poverty, as much as weak enforcement of the law.View image in fullscreenGirls studying in a secret school at an undisclosed location in Afghanistan.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesThere are “child marriage-free zones” in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, where young people come together to support any school friend who is being married off against her will. Young people become known as“wedding busters”because of their willingness to intervene. With assistance and will, so much is possible.It is no accident that the Taliban have focused so much attention not just on denying women rights but specifically on denying them an education, because they know, as we do, that schooling is the most potent enabler. Across the world, it is the single most powerful protection against early marriage. Organisations such asGirls Not Brideshave established that every additional year a girl spends in secondary education significantly reduces the likelihood that she will be married as a child.If we could open the doors to quality schooling, ensure girls had access to safe spaces and provide financial support for their families, tens of thousands more could get that education. Even in Afghanistan, that is no pipe dream. Through Unicef andEducation Cannot Wait, and with secret, on-the-ground support, girls are learning in unconventional ways: often online, sometimes in underground schools or in family homes, unseen by the authorities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Nobody is coming to help us’: Afghan teenage girls on life without schoolRead moreBut there is so much more to be done, not least because thousands of girls have had to leave the country to obtain schooling, and with tension rising betweenAfghanistanand Pakistan, one favoured route out of the country is fast closing.Britain’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced that under the newimmigration and asylum bill, there will be two routes under a refugee resettlement scheme for students that could help girls get the education they have been denied. The first is through recognised charities sponsoring girls coming to the UK. The second is through colleges and universities offering scholarships.That’s good, but we must go further. I believe a fund must now be set up in support of Afghan girls who are threatened with being married off against their will. It should offer them bursaries to continue their education, if necessary outside their home country. And as UN special envoy for education, I am happy to work with any charity or educational institution that wants to assist girls in defence of their human rights.It may be a small gesture, but five years after they were condemned toTalibanrule, isn’t it time to truly support all the girls who risk their freedom and their lives for an education, and the hope of a meaningful existence? They yearn for things we take for granted. It is our moral duty to help them.Gordon Brown is the UN’s special envoy for global education and was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010The future starts with us:Gordon Brown in conversationOn Thursday 10 September, join Hugh Muir and Gordon Brown to discuss the intricate connections between global instability and civic decline, aas explored in Brown’s new book, The Future Starts With UsBook ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsAfghanistanOpinionTalibanChild marriageViolence against women and girlsWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: With Russia at the door and the US backing away, Europe has to build its own ‘way of war’ | Nathalie Tocci | The Guardian
description: Even in a Europe-focused Nato 3.0, Washington would still want to call the shots. We need an insurance policy, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Author: Nathalie Tocci
Headline: Even in a Europe-focused Nato 3.0, Washington would still want to call the shots. We need an insurance policy, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Content: US troops prepare combat vehicles before deploying to Romania on 9 February 2022 in Vilseck, Germany.Photograph: Alexandra Beier/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS troops prepare combat vehicles before deploying to Romania on 9 February 2022 in Vilseck, Germany.Photograph: Alexandra Beier/Getty ImagesOpinionNatoWith Russia at the door and the US backing away, Europe has to build its own ‘way of war’Nathalie TocciEven in a Europe-focused Nato 3.0, Washington would still want to call the shots. We need an insurance policyTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.31 EDTShareHow can Europe defend itself againstRussiawithout the US, or with much less of it? This question sums up the existential challenge now facing the continent.Russia’s imperial ambitions start with Ukraine, but they don’t end there. Moscow’shybrid attacks, its political interference in support of Russia-friendly parties and its military sabre-rattling – including awarship’s live-fire exercise45 miles off the UK coast – all point in the same direction. A kinetic war to defend ourselves against Russia in the coming months or years cannot be ruled out. This is why European defence budgets are rising across Europe, especially in countries closer to the frontline.Defence spending has accelerated since Donald Trump returned to office. This is less because of Trump’s jibes and insults – nowextending even to far-right European leaderslike Giorgia Meloni – and more that Europeans are waking up to the reality that in the event of a war against Russia, the US may not be there for them. While the US nuclear umbrella could hold – although France has launched an initiativeto Europeanise its nuclear deterrentin case it does not – European governments and institutions are reckoning with the possibility that they might need to fight Russia without US conventional forces’ support or with much less of it.This explains the emergence of something that is unofficially being called Nato 3.0. At the Ankara Nato summit a few weeks ago, the initiative was pompously talked up – in part to placate Trump, in part to signal to Vladimir Putin that even if the US takes a back seat, a Europeanised Nato remains credible. The slogan that its supporters use, “A strongerEuropein a stronger Nato”, is misleading. Yes, Europeans will become militarily stronger, but as the US partly disengages, Nato overall will weaken. Working towards a Europeanised Nato is still sensible: even if the alliance weakens in absolute terms, it may still be strong enough to stand up to an encroaching Russia.But here’s why we need to be cautious and work on alternatives at the same time. Take a worst-case scenario in which Russia attacked a European Nato country in the coming months or years. That country’s European Nato allies would probably come to the rescue. Eastern and northern European countries would stand by each other, of course. Even Germany has arguably made the cultural and psychological leap of acknowledging that its troops may have to fight the Russians again. Its plans to permanently station a5,000-strong brigade in Lithuaniais a signal.If Germany were to respond, France and the UK would very likely come in too. And if these core countries stepped in, Italy and Spain would follow suit. The good news is that Europeans would probably remain united. But the bad news is that the US might not answer the call to defend Europe – and this in turn would instantly break Nato. The core pledge of the alliance’s founding treaty,article 5, says that an attack on one Nato state is an attack on all. The nature of the rupture would be the same whether it came from an explicit triggering of article 5 to which the US did not respond, or from article 5 never being triggered in anticipation of that very outcome.A second, less catastrophic scenario is one in which there is no Russian provocation,Nato3.0 moves forward in earnest, and in a few years’ time the alliance looks radically different to how it looks today, with the Europeans – along with Turkey and Canada – shouldering the lion’s share of the burden. But if non-US allies shoulder the bulk of the responsibilities, they will want the bulk of the rights. Europe’s defence markets would become less open to US companies, and Nato’s priorities would start reflecting European interests. Europeans would certainly not be happy to let the US call the shots indefinitely while they merely carry out orders. But it is hard to imagine any US administration, let alone one with Trump at the helm, happily giving up these rights and benefits.Since its inception in 1949, Nato has been organised around US capabilities, technologies and strategic culture. Europeans have been integrated into a US command structure and have adopted the US way of war. They lack the capabilities, manpower and command structures available to the US. If they had to deal with armed aggression in the near term they could not replicate Nato’s model. One way or another they would develop alternatives – but with the US still formally in Nato, albeit less committed to it, this could not happen within the alliance itself.None of the alternatives is ideal. The EU does important work on defence industry cooperation and even has amutual assistance clauseenshrined in its treaties, but due to a range of constitutional and political constraints, I don’t believe it constitutes a feasible path forward to defence.This leaves so-called coalitions of the willing – an idea with a problematic history that is now being resurrected. The US has led previous coalitions of the willing when it wanted to bypass formal multilateral structures like the UN. The most infamous example is the US-led coalition that invaded Iraq in 2003, without UN security council authorisation and in blatant violation of international law.Today, coalitions of the willing have formed around critical security flashpoints – including Ukraine, Greenland and the strait of Hormuz. As in the past, their establishment is driven by the fact that existing organisations – the UN, Nato and the EU – have proven unable to deal effectively with these challenges on their own. Interestingly, this time, rather than being US-led and aimed at bypassing international law, they are European-led, bypass Washington, and are aimed precisely at affirming collective European action on key security issues in compliance with international law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCoalitions of the willing, however, are ad hoc and ephemeral, lacking both a system for political strategic decision-making and an operational chain of command. While participating states’ militaries are now meeting regularly to develop joint plans, these coalitions still lack the permanence needed to structurally build a European way of war, ensure its consistent adherence to international law, and to convey a real sense of confidence in the public. Institutionalising such coalitions at political level will be critical. One option would be through a European security council, an idea that was born in the wake of Brexit to keep the UK involved in European security decisions. It isbeing resurrected nowprecisely to devise ways for Europeans to address the continent’s security.None of this should de-prioritise the Europeanising of Nato – but coalitions of the willing could be a critical insurance policy, should Nato 3.0 falter and fail.Nathalie Tocci is a GuardianEuropecolumnistExplore more on these topicsNatoOpinionEuropeRussiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Liberated from its ludicrous libretto: how the magnificence of Oberon can be properly heard at last | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Full of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brilliance
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Full of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brilliance
Content: Blowing the dust off the original … Jennifer Davis as Reiza and Rachael Wilson as Fatima in rehearsals for Oberon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBlowing the dust off the original … Jennifer Davis as Reiza and Rachael Wilson as Fatima in rehearsals for Oberon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianClassical musicLiberated from its ludicrous libretto: how the magnificence of Oberon can be properly heard at lastFull of panache and originality, Weber’s grand opera is the work of a composer at the height of his powers – but its plot is a load of nonsense. The conductor of its Proms premiere celebrates its brillianceMark ElderTue 4 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarl Maria von Weber was a great opera composer with a minimal ability to find the right libretto writers. He never made a good choice in any of the three pieces for which he’s still known.View image in fullscreenCarl Maria von Weber, by Caroline BarduaOberon was his final work. He wrote it in London 200 years ago for Covent Garden theatre and died of tuberculosis shortly after its premiere in 1826, aged only 39. He was buried in the cemetery just north of the Barbican, although his grave today is in Dresden. Some 18 years after his death, Wagner – who adored, and was inspired by, the older composer (there could not have been Lohengrin without Weber’s earlier opera Euryanthe) – raised the money to repatriate his body. A large crowd met the coach at the gates of Dresden and processed through the rain to the city’s old Catholic cemetery where a second funeral was held and Wagner’s specially composed fantasia for wind band based on themes from Euryanthe was performed.German audiences did not doubt Weber’s worth, but only in the past few years have Weber’s three great operas – Der Freischütz, Euryanthe and Oberon – begun to be treasured more widely. I conductedEuryanthe at Glyndebournein 2002 and loved every minute. It’s the most wonderful piece of dramatic music, saddled with a terrible libretto. Der Freischütz was a sensation on its Berlin premiere in 1821: Weber had written a new kind of German national romantic opera, an everyday story of country folk (with apologies to the Archers) but it’s hard to get a staging right today and it is little performed outside Germany – everybody just laughs at the plot’s daft mix of supernatural and silly. Yet its music is exuberantly inventive, full of colour and beauty, and – as with Weber’s other two grand operas – deserves to be heard.View image in fullscreen‘Wonderful dramatic music, saddled with a terrible libretto’: Clive Bayley in Glyndebourne’s 2002 staging of Weber’s Euryanthe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOberon’s libretto is best described as a phantasmagoria. It’s by James Robinson Planché, a prolific commercial dramatist who wrote well over 100 theatre shows involving exuberant opulence and fantastical stories. The work’s sprawling tale of fairyland, desert islands, pirates, crusaders and an imaginary Arabia would have been completely acceptable in the 1820s, but now seems very far away. There are elements of Mozart’s Magic Flute (two couples, trials, magic) and James Bond movies (escapism, effortless flitting between exotic locations), while Ivor Novello is a useful comparison point. Novello’s musicals are full of wonderful tunes. However, the shows themselves – King’s Rhapsody, Glamorous Night and such like – are wild extravaganzas that haven’t aged well.To stage, or even semi-stage Oberon, its text needs to be rewritten, and for our Proms performance, author Timothy Knapman has created a new single narrative that respects the original but blows the dust off it. His witty version, narrated byTamsin Greig, will entertain today’s audiences just as Londoners were entertained in 1826.The music needs not a jot of revision: it has an immediacy and daring that still startles. Full of panache and confidence, this is the work of a showman at the top of his powers. Weber’s heart lay in the theatre and he understood how to write for it.From the first notes ofthe overtureyou know you’re in the hands of a master. It begins with stillness and a sense of something coming. Perhaps we’re in a forest on a summer afternoon. The harmony is gentle and serene, leading us into a dreamy world where anything can happen. There are three notes, long-short-long, on a horn. These, we later learn, are the call Oberon gives to one of his mortal charges: if you’re in trouble, blast those three notes and I will save you. And then, suddenly, some manic fairy energy breaks in and you don’t quite know what’s hit you. You hear lots of different characters and tunes; it’s brilliant and fast.double quotation markOberon’s music is full of panache and confidence: the work of a showman at the top of his powers.Nobody had really done anything quite like this before. Mendelssohn had that same lightness of spirit in his A Midsummer Night’s Dream concert overture, written in the same year as Oberon.The period instruments of theOrchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, with the players so expert in this kind of repertoire, will bring a suitable litheness. There might be three trombones but the sound has to be lively, not ever fat. Weber’s orchestral palette is full of colours and reflects the characters on stage and the different settings; he writes particularly beautifully for woodwind. You can almost feel him thinking:“Ah, this moment has got a bit of melancholy … we need to make sure this is clear. Let’s bring the clarinet in as well as the strings, to give another yearning quality.”View image in fullscreenMark Elder rehearses with John Findon (Sir Huon of Bordeaux) and Jennifer Davis (Reiza) and the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe overture aside, the act one finale is also a great favourite of mine. It’s a substantial piece in different sections. We’re just getting to know Reiza, the heroine. She has been told in a dream that Sir Huon will rescue her from a forced marriage, and she calls out to him, saying please don’t delay. She and her servant Fatima sing this brilliant little duet, and then, suddenly, we hear a march that represents the harem guard closing things up for the night. There’s a tiny extra wind orchestra and percussion, which I’m going to put at the top of the stage, separate from the other musicians. This is my last chance, Reiza says, I’ve got to escape before they close the gates…Skilled in understanding the voice, Weber gives his singers amazing opportunities to shine. The leading role of Sir Huon needs an Olympic heldentenor: nimble and athletic. We’ve got John Findon, a really terrific tenor who is going to make a big impact. (And I always say it’s like Wimbledon. You have to get your first serve in when you sing this sort of music.) The chorus, the superb Monteverdi Choir, also have their work cut out – they’ve got to be fairies, elves, slaves, courtiers and even mermaids.View image in fullscreenNicky Spence (Oberon) rehearses at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianListen out too for Reiza’s showstopper aria Ocean, Thou Mighty Monster in act two. By now she and Huon have been shipwrecked on a desert island. Despairing, she spots a sail and waves like mad hoping to be rescued – but it’s pirates, who kidnap her and leave Huon tied up on the shore. Luckily, he’s still just able to sound his magic horn to summon help. (Not for nothing does Grove’s dictionary of music describe Planché’s libretto as “a picaresque farrago of nonsense”.)I have known and loved Oberon all my life – I played it as a bassoonist in a university orchestra decades ago. To be performing it is a dream come true. The music is such fun to conduct – it has an immediacy and an originality; it was made for the theatre. You can’t just beat through it, you’ve got to bring it alive.Two hundred years is a long time to wait for a Proms premiere. This might be a first for the opera, but the overture has been a festival staple, such a favourite that in 1902’s Proms concerts it was played six times! While that might be too much to hope for Oberon, if we can create a performance that’s lively, risky and full of physicality as well as beautiful music-making and so give this work the life it deserves I will be happy.As told to Imogen Tilden. Mark Elder conductsOberon at the Promsand live on BBC Radio 3 on 6 August. All Proms concerts are on BBC Sounds until 12 October.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicMark ElderProms 2026OperafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and serial killers: inside Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis’s lurid TV thriller | US television | The Guardian
description: The Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleaze
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleaze
Content: Homer Gere as Robert Mallory and Igby Rigney as Bret Ellis in The Shards.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreenHomer Gere as Robert Mallory and Igby Rigney as Bret Ellis in The Shards.Photograph: FXUS televisionSex, drugs and serial killers: inside Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis’s lurid TV thrillerThe Shards brings the cocaine-addled teens of a 1980s prep school to life with a cast of newcomers and a heavy dose of sleazeEmma MaddenTue 4 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the first thingsRyan Murphy’s TV adaptation ofBret Easton Ellis’sThe Shardswill make you ask is: where the hell are these kids’ parents? The answer is simple. This is Los Angeles in 1981, and these fabulously benumbed kids aren’t being helicopter-parented. They’re going to parties, drinking whiskey, listening toUltravox’s Viennaon repeat and doing copious amounts of cocaine. It’s a complete vision of Ellis’s dully hedonistic America.The FX series follows a character named Bret Ellis – a thinly coded version of the author – in senior year at an exclusive Los Angeles prep school whose controlled, Joan Didion-coded world begins to unravel with the arrival of enigmatic transfer student Robert Mallory. At the same time, in the post-Charles Mansonand Jeffrey Dahmer era, a serial killer known as The Trawler draws ever closer to Ellis and his increasingly paranoid circle of friends. Ellis (the real one) first released his autofictional story The Shards as a serialized podcast between 2020 and 2021 before expanding it into a novel in 2023.Gregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’Read moreOriginally, the novel seemed destined to be adapted byLuca Guadagnino. Instead, in a twist of fate (and professional conflict), Guadagnino’s more measured style gave way to Murphy’s unashamed extravagance, as he came onboard in February 2025. On paper, Murphy and Ellis might seem like opposites, but in The Shards, they find everything they have in common. Both are “obsessed with moments in their youth of hidden identities”, said Brad Simpson, The Shards’ executive producer, and both came of age in the time of Aids. “That’s affected gay artists more than most people think.“This story is about a group of young, beautiful people who are about to embark on the world, and there is a killer that hunts them. There’s an obvious metaphor to Aids in the 1980s for that,” says Simpson, speaking on Zoom along with the cast a week before the show’s release.For Murphy’s interpretation of The Shards, he assembled a combination of seasoned actors and the next wave of young Hollywood. The cast includes Kaia Gerber, returning to Murphy’s world after appearances in the American Horror Story franchise, as the reluctantly perfect Susan Reynolds. Igby Rigney, television’s future Evan Peters, plays Ellis. Meanwhile, the seven-time Tony award-winning producer Jordan Roth plays personal assistant Steven Reinhardt, a kind of Lynchian version of Andy Warhol who Murphy says he modeled around Roth. “He sent me a DM saying, ‘I have a part for you. Call me,’” says Roth.Homer Gere steps into what feels like a role poised to launch a career overnight as Robert Mallory, the irritatingly self-assured object of Ellis’s obsession. “Gen Z wants to have new stars, they want fresh faces,” explains Simpson.The cast hadn’t met before, but Gere and Gerber had certainly heard of one another. There was some air that Gere (son ofRichard) and Gerber (daughter of Cindy Crawford) felt they had to clear. Their parents were one of the defining star couples of the 90s, so when they first met two weeks before filming: “I think one of the first things we said was, ‘Should we address it?’” says Gere. They ended up laughing about it, and got the inevitable conversation out of the way before they went to set. “So it’s not like we ended up talking about it every day.”View image in fullscreenKaia Gerber as Susan, Rigney as Bret, Hayes Warner as Debbie Schaffer, Gere as Robert Mallory and Graham Campbell as Thom Wright in The Shards.Photograph: FXOne of Murphy’s main casting criteria for selecting this cast was their aspirationalism: namely, would you want to go to a party, drink whiskey and do mounds of coke with them? Probably. But also, please don’t do that. WhileLove Story, Simpson and Murphy’s previous series, helped make smoking cool again. “We regretted that,” Simpson says, laughing. He hopes this one won’t inspire kids to “have drug-fueled parties and drive quickly on the PCH”.Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’Read moreRight now, a week out from the season premiere, life is much the same for the acting newcomers. “I’m just hanging out, seeing friends, reading books,” says Gere. Upon release, that will all be turned on its head. Entering Hollywood through one of its biggest doors, the cast are suddenly staring down the possibility of overnight fame. The closest glimpse of what’s to come is seeing themselves plastered across billboards all overLos Angeles. How do you prepare for something like this? “You can’t,” says Campbell, who’s kept the blond perm that he sports as character Thom Wright, whose jock archetype devolves throughout the season.In The Shards, each of the characters is desperate to be seen, no more explicitly than Debbie Schaffer, a seethingly insecure teen played by Hayes Warner, primarily known as a musician somewhere in the vein ofAvril Lavigne. Those feelings were easy to access, she says. “I was in the music industry, and it’s so oversaturated, and there’s so much desperation to get your music out there, like, how do you get people to listen and care and hear about it?”View image in fullscreenRigney and Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXThe Shards clearly demands attention with its classic cocktail of sex, drugs and rock’n’roll, though it leans heaviest towards the drugs. Throughout filming, the cast consumed a staggering amount of “terrible cigarettes and iced tea [standing in] for whiskey”, says Campbell, who only landed his first professional role three years ago on Broadway. Then there were the cocaine re-creation experiments, as the actors went through a series of milk and coconut powders. Out of everyone, Warner’s character had by far the most coke. That first trial with coconut powder “was too sticky”, she says. Eventually, they traded it for milk powder, which Warner snorted in large quantities while reshooting her many coke-sniffing scenes. “The powder would begin to liquefy in my nose,” she says, grimacing.The Shards is billed as an erotic thriller, though it’s a surprisingly chaste entry in the genre. In the era ofHeated Rivalry, expectations have been heightened for graphic man-on-man sex, but The Shards instead thrives on tension and suspense. There’s nary a dick shot to be seen. No blowjobs and not even a measly handjob. There’s some aggressive making out, but that’s as far as it goes.“I think it’s deeply erotic, and I think it’s deeply beautiful. I think there is a lot of sex, drugs and rock’n’roll, but it’s done in a way that’s much more elevated than people are accustomed to these days,” says Campbell.View image in fullscreenRigney and Warner in The Shards.Photograph: Ray Mickshaw/FXFor the sexy scenes there are, Rigney says: “The intimacy coordinator gave us an ungodly amount of Listerine strips, and you have to watch what you eat for lunch,” although he was tempted to find out how good his fellow actors really were by “going the pickle, onion, tuna route”, he says. “But in the end, I just love them too much to do that.”Rigney plays the leading role with keenly observed physical code-switching, veering between his real (gay) and fake (straight) selves. In Ellis’s straight romances, Rigney plays the rigidity of a straight teenage boy. In his homosexual encounters, his entire body shifts. He’s suddenly sylph-like and coy, eyebrow arched, smarmy, crotch forward. Rigney said it’s not something he had to be directed to do. “That was all natural, baby.”As the next generation of actors, they’re desperately hoping for a second season. “Is the cash coming in?” Rigney pauses. “Well, what I will say is it’s amazing to have a stable job as an actor, regardless of what the income is.” He taps the wooden table next to him. “If we get a second season,” teases Simpson, “we promise there’ll be more sex.”The Shards premieres on 5 August on FX/Hulu in the US and on 6 August in the UK and Australia on Disney+Explore more on these topicsUS televisionRyan MurphyBret Easton EllisTelevisionLos AngelesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Peter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honesty | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Gill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a director
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: Gill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a director
Content: Highest standards … Peter Gill in 2008.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/the GuardianView image in fullscreenHighest standards … Peter Gill in 2008.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/the GuardianTheatrePeter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honestyGill’s dramas of divided class loyalties such as The York Realist had a clear-eyed precision matched by his rigorous work as a directorPeter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86Michael BillingtonTue 4 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Gill, who has died aged 86, was one of the unsung heroes of British theatre. As both director and playwright his work was characterised by its uncompromising honesty and unflinching integrity. Much admired by his fellow artists, he at last achieved a degree of public fame inhis annus mirabilis of 2002when his terrific playThe York Realistwon a number of awards and the Sheffield Crucible staged a month-long retrospective of his work as well as a brand-new play,Original Sin.Few remember that Gill, born into a Welsh, working class Catholic family, began life as an actor: look closely and you can spot him in the film of Zulu. But it was at London’s Royal Court, where he began work as an associate director in 1964, that he learned his craft and acquired the values that were to shape his whole career: a belief in the sanctity of text, the purity of design and a respect for actors.His first play The Sleepers Den, showing three generations of women all in bed next to each other, was a meticulous re-creation of working-class life. But it was his rediscovery of three neglected plays of DH Lawrence – A Collier’s Friday Night, The Daughter-in-Law and The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd – staged as a trilogy in 1968, that marked him out as a first-rate director: as Irving Wardle wrote, “the ordinary processes of living became not only interesting but objects of respect and something beautiful.”View image in fullscreenPeter Gill at the Royal Court theatre, London, with a photograph of George Devine on the wall.Photograph: Sarah Lee/the GuardianGill’s work as a playwright and director were ultimately inseparable because they were linked by an unsparing honesty. In Small Change (1976), he recalled the unhealed emotional scars left by an adolescent sexual relationship. In Kick for Touch (1983) he wrote with equal truth about a Welsh world of male bonding, rugby-as-religion and women as outsiders. Gill invariably directed his own work but he approached classic texts in the same rigorous, investigative spirit. One of his finest achievements was to turn a former TV studio into a performance space at the Riverside Studios in Hammersmith, London, and to stage a number of productions, including The Cherry Orchard, The Duchess of Malfi and Measure for Measure, of glittering clarity there. If the Riverside is still a going concern, it is because of Gill’s visionary enterprise.He also worked extensively at the NationalTheatre, where his many productions included a brilliantly hard-edged version of Christopher Hampton’s Tales from Hollywood and an astonishing revival of Otway’s Venice Preserv’d, where Ian McKellen, Michael Pennington and Jane Lapotaire achieved a heroic acting style that perfectly matched the tone of Otway’s verse-tragedy. Gill’s tenure as director of the National Theatre Studio, which he founded in 1984 to develop new work, ended less happily. But during his time there he tirelessly championed new writers and ensured their work reached the stages of the Royal Court and the Bush.Peter Gill: ‘Nothing happens unless the middle classes do it’Read moreIf I had to seize on one play that shows Gill as both writer and director at his best it would be The York Realist. Its involves a farm labourer, George, who has an affair with a London-based director, John, while working on a production of the York Mystery Plays in the early 1960s. It owes an obvious debt to DH Lawrence in its emotional intelligence, raw honesty and fascination with the intersection of class and sex. For John, the Yorkshire countryside has an exotic otherness of which he can never fully be a part while his lover, George, relishes the intellectual excitements of London but is wedded irrevocably to the land. It was as if much of what Gill had learned during his early years at the Court had been not just absorbed but miraculously enhanced.Gill carried on working as both dramatist and director but in later years became increasingly detached from the British theatre. Periodically my phone would ring and he would be on the line, often talking volubly for half an hour, about something that had caught his attention. He cared passionately about the theatre and his occasional gripes were dictated by his adherence to the highest standards and his belief in the sacrifice of personal ambition to the primacy of the work itself.Explore more on these topicsTheatrePeter GillRoyal Court theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content
