title: The hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia Tait | The Guardian
description: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Author: Amelia Tait
Headline: Any marriage that starts without the Killers’ biggest hit is guaranteed to end in divorce, says freelance features writer Amelia Tait
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onWeddingsThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your weddingAmelia TaitSure, it’s about jealousy, infidelity and paranoia, but the Killers’ biggest hit is a dancefloor banger: any marriage that starts without it is guaranteed to end in divorceTue 4 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareI’ve been to two weddings where the bride and groom refused to play theKillers’ pop-rock hit Mr Brightside, and both ended in divorce. Well, not yet or anything – but I’m sure it’s coming. How happy can a couple really be if they’re not willing to play the biggest banger to ever bang moments after their hearts have been bound together as one? There are some things that should never be missing from a wedding unless you outright detest your guests. Canapes, yes. Cake, sure. And the opportunity to scream, “Comin’ out of my cage and I’ve been doin’ just fine” next to someone’s Auntie Debs? Undoubtedly.Why should a song about jealousy, paranoia and infidelity pump through the speakers on your special day? Because everyone knows it. Mr Brightside is thethird most sold and streamedsong in the UK, and it’s the longest-charting single in this country’s history, even though the Killers are (somehow) American. Unlike much else these days, the track transcends borders. In 2025, YouGov asked more than 1,000 Americans which songs they knew all the words to, and Mr Brightside came in15th place. The songs above it included The Star-Spangled Banner, Happy Birthday and Jingle Bells.Four years ago, my husband and I fought over our wedding playlist because he (I possibly unfairly believed) wanted to look cool and cultured, and I wanted to serve up a cheeseboard of belter after belter. In the end, our elderly Sicilian DJ forged his own path, playing The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air theme tune twice in quick succession, to my husband’s consternation and my utter delight. Was that DJ simply confused by our shared language barrier?No. He knew something, I think, that so many couples refuse to accept: your wedding playlist is not about you. Your wedding day is, sure. The dress, the venue, the food, the poems – they can all be a careful curation of your tastes. But the playlist belongs to the people. And the people demand to dance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Killers’ Mr Brightside becomes biggest song to never reach UK No 1Read moreDancing Queen. Come On Eileen. Jolene. Many failsafe wedding staples unite the generations by ending in an emotive “een”. But another way to be sure a song will set fire to the dancefloor is to ask yourself a very simple question: can my guests do a series of impassioned hand gestures as they scream-sing? Mr Brightside encourages listeners to not only touch their chests, but also take a drag of a phantom cigarette. The song allows us to bring a little finger-and-thumb-shaped phone to our earstwice– once to call an imaginary cab and once to answer the phone to destiny.This, in the end, is all that most of us come to a wedding to do. And as the track comes to a close, we can heed its final call to open up our eager eyes. Because in that moment, we’re all Mr Brightside.Amelia Tait is a freelance features writer and the author of Lily Tripp: Diary of an Accidental Time TravellerExplore more on these topicsWeddingsThe hill I will die onThe KillersPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: No smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy Cricket | Comedy | The Guardian
description:
Having cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015
• Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Having cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015• Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80
Content: Letters from ‘Mammy’ … Jimmy Cricket performing in A Night Of 100 Stars in 1990.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLetters from ‘Mammy’ … Jimmy Cricket performing in A Night Of 100 Stars in 1990.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockComedyNo smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy CricketHaving cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80Mark LawsonTue 4 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the comedian Jimmy Cricket chose the catchphrase, “And there’s more!” he may have reflected that the words would one day have a poignant irony. As has now happened after his death, aged 80.The stage name was adopted by James Joseph Mulgrew, from Cookstown in Northern Ireland, when he worked as an entertainer at the Butlin’s and Pontins holiday camps from the 1960s at a time when these summer resort venues were an academy for UK entertainers.Both Jimmy and Jiminy Cricket were rooted in polite euphemisms for the expletive “Jesus Christ!”, but Mulgrew, a committed churchgoer and carefully clean comic, is unlikely to have been motivated by the oath. Whether deliberately or by luck, his chosen pseudonym was likely to pique the interest of fans of Disney’s Pinocchio(in which Jiminy Cricket is a key character), those interested in orthopteran insects in general and lovers of the greatest summer game. The Irish climate and distraction of more historically Irish sports might have restricted the resonance of that reference back home but it proved useful to schedulers in Britain. Jimmy’s Cricket Team was the title of his successful BBC Radio 2 series from 1990, making the return to wireless writing of Morecambe & Wise’s greatest writer, Eddie Braben.View image in fullscreenSuited and Wellington booted … Cricket in And There’s More in 1985.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockAt that time, BBC Radio was tapping into the peak of Mulgrew’s public popularity, encouraged by his biggest television visibility, from 1985-88, on an ITV show titled after his catchphrase, And There’s More. The words perfectly suited a show featuring short sketches, songs and standup. Fronted by Mulgrew as Cricket, the 24 episodes included regular appearances by comedy actors Nicholas Smith (Are You Being Served?) and Joan Sims (Carry On) and guest slots for Hazel O’Connor, singing, and Rory Bremner, impersonating.As Cricket, he wore a stage costume of too-short formal trousers (possibly a homage to the similarly attired Max Wall), funny hats and Wellingtons on the wrong foot. That – alongside the somewhat silly professional moniker – led some wrongly to assume that he was a children’s entertainer.It was not, though, entirely misleading. He aimed at adults the sort of material that classified him as what used to be called a “family entertainer” – no smut, no swearing and little songs in which his retained native accent allowed him to rhyme “faffing” with “laughing”.The purity and implied puritanism of his comedy was perhaps rooted in a Roman Catholic upbringing in Northern Ireland in the 1950s, a creed and era noted for their censoriousness. The lasting impact of his upbringing was also evident in many references in his routines to letters from his “Mammy”. Though uncontroversial at the time, one aspect of the act – many gags relating to “Irish logic” – might now be regarded as offensive, although, in common with Jewish comedians, Mulgrew would have claimed a birthright to explore stereotypes within his own tribe.Though the hold of the faith diminished for many of his Ulster generation, Mulgrew remained practising, receiving in 2015 a papal knighthood, Catholicism’s highest honour, from Pope Francis. The citation mentioned the recipient’s charitable work; although the Argentinian pontiff was something of a joker himself, the honour is unlikely to have been for comedy. (Mulvey’s Northern Irish peer, Frank Carson, though rather less scrupulously clean mouthed, had received the same honour from Pope John Paul II, creating an intriguing trend among Northern Irish jokers of that generation.)The highest profile period of Mulgrew/Cricket’s career overlapped with the so-called Troubles in Northern Ireland, its associated atrocities often featuring in the headlines of news bulletins abutting his TV and radio appearances. The performer, though, was wary of sectarianism – holiday camp performers largely targeted those unlikely to be paying customers – and, in turn, didn’t suffer much bigotry, although, as with Carson, few impressionists could resist a go at the Ulster brogue.“Always let your conscience be your guide,” sings Jiminy Cricket in Pinocchio and that was the credo of his near namesake during a career in which he aimed to provide unthreatening fun – and succeeded.Explore more on these topicsComedyTV comedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A pressing issue: why are vinyl albums becoming so different from their digital versions? | Vinyl | The Guardian
description: They’re expensive, elaborate – and may not contain all the music. After Olivia Rodrigo, Charli xcx and more sent out incomplete or unfinished vinyl versions, fans are feeling shortchanged
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: They’re expensive, elaborate – and may not contain all the music. After Olivia Rodrigo, Charli xcx and more sent out incomplete or unfinished vinyl versions, fans are feeling shortchanged
Content: Charli xcx and Olivia Rodrigo, who have each put out vinyl editions that differ from digital ones.Composite: Harley Weir/PA, PRView image in fullscreenCharli xcx and Olivia Rodrigo, who have each put out vinyl editions that differ from digital ones.Composite: Harley Weir/PA, PRVinylA pressing issue: why are vinyl albums becoming so different from their digital versions?They’re expensive, elaborate – and may not contain all the music. After Olivia Rodrigo, Charli xcx and more sent out incomplete or unfinished vinyl versions, fans are feeling shortchangedAdam BenzineTue 4 Aug 2026 05.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was one of the most anticipated collaborations of the year: Charli xcx teaming up with film-maker David Cronenberg for No One Lasts Forever, the closing track on her new albumMusic, Fashion, Film, which debuted at No 1 in the UK.But for fans who pre-ordered what was advertised as the “full-length” album on vinyl, an unwelcome surprise awaits. The song doesn’t contain the spoken-word contribution from Cronenberg – an astonishing reflection on art, death and eternity – that is included on streaming platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music.The collaboration, praised by Variety as“the heart of what the album is really about”, apparently missed the vinyl deadline. “It was at a point where we had to deliver the vinyl audio [and] we didn’t get David in time,” Charli told the Tape Notes podcast, adding: “There’s actually a different version of the song on the vinyl, which we haven’t really spoken about yet.”double quotation markArtists and labels owe it to fans to communicate these differences upfrontAnimesh Khare, a 27-year-old fan from Paris, was among those disappointed by the decision. “Learning that the vinyl version isn’t the complete record definitely makes me hesitate to purchase it,” he says. “Artists and labels owe it to fans to communicate these differences upfront so people can make informed decisions before dropping money on physical media. It’s just a matter of respect and transparency.”Charli xcx isn’t the only offender. Fans who pre-ordered Olivia Rodrigo’s third albumYou Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Lovedocumentedunexpected editsacross half a dozen tracks on the album’s vinyl editions, including missing bridges, outros and other musical passages. Meanwhile, fans discovered vinyl copies of Raye’s second album didn’t contain its final mix:This Album May Contain Hope, the title promised, but maybe not the finished songs. In response, Raye said: “I really apologise … the digital versions of some of these songs, some are quite different. And you just need to embrace that because I tried my best.”View image in fullscreenThis album may contain an earlier mix … Raye.Photograph: Aliyah OtchereIt’s the year’s worst pop trend: fans paying the highest price to pre-order what is ostensibly the most desirable, collectible or elaborate edition of an album are instead receiving incomplete or unpolished versions of the music.In Raye’s case, the singer tried to offer a positive spin, joking to Zane Lowe that the almost-finished vinyl could become a collectible. But cash-strapped fans aren’t seeing the funny side. “It’s fair to assume when you’re buying a record that it’s the final recording,” wroteone person on Reddit, in a comment typical of dozens posted to the site. “I ride for Charli, I love her as an artist, but a bait-and-switch isn’t cool.”Elsewhere, the first pressing of the Weeknd’sHurry Up Tomorrowcontained only 11 of the 22 tracks on the digital version, and also featured shorter or earlier mixes, different transitions and missing guest contributions; it was followed by a “complete edition” double-vinyl release. The first vinyl pressings of Beyoncé’sCowboy Carterwere missing five songs that were released in the digital version, causing dismay among fans – she did not respond to requests for comment at the time – while other albums, such as Nicki Minaj’sPink Friday 2and Lil Wayne’s Tha Carter VI, are pressed to vinyl in much shorter editions than their digital versions, possibly to avoid costly double or triple vinyl editions.View image in fullscreenRodrigo with a limited-edition Lego version of her latest record.Photograph: The Lego Group/Hunter Simmons/PAAnother reason is that vinyl plants need to receive audio masters and artwork at least six weeks before a planned release date, with elaborate packaging or multiple variants requiring extra. “The more complicated the package, the more time it’ll take to manufacture,” explains Ben Savage, manager of Birkenhead-based retailer and indie label Skeleton Records, “especially if there are box sets involved”. Spotify, by contrast, needs just five business days to process digital files.In the case of Rodrigo, her June chart-topper was released in at least a dozen different vinyl configurations, including signed copies, picture discs, editions with lenticular artwork, alternative covers, retailer exclusives, pop-up book editions and a veritable rainbow of coloured pressings.But all feature shorter versions of songs such as Honeybee, Maggots for Brains and The Cure – the last of which, for example, loses its romantic violin outro. The cuts are so widespread that fans at first assumed their copies had been mispressed. Rodrigo’s label and publicists did not respond to requests for an explanation, but the singerlet slipthat album closer Cigarette Smoke was written only a week before she had to “turn everything in for the vinyl”.It’s a revealing turn of phrase: the physical campaign may no longer be simply packaging a completed album. The manufacturing timetable may be intruding into the creative process itself: one deadline to get some version of the album on to wax, and another to finesse the final mix for the streaming release. If that’s the case, should artists make it clearer to fans that they might receive a vinyl copy that is different to a digital release?‘This is so creepy!’: the Taylor Swift vinyl haunted by Britain’s weirdest musiciansRead moreOne Rodrigo fan said they weretoldby the singer’s online store that the vinyl “was received as intended” and denied a refund. And unlikeaccidental mispressings, which sometimes become valuable because only a handful escape the factory, these early editions are intentionally manufactured in large quantities – often tens of thousands. They may still appeal to collectors, but are unlikely to command the kinds of prices associated with genuine misprints.The combination of variant saturation and fan Fomo has been a boon for labels, helping drive UK vinyl sales to 7.6m LPs last year, according tothe BPI– a 13.3% year-on-year increase and an 18th consecutive year of growth. But Savage warns that the industry may be pushing its luck. “It’s ripping off fans,” he says. “We fear it may lead to buyer exhaustion and cause the bubble to collapse.”Explore more on these topicsVinylPop and rockCharli xcxOlivia RodrigoMusic industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was a death row lawyer. Here’s why I now joke about capital punishment | Comedy | The Guardian
description: In my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortable
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortable
Content: Josh Pickar: ‘What excited me most [about standup] was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Steve UllathorneView image in fullscreenJosh Pickar: ‘What excited me most [about standup] was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Steve UllathorneComedyI was a death row lawyer. Here’s why I now joke about capital punishmentIn my standup, I’m not trivializing the death penalty. I’m getting people to stay engaged when the subject is uncomfortableJosh PickarTue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTShareThe first time I came out as gay to a client on death row, he said: “Josh, I don’t care what you do with your ass, as long as you’re helping mine.” That joke did something legal arguments and moral philosophy rarely could: it made him impossible to keep at a distance.I spent seven years working as a lawyer for men on both Alabama and federal death rows. I stumbled my way into it. I was only 24, fresh out of law school and working at a big corporate law firm in Manhattan. A friend from law school asked if I wanted to join two pro bono death-penalty cases. I had no relevant experience and knew nothing about capital punishment.I was, after all, a fresh-faced gay Jewish kid from the Boston suburbs. What did I have to offer a man awaiting execution?double quotation markIt was often my clients’ humor that made them impossible to flattenMy friend wouldn’t hear it. She told me the clients were really nice, there were interesting legal issues, and I would have the opportunity to work with an important partner at the firm. Those seemed like pretty good reasons to join the team.One of my first taskswas to review the evidence the prosecution presented at trial. One piece of evidence demanded my attention: a 30-second surveillance video. I spent hours studying those 30 seconds. I knew every damn frame. Something was just off. Then it clicked: it was not a video. It was a slideshow. The surveillance camera had captured a series of still images, which the prosecution presented as continuous footage. That footage had huge gaps that the jurors unconsciously filled in.The “video” was extraordinarily misleading. The government’s conduct was unconscionable. I was hooked.During one of my first visits, after some light panicking and a full-body pat-down at the prison entrance, I sat down across from a strongly built, baby-faced Black man in his mid-30s.Before the visit, the prison had told me not to wear khaki. Now I understood why. He wore a khaki prison jumpsuit over a white undershirt. The guards did not want to mistake a lawyer for a prisoner. He was covered in tattoos, including one of a woman’s name stretched across his neck.I introduced myself and asked how he was doing.“I’m blessed, I can’t complain. Doing better than Muammar Gaddafi,” he replied.I wasdelighted. Five minutes earlier, I had been terrified of saying the wrong thing. Now, we were laughing about whether it was worse to be on death row or to be a slain Libyan dictator.Climate anxiety was consuming me. Then I learned to laugh about itRead moreThat instinct for humor in an unspeakably harsh context was not unique to him. Another client of mine had made several attempts to take his own life. After one such attempt, a correctional officer gave him a pamphlet of yoga poses and mindfulness exercises. He mailed me the pamphlet and wrote across the top in all caps: “NOT WORKING! :P” Even in despair, he wanted me to see the joke.The death penalty depends, in part, on keeping the people it condemns abstract. Knowing them, and laughing with them, made that distance impossible to maintain.It was often my clients’ humor that made them impossible to flatten. They were people convicted of terrible crimes, but no verdict could account for the whole person. Many of them had spent more than 20 years on death row accumulating friendships, frustrations and routines. They could be funny, perceptive and infuriating all in the same conversation.One of my former clients has spent decades in solitary confinement. Locked away in a tiny cell whose narrow window is frosted over, he has become a prolific artist. He makes abstract, distorted figures he calls his “Sassy Boys”. They have tiny hats, canes and earrings. They’re always late and unbothered.He says they’re like jazz: either you get it or you don’t.Watching him make work that strange and alive from his cell made it harder for me to justify postponing the life I claimed I wanted.I began performing standup and improv around New York City. Public speaking did not bother me much, but I was no theater kid. I made friends laugh in conversation, but doing it intentionally was different. What excited me most was the immediacy. A court could take months to issue a ruling on my brief. In a single breath, an audience could reject my joke.During the day I was fighting to get people off death row. At night, I was improvising a scene in a firehouse where the firefighters greeted one other by saying “lesbians”.Comedyoffered an outlet, a community, and a place where the stakes were low.Bryan Stevenson’s book Just Mercyin particular had shown me how storytelling could bring audiences closer to the people the legal system reduced to verdicts. As I spent more time performing, I began to wonder what comedy might do differently – not by making the subject lighter, but by helping audiences remain engaged when the subject became uncomfortable. I started telling jokes about the death penalty, wondering whether humor could bring audiences even a fraction as close as my clients’ jokes had brought me.double quotation markI do not know whether laughter can change someone’s mind. But a joke can unsettle an assumptionMy clients’ jokes revealed the people inside the system. My own jokes often revealed the system’s grotesque logic. I began telling a joke about mitigation evidence: the information that defense lawyers present to help a judge or jury see a life larger than the crime.The uncomfortable truth was that the more horrific the information we uncovered about a client’s life, the more useful it became for his case. After an interview with a client’s cousin, I called another lawyer on my team: “I have amazing news. He was molested! The dad AND the uncle.”In ordinary conversation, talking about the death penalty often made people shut down. But even in noisy comedy rooms, audiences listened. After shows, people came up to me with questions about the cases and the system. The laughter did not trivialize the subject. It gave me permission to keep talking about it, and seemed to give them permission to keep listening.I eventually decided to leave the law. I was burned out. When the stakes of work are literally life and death, it becomes hard to keep the rest of life in proportion.Still, leaving felt like a betrayal of my clients. I dreaded telling them. But the goodbyes were anticlimactic. They had seen lawyers come and go before. I have stayed in touch with several of them, and I think about them all the time.After years of treating control and expertise as the highest virtues, I wanted to learn how to fail. So I left for France to study at École Philippe Gaulier, the clown school where Sacha Baron Cohen and Emma Thompson studied. The school taught that a performer’s cleverness is not enough. Audiences respond to the pleasure a performer takes in being on stage, especially when things go wrong.The teachers were ruthless in their criticism. “Change completely!” they would yell. “Do you hear anybody laughing? Why do you keep doing the same fucking thing over and over if nobody is laughing?”‘It turned out I had a brain tumour …’ Six standup comics on what spurred them to get on stageRead moreAs a lawyer, I had spent years making sure I had a plan for every contingency. At Gaulier, I began to see how the instinct that had served me as a lawyer could stand between me and an audience. Uncertainty, it turned out, was not a weakness. It was an invitation.Legal advocacy is essential. A single filing could be the difference between life and death. But after years of working case by case, I became increasingly interested in reaching people for whom the death penalty could remain safely abstract. A court can overturn a sentence. But a legal ruling cannot dissolve the emotional distance that allows executions to remain politically possible.Comedy offers another way to lessen that distance. Not by lecturing an audience toward a conclusion that took me years to reach, but by letting them watch me stumble toward it through the contradictions, jokes and relationships that changed me.I do not know whether laughter can change someone’s mind. But a joke can unsettle an assumption and make indifference harder to sustain.A few weeks ago, the former client who makes the Sassy Boys called and suggested we make a musical. Not to make a political point. Just because it sounded fun to make something with another person. With me.I can’t sing. But you may see a death penalty musical coming to a theater near you.Josh Pickar’s debut standup showGetting Offwill be running at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe at the Assembly Roxy (Snug) on 5-30 August

title: Ariana Grande expands on decision to ‘step back from visibility’, telling fans it was ‘not reactive or impulsive’ | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: Singer and actor, whose world tour ends next month, told audience in Chicago that she had been quietly planning the move for a long time
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Singer and actor, whose world tour ends next month, told audience in Chicago that she had been quietly planning the move for a long time
Content: ‘Boundaries need to be set’ … Grande pictured in January.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Boundaries need to be set’ … Grande pictured in January.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersAriana GrandeAriana Grande expands on decision to ‘step back from visibility’, telling fans it was ‘not reactive or impulsive’Singer and actor, whose world tour ends next month, told audience in Chicago that she had been quietly planning the move for a long timeLaura SnapesTue 4 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAriana Grande has expanded upon her recent decision to take “a step back from visibility” when her tour ends next month, as a result of what a spokesperson called “endless, ongoing public scrutiny”.On Monday night during the first show of a three-night run in Chicago, the 33-year-old musician and actor read from notes as she told fans: “The announcement that was made yesterday was not a reactive or impulsive thing. It is something that I had decided to plan quietly, a long time ago.”The planned step-back includes Grande’s withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George at London’s Barbican next summer, where she would have appeared alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey.Grande appeared to reference ongoing public concern about her weight, which heightened after the release of the video for Petal, the lead single from her new album of the same name, last week. When shared on Instagram, the video received a community note pointing eating disorder sufferers towards resources.“I heard my fans were worried negativity was ruining things for me but that could not be more than the opposite,” she said. “Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes.”Grande said she had made her decision from a “thoughtful and empowered place”. She continued: “No matter what noises exist out there, nothing will ever be able to distort my reality, or be more real to me than this love that we share.”Grande’s new album frequently expresses her frustration with the expectations of the public; in the video for Petal, she murders a group of critics with a chainsaw. On stage in Chicago, she said: “I love you, this is what I want always ... the rest of that [commentary] is not mine to carry.”She called her current tour “one of the most healing, beautiful, correct and special experiences” of her life. The run continues with a 10-night residency at the O2 Arena in London from 15 August.Explore more on these topicsAriana GrandePop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the true horror of the Salisbury Poisonings laid bare | Television | The Guardian
description: Gripping first-hand testimonies walk through the events of the 2018 poisoning. Plus: a campfire showdown in Survivor Australia. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Gripping first-hand testimonies walk through the events of the 2018 poisoning. Plus: a campfire showdown in Survivor Australia. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: A tale of betrayal … the former home secretary Amber Rudd in The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door (Sky Documentaries)Photograph: Propagate/Passion PicturesView image in fullscreenA tale of betrayal … the former home secretary Amber Rudd in The Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door (Sky Documentaries)Photograph: Propagate/Passion PicturesTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the true horror of the Salisbury Poisonings laid bareGripping first-hand testimonies walk through the events of the 2018 poisoning. Plus: a campfire showdown in Survivor Australia. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Hannah Verdier,Priya ElanandEllen E JonesTue 4 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Salisbury Poisonings: A Spy Next Door9pm, Sky Documentaries“I said to myself: ‘Don’t worry, nothing happens in Salisbury,’” remembers journalist Emma Volney of her first week in local radio in 2018. “You don’t expect to see two people on a bench foaming at the mouth.” This documentary uses first-hand testimony to walk through the events of the poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia. The former prime minister Theresa May, intelligence officials and counterterrorism leaders also speak about the incident.Hollie RichardsonBest Medicine8pm, Sky OneThis cosy series about a cranky small-town medic is a faithful remake of Doc Martin – albeit with added American schmaltz. This week sees Maine’s Dr Martin (Josh Charles) deal with an elderly patient displaying a recent pattern of strange behaviour, and primary schooler Peter’s apparent hypochondria.Hannah J DaviesSurvivor Australia9pm, BBC ThreeRacing through a mud pit with inevitable injuries is nothing compared with the campfire showdown in the 10th season of the reality hit, billed as heroes v villains. The tribes play beautifully to type, with conservationists and activists working as a team and the self-confessed selfish camp going all-out on the conniving.Hannah VerdierJoe & David’s Magical Sitcom Tour9pm, U&GoldComedian mates Joe Wilkinson and David Earl have a hard time describing their new show in a nutshell. All you need to know is they celebrate one of their favourite sitcoms in each episode, visiting the locations and speaking with its creators and stars. First up, one of Joe’s top picks: Porridge.HRThe Vampire Lestat: Interview With the Vampire9.30pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenRock horror show … Sam Reid as Lestat de Lioncourt.Photograph: Sophie Giraud/BBC/AMC Networks EntertainmentThe outrageous musical vampire romp continues to thrill. Jennifer Ehle guest stars as the fabulous mother of glam rocker Lestat (Sam Reid) and we learn how they both became vampires in 18th-century France. Sure, there’s a bit of incest going on, but the pair together on screen are electric.HRIt Happened to Me: I Was Jailed in Japan for Ketamine10.15pm, BBC TwoIzabel Rose was a high-functioning ketamine user. Enchanted by Japan, she believed that leaving London would make her go straight. But, as she admits, “addiction doesn’t understand geography”. After phoning a contact about a fix, she was detained in Osaka by the police. So in this documentary, why does she say that was the best day of her life?Priya ElanFilmStand By Me (Rob Reiner, 1986),3am, Sky Cinema GreatsView image in fullscreenIconic … River Phoenix in Stand By Me.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Alamy“I never had any friends later like the ones I had when I was 12.” With that closing line, this 1986 adaptation of a Stephen King novella cemented its status as the ultimate coming-of-age movie. Its 1950s-set story concerns four boys (including an memorable performance from the late River Phoenix) who set out on a macabre journey to find the body of a missing classmate. Stand By Me was always a classic, but subsequent events – including the tragic death of much beloved director Rob Reiner – have invested rewatches with added poignancy.Ellen E JonesLive sportThe Hundred Cricket. title: Children of the Wild by Kevin Powers review – gripping tale of a friendship forged in war  | Books | The Guardian
description: Written by a US army veteran, this novel of courage and cruelty during the first world war is filled with unsettlingly authoritative depictions of violence – but its characters are less believable
Author: Marcel Theroux
Headline: Written by a US army veteran, this novel of courage and cruelty during the first world war is filled with unsettlingly authoritative depictions of violence – but its characters are less believable
Content: A remote valley in Virginia, where Children of the Wild is set.Photograph: TerryKelly/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA remote valley in Virginia, where Children of the Wild is set.Photograph: TerryKelly/Getty Images/iStockphotoBook of the dayBooksReviewChildren of the Wild by Kevin Powers review – gripping tale of a friendship forged in warWritten by a US army veteran, this novel of courage and cruelty during the first world war is filled with unsettlingly authoritative depictions of violence – but its characters are less believableMarcel TherouxTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKevin Powers’s fourth novel marks a return to the themes and subject matter of his acclaimed debutThe Yellow Birds, winner of the 2012 Guardian first book award. Through the lives of its central characters, it explores the courage, folly, cruelty and absurdity involved in war, and the challenges of adjusting to civilian life afterwards. But while The Yellow Birds focused on the experience of US soldiers fighting in Iraq, where Powers himself served between 2003 and 2004, Children of the Wild is set amid the carnage of the first world war.It follows the fortunes of two young men from a remote valley in Virginia. Roy is the arrogant young heir to a wealthy local landowner; Ennis is an orphan of unknown origin who has been living, like a character in a fairytale, in a shack on the top of a mountain. Ennis and Roy are first linked in a love triangle when Ennis is lured off his mountain top by his desire for Samantha, the daughter of the local minister, whose eyes have the “lustre of smoky quartz”. Roy has expected to marry Samantha, but she chooses feral Ennis. Roy accepts the setback remarkably swiftly, transferring his affections to Esther, the wealthy and shallow sister of his college roommate, Fintan. Roy and Ennis settle their differences with a mighty punch-up that cements an unlikely friendship between them.When Roy joins the army to fight in France as an officer, he persuades Ennis to come with him as a private. This becomes a source of guilt to Roy as the novel unfolds. Unequal in terms of class and status, Roy and Ennis are also asymmetrically talented at killing. Roy, though nominally the leader, is haunted by terrifying dreams and finds the responsibility of his role overwhelming. Ennis turns out to have an Achilles-like genius for warfare.double quotation markPowers is a tremendously gifted writer – he has an amazing knack for storytelling that seems to unfold visuallyBorn out of a brawl, the relationship between Roy and Ennis turns out to be by far the strongest attachment in the novel. It’s reinforced by subsequent acts of violence that include killings on and off the battlefield. Roy is both in awe of Ennis and fearful of him. Indifferent to praise or glory, Ennis is “at home in a dark corner of his soul that Roy didn’t even want to acknowledge existed in his own”.Powers is a tremendously gifted writer. He has an amazing knack for storytelling that seems to unfold visually and conveys landscapes, gestures and complex military engagements with great flair. His economical prose makes brisk work of a gripping tale that includes violent set pieces on the battlefields of France, war crimes, a pandemic, a quest through the mountains of Ohio, murders, a flashback to the bloodshed at Little Big Horn, and a powerful ending that reminds you, once more, of the heartbreak war brings in its wake.Powers writes about violence and its impact on both perpetrators and victims in a way that feels unsettlingly authoritative. When Ennis commandeers a German machine gun, you sense that the scene is informed by more than academic research: Powers was himself a machine-gunner in the Iraq war. Various characters, including a civil war veteran, punctuate self-aggrandising Roy’s delusions about warfare and loss with memorably gritty wisdom. “Every single person on this earth has a hole inside them where someone they loved used to be,” one person tells him. “You sit there thinking that hole inside of you is special.”Buried in the pages of the book is a telling allusion that hints at Powers’s ambition for it. On two occasions, in the context of terrible acts of violence – a scalping and a lynching – different characters utter these words to Roy: “Come and see.” Both times, Roy draws our attention to the phrase by repeating it: “‘Come and see’? It was familiar, but Roy couldn’t place it.”Powers wants the reader to notice the words and supply the missing context: “Come and see” is the dark invitation that John the Revelator receives in the final book of the Bible to witness the apocalypse. It’s also the title of a Soviet film directed by Elem Klimov that has a strong claim to be the most harrowing war movie ever made. Very much like Klimov’s film, Powers mixes incredible visual intensity with the mythic and surreal in order to illuminate the apocalyptic extremes of human behaviour.Yet his desire to make the story resonate at an epic level also makes parts of the novel melodramatic and implausible. When you notice the characters are mythic archetypes –RoyYoung,EnnisDuke,the flawed Arthurian king and the Lancelot who steals his Guinevere – they seem a little less real as people. Ennis’s journey down the mountain and his progression from feral cow-wrangler to cold-eyed killer never feels fully persuasive and is punctuated by moments of improbability. This isn’t limited to Ennis: characters have a habit of doing things that are dramatically striking, but psychologically far-fetched. Samantha distributes presents to the local children with the corpse of her dead father in the wagon.Roy heads off to the Bighorn Mountains for a mission that’s supposed to be heartfelt, but feels like hollow spectacle. Ennis returns from the war and perpetrates a bizarre and self-sabotaging act of violence. And then there’s Fintan Thoreau, Roy’s ghastly future brother-in-law, whose villainy motivates an important section of the plot but feels cartoonish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere’s also something uncomfortable about the book’s representation of violence. Officially, violence is repellent, but it’s pretty cool too, especially when our heroes are cutting a swathe through German soldiers, who are depicted with a one-sidedness that reminded me of the jingoistic Warlord comics that were a guilty pleasure of my childhood. At one point, Roy is struggling to find the cold-heartedness to dispatch a German soldier who is pleading for his life. Roy looks over at Ennis, with a look “that begged him for permission to be free of this man’s death”. The permission is supplied by the author: the two-faced Boche sneakily pulls out a knife thus making him utterly unworthy to live.Though I enjoyed the book a great deal and admired Powers’s bravura, economical prose, I ended up comparing it to other books about the same conflict. The first world war has many chronicles: All Quiet on the Western Front, Good-Bye to All That, Birdsong, Pat Barker’s Regeneration trilogy. The best of these manage to depict the awfulness of warfare with both more banality and more humour. I recently reread Frederick Manning’s 1929 novel The Middle Parts of Fortune alongside Alice Winn’s 2023 debutIn Memoriam. I found their foul-mouthed soldiers and doomed public schoolboys more lastingly real than the avatars of Children of the Wild, with their murky backstories and portentous dream lives.Children of the Wild by Kevin Powers is published by Atlantic (£14.99). title: Geography of Heaven by Rory MacLean – soul-searching journeys into the afterlife | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: From an ashram in India to an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru, a travel writer searches for meaning after the death of his wife
Author: Kathryn Bromwich
Headline: From an ashram in India to an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru, a travel writer searches for meaning after the death of his wife
Content: MacLean at a Buddhist festival in Bhutan.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenMacLean at a Buddhist festival in Bhutan.Photograph: PRAutobiography and memoirReviewGeography of Heaven by Rory MacLean – soul-searching journeys into the afterlifeFrom an ashram in India to an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru, a travel writer searches for meaning after the death of his wifeKathryn BromwichTue 4 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn this moving, sometimes grandiloquent grief-memoir-cum-travelogue, Rory MacLean pairs an affinity for new-age thinking with a habit of loftily holding forth (“none of us are created for naught”, “love can but lead to truth”) and a proclivity for arresting one-liners (“I watched gods walk on fire”). In his search for meaning in the five years after his wife’s untimely death from cancer, he shows himself to be both refreshingly broad-minded and unnecessarily crotchety, like a more cantankerous Michael Palin.MacLean’s work as a travel writer has taken him across the world, whether flying a handbuilt plane over Crete or riding shotgun with a drug warlord in Burma. This is his first book since losing Katrin, for 32 years the “fixed point” in his life, whose final weeks and moments he describes tenderly. Unable to process her death, he turns to travel to seek out “thin places”:áiteanna tanaíin Celtic mythology, where the veil between worlds is porous. Starting in Jerusalem, his quest takes him to more than a dozen sacred locations, including an ashram in India, a Native American community in South Dakota, an “excruciating” Vipassanā retreat in Suffolk and, inevitably, an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru.You can’t fault his commitment. He takes the alarming decision – mere weeks before the 7 October attacks – to infiltrate an Israeli settlement in the West Bank, hiding in the shadows from IDF patrols, in an attempt to recreate the circumstances under which Jacob (“a traveller like me”) dreamed of a ladder to heaven. In the US, he faces an oncoming tornado, “too transfixed by the unfolding storm” to seek shelter; in Bhutan, he spends two days travelling to a Buddhist festival along a road that is “little more than a narrow ledge hacked into the rock face”.MacLean’s skills as a travel writer are evident. He brings to life a Herzogian boat journey down a river into the Amazon, “twisting like a serpent towards another world”. He describes a cremation ground in Bhutan in rich, resonant detail, from the “barley burned in a metal basin, its smell said to keep hungry ghosts at bay”, to the throaty chanting of the monks. In South Africa, he consults a sangoma or diviner; to this day, the country has four times more traditional diviners and herbalists than medical doctors. At the Rosebud Sioux Reservation, he witnesses a remarkable ritual involving trance-like dancing and offerings of flesh. The discussions of Victorian spiritualism and the use of AI to bypass grief are thoughtful and well judged.But there are jarring tonal shifts, from the pompous (“Does sanctity fall from above or is it conditional on social convention, I wondered?”) to the colloquial (“kick the bucket”, “bunkum”). And more than once, the book is let down by outdated language about minority groups (described as “crippled” and “swarthy-skinned”). Do we really need to know whether every woman he encounters is “slender” or “chubby”?Throughout, MacLean treads the line between credulous and open-minded. Science is invoked occasionally, only to be dismissed as “reductionist” and “pathetic”. Instead, he becomes fixated on numerology, calculating “the maths” of when Katrin will be reincarnated (according to different people he consults, 49 days after her death, or years later, potentially as a dog). He compiles a dossier of evidence that, in his mind, proves “without doubt” that Katrin’s soul lives on: a dream, a sunbeam, a blue ribbon, a friend’s furniture in Mexico being inexplicably rearranged.In each new location, his soul-searching follows a pattern: initial disappointment, followed by a last-minute breakthrough. Much of the book hinges on him feeling a vague, indefinable presence – a tingling, a shift in the air – undoubtedly profound to him but almost impossible to put into words (“something infinitely subtle … it was there, and more than nothing”), which can be frustrating for the reader. A somewhat belaboured flight metaphor eventually leads him, many figurative and literal air miles later, to the realisation that what matters is the journey, not the destination.Geography of Heaven: Travels to the Hereafter by Rory MacLean is published by Abacus (£22).
