title: Web of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in Hollywood | Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day | The Guardian
description: Tom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Tom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?
Content: Tom Holland in a scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony Pictures via APView image in fullscreenTom Holland in a scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony Pictures via APSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayWeb of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in HollywoodTom Holland’s fourth outing as Peter Parker broke box office records but how did the web-slinger avoid growing superhero fatigue?Jesse HassengerTue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAyear ago, the superhero-industrial complex looked like it was on the wane. All three of Marvel’s big movies for 2025 underperformed to some degree or another, outgrossed by DC’s newest reboot of Superman – which itself made less than any number of previous-regime DC movies, and was followed up by this summer’sSupergirl, a costly bomb. It looked as if the age of heroes might be coming to an end, and only seemed fitting that the next big Avengers movie was subtitledDoomsday(and had resigned itself to sharing a release date with the Imax-grabbing release ofa third Dune movie).But look out, as the song goes: here comesSpider-Man.Spider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilersRead moreSpider-Man: Brand New Day, the fourth solo film starring Tom Holland as the third live-action iteration of the character in the past 25 years, was always expected to do well at the box office this summer. Its predecessor, 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home, was the first movie since Covid to post 2010s-style numbers. At the same time, it seemed like an anomaly, given its advantage of two additional Spider-Men, as previous stars Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield returned for an unexpectedly moving curtain call to their versions of Peter Parker. Still: the (relatively) lower-grossing movies that sent those past Peters packing made a substantial amount of money, too, so there was a general understanding that Spider-Man would be a perennial favorite and Brand New Day would do accordingly well.Yet a few months ago, hardly anyone predicted that it would swoop so far asthe all-time opening weekend record in North America, outgrossing Avengers: Endgame with $360m, and coming in a strong second worldwide, making nearly a billion dollars within four days. What’s more, Brand New Day is keeping pace with a movie that was an all-in team-up event, also sold as a de facto finale. Most of it focuses on the six core Avengers who first assembled in the 2012 smash (plus Ant-Man, Captain Marvel and Rocket Raccoon) but its climax features appearances from just about every major MCU character brought back from the dead, including Holland’s Spidey.Brand New Day certainly takes advantage of that same wide cinematic universe, with supporting parts for the Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), the new Black Widow (Florence Pugh), the Punisher (Jon Bernthal), and one major figure fromMarvelcomics. But that mystery character’s identity wasn’t part of the ad campaign in order to keep the movie’s surprise intact, and the Punisher is from a few Marvel TV shows – not exactly a blockbuster-level draw. No, it’s safe to say that Brand New Day is breaking records – it will become the biggest movie of the year in a matter of days – because of Spider-Man himself.That means the character, not Holland (though his version is obviously popular). Spidey has been posting numbers like this longer than any single movie star: back in 2002, the Spider-Man film starring Maguire and directed by Sam Raimi was the first movie to ever open with over $100m at the North American box office, and it sure didn’t have any other marquee heroes helping it along. Combined with the surprise success of an X-Men movie two years earlier, Spider-Man 02 kicked off a superhero-movie craze – and due respect to Professor X and his noble mission of mutant-human brotherhood, but the Raimi film pulled in well over twice as much. It was a sign that he was attracting audiences beyond the comics-fan faithful, even – cue the nerd sweats – girls!It’s probably an oversimplification to chalk Spider-Man’s enduring cinematic appeal to a female audience, not least because all three live-action Spider-Man series center a male point of view, unswervingly make the female lead a love interest for Peter Parker, and ignore all of the super-powered women in this corner of comics lore; only the animated Spider-Verse movies get into Ghost Spider, Spider-Woman and so on. (It would also be unfair to deny the existence of female comics fans, excited to see Spider-Man on screen.) But while Kirsten Dunst’s Mary Jane from the Raimi films does play like a damsel frequently in distress – she’s climactically endangered for three movies in a row, and Raimi’s take on gender roles is not exactly forward-thinking – she does have her own hopes, dreams and disappointments.Her feelings are a big part of what drives the emotional core of the much-maligned, underrated Spider-Man 3, just as Peter’s feelings for her drive the action for the first film. In the new movies, the evolving relationship between Peter and MJ (Zendaya, Holland’s real-life spouse) is rarely far from the center of the film. Hell, the obvious affection between Garfield’s Spider-Man and Emma Stone’s Gwen Stacy is just about the only thing that makes the abruptly curtailed Amazing Spider-Man movies watchable (and the comics-accurate death of Gwen at the end of the second film probably helped doom it with audiences; it’s a colossal and unearned-feeling downer to kill off your superstar female lead in just the second film).View image in fullscreenTom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Courtesy of Sony Pictures/Sony PicturesIt doesn’t feel like a coincidence that all three live-action Spider-Man actors dated their co-stars at some point; these are superhero movies that reboot and reconfigure and recast, but never fully dispense with romance. At first, that was very much part of MCU at large; the first two Iron Man movies run on screwball-adjacent byplay between Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr) and Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow). But as romance leached out of the MCU following Phase One, replaced with weirdly businesslike allusions to off-screen hookups and breakups, Spider-Man remained at least a little bit lovelorn, perhaps reminding audiences of a crucial human angle missing from big-scale smash-em-ups.Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superheroRead moreIt’s not just the love stories that continually draw audiences to Spider-Man, of course. The character has long resonated as a keen fusion of longtime DC titans Superman and Batman: he’s got the diverse (and potentially playful) power set like Superman, paired with a Clark Kent-like humble-nerd identity; and the relatable angst of Batman, who of course has no fantastical powers and, as such, bumps up against his human limitations. He wasn’t the first Marvel hero, but he’s probably the archetypal one, mixing in more overt teen melodrama in an era where Superman was flying further into sci-fi territory.Adapting Spider-Man into other media has only increased his cachet; toddlers are now routinely shown Spidey and His Amazing Friends, a sort of Marvel version of Paw Patrol that gets them hooked on a version of that mythos early, via Disney+. Yet another Spider-Man advantage, though, is very much the opposite of Disney-umbrella synergy: the movie rights for the character have stayed with Sony since the first film. That’s a big part of why there have been three different Spider-Man actors; Sony has to keep making movies to hang on to the characters. (That’s also why a whole bunch of negligible movies about tertiary Spider-verse characters like Madame Web exist.)Disney’s Marvel Studios still deserves credit for the recent successes; they produce the Holland movies, which are in continuity with their other projects. But there’s still probably some manner of negotiation in terms of their timing and, at least with Brand New Day, maybe their creative direction. Holland has told the press that his experience making The Odyssey inspired him to push for a more disciplined approach to Marvel’s assembly line. For her part, Zendaya seems to have brought in Justin Kuritzkes, screenwriter for her film Challengers, to punch up some of the character work. (He receives an “additional literary material” credit.)The stars and film-makers working to make Brand New Day feel more like its own movie with some fun Marvel tie-ins, rather than the latest Marvel homework assignment, may have put it over the top in terms of good buzz and a huge opening in the wake of The Odyssey. (The promotion of having three of its main actors – Holland, Zendaya and Bernthal all appear in both! – shared with the second-biggest movie of the summer couldn’t have hurt, either.) But Spider-Man movies are also notable for their consistency. The series’ biggest disaster, The Amazing Spider-Man 2, still pulled in $700m worldwide. (As far as low points go, that actually beats Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman, Iron Man, Captain America … pretty much everyone.) The first film premiered less than a year after the 9/11 attacks on the US – an early trailer was pulled because it consisted of a visual-effects sight gag where a bad guys’ helicopter got caught in a Spidey web spun between the two towers of the World Trade Center – and while the world has changed plenty in the past quarter-century, it does feel as if Spider-Man is the most enduring film character of the new millennium so far.View image in fullscreenTom Holland and ZendayaPhotograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockIt might be a little trite to suggest that a movie in production well before 9/11, featuring a character that had been beloved for decades and earmarked for a big-screen debut for ages (James Cameron wrote a detailed treatment in the 1990s in preparation for a version that never came to pass), received such a franchise-long boost from a single historical event. But in retrospect, it is difficult to picture these Spider-Man movies working quite so well in the 1970s/80s of the original Superman movies (which clearly influenced Raimi’s films) or the 1980s/90s of the early Batman cycle, with their ornate, almost otherworldly spectacle. It’s as if Spider-Man needed to accumulate some eras to throw back to while also moving past those previous icons.The forward progress has always been subdued; the first movie is the only one to really make much of post-9/11 New York, and only obliquely, in a scene where citizens rise up and help Spider-Man, declaring “you mess with one of us, you mess with all of us!” (This protective togetherness is further echoed in the sequel’s subway rescue sequence, though there it takes on more of a pseudo-religious aura that’s surprisingly touching all these many years later.) Well into the 2020s, Spidey is still foiling old-timey bank robberies; there may not be sacks of money with dollar signs on them, but there might as well be. That he’s doing this casually using invasive, illegal surveillance equipment marks him as a truly well-integrated post-9/11 superhero, while Marvel mutes real-world allegory elsewhere in their increasingly insular universe.Even if his nominal co-parent is just another flavor of multinational corporation, the current Spidey being of the MCU but not Disney-exclusive sets him ever-so-slightly apart from his many famous co-stars. Worlds end and new phases begin for the original Avengers; two appear to be actually-for-real-dead, while others threaten to age out of their costumes (or, worse, age back in when they don’t know what else to do).This should be a bigger problem for Spider-Man, a character who, despite the second part of his moniker and a whole lot of comics stories where he’s an adult, is largely thought of as a perpetual teenager. Yet as often as he’s been recast back to high school in the movies, he stays in the culture’s good graces and captures a range of demographics. Maybe it’s because that endless cycle that’s supposed to be the sign of a soulless, deathless franchise actually (however accidentally) has come to resemble the kind of endless struggle that made the character so refreshing in the first place. Even when he’s making billions in days, he’s a superhero who remains an unambiguous work in progress.Explore more on these topicsSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandMarvelSuperhero moviesZendayaSpider-ManfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Careless whispers: what really happened between George Michael and Lindsay Anderson? The Wham! movie producer reveals all | Movies | The Guardian
description: How did the pioneering director get involved – then fall out – with the 80s’ poppiest band? How are Sam Peckinpah and Michael Jackson’s Thriller involved? Prepare for a tale of ambition, deception and shuttlecock-stuffed shorts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: How did the pioneering director get involved – then fall out – with the 80s’ poppiest band? How are Sam Peckinpah and Michael Jackson’s Thriller involved? Prepare for a tale of ambition, deception and shuttlecock-stuffed shorts
Content: ‘Apostles of the New Materialism’ … George Michael, Lindsay Anderson and Andrew Ridgeley in China.Photograph: Lindsay Anderson Archive, University of StirlingView image in fullscreen‘Apostles of the New Materialism’ … George Michael, Lindsay Anderson and Andrew Ridgeley in China.Photograph: Lindsay Anderson Archive, University of StirlingMoviesCareless whispers: what really happened between George Michael and Lindsay Anderson? The Wham! movie producer reveals allHow did the pioneering director get involved – then fall out – with the 80s’ poppiest band? How are Sam Peckinpah and Michael Jackson’s Thriller involved? Prepare for a tale of ambition, deception and shuttlecock-stuffed shortsWhen Wham! squashed Lindsay Anderson’s China filmAndrew Ridgeley on Wham’s surreal trip to ChinaMartin LewisTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the evening of 3 April 1985 in a hotel in Hong Kong.Lindsay Anderson, who I’d engaged to direct the theatrical documentary I’d instigated of Wham!’s historic trip to China, had called a meeting of the film crew. He wanted to give a pep talk the night before we flew to Beijing.The 30-strong team my production company had recruited for this adventure duly assembled. Lindsay gave a speech in the stentorian tones of an elder statesman addressing the House of Commons and rooted in Henry V’s St Crispin’s Day oration. And typical Lindsay, he mixed shrewd observation with sardonic wit. “Tomorrow we embark on a great adventure,” he said. “We travel into communist China with George and Andrew – ‘Apostles of the New Materialism.’”Six months later, after the first cut of the film he made was screened forGeorge Michaeland Andrew Ridgeley, Lindsay was suddenly and summarily dismissed from the project. His stately, 80-minute work-in-progress If You Were There … was denounced and Lindsay was purged. His insightful film showing China on the verge of modernisation was condemned, and with the exception of a screening in a BFI series marking his centennial, it has become an “un-film”. This was quite the media storm in the Wham! teacup of the mid-80s. But it rapidly became forgotten.View image in fullscreenA shrewd observer … Lindsay Anderson in 1968.Photograph: Jane BownA frothy one-hour reel titled Foreign Skies was confected from our film by a duo of music video operators and it premiered in June 1986 on big screens in Wembley Stadium at Wham! The Final. It was squeezed in as a support act between Elton John (costumed as Ronald McDonald) and Gary Glitter. When I told Lindsay of this auspicious positioning of the bowdlerised derivative of our film, he responded with a withering: “Quite!”‘I thought it didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell’: Andrew Ridgeley on Wham’s surreal trip to ChinaRead moreAnd now comes a well-constructed new film sanctioned by the George Michael estate,Wham! 10 Days in China, whose bragging rights include drawing on the vast archive of magnificent unseen footage shot by Lindsay and our team of cinematographers, rescued from the vaults. Its remit is to look at the overall China excursion and its impact. And of course to appeal to the legions of Wham! fans. So the story behind the trashing of a film by one of our finest directors is not a focus. Fair enough. But I will try to convey the essence of why it happened.In February 1985, I was based in New York and nine years into a producing career that started with multiple shows, albums and films of the Secret Policeman’s Ball series I’d co-created with John Cleese to raise funds for Amnesty International. I’d just produced the music videos created to launch the career of Julian Lennon, for which I’d recruited Sam Peckinpah as director.I was a lover of the documentary artform and the work ofFrederick Wiseman, Richard Leacock,the Maysles brothersand DA Pennebaker. And as a publicist and marketing strategist fortunate enough to have been mentored by the former Beatles press agentDerek Taylor, I understood how film could be harnessed to help shape consumer perceptions of musical artists.Out of the blue, I got a phone call from an old pal from the London music business of the 1970s who’d just arrived in Manhattan. It wasJazz Summers– one half of the management duo behind Wham! In that role, most people think ofSimon Napier-Bell, the flamboyant 1960s impresario, but the double-act of Wham! were represented by a double-act of managers. Simon the flashy show-horse. Jazz the scrappy work-horse.View image in fullscreenMartin Lewis with Andrew Ridgeley and George Michael by the Great Wall of China.Photograph: Martin Lewis CollectionJazz took me to see Wham! perform and I was impressed. Afterwards, Jazz, George, Andrew and I had supper, and Jazz told me Simon was currently finalising a wheeze to have Wham! be the first pop group to play China: a shrewd stunt designed to help them break the US with the hoped-for media coverage, clearly inspired by the hoopla that Elton John got from being the first pop act to play in Russia in 1979.I instinctively said: “That’s a great film!” Jazz said: “Wanna make it?” I said: “Yes!” Approximate duration of the development process: about seven seconds.I told him that we could make a standard-issue travelogue tailored to MTV sensibilities. “But that just gets you recoupment of your costs and reinforcement of your existing audience. Pop fans and the red tops. You’ve already got them. So what would you gain?”“But make a serious documentary about the visit – that shows your lads as cultural ambassadors – that film gets shown at film festivals and elevates your boys into the broadsheets.” I made it clear there was no point shooting a Sino version of Club Tropicana – Club Tiananmen. And that we needed a real film-maker who would see the big picture. Who would understand and portray the bizarre cultural juxtaposition.Jazz bought it, and I was given the green light to find and hire such a director. Having just had the adventure of working with Peckinpah, I decided I needed another old-timer and I loved the films of Lindsay Anderson.So that’s how he came on board. But how and why was he forced to walk the plank? I think the problems began because Jazz and Simon did not see themselves as respectful collaborators with Wham! as, say, Brian Epstein had been with the Beatles. They were akin to Tin Pan Alley-era puppet-masters, skilled at hustling sponsorship deals with Fila for the Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go video, and encouraging the benefits of shuttlecock insertion into shorts.View image in fullscreenA cinematic tour de force … If You Were There, Lindsay Anderson’s version of the documentary.Photograph: Lindsay Anderson Archive, University of StirlingSo they did not share with George and Andrew the reasoning behind the engagement of Lindsay and the strategy of making a serious documentary. The lads were expecting a bog-standard fluff-piece with Lindsay’s name attached simply as a bit of window-dressing.The cultural interests of George and Andrew were considerable, but as of 1985, the ethos of documentary makers such as Robert Flaherty, John Grierson and the subsequent pioneers of cinéma vérité and direct cinema had not entirely penetrated the Bushey area. So they were ill-equipped to comprehend or appreciate the first cut of a sophisticated film. Imagine their culture-shock when confronted with Lindsay’s carefully constructed cinematic tour de force.Even more significantly, something traumatic changed in the dynamic between George Michael and his managers. When Jazz and Simon first took on Wham! as clients, the implicit game plan was to run the table as long as organically possible. They knew George would eventually want to become a solo artist, but they figured that if they hit the jackpot of breaking in the US – which they did – then surely their young charges would be happy to keep the money rolling in.But after their 11-show stadium tour of North America in August-September of 1985, George suddenly conveyed a new timeline to them. He was done with Wham! He wanted off the merry-go-round. He would deliver a few more singles, do a final concert and then adios. Left unspoken was whether he would keep them as managers of his solo career.View image in fullscreenGeorge Michael and Martin Lewis in a Chinese satellite TV facility in April 1985.Photograph: courtesy of Martin LewisSince they were, for historical reasons, working on a handshake rather than a legal document, this was most unwelcome news. The expected additional years of vast profits rolling in from records, tours and merchandise was about to go up in smoke. There was no guarantee that their golden-coiffed goose would be laying golden eggs for the managers to continue collecting.They rapidly needed one last hit, a product they could rush-release to grab a quick profit. A year earlier, in the still early days of home video, something remarkable had happened. A company called Vestron released a VHS: Making Michael Jackson’s Thriller, a behind-the-scenes of the popular music video. It was one of the first home videos to be sold rather than rented by consumers. And it rapidly sold millions.Bingo! Forget about that airy-fairy, worthy and virtuous film-festival claptrap designed to get Wham! covered in the Guardian and the New York Times! No longer needed. The film could be easily repurposed in post-production to be a sure-fire commercial product to sell to the fans.The problem was that they were committed to making a film with Lindsay, and there was no way a respected auteur was going to mutate the vision he was engaged to create into an anodyne pop tart to be consumed by teeny boppers.double quotation markIt was not the ‘what we did on our Chinese holidays’ home movie they had been misled to expectJazz knew that. So a touch of kabuki theatre had to be enacted. It was decided that George and Andrew had to be shown Lindsay’s film-in-progress for the express purpose of eliciting their displeasure, in order to give Jazz and Simon the excuse to dispense with Lindsay.That was very easy to engineer. Neither George nor Andrew had been party to – nor made aware of – the artistic vision that had been agreed in February. Nor were they accustomed to seeing a full-length theatrical documentary in the middle of the complex editorial process.So stage one was rapidly achieved. I was at that fateful private screening, and George and Andrew were totally unprepared for what was unspooled – it was not the “what we did on our Chinese holidays” home movie they had been misled to expect.Stage two was firing Lindsay because “the boys didn’t like his film”. As the producer, I was duly summoned to Jazz’s office. It was a short but tough conversation for two old pals. He told me point-blank that I had to fire Lindsay. I had a split second to decide what to do.Should I stick with the chap I’d known for nigh 14 years who’d engaged me on the project? And stay in the running to produce more films and videos with George Michael? Or stick to my principles and defend Lindsay, whom I had hired but known for only six months?View image in fullscreenAndrew Ridgeley and George Michael in the new documentary Wham! 10 Days in China.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/© Andrew Ridgeley, Big Geoff Overseas Limited, Robobuild Limited t/a George Michael EntertainmentAt the age of 33, I was neither courageous nor particularly noble. Yet I reflexively declined to fire Lindsay and resigned on the spot.Lindsay was fired a few minutes later via a phone call from Jazz. I negotiated that Lindsay and I would retain our respective director and producer titles. After six months of hard work, it was the least we deserved, although after I saw the candyfloss of Foreign Skies – the mutant derivative that was spun out of Lindsay’s footage – I had mixed feelings.Despite that regrettable denouement, life continued. Lindsay and I stayed friends until his death nine years later in 1994. He was just 71. Though I tried to get him to see that it was Jazz and Simon who had let him down, he continued to be upset with George. He had wanted an artist-to-artist relationship that was just not on the cards.Wham! 10 Days in China review – pop meets politics in George and Andrew’s great leap eastRead moreTo my delight, George and I retained the bantering rapport that had become our dynamic. I defended him on US TV after he was arrested in a Beverly Hills public restroom by a plainclothes policeman – I joked that the cop was not really in plain clothes as he was wearing a $2,000 Gucci jacket! George appreciated my public support on his behalf and was much amused that the TV show accorded a straight pal the nonsensical on-screen caption “producer and longtime companion”.He held no bitterness about the experience of our film. We even discussed new projects including an intriguing collaboration with Bob Dylan – a story I’m saving for my memoirs.Wham! 10 Days in China is in cinemas now.Martin Lewisis a producer, humorist and marketing strategistExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGeorge MichaelLindsay AndersonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Love Me Tender review – Vicky Krieps custody-battle drama is intelligent, sensual and bitter slice of life  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Anna Cazenave Cambet’s adaptation of Constance Debré’s novel is a superbly acted and affecting – if restrained – portrait of child access and interpersonal strife
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Anna Cazenave Cambet’s adaptation of Constance Debré’s novel is a superbly acted and affecting – if restrained – portrait of child access and interpersonal strife
Content: Vicky Krieps as Clémence and Monia Chokri as Sara, in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesView image in fullscreenVicky Krieps as Clémence and Monia Chokri as Sara, in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesMoviesReviewLove Me Tender review – Vicky Krieps custody-battle drama is intelligent, sensual and bitter slice of lifeAnna Cazenave Cambet’s adaptation of Constance Debré’s novel is a superbly acted and affecting – if restrained – portrait of child access and interpersonal strifePeter BradshawTue 4 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVicky Krieps gives an intelligent, finely calibrated and sensitive performance in this marital-breakdown drama from writer-director Anna Cazenave Cambet. Cambet has adapted the autobiographical novel of the same title by Constance Debré, about her bitter experience of being denied contact with her young son after her marriage breakup – at the same time quitting her job in law and then coming out as gay, andalsobecoming a writer (these things apparently held against her in France’s patriarchal family courts).Krieps mimics the author’s elegant, close-cropped hairstyle in the film’s final act, and is never anything other than excellent. But I wondered sometimes if, in the course of this slightly prolix movie, the reserve and control required from her by the material were quite doing full justice to the extraordinary 18-month ordeal of not being able to see your own child.Well, perhaps that opacity is what you need to survive, when emotionalism would be held against you, and interpreted as instability. And there is something inspired in the movie’s final internal monologue, heard in voiceover as Krieps’s character is cycling through the streets, wondering if she is emerging from a “mourning” period for her son. There is another flash of inspiration from the director in contriving things so that the first clear look we get of her son’s face is an hour into the film, at the first court-supervised contact meeting.Krieps is Clémence, whose shared arrangements around her son Paul (Viggo Ferreira-Redier) with her ex-partner Laurent (Antoine Reinartz) are amicable enough until she reveals to him that she is now dating women. Something in her new sexual identity, and the fact that she having some success as a writer describing it, triggers a spiteful rage in Laurent, who turns Paul against his own mother. He applies for sole access, coercing their son into writing a bogus deposition statement attacking Clémence. He succeeds in denying access for a year and a half.‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting HollywoodRead moreClémence defiantly tries to resist the bullying, to continue with her life of sensual openness, honesty and artistic expression, in effect biting her tongue in the face of state-sanctioned homophobia. She finally discovers some intimacy with Sarah (Monia Chokri), while also trying to look after her elderly, ailing father (Féodor Atkine). Clémence gradually gains some access to Paul, talking to him while two court officers are present, and finally gets to take him out on her own for a gleeful bike ride (but thank heavens Laurent’s lawyers didn’t see that they had no helmets).In its moment-by-moment transcription of the crushing banality of this kind of injustice, the film is offering a bitter slice of life. I wasn’t sure about Paul’s flash of anger in one of the “contact” scenes when he tips the chair over and then Clémence does the same thing; it is a rare moment of actorly discomfort for Krieps. But again, perhaps this sort of discomfort, this half-hearted bad art in the midst of real life, is authentic in its way.As for Laurent, he is a mystery: petulant, angry, resentful. There is a strange moment when he opens the apartment door to Clémence, and we glimpse two rather forbidding men inside. These are his lawyer and friend, there at his request as witnesses to any of Clémence’s supposed bad behaviour, although we never hear any more of them. Perhaps there could be another story to tell – perhaps even a sympathetic story – about the pathos of Laurent and his suspicions. This is an intelligent, sophisticated, sensual movie that never quite arrives at the explosively passionate moment it appears to promise.Love Me Tender is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFamilyParents and parentingFranceDivorceEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Imelda Staunton | Movies | The Guardian
description: She’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: She’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?
Content: Warm and calm, but won’t stand for any nonsense … Imelda Staunton.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APView image in fullscreenWarm and calm, but won’t stand for any nonsense … Imelda Staunton.Photograph: Domenico Stinellis/APFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Imelda StauntonShe’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her?Rich PelleyTue 4 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is perhaps fitting that Imelda Staunton ended up playing Queen Elizabeth II in the last two series of The Crown, considering she has been acting royalty for years. Her film career has seen her voice champion egg-layer Bunty in 2000’s Chicken Run, followed by roles in Mike Leigh’s 2004 drama Vera Drake and the 2005 comedy Nanny McPhee. In 2014, she played the formidable Welsh miners’ strike campaigner Hefina inPride. She also plays Lady Maud Bagshaw in the first two Downton Abbey films, and voices Paddington’s beloved Aunt Lucy in all three Paddington films. For a whole generation, however, she will always be Dolores Umbridge in two of the later Harry Potter films, where she somehow made a pink cardigan almost as frightening as Voldemort.View image in fullscreenBafta-winning role … Imelda Staunton, left, with Daniel Mays in Vera Drake.Photograph: Moviestore collection Ltd/AlamyOn TV, she has cropped up in everything from Little Britain and Doctor Who to Psychoville, Brassic and a memorable guest appearance in the fourth series of A Bit of Fry & Laurie, where – for reasons known only to F&L – she was introduced as “Snutty”. Whether she’s playing a chicken, a bear or the head of state, there is always something unmistakably Imelda about her performances: warm and calm but with the distinct impression that she won’t stand for any nonsense.After training at Rada, Staunton spent six years in repertory theatre before making her film debut in Bill Douglas’s 1986 historical epic Comrades. She went on to appear in 1992’s Peter’s Friends, 1993’s Much Ado About Nothing, 1995’s Sense and Sensibility and 1998’s Shakespeare in Love. Then came Leigh’sVera Drake, in which she plays a warm-hearted cleaner who secretly carries out illegal abortions in 1950s London. Her performance won her a Bafta and the best actress prize at the Venice film festival, as well as earning her an Oscar nomination.In addition, Staunton has had a garlanded career in musicals, beginning in 1982 with The Beggar’s Opera. Her performances in Follies, Guys and Dolls, The Wizard of Oz, Gypsy, Sweeney Todd and Hello Dolly! have been widely acclaimed. She has received 15 Olivier award nominations, winning five of them. In 2024, she was awarded a DBE.View image in fullscreenA terrifying pink cardigan … Staunton as Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter: Order of the Phoenix.Photograph: Warner Bros/AllstarHer latest film,& Sons, reunites her with her Pride co-star Bill Nighy, who plays a famously difficult novelist who summons his family together to make a startling announcement; Staunton plays his estranged wife.Now Staunton is here to answer your questions so please post them below by 6pm on Wednesday 5 August, we’ll put the best to Snutty and publish her answers in Film & Music.& Sons is in cinemas from 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewImelda StauntonHarry PotterMike LeighVera DrakeTelevisionMusicalscalloutShareReuse this content

title: The Summer Book review – Glenn Close powers sweet-natured take on Tove Jansson’s grief classic | Movies | The Guardian
description: This sensitive adaptation of Jansson’s 1972 novel, set in the beatific Gulf of Finland, is a quiet treatise on life and death
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This sensitive adaptation of Jansson’s 1972 novel, set in the beatific Gulf of Finland, is a quiet treatise on life and death
Content: Affecting and distinctive … Glenn Close in the The Summer Book.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAffecting and distinctive … Glenn Close in the The Summer Book.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesReviewThe Summer Book review – Glenn Close powers sweet-natured take on Tove Jansson’s grief classicThis sensitive adaptation of Jansson’s 1972 novel, set in the beatific Gulf of Finland, is a quiet treatise on life and deathPeter BradshawTue 4 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 03.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlenn Close brings her totemic presence to this gentle movie – as well as a makeup-enhanced grandmotherly face. This is a sweet-natured adaptation of Tove Jansson’s 1972 novel; it has charm, though it’s sometimes becalmed in its own sensitivity.Close plays a tough, wise, humorous-yet-cantankerous eightysomething woman who likes cigarettes and walking around outside stark naked when there’s nobody else around. She brings her recently widowed son (Anders Danielsen Lie) and six-year-old granddaughter Sophia (newcomer Emily Matthews) to a tiny, idyllic island in the Gulf of Finland, where they have a summer cottage. The grandmother may, incidentally, have unresolved feelings for local man Eriksson, in a fleeting cameo for veteran Icelandic actor Ingvar Sigurdsson.It is here that grandmother, son and granddaughter hope to work through their grief and somehow find a version of the happiness that they once had there as a family, and come to terms with what happened to Sophia’s mum (though we do not discover how she died). Close’s formidable and very watchable performance shows us how the grandmother is unsentimentally taking on the burden of simply being there for Sophia – chatting to her about this and that, while her son retreats into his own sadness and what she robustly calls his self-pity. In fact, the film does not give us much idea of what he is thinking and feeling, perhaps wasting the considerable acting talents of Danielsen Lie.We are, of course, approaching a moment of catharsis when they can all say the painful, angry, grief-filled things in their hearts; this arrives with a storm that endangers their boat trip to the nearby Söderskär lighthouse. It is an unwritten movie rule that lovable old people who are paired with the very young have to die before the closing credits, their work of imparting wisdom complete. But in a film like this, which is already about death, it isn’t clear if the rule applies; consequently, there is a kind of generic uncertainty about the grandmother’s fate which is maintained until the very end. Without Close, this may have been a little insipid; with her, it is affecting and distinctive.The Summer Book is in UK cinemas from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsTove JanssonGlenn CloseSwedenFamilyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What, no sequinned crooners? How cruises became the home for world class theatre | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Forget cheesy acts, these days cruise ships boast the cutting edge tech to stage hip West End productions and Olivier award-winning musicals – and young people are loving it
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Forget cheesy acts, these days cruise ships boast the cutting edge tech to stage hip West End productions and Olivier award-winning musicals – and young people are loving it
Content: Cabin fever … the All on Board Show by Ambassador Entertainment: some onboard theatres can seat up to 1,000.Photograph: Cruise Travel Image SAView image in fullscreenCabin fever … the All on Board Show by Ambassador Entertainment: some onboard theatres can seat up to 1,000.Photograph: Cruise Travel Image SATheatreWhat, no sequinned crooners? How cruises became the home for world class theatreForget cheesy acts, these days cruise ships boast the cutting edge tech to stage hip West End productions and Olivier award-winning musicals – and young people are loving itBrian LoganTue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe phrase “cruise ship entertainment” conjures vivid images, even to those who have never set foot on an oceangoing vessel. Starry backcloths, sequined frocks, tunes and croons from yesteryear, the lite-ent values of the 1970s preserved in aspic. Perhaps those stereotypes held water way back when the singer Jane McDonald ruled the reality TV waves. But – lazy thinking ahoy! – do they still?Look at the shows currently a-sail on the high seas, from the Olivier award-winning 9/11 musical Come from Away, to hip theatre-maker Emma Rice’s acclaimed Brief Encounter. And look at the onboard production values, which “way surpass what you see in London theatres”, says Susannah Daley of Peel Entertainment, which provides shows for the Ambassador cruise line. “These ships are now being built with theatre in mind, to a really high spec, to hold between 600 and 1,000 people. What can be produced in them is pretty phenomenal.” Producer David Pugh, a veteran of the West End who has collaborated with Cunard cruises, says: “These are probably the most technical theatres, in terms of lighting and sound, that you’ve ever seen outside of the best theatres in the world.”View image in fullscreenA scene from Venison by Huw Turnbull, the winner of the 2025 Ambassador Peel Playwriting Challenge, which debuted on MS Ambition in May.Photograph: Ambassador Cruise LineBrief Encounter is Pugh’s. He has also recently delivered the RSC’s production of The Constant Wife onboard Cunard cruises. Meanwhile, Cunard is now well established as the “headline partner” of theatre’s most prestigious gong show, the Olivier awards – while Peel has just run a competition (which received 260 applications) for new plays to be performed at sea.It’s all a far cry from the days when cruise ships ranked alongside Butlin’s for arts industry prestige. “It’s really shifted,” says Cat Robey, Cunard’s senior entertainment development manager (and a former deputy director of London’s Jermyn Street theatre). “No one says ‘No’ any more. It’s now much more, ‘I’ve heard it’s brilliant and I’d love to do it.’”View image in fullscreenDecks appeal … entertainment onboard MS Astor passing the Panama Canal in January 2006.Photograph: Ullstein Bild/Getty ImagesWhen Peel took to the sea 26 years ago, says Daley, “people tended to think of cruises as girls with feathers and some crooner. But we were told, ‘No, we want to get away from that whole cheesy reputation.’” Back then, cruises laid on a handful of performances per week. Now there are multiple shows daily. These include shows in repertory by resident companies, and others by visiting outfits moonlighting at sea. All artforms are welcome: Cunard currently offers immersive theatre, for example, from the company behind wraparound performance experiences Peaky Blinders: The Rise and Doctor Who: Time Fracture.That, says Daley, is because the mainstream theatre industry has woken up to what can be achieved on cruise ships. On the one hand, it’s about meeting new audiences – “People are seeing theatre on a cruise who may never have been to the theatre before” – and in large numbers. “You’ve got a guaranteed audience,” says Daley, “and where on earth would you get that? We can get 600 people coming to a play in the afternoon. In the evening, we may get 1,200 people over two sittings. This is a fabulous opportunity for your work to be seen.” It’s a great chance for artists to flex their performing muscles, too. “Cruise offers, especially to younger performers, massive variety. Because you have to sing rock one day, opera another day and act in a play the next. You’re stretching yourself all the time.”View image in fullscreenKara Tointon in a promotional shot for the Royal Shakespeare Company’s production of The Constant Wife, which was staged on Cunard cruises.Photograph: Courtesy of  CunardIt’s increasingly the case, says Robey at Cunard, that customers are booking cruises based not solely on their sunkissed itineraries, but on the theatre onboard. “We absolutely know from guest feedback and booking trends that performances draw bookings,” she says, citing themed event voyages that include “LondonTheatreat Sea” (Southampton to New York, May 2026), not to mention Virgin Voyages’ seven-night comedy cruise (tagline: “Laugh your aft off!”).double quotation markFurniture goes one way, the actors go the other, and there’s bloodPeel’s and Ambassador’s recent playwriting prize, meanwhile, reflected a hunger among passengers for new bespoke drama onboard. “You try and get into a lounge to watch them sometimes and it’s absolutely packed,” says Daley. The prize winner, a thriller titled Venison by Edinburgh-based Huw Turnbull, is being staged on the waves this summer. “We hope the competition will make people aware,” says Daley, “of a growing opportunity at sea for writers, directors and all sorts of creative talents.”There are, of course, downsides. “A ship doesn’t wait for anybody,” says Daley. “Whenever we’re sending out scenery, costumes and lighting, it has to arrive on time at whatever port we’ve agreed. We’ve got some freight which at the moment is floating around Spain because it’s not allowed to dock there.”View image in fullscreenA scene from the Olivier award-winning Pride and Prejudice* (*sort of) on board the Cunard vessel Queen Anne.Photograph: Christopher IsonThere are other logistical quirks. Rehearsals must take place at antisocial hours, because the theatre is in fairly constant use. Shows require ruthless editing to fit allotted running times. And the motion of the ocean isn’t always a performer’s friend. Pugh remembers rehearsing the acclaimed Regency comedy Pride & Prejudice* (*sort of), “on the Bay of Biscay, gale force seven. Furniture goes one way, the actors go the other, this girl gets hit on the head, and there’s blood.” Cue a medical lockdown and a long delay to the opening of the show.double quotation markI went in armoured with what I thought was this patronisingly accessible actBut there are further reservations about the cruising experience that make bloodied heads pale by comparison. Thecomedian John Tothill’s new show, nominated for the Edinburgh comedy award last summer, recounts a recent experience gigging at sea. It was not a positive one. While Tothill is not obvious cruise ship material – his comedy is self-parodically erudite – he made a real effort to make it work. “I honed a routine down to my most down-the-line accessible material. Gone was all my stuff about the Lutheran reformation. I went in armoured with what I thought was this patronisingly accessible act.”View image in fullscreenThe theatre onboard Ambassador’s cruise ship Ambience, which made its maiden voyage in 2022.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThen he went onstage. And what happened “wasn’t just bombing” he says. “It was like a religious silence every night. A kind of existential darkness. I have never experienced anything like it before or since. Being met with total bafflement and confusion which, across the course of an hour, boiled over into angry contempt on both sides. It was like a culture war playing out in real time. I felt that [the audience] had unfairly caricatured me as a rubbish, lazy young comedian. And I returned the favour. We just didn’t see eye to eye.”double quotation markWhat you don’t want is anything that’s sectarian in any way that would divide an audienceTo Tothill, cruise ship audiences trend reactionary (“the things that go down really well are still tribute acts for bands in the 80s”), and the breadth of entertainment available militates against quality. To Daley, that’s an out-of-date stereotype: “There’s as many varied guests onboard as there are in any other walk of life.” Recent research backs that up: a2023 report by the Cruise Lines International Associationshowed that millennials made up 22% of passengers that year, with gen Z accounting for a further 14%.View image in fullscreenA scene from the musical Come from Away onboard the Cunard ships Queen Victoria and Queen Elizabeth.Photograph: Courtesy: CunardThe old-duffer stereotypes may be wearing thin – although Daley and Robey admit that when programming performances onboard, it’s best to avoid particularly challenging work. “What you don’t want is anything that’s sectarian in any way that would divide an audience,” says Daley, while Robey adds: “We’re with people who are on holiday, ultimately. They’re here to have a good time.”Producer Pugh’s misgivings relate to working practices and standards at sea. After signing his own contract with (US-owned) Cunard, he became aware that the company’s resident performer and stage manager contracts were non-union, and that the jurisdiction of the actors union Equity does not extend into international waters. While Pugh acknowledges that pay rates onboard are seldom a problem, he expresses concern for the overall wellbeing of artists, who can get too easily isolated and trapped in these jobs. Cunard made no comment when invited to respond to these issues.Experience: we sold everything to live on cruise shipsRead moreEquity was involved in negotiations when, for example, the RSC partnered with Cunard. Speaking to the Guardian, the union acknowledges the difficulty of imposing UK working standards on global seafaring, but says its interactions with the industry have been broadly positive. Negotiations are relatively straightforward, it says, when shows transfer wholesale from land – and that, increasingly, seems to be where entertainment at sea is coming from.“When I started this job,” says Robey, “I came in with the mindset that cruise ship entertainment was a bit passé and end-of-the-pier. But things have massively changed. There’s a realisation that it is actually unbelievably varied, with so much opportunity to push boundaries in different artforms. I now have companies and West End producers asking to come aboard.”Explore more on these topicsTheatreCruisesShipping industryTravel & leisureMusicalsRoyal Shakespeare CompanyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artform | Games | The Guardian
description: The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Content: Designed to foster connections and playfulness … Big Walk.Illustration: PanicView image in fullscreenDesigned to foster connections and playfulness … Big Walk.Illustration: PanicGamesReviewBig Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artformSwitch 2, PlayStation 5, PC; House HouseThe creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measureLewis GordonTue 4 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRadiant sunsets glinting on lapping waves; bushland valleys that beckon with secrets; modernist buildings sat atop craggy ridges: Big Walk’s setting is as arresting as it is beguiling – a kind of architectural fever dream transplanted to a handsome Australian wilderness – but it is the images created by players that lodge deepest in the mind. Here’s one that has stuck with me: in the black of night, cicadas kicking up an almighty din, I had lost my partner. Panic. Despair. Fear. Then, there in the far distance, I saw him signalling in my direction. He was relentlessly spamming a gigantic, ball-shaped lamp on and off, the ground around him flicking from inky dark to warm pastel pink and back again, like a single Christmas light blinking from afar.This kind of encounter is common in Big Walk, the brilliant and whimsical new online co-op puzzler from House House, the Melbourne-based studio behind the 2019 viral hit,Untitled Goose Game. Rather than playing as a honking, mischief-making goose as you do in that game, you are a bug-eyed, gangly limbed kind of bird person (think Pingu as drawn by Mondrian) for whom getting separated from your mates is all part of the fun. That’s somewhat because this rugged terrain is dense with vegetation and cliffs to fall down, and also because the game makes ingenious use of proximity and direction-based voice audio. Step out of earshot of your party and you will find it difficult to call for one another (unless, of course, you’ve picked up a Fisher-Price-like walkie-talkie).View image in fullscreenStep into the wilderness … Big Walk.Photograph: PanicSo you and up to 12 players step out into this somewhat eerily photorealistic open world to uncover its mysteries. Quickly, you come across challenges which veer from the straightforward to the brain-scrambling: shoot the aforementioned ball-shaped lamp into a hoop; arrange wooden pegs decorated with odd, nature-themed symbols into some kind of shape. For each successfully completed task, you win what looks like a large red peanut. Get enough of these red peanuts and you score a key which in turn unlocks some important piece of infrastructure: for example, a slow-moving, toy-like train whose parping horns are a joy to obnoxiously blare across the otherwise bucolic landscape.This structure naturally sustains its own rhythm: moments of intense cooperative concentration followed by longer stretches of ambulatory downtime. Such is the layout of this world, you end up doing a lot of backtracking. This is when a little of the game’s quirky lustre wears off since the actual walking is the least interesting part of Big Walk (and you’re also liable to get stuck on bits of rock). Frustration builds as you traipse through the same patch of scrub for the umpteenth time.Still, Big Walk’s less action-packed moments can be gratifying in their own way: I never tired of watching the twinkling night sky segue with impossible speed into the warm, orange glow of a new day, or stopping to enjoy the sounds of a softly gurgling creak.The beauty of Big Walk lies in how it tasks you with working together, conversing verbally and physically, to access its most enchanting sights. It stands out in an era when so much of online communication, be that in video games or on social media, has been distorted by a kind of attention-holding logic – for instance, the serotonin-releasing kerching of notifications or the relentless rewards of levelling up. Yet Big Walk eschews these pernicious aspects of digital life for a gentler, less overbearing experience that seems expressly designed to foster enriching connections and childlike playfulness.Here’s another moment that has stuck with me: wiping away tears of laughter after my brother and I clumsily dropped one of those essential red peanuts to the bottom of the devilishly constructed, practically “masocore” 100ft shaft that we had painstakingly platformed our way out of. We nattered about it until we found the next thing that piqued our interest: wobbly rave tunes blaring from deep inside the belly of a mountain. I shan’t say any more: you and your pals will want to discover these delights for yourselves.Big Walk is out now; £15.99, A$29.50Explore more on these topicsGamesPuzzle gamesPlayStationPCNintendo Switch 2reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Beast of Reincarnation review – a taxing reflection of human-made damage | Games | The Guardian
description: Game Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holding
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Game Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holding
Content: A taxing and often monotonous journey … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakView image in fullscreenA taxing and often monotonous journey … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakGamesReviewBeast of Reincarnation review – a taxing reflection of human-made damagePC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Game Freak/FictionsGame Freak channels a post-apocalyptic reality that reflects our own repetitive erosion cycles, with a fair bit of hand-holdingDiego ArgüelloMon 3 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of your time in Beast of Reincarnation is spent collecting last words. You cross paths with robots lying on the ground, who muster whatever energy they have left to provide guidance. These interactions are fleeting. Attempt to talk to them a second time, and protagonist Emma makes their fates painfully clear: “They’ve already passed on.”The latest detour by Game Freak, the studio best known as the primary developer of Pokémon games, is an action RPG set in a post-apocalyptic Japan. Taking cues from Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Final Fantasy VII Remake, and NieR: Automata, you wield the sword of an outcast accompanied by an ever-loyal canine. The pair embark on a taxing and often monotonous journey to defeat the titular beast, which nonetheless serves a thematic purpose to bolster a decaying reality, while reflecting a possible future for ours.View image in fullscreenA decaying reality … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakGame Freak hasn’t marketed Beast of Reincarnation as a Soulslike – the video game subgenre fostered by FromSoftware’s Dark Souls series – but there are many similarities. Smackdowns are challenging, boss encounters are frequent, and you rest at campsites scattered across each zone. However, as director Kota Furushima told Famitsu (translated by GamesRadar+), the team aims for the experience to be “enjoyable for even those who aren’t good at action games”.That design ethos is clear from start, as you’re able to select the difficulty level. My 20 hours with Beast of Reincarnation were spent in normal difficulty, with quite a few retries at first. As time passed, I realised just how much the mechanics want you to succeed – veering into hand-holding territory.View image in fullscreenAiming to be ‘enjoyable for even those who aren’t good at action games’ … Beast of Reincarnation.Illustration: Game FreakTake Koo as an example. The pup is an invaluable combat companion for Emma. Yet, he is also a four-legged wiki. He sniffs out nearby enemies, valuable materials, chests, and characters – even before they’re in view. Despite exploration being encouraged and often rewarded, Koo’s actions ensure virtually no sense of discovery. Even forgetting to pick up an item from the ground is done for you, as he fetches it before you can even turn around.This streamlining extends to pretty much everything. Both Emma and Koo have robust skill trees to unlock abilities, which progressively turn the pair into a powerhouse. Yet mechanics such as cooking and harvesting are automated in the background as you fight. There are campsites aplenty, often with a merchant nearby, and returning to them after a defeat doesn’t have any consequences. You quickly repurpose yourself and try again, your body still drenched in blood from the previous attempt.View image in fullscreenThere are campsites aplenty, often with a merchant nearby … Beast of Reincarnation.These decisions aptly correlate to Emma as a character. She is, by design, a person devoid of memories and emotions – oblivious to the grief of the robots she encounters (referred to as golems), who carry human souls inside, trapped in machines designed to serve a single purpose, before shutting down. By learning about feelings from the characters around her and what drives them, Emma’s purpose in the world is questioned. Yet, she, and by extension you, is not offered any alternative.The senseless cycle of violence is even more pronounced in the second half, with enemies and boss encounters being largely recycled. Again, this feels like an attempt to placate you, by presenting obstacles you’ve already overcome. Almost every mechanic is designed to grant you what you need, exactly when you need it.When you’re approaching a boss’s lair, the environment around you morphs. Flora transforms, and the sky turns orange, clouds obscure the sunshine. It’s a striking vista, and one similar to reality, aswildfireshave affected air quality in North America and Canada, and their damage isyet to be calculated. A similar anxiety prevails when learning about the origins of golems, with the idea of human souls being digitised in the face of imminent calamity. There are many parallels to current reality, in a time when we are encouraged to lease ourcreativity,emotions, andautonomyto machines, as we’re algorithmically encouraged to stay oblivious to theactionandinactionof those in power in the face ofhuman-made disasters.Every time Emma defeats a boss, she obtains its power, depicted as a flower added to her braided hair. Using said power in combat creates an inflorescence out of thin air. It’s almost ironic to use a sword to re-establish colour to a world that is actively in a state of erosion. Despite being rooted in conflict and grief, Beast of Reincarnation doesn’t culminate in a nihilistic afterthought. Rather, it uses whichever energy it has left to muster a glimmer of hope – like the sight of a flower blooming on an empty, barraged field.Beast of Reincarnation is out nowExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesRole playing gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What’s the best vegetarian alternative to gelatine? | Vegetarian food and drink | The Guardian
description: There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatine
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatine
Content: Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Benjamina Ebuehi. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Julia Aden.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Benjamina Ebuehi. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Julia Aden.Kitchen aideVegetarian food and drinkWhat’s the best vegetarian alternative to gelatine?There is no exact plant-based substitute – the ideal option will depend on the dish. But, ultimately, it’s easiest to choose a recipe that doesn’t require gelatineAnna BerrillTue 4 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do I go about substituting gelatine sheets for a vegetarian setting agent?Sarah, Aberdeen“The truth is, there’s no exact substitute for gelatine, because it has an incredibly unique texture,” says Richard Phillips, head of pastry atTimberyardin Edinburgh. Sure, there are plenty of plant-based gelling agents out there – “agar-agar [or just agar], gellan gum, pectin, carrageenan, locust bean gum, vege-gel… the list goes on,” says Phillips – but the result will never quite be the same.“The temperature you have to use them at is different [to gelatine],” says Philip Khoury, author ofBeyond Baking, so his usual workaround is to simply formulate recipes that don’t use gelling agents. Now, that’s all well and good when you’re a pastry chef, but what about the rest of us? “If, for example, I’m making a thick, pipeable cream, then I’ll use cornflour,” says Khoury, and just manipulate it to get different textures. Let’s take the panna cotta and creme brulee recipes in his first book,A New Way to Bake, as an example: “You get two very different textures from essentially the same recipe. The only difference being that if you pour the custard into a tray and chill it, it will set, whereas if you beat it with a whisk, it will turn into this luscious, creamy texture that’sjustset.”But one gelatine substitute doesn’t fit all. “There are specific alternatives for specific things,” says Phillips: “Reversible pectin for glazes; kuzu [root starch] to thicken sauces; pectin to make jellies, using different dosages for different sets.” Khoury, meanwhile, prefers agar for the latter, and the seaweed-derived gelling agent has become something of a poster child here. But again, don’t expect exactly the same result as you’d get with gelatine. And that’s not a subjective statement, as Harold McGee explains in his bibleOn Food and Cooking: “Agar forms gels at even lower concentrations than gelatine does, less than 1% by weight. An agar jelly is somewhat opaque and has a more crumbly texture than a gelatine jelly.” Where gelatine sets and remelts at around the same temperature, an agar gel “only melts again when its temperature reaches 85C [185F]”, which is to say, a jelly made with agar won’t have that joyous melt-in-the-mouth texture.Even so, Reece Kallah, head pastry chef atMount St Restaurantin London, uses agar in fruit puree gels, which feature in her set vanilla custard. “As a general guide, use 0.5% agar by weight of your liquid – for example, 5g agar per 1 litre of liquid.” Kallah mixes the agar with a little sugar “to help it disperse evenly, as it doesn’t dissolve particularly well on its own”, before whisking it into the boiling liquid, pouring into a tray or ramekin, and leaving to set. “I still prefer gelatine, though – it has a softer, more delicate texture because of that lower melting point.”Stars don’t always live up to their hype, after all, and Khoury adds another word of caution. “If Sarah goes about this by saying: ‘I want to swap gelatine for something else’, then it won’t work; if she wants success, then follow a recipe that doesn’t contain gelatine.” It’ll likely be less faff, too.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Herby feta frittata and a knockout fruit and rocket salad: Sami Tamimi’s Arabic summer recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Levantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket salad
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: Levantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket salad
Content: Sami Tamimi's courgette and feta cheese Ijeh-Aravic frittata with a fruit, red onion and rocket salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi's courgette and feta cheese Ijeh-Aravic frittata with a fruit, red onion and rocket salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodHerby feta frittata and a knockout fruit and rocket salad: Sami Tamimi’s Arabic summer recipesLevantine summer magic in a herby and moreish Arabic frittata with a peachy fruit, red onion and rocket saladSami TamimiTue 4 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve always loved food that can be enjoyed at room temperature, or even cold the next day. As the UK, along with many other parts of the world, swelters through another hot summer, these are exactly the kinds of dishes I want to cook and eat. Fresh, light and unfussy, they require little effort, yet never compromise on flavour. This herb-packed courgette and fetaijehpaired with a lush fruit, red onion and rocket salad alongside makes the perfect meal for warm days and relaxed summer gatherings.Courgette and fetaijeh(Arabic frittata)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIjeh is a much-loved Palestinian herb frittata-like omelette that perfectly captures the freshness and simplicity of everyday home cooking. Made with eggs, generous handfuls of fresh herbs, onions and fragrant spices, it is crisp around the edges and soft in the centre and can be enjoyed at any time of day. Together, with some cool mint yoghurt and a salad of fruit and caramelised onions, they celebrate the generosity at the heart of any table.Prep20 minCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4-62 large courgettes(about 700g),trimmed and coarsely gratedSalt and black pepper1 red pepper (about 120g),pith and seeds discarded, flesh finely choppedOlive oil1 small onion (80g),peeled and finely chopped3 spring onions (45g),trimmed and finely chopped3 garlic cloves,peeled and crushed25g flat-leaf parsley,finely chopped20g fresh dill,finely chopped4 large eggs,lightly beaten200g feta,crumbled100g plain flour1 tsp baking powderFor the mint yoghurt300g Greek-style yoghurt2 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp lemon juice1 small garlic clove,peeled and crushed¼ tspdried mint¼ tsp aleppo chilli flakes⅓ tsp saltHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and line the base and sides of a 26cm round baking dish with parchment paper.Put the grated courgette in a colander, sprinkle with one teaspoon of salt and leave for 10 minutes. Using a clean tea towel, squeeze out as much moisture from the courgettes as you can, then put them in a large mixing bowl. Squeeze out the excess moisture from the red pepper, too, then add them to the bowl. Add all the remaining ingredients, along with three quarters of a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper, and combine well using your hands. Transfer the mixture to the prepared dish and smooth the top with the back of the spoon. Bake for 50 minutes, until golden brown, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.To make the mint yoghurt, mix the yoghurt in a medium bowl with the rest of the ingredients, until well combined. Set aside.Once theijehhas cooled, cut it into slices and serve warm or at room temperature with the mint yoghurt and fruit, red onion and rocket salad (below).Fruit, red onion and rocket saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenWhile I like to make loquats the star here, peaches, nectarines, or apricots make excellent alternatives. Serve as a light starter or alongside the ijeh, grilled meats or hearty, nutty grain dishes.Prep15 minCook40 minServes4, as a starter or side1 red onion (150g),peeled and cut into 8 wedges3 tbsp olive oil6 large loquats, peaches, nectarines or apricots (350g),peeled and sliced in half lengthways100g rocket leaves5g coriander leaves,picked5g mint leaves,picked40g pecan kernels,toasted and roughly choppedFor the dressing2½ tbsp balsamic vinegar1½ tbsp pomegranate molasses1½ tsp runny honey1 small garlic clove,peeled and crushedFlaked sea salt and black pepper3 tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/gas 6. First, make the dressing by mixing the balsamic, molasses, honey, garlic, a quarter teaspoon of flaked salt and a grind of black pepper. Slowly pour in the oil, whisking constantly, until combined and smooth.Put the onion wedges into a medium bowl and add one and a half tablespoons of the dressing, along with an eighth of a teaspoon of salt. Toss well to combine, then transfer to a parchment-lined baking tray and roast, tossing once, until softened and slightly caramelised – about 20 minutes. Set aside to cool.Heat one and a half tablespoons of olive oil in a medium frying pan. Add the halved fruit cut side down and fry for two to three minutes, then flip and cook for two minutes more, or until slightly caramelised. Remove from the pan and set aside.Put half the roast onion in a large mixing bowl along with the rocket, herbs, half the pecans, a half-teaspoon of flaked salt, a good grind of black pepper, and half the remaining dressing. Toss well to combine, then transfer to a serving dish, layering the salad and fruit cut side up. Repeat with the remaining salad, onions and fruit, and finish with the remaining toasted nuts.The headline of this article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version referred to a “herby frittata and a fruit and feta salad”; this should have said herby feta frittata and a fruit and rocket salad.Explore more on these topicsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkSaladMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
